title: October 16, 2026
description:
Access Approval

Feature

Service connectivity automation is generally available (GA).

Access Transparency

Feature

Service connectivity automation is generally available (GA).

BigQuery

Feature

Conversational analytics in BigQuery is now available in the following locations:

  • northamerica-northeast1 (Montréal)
  • northamerica-northeast2 (Toronto)

For more information, see Locations.

Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL

Change

Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL now supports enabling Managed Connection Pooling on existing Private Service Connect instances. Previously, Cloud SQL supported enabling Managed Connection Pooling only on new instances using Private Service Connect.

For more information, see Managed Connection Pooling overview and Configure Managed Connection Pooling.

Dialogflow

Feature

gemini-3.5-flash-lite has become generally available (GA). See Generative quotas for how to request quota for Gemini 3 and later models.

Gemini Enterprise

Feature

Gemini Enterprise: Configure citations for custom MCP data stores

You can configure the citation_mappings parameter for custom Model Context Protocol (MCP) data stores using the REST API to display source citation chips when Gemini Enterprise answers questions using tools on your custom MCP server. This feature is generally available (GA).

For more information, see Configure citations for custom MCP data stores.

Feature

Gemini Enterprise: Connect workflows in Workflow Builder to Confluence Data Center and Jira Data Center

You can connect workflows in Workflow Builder to Confluence Data Center and Jira Data Center to search data and automate actions across these third-party apps.

For more information, see Workflows overview.

Google Cloud Contact Center as a Service

Announcement

Advanced reporting dashboards prerelease notes 6.16

Here are the pre-release notes for updates to the advanced reporting dashboards and other reporting in CCAI Platform. When we release these updates, we expect the new capabilities to be as shown here.

Important: The next version of the advanced reporting dashboards could be greater than 6.16.

Fixed

This release addresses the following issues:

  • Fixed an issue where the Agent Performance tile on the Real-time Agent Monitoring dashboard executed redundant database queries during auto-refreshes.

  • Updated advanced reporting filter prompts so they behave consistently across all dashboards and display the complete list of configured values:

    • List-backed filters now open directly into a searchable list on the first click.

    • Dropdowns that previously returned empty or partial lists now display the full configured list, including Agent Name, Agent Email, Agent Custom ID, Agent Teams, Location, Language, Answered By, and Projection Result.

    • Disposition Codes and Disposition List filters now display the codes configured for your instance.

    • Agent Teams and Team Name filters now match agents in any of their assigned teams.

    • Configuration renames (Queue Group, Queue, Agent Team, Disposition Code, Location, Role, and Skill) now appear in filter dropdowns within 30 minutes instead of up to six hours.

    • The Projecting filter on the live Queued dashboards is now clearable, so you can reset it to show all queued interactions, and offers only Yes.

    • Fields without a predefined list of values (such as consumer phone numbers and ID fields) now display a plain text box with an operator so you can type a value directly.

    • Call Status and Deflection Type filters now display values that existed in the data but were previously missing from the list.

    • Channel now reports a value on the live Voice and Chat dashboards, and on historical Chat dashboards, for interaction types that previously appeared blank (including internal, API-initiated, campaign, UCaaS, callback, and extension calls).

    • On the Agent Audit dashboard, the Change Details table now displays its timestamp column and sorts it correctly.

    • Consumer phone number filters now accept a single value instead of multiple values. Saved filters or links that pass multiple numbers apply only one.

    • On the Missed Interactions dashboards, the Activity Status column and filter are renamed to Projection Result.

    • Actor values describing who answered, ended, or disconnected an interaction are now standardized as Human Agent, Virtual Agent, End User, and System. Saved filters, Looks, and schedules that used the previous wording must be reselected.

Google Kubernetes Engine

Change

For GKE Standard CPU node pools, GKE can now upgrade nodes by updating the existing Compute Engine VM in place, instead of deleting the VM and creating a new one. Because the node keeps its underlying VM, it also keeps its compute capacity during the upgrade. This lowers the risk that a node upgrade fails or stalls because resources aren't available.

To enable this type of upgrade, use surge upgrades with the maxUnavailable field set to a value greater than 0. For more details about when GKE reuses the same Compute Engine instance, including exceptions, see maxUnavailable: GKE makes an existing node unavailable to recreate it.

This change applies to all GKE versions. To opt out, contact Cloud Customer Care.

Vertex AI Search

Change

Agent Search: Update to the stable model

The stable model for answer generation is updated to gemini-3.5-flash/answer_gen/v1 from gemini-2.5-flash/answer_gen/v1.

For more information, see Answer generation model versions and lifecycle.

Feature

Custom organization policies for Agent Platform Workbench instances

You can now use custom organization policies to allow or deny the creation and update of Agent Platform Workbench instances based on their configuration. Custom constraints for the notebooks.googleapis.com/Instance resource are enforced when you create or update an instance, and support dry-run mode. This feature is now generally available (GA). For more information, see Create custom organization policy constraints.

Apigee X

Feature

Model Context Protocol (MCP) tool arguments are sent to the location their OpenAPI parameter declares

This change applies to Apigee X in all supported regions.

An MCP tool argument whose OpenAPI parameter declares in: header is now sent to your backend as a request header, and one that declares in: cookie is sent in the Cookie header. Previously both were appended to the query string. in: query and in: path parameters are unchanged, and every parameter still appears in the tool's inputSchema, so MCP clients supply arguments exactly as before. If a backend reads one of these values from the query string, declare the parameter in: query or read it from its declared location.

On a tool call that supplies at least one cookie argument, the Cookie header is replaced with only the declared cookie parameters, omitting any others. Any cookie your backend relies on must be declared as an in: cookie parameter.

An MCP proxy that was already deployed continues to use the previous query-string behavior until its configuration is next regenerated. To adopt the new routing on an existing MCP proxy, deploy a new revision of it.

For the full mapping, see Tool argument placement on the backend request.

Security

On October 24, 2026, we published a security bulletin for Apigee.

Two vulnerabilities in PHP core (CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, "PHP2Shell") allow an unauthenticated attacker to execute code remotely on a server running a vulnerable PHP version. The impact is limited to Drupal-based Apigee developer portals, which customers deploy and operate. Apigee, Apigee Hybrid, and the Apigee integrated portal don't use PHP and aren't affected.

Security bulletin published: GCP-2026-072

BigQuery

Feature

Conversation logging for Conversational analytics in BigQuery is now generally available (GA). You can log data agent conversations to a BigQuery table in the agent's project. For more information, see Conversation logging overview and Configure settings.

Feature

Python user-defined functions now support volume mounts, which let you access dependency files from Cloud Storage directly from your Python UDF code. This feature is in Preview.

Feature

The REGEXP_EXTRACT_GROUPS function produces substrings that match multiple capturing groups in a regular expression.

This function is in Preview.

Cloud Database Migration Service

Feature

You can now create heterogeneous conversion workspaces by importing database schema metadata files from a Cloud Storage bucket without requiring direct network connectivity between Database Migration Service and your source database during the schema conversion phase. For more information, see the following pages:

  • Create a conversion workspace for Oracle to Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL
  • Create a conversion workspace for Oracle to AlloyDB for PostgreSQL
  • Create a conversion workspace for SQL Server to Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL
  • Create a conversion workspace for SQL Server to AlloyDB for PostgreSQL

Compute Engine

Security

A vulnerability (CVE-2026-85299) about incorrect authorization in Compute Engine was discovered and has been addressed. For more information, see the GCP-2026-073 security bulletin.

Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform

Feature

Control user intent matching for semantic governance policies

You can now turn user intent matching on or off for semantic governance policies by setting the sgpUserIntentMatching key on the authorization extension metadata. User intent matching is on by default; set the key to DISABLED to turn it off. Turning it off reduces protection against indirect prompt injection. When the key is set, policy evaluation logs report the mode each evaluation used in the sgpUserIntentMatchingMode field.

For more information, see Control user intent matching.

Feature

Cloud Storage output support for Gemini image generation models

Direct Cloud Storage output persistence is generally available (GA) for Gemini Nano Banana 2.1 (gemini-nano-banana-2.1), Gemini 3.1 Flash Image (gemini-3.1-flash-image), Gemini 3.1 Flash-Lite Image (gemini-3.1-flash-lite-image), and Gemini 3 Pro Image (gemini-3-pro-image). You can set outputConfig.outputUriPrefix and generationConfig.responseFormat[].image.delivery to "URI" in generateContent and streamGenerateContent requests to write generated and edited images directly to a Cloud Storage bucket and receive the object URI in fileData.fileUri instead of inline bytes. For more information, see Save generated images to Cloud Storage.

Feature

Gemini 3.8 Flash TTS and Gemini 3.8 Flash-Lite TTS are Generally Available (GA)

Gemini 3.8 Flash TTS and Gemini 3.8 Flash-Lite TTS are available in General Availability (GA) in the global location and the us and eu multi-regions. The models support structured speaker and style metadata, inline vocal tags, multi-speaker dialogue, and streaming. Voice design and voice replication capabilities remain available in Preview.

For more information, see Generate speech with Gemini TTS.

Feature

Semantic governance policies support more model providers

Semantic governance policies now evaluate tool calls from agents that use models from providers other than Gemini. The policy engine reads each provider's request and response format, so the same policies apply whichever model your agent uses. Supported APIs include the Gemini Developer API and Gemini models on Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform, the Anthropic Messages API, Claude models on Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform, the OpenAI Chat Completions API, the Mistral AI API, the OpenAI-compatible endpoint on Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform (including Llama models), and self-hosted OpenAI-compatible servers such as vLLM. Streamed model responses aren't supported.

To govern these providers, update the when condition of your authorization policy to match each provider's request path. The updated condition also matches requests that include a query string.

For more information, see Supported model providers and Connect the policy engine to Agent Gateway.

Google Distributed Cloud (software only) for bare metal

title: The Vercel Sandbox CLI is now more agent-friendly
description:
The Sandbox CLI version 4.0.1 ships four output and error improvements:

  • New sandboxes point users towards how to connect into them.

  • A sandbox not found error shows where to look for existing sandboxes.

  • Common mistakes, like typing a command after sh, redirect to the command that was intended.

  • Outdated installs show an update notice when they create a new sandbox.

Each of these messages now carries the action to take next instead of leaving you to work it out.

New sandboxes tell you how to connect

create and fork output now ends with a connect hint, so a fresh sandbox never leaves you wondering what to type next.

Not found errors point you to your sandboxes

When a command references a sandbox that does not exist, the error is quiet and actionable instead of a raw API dump. Setting DEBUG=sandbox:errors restores the request detail for debugging.

A misused command explains the right one

sh opens a plain interactive shell, so it takes no command of its own. The CLI can now return precise answers that rewrite the attempt into the command that does what you meant, whatever the command is.

Outdated installs warn you at creation time

create, sh, and run check for a newer published CLI and print an update notice when the install is behind. The check is cached to a file and refreshed at most once per hour; when a lookup does run it happens concurrently with the creation request, so it adds no latency. Creation defaults, such as the base image, are chosen client side, so an outdated global install silently keeps old defaults. Prerelease versions skip the check, and SANDBOX_SKIP_VERSION_CHECK=1 disables it.

Learn more in the Sandbox CLI documentation.

title: $1 million hacker challenge for Vercel Sandbox
description:
Agents need to run untrusted code, and the microVM has become the standard way to do it: a dedicated guest kernel per workload, isolated from the host and from every other workload on the same machine.

But recent security research and real-world incidents have revealed that agents running untrusted code do not need to cross a VM boundary to escape containment; they only need one network path the security model failed to account for, which we explained in our post A sandbox without a network boundary is only half a sandbox.

Isolation only holds if both sides of it hold: the Firecracker microVM and the host-side network controls. Recently our CTO pointed an open-weight model with no safeguards at Vercel Sandbox. It did not escape, but it mapped the guest kernel, built a VM to reproduce its ideas, and wrote a fuzzer.

Defenders have first-mover advantage, but it won't last forever, and the choice is when to test the boundaries (we strongly encourage building a scanning program, which you can do on any budget with an open-source tool like deepsec and AI Gateway).

We are proactively choosing to test Vercel Sandbox on our own schedule, not an attacker's, and we are doing it in the open, with the best researchers in the world.

So for two weeks, we are paying up to $1,000,000 USD to the researchers who can escape a Vercel Sandbox.

The challenge

Starting today, Vercel is running a two-week public HackerOne program focused on Vercel Sandbox isolation.

  • Program: Public HackerOne program, open to all eligible researchers

  • Window: Tuesday, August 18 to Tuesday, September 1, 2026, or earlier if the reward pool is exhausted

  • Max per report: $50,000 USD, for a vulnerability that lets a threat actor read or modify another Vercel tenant's data

  • Total pool: Up to $1,000,000 USD in total payouts

Bounties are paid per report, scoped to a single root cause, and assigned by Vercel triage based on the maximum demonstrable impact. The full bounty table, detailed scope, and the list of known-duplicate classes are on the HackerOne program page.

How Vercel Sandbox is built

Vercel Sandbox runs on bare-metal EC2 hosts. Each sandbox gets its own Firecracker microVM with a dedicated guest kernel, and inside that microVM a Linux container runs the operator's code. The microVM, not the container, is the security boundary, so operator-supplied code runs two layers removed from the host. We assume that code is fully hostile: root inside the container, full kernel access inside the microVM, and motivated to reach the host or another tenant.

The network side of the boundary is enforced on the host, outside the microVM, where code inside the sandbox cannot modify or disable it. The sandbox firewall intercepts outbound TCP and DNS, checks each connection against the operator's domain and CIDR policies, and can inject credentials at the boundary so they never enter the microVM.

What we're looking for

In short: anything that breaks the sandbox boundary.

  • Compute boundary: Escaping the Firecracker microVM to the EC2 host, or reaching another tenant's sandbox through the compute layer (reading, modifying, or executing code in it), or crashing another tenant's sandbox from within another sandbox

  • Network boundary: Defeating the sandbox firewall without crossing the microVM: reaching destinations the operator did not authorize, exfiltrating data, or retrieving brokered credentials

Container namespace escapes that only reach the Firecracker guest OS are not in scope. Namespaces are a developer-experience feature, not the security boundary.

Bounties

Severity

Bounty

Critical

$25,000 – $50,000

High

$10,000 – $25,000

Medium

$5,000 – $10,000

Low

$1,000 – $5,000

The full bounty table, with example vulnerability classes for each tier, is on the HackerOne program page.

How to participate

The program is open now and closes on Tuesday, September 1, 2026, or earlier if the $1,000,000 USD reward pool is exhausted. Reports go through the HackerOne program page.

To reproduce a finding, boot a sandbox with the @vercel/sandbox SDK and demonstrate the impact with a live proof of concept. The default sandbox OS is enough for most reports; bring a custom image from the Vercel Container Registry only if your PoC needs extra tooling. We will not reward static-analysis-only findings; to issue a payout, we need to see the boundary break.

Full rules, eligibility, the complete scope and bounty table, and the submission process are on the HackerOne program page.

Results and payouts

We will triage reports from the day the program opens through one month after it closes. As findings are confirmed, we will pay bounties, ship fixes, and credit every researcher whose report holds up. The techniques discovered during this program will become permanent additions to the sandbox boundary, protecting every workload on Vercel long after the challenge ends. After the program closes, we will publish a follow-up writeup of the techniques and the fixes we shipped.

Thanks to HackerOne for standing up the program, and to the researchers who will spend the next two weeks trying to break what we built.

title: Vercel for Platforms can now deploy from your users' GitHub repositories
description:
Teams building on Vercel for Platforms can now create deployments directly from their users' GitHub repositories, without requiring them to install the Vercel GitHub App. When creating a deployment, pass a gitAccessToken alongside gitSource. Vercel uses the token to retrieve the source and build the deployment.

Tokens should be read-only, scoped to the requested repository, and valid for 24 hours or less. Vercel temporarily stores the token in encrypted form so source retrieval can complete. The token is never stored on the deployment.

Learn more about using a GitHub access token.

title: Exa joins the Vercel AI Gateway and Agent Marketplace
description:
Exa is now available on the Vercel AI Gateway and Agent Marketplace as a native integration. Exa's neural search engine grounds models in current information.

  • Exa search is now a built-in tool on AI Gateway, which runs the search for you without an Exa account of your own.

  • You can also add Exa to a Vercel project from the Agent Marketplace to power search or a research agent, with a single API key that works across every Exa product and billing through your Vercel account.

Exa search on AI Gateway

Every model on AI Gateway can search with Exa through a built-in tool, with no Exa account or key of your own required. Pass gateway.tools.exaSearch() alongside your prompt and the gateway runs the search, hands the results back to the model, and keeps going until the model stops searching. You get one finished response with a synthesized answer rather than raw results to stream back yourself.

The tool takes the same controls as the Exa API, so you can set how many results come back, focus a search on a category such as news or research papers, restrict it to a country, and include or exclude domains.

Searches bill through AI Gateway next to your model usage at list price with no markup.

Exa on the Agent Marketplace

Install Exa from the Marketplace or deploy the Next.js Search template to integrate Exa's instant search, deep answers, and content extraction to your Vercel project.

About Exa: For developers building AI features on Vercel, Exa gives agents the web, organized for them. Whether you're answering questions, monitoring changes, or extracting structured data, Exa's one API for search, crawling, and research returns token-efficient highlights with grounded citations, so your agents get the context they need with fewer round trips, lower cost, and lower latency.

title: Chat SDK adds Instagram adapter
description:
You can now build bots for Instagram with the new Instagram adapter for Chat SDK.

Bots can send and receive DMs and media, render cards as quick replies and link buttons, show typing indicators, receive reactions, and handle story replies.

The adapter connects through Meta's Instagram Messaging API and requires a professional Business or Creator account.

Messages are buffered, so streamed responses send as one message when the stream completes. Meta enforces a 24-hour messaging window, so bots can only reply within a day of the user's last message.

Read the documentation to get started or browse the adapter directory.

title: Vercel Connect now supports Microsoft
description:
Vercel Connect now includes a managed connector for Microsoft, so your apps and agents can access all Microsoft products such as Teams, OneDrive and more.

As a Vercel Managed Connector, Vercel registers the Entra application and configures federated credentials for it, so you don't have to create an app registration or manage client secrets yourself. Authorize the app for your Microsoft tenant once, then attach the connector to the projects and environments it needs.

Create a connector from the dashboard or the Vercel CLI:

With the connector attached, your code requests a token only when it needs one. The @vercel/connect SDK authenticates with your deployment's OIDC identity and returns a short-lived token for the app itself, using the application permissions your admin granted:

title: Introducing Vercel for Slack
description:
Vercel Agent now works in Slack. Mention it the way you'd pull a teammate into a thread, and it reads the discussion, answers with the context of the platform running your app, and turns the team's decisions into changes you approve. Vercel for Slack is available today in Public Beta for Pro and Enterprise teams.

Work starts in conversation. An alert gets noticed in a channel, a fix gets agreed on in a thread, and then someone leaves Slack to do the work. With Vercel Agent, you can tag it in for answers about your infrastructure or hand it the work, all without leaving the conversation.

What is Vercel Agent?

When we introduced Vercel Agent, we called it an AI teammate for your development workflow. Today it's the first responder for your production apps. When something changes, it investigates your logs, metrics, and deployments, finds the root cause, and proposes a fix, often before anyone's opened a laptop. Give it a PR and it flags the regressions and risky changes that a passing CI run won't show.

In Slack, that agent joins the conversation itself. It is a core part of Vercel, so your deployments, build statuses, logs, metrics, code reviews, and PRs are in front of it before you've typed anything. Mention @Vercel in a channel, a thread, or a DM, and it answers like a teammate with every tab already open. And answering is only half of it, because once you know what's wrong, the agent can go fix it:

  • Diagnose issues: Investigate incidents, trace errors to the deploy that caused them, explain a cost spike, and answer questions about your codebase.

  • Code alongside your team: Fix failing builds and CI, review PRs with knowledge of how the code runs in production, and turn a thread's decision into a tested pull request.

  • Operate your projects: Roll back deployments, update configuration, manage feature flags, and resolve unusual usage before it becomes a bill.

The agent is read-only by default, and anything that changes code or configuration goes through a plan that you approve. Vercel for Slack brings that whole loop into the threads where you and your team are already discussing work.

Accelerating development with a conversation

Teams form decisions through collaboration. Incidents get triaged in a channel, code reviews are hashed out in threads, and features get scoped between standups. But once a thread settles on what needs to be done, the actions still need to be translated into tickets, terminal commands, and PR descriptions. Every handoff drops context, and the conversation that held the full picture becomes the thing everyone summarizes from memory. Vercel for Slack gives the agent the full context of the original conversation for every turn.

Answers in one place speed up the whole team

A deployment goes out at 1:42pm. By 1:51, checkout error rates are climbing and an alert lands in the platform engineering channel.

What used to happen next was a scatter. One responder opens logs to see how bad it is, another asks their coding agent to line up the anomaly up against the deploy timeline, a third starts reading the diff of the suspect PR. Each person investigates alone, in their own view of the same system, and the thread is where they reconcile by pasting screenshots, summarizing agent findings, and correcting each other as they establish the actual state of the situation. The minutes that matter get spent assembling the picture before anyone can act on it.

With Vercel for Slack, the first question goes to the agent, right in the thread.

"@Vercel, checkout errors spiked after the 1:42 deploy. What's going on?"

It sizes the blast radius, correlates the spike with the deployment, identifies the PR that shipped in it, and explains which change, in which file, caused which behavior. The answer arrives in the channel, where the whole team reads the same diagnosis at the same time.

Nobody has to re-run a teammate's investigation or wait for the recap, because everyone is looking at the same report. The engineer who knows the checkout code speaks to the change itself, the on-call weighs how many users are hit against how long a fix would take, and what's left for the thread is the decision, whether to roll back or fix forward.

Vercel Agent understands how your team already talks

The thread, channel, or DM is the beginning of the prompt itself. You don't have to re-explain anything that was already said, or pass in any context from your app or codebase. Bring it into a conversation like any other team member and it reads the room, picks up what the team has been discussing, and can act on it when asked.

One example of this was our iteration on Vercel Agent's plan card, the message it posts in Slack to request approval for the work it wants to do. The first version we tested internally was a wall of text, but when one of our engineers noticed that people were often approving actions without reading all of the details, we had a redesign thread that ran 47 replies deep on what a person needs to see before confirming an action on the group's behalf. Tagging Vercel Agent in at the end of that thread is what resulted in the card you see today.

By the time a PR from a conversation like this lands in a thread, the tests have already run and the preview deployment is live, so the team can start reviewing it in the conversation that kicked off the feature in the first place.

Vercel Agent reviews pull requests in the thread

Ask Vercel Agent for a review in the thread where the PR is being discussed, and the conversation is passed along with the request. What your team has been raising becomes context for what Vercel Agent checks, and its findings land back in the same thread, so discussing them, deciding, and fixing them is one loop instead of a trip to another tool.

One example from one of our own PR discussions was a review someone requested mid-thread. The agent came back with a bug sitting just outside the diff, the same title rendered twice in the UI.

A finding doesn't have to end as a comment. If the team agrees it should be fixed, the agent can patch the PR itself, and that change arrives the same way everything else does, as a proposal waiting on an approval.

Changes always go through a plan your team approves

When a thread lands on a change, Vercel Agent replies with a plan that says what will happen, in which project, and at what scope. Decisions in a channel form in fragments, across people and hours, and nobody types "DECISION:", so the plan is where all of that becomes one explicit thing to say yes to. Once approved, the agent does the work under its own identity, and the audit trail shows who asked, who approved, and what ran.

One example from our own threads was a cached page showing stale data after we shipped an update. Someone called for a cache purge scoped to just the specific pages, since it was peak hours, and asked the agent to set it up. The plan that came back matched the ask exactly, a purge of the specific path and its sub-paths with the rest of the site's cache left warm, and nothing ran until someone approved it.

Whether a thread ends in a diagnosis, a pull request, or a cache purge, the last step belongs to a person.

Getting started

The easiest way to get started is to simply ask Vercel Agent questions. Ask about the error you're chasing or the build that just failed, see what comes back, and let your team decide over time how much of the work the agent takes on. Until someone approves a plan, it's only ever reading.

Vercel for Slack is available in Public Beta for Pro and Enterprise teams. To start using Vercel Agent in Slack:

  • Open the Slack app in the Vercel Marketplace and click Connect Account.

  • Choose the Slack workspace to connect, then click Allow.

  • Mention @Vercel in a channel, a thread, or a DM.

  • Sign in to your Vercel account when it prompts you the first time.

See the Vercel for Slack docs for setup and permissions.

title: How v0 authenticates to Snowflake without exposing the user's OAuth token
description:
AI-generated applications often need to authenticate to external services on behalf of their users. That creates a problem: generated code shouldn't have access to the user's credentials.

We faced that decision when building the v0 Snowflake integration. It lets users connect Snowflake, inspect schemas, query data, and generate applications that run against their warehouses. That generated code has to authenticate to Snowflake, but it is written by a model and runs without human review, and prompt injection can steer it into exfiltrating whatever it can read, so the user's OAuth token should never enter the environment the code runs in.

We solved this with a Snowflake request proxy for v0 sandboxes, built on the Vercel Sandbox firewall. The sandbox can run normal Snowflake clients, but the real credential is resolved at request time in a server proxy outside the sandbox runtime. This lets existing Snowflake clients work inside the sandbox without exposing the user's credential to generated code.

The harder problem was deciding where the proxy could safely inject the credential. The obvious implementation, replacing a placeholder token wherever it appears, introduces another credential leak.

Isolation doesn't protect secrets

v0 runs generated applications in isolated sandboxes. Isolation protects the rest of the system from untrusted code, but it doesn't protect secrets inside the sandbox.

If a generated app can read a token from the filesystem, that token can be copied into logs, returned in an API response, embedded into generated client code, or sent to another host. Sandbox isolation limits what the application can access, but it does not help once the credential itself is available inside the sandbox.

For Snowflake, the credential represents the Snowflake role the user connected with. v0 should be able to help the user explore and build with data they are authorized to access, but generated code should not receive raw provider credentials just because it needs one.

Every Snowflake request goes through the proxy

The sandbox cannot talk to Snowflake directly. When code inside it sends a request to the user's Snowflake account host, the sandbox firewall forwards that request to the v0 Snowflake proxy:

The firewall terminates TLS with a certificate authority unique to each sandbox, which lets the proxy read and rewrite traffic that would otherwise be encrypted. The sandbox trusts that certificate authority automatically, so the Snowflake SDK and CLI run with their default certificate validation, OCSP included. The proxy then verifies the sandbox's OIDC token, looks up the v0 chat the sandbox belongs to, restores the user session bound to that chat, and retrieves a fresh Snowflake credential for that user.

The sandbox does not choose where a token-bearing request is sent. The proxy derives the Snowflake account host from the server-side credential and rejects invalid account URLs, keeping the credential scoped to the connected Snowflake account rather than trusting host information supplied by generated code.

Compatibility without credential exposure

As a stopgap, the first version of the integration wrote the user's real token into the sandbox's Snowflake token files. The proxy replaced that approach. Ideally, we would remove token files from the sandbox entirely, but Snowflake clients expect credentials in different locations depending on the authentication flow.

Some requests, such as Snowflake SQL API calls, authenticate with an Authorization: Bearer header. Other client flows read local token files and send the token as part of a login request. Once the client has authenticated, subsequent requests use Snowflake-issued session tokens, and the proxy passes those requests through untouched.

To preserve compatibility, v0 still writes a token-shaped placeholder into the sandbox. The placeholder is a fixed, public, 72-byte string that grants no access, and its only job is to let existing Snowflake SDK and CLI flows behave as if a token exists. The proxy never authorizes a request based on the placeholder itself. Instead, the proxy authorizes the request using the sandbox's server-side identity and its binding to the user's chat.

The real OAuth token, the reusable credential that represents the user, is never written into the sandbox. Snowflake does issue session tokens that live inside the sandbox after login, but each of those belongs to a single authenticated session.

Those sessions are short-lived in practice. The Snowflake helper in generated apps destroys its connection after each query, which ends the session right away. Closing the chat does not end a session on its own, but tearing down the sandbox takes the token with it, and Snowflake expires the session server-side after four hours of inactivity by default. When a request reaches the proxy, it decides whether and where to attach the credential.

Why blind replacement fails

The first version of the proxy searched each request for the placeholder and swapped in the real token wherever it appeared:

The problem is that generated code controls parts of the request, including where the placeholder can appear. A SQL statement, for example, is caller-controlled data. If a query contains the placeholder as a string literal, blind replacement turns that query into one containing the real OAuth token. If the database then returns that string, the real token comes back into the sandbox as query output, and the proxy would have leaked the token it was built to keep out.

Stricter matching does not close the hole. The proxy shouldn't inject a credential based on attacker-controlled text. Instead, it needs to know which field in each Snowflake request carries authentication.

Injecting credentials only into authentication fields

Snowflake requests reach the proxy in three shapes, and each shape puts authentication in a different place.

For Snowflake SQL API requests, the proxy sets the OAuth token on the Authorization: Bearer header. The body remains caller-controlled SQL and is not rewritten. If the placeholder appears in the SQL payload, the proxy rejects the request before it reaches Snowflake and logs it as placeholder misuse.

For Snowflake login requests, the proxy parses the JSON request body, sets the token structurally at the login token field, and serializes the body again. If the placeholder remains anywhere else in the request body, the proxy fails closed.

Post-login session requests authenticate with Snowflake-managed session tokens, so the proxy has nothing to inject.

Failing closed

The proxy rejects any request where:

  • The sandbox is not bound to a chat

  • No user-scoped credential can be obtained

  • The Snowflake account host cannot be derived

  • The placeholder appears outside an approved authentication field

  • A structured login body cannot be parsed safely

Requests are also bounded before inspection so that compressed or oversized bodies cannot turn the proxy into an unbounded parser. Every proxied request emits an observability event with the upstream outcome, status, duration, and injection location. This surfaces misuse and integration failures without exposing secrets.

Handling refresh and deploy

Token refresh cannot depend on an ambient browser cookie, because proxy requests originate from the sandbox, not from the user's browser session. v0 binds the user session to the sandbox instead, and the proxy mints and refreshes OAuth credentials from that binding.

The publish path uses Snowflake CLI flows with the same credential boundary. Deploy can write the placeholder into credential files, but never the real token.

After deployment, the application runs in Snowpark Container Services and authenticates as its own service user, with a token that Snowflake manages and rotates automatically, mounted at /snowflake/session/token. The user's OAuth token and the v0 proxy are no longer involved.

The resulting security boundary

For users, none of this is visible. Connect Snowflake, ask v0 to inspect schemas or build an app, preview the result, and deploy when it's ready.

The security model rests on five rules:

  • Credential injection happens only at each endpoint's authentication fields

  • Requests that use the placeholder outside an authentication field are rejected and logged

  • Token-bearing requests go only to the connected Snowflake account host

  • Credentials are minted and refreshed server-side

  • Generated code uses Snowflake without ever reading the user's OAuth token

In its first 15 days in production, the proxy attached credentials server-side for roughly 13,000 requests and recorded zero placeholder-misuse rejections.

Although we built this proxy for Snowflake, the same problem applies to other integrations: generated code often needs to authenticate without receiving the user's long-lived credential. The important part is to inject credentials only into protocol-defined authentication fields, rather than rewriting arbitrary request data.

The v0 Snowflake integration is now available in beta. Get started by reading the integration docs.

title: Microfrontends previews now link across repositories
description:
Microfrontends can now link Preview Deployments across repositories when their Git branch names match exactly.

In a monorepo, projects share the same Git repository, commits, and branches, so Vercel can automatically link their previews. Cross-repository projects have separate commit histories and branches in separate repositories. With this update, Vercel matches Git-connected projects by branch name and links their corresponding previews.

For example, when you preview the new-checkout branch of one project, requests to other projects in the Microfrontends group will use their new-checkout previews when available. This makes it easier to review coordinated changes across repositories in one preview experience.

This feature is enabled by default for new Microfrontends groups. You can manage it in your Microfrontends settings. Learn more about how deployment routing works for Microfrontends.

title: Always-on tracing for production and preview traffic
description:
With always-on tracing, you can now debug your real user requests without reproducing them.

Always-on tracing continuously collects traces from your production and preview traffic. Unlike session tracing, which only captures requests from your own browser, it samples your live traffic.

You control what's collected with sampling rules. Each rule sets a trace rate for an environment (All, Production, or Preview), optionally scoped to a path prefix like /checkout. Nothing is collected until you add a rule, so you pay only for what you choose to trace.

You can also manage sampling rules from the CLI. vercel traces config set adds a rule, or changes the rate of an existing one when you run it again with the same environment and path prefix:

Infrastructure and outbound fetch spans are captured automatically. To add framework and custom spans, instrument your app with @vercel/otel.

To view a trace, open the Logs or run vercel traces get <request-id>.

Always-on tracing is is now in beta and available to teams on all plans. Tracing is priced at $0.50 per 1M span units. Traces follow your runtime log retention: 1 hour on Hobby, 1 day on Pro and 3 days on Enterprise.

Get started by adding a rule in Settings → Tracing or from the settings icon in Logs. Learn more in the documentation.

Read more

title: How Ora benchmarks every major AI agent on Vercel
description:
Ora on Vercel

  • Front end, back end, and agent runtime on one platform

  • Every major agent tested side by side on live sites

  • Hundreds of commits a day from a 16-person engineering team

Ora sends agents onto live websites with instructions to sign up for a product, integrate with it, and pay for it. Agents often fail, and by Ora's estimate, 99% of the web isn't agent-ready. The platform shows customers where and why agents fail, and what to change.

Assaf Elovic, co-founder of Ora, spent years helping agents discover the web. His previous company, Tavily, built a web search engine for AI agents and was acquired by Nebius earlier this year. Search solved half the problem, but an agent that finds a product still has to actually use it. He and co-founder Liad Yosef started Ora to measure how ready the web is for agents, and to fix the parts that aren't.

Today that means spawning agents against live customer sites from journey.ora.ai, where Ora runs a journey and records the cost, latency, and steps an agent needs to finish a task. The platform runs on Vercel, including the agent runtime.

Benchmarking every major agent side by side

Every harness expects its own infrastructure

Agents decompose into two parts: a model, which does the reasoning, and a harness, the software that gives the model its tools and drives it from step to step. Ora's lineup covers the agents customers use most: Claude Code, ChatGPT, Gemini, Hermes, OpenClaw, and eve, Vercel's agent framework. Ora runs each agent on a customer's website and watches how it handles common workflows.

No two harnesses want the same infrastructure. Each expects its own environment and exposes its steps differently, so Ora runs a separate runtime for every harness and traces every step. Ido Finder, who leads engineering at Ora, calls that side-by-side coverage one of the most valuable things ora brings to its customers.

When an agent stalls in a signup flow, the customer sees which step and what it tried. Without the trace, the result is a score with nothing behind it.

One platform under every harness

Ora built this testing system entirely on Vercel. Front end, back end, and the agent runtime share the same deployment path, logs, and authentication. The agent runtime isn't separate infrastructure to operate; it lives where the rest of the product lives.

Ora benchmarked eve, then built on it

Testing eve like any other harness

When Vercel launched eve, Ora gave it no special treatment. eve went through the same benchmark, under the same conditions, as every other harness in the lineup. Ora works with Vercel Engineering as a design partner, and Finder gave the eve team direct access to the platform to dig into the results.

The initial test put eve against Claude Code across hundreds of real journeys on multiple domains. Both harnesses ran the same models, Claude Fable 5 and Haiku 4.5, and every run gave the agent the same job: integrate with a product.

Ora published three numbers from the comparison:

  • 7% fewer steps to reach the goal

  • 2x native success: twice as many tasks finished on the customer's own site instead of falling back to web search

  • 9% more valid endpoints: more of the endpoints the agent found were ones it could actually call

The benchmark fed back into eve, too. One run surfaced a prompt-caching issue, the eve team shipped a fix, and Ora's next round of results measured roughly 15% lower total cost.

The framework behind Ora's own agents

For a company that benchmarks every major harness for a living, this is not a casual choice. After those results, Ora builds on eve.

Because eve follows the Next.js paradigm, there was little to configure, and tools, skills, and connectors take little code. The feature that sealed it was the sandbox override. An agent framework like eve ships with its own sandbox, the isolated environment where the agent executes, runs tools, and touches files. That's a good default for most teams, because you get safe execution for free. But an agent in the framework's own sandbox runs outside the instrumented environment where Ora traces every step. The override lets the team swap that environment in, so eve agents get recorded like every other harness, with nothing new built.

Journey.ora.ai now has eve on both sides, eve is one of the harnesses it tests, and eve is what it runs on.

How 16 engineers ship hundreds of commits a day

The engineering team is 16 people shipping hundreds of commits a day, and day-to-day infrastructure work belongs to their coding agents. A stack that sits in one place lets those agents run it end to end.

Finder puts the time saved at a few hours a week at least. Elovic credits a similar amount to how well coding agents build with Vercel's libraries.

What's next

Ora is adding more products, and the architecture is growing with them. The team is splitting its platform into microservices, all of them on Vercel. New services deploy to the same infrastructure and talk to each other with no extra configuration, and the internal agents built on eve will run as one more service.

By Ora's own measure, 99% of the web still can't handle an agent that shows up to sign up, integrate, and pay.

About Ora: Ora makes the web agent-ready. Companies use ora to benchmark how AI agents discover, navigate, and interact with their websites, and to build the infrastructure agents need to find, use, and transact with them.

title: Updates to Hobby and Pro Terms of Service
description:
We are updating the Terms of Service for Hobby and Pro customers, effective October 19, 2026. The updates clarify some existing Vercel practices, expand terms on topics such as managed accounts and credits, and reflect applicable legal requirements, including certain cancellation and service-change rights for eligible consumers in the UK and EU.

Credits and billing

A new section sets out how credits work: plan-included credits expire at the end of the subscription term and purchased credits expire one year after purchase unless stated otherwise in the relevant credit purchase terms. Credits can only be used to pay Vercel fees, have no cash value, and are nontransferable. Credits are generally nonrefundable, but unused purchased credits are refunded if Vercel terminates your account without cause.

The Terms also clarify that credit purchases are billed in advance, subscriptions auto-renew unless you turn off renewal, and third-party pass-through rates may change when provider rates change. ⁠⁠

Managed accounts

We also clarified that if your company wishes to manage your account using your company work email, Vercel will now notify you first and give you a reasonable amount of time to move your personal content to an account with a different email address

Renewal and cancellation

You can turn off auto-renewal and cancel or downgrade through account settings or Support. Cancellation or downgrade generally takes effect at the start of the next renewal period. The Terms also explain statutory withdrawal and refund rights for eligible consumers.

Service changes

Eligible consumers in the UK and EU may cancel the affected subscription free of charge if a change has more than a minor negative impact on their access to or use of the Services. They have 30 days from notice or the change, whichever is later, and may receive a prorated refund of prepaid amounts for the remaining period.

Other updates

The service-specific provisions have been moved to a dedicated Service Terms page. The Terms also clarify sanctions-related obligations, including that use of the Services must not be in connection with or for the benefit of a sanctioned person under applicable laws.

title: Death to long-lived static credentials
description:
Fifteen years ago, TLS was something you'd use to protect the most sensitive areas of your app. Then Google, Let's Encrypt, the EFF, and others led the push for HTTPS everywhere, making encryption the default for every request. Without it, anyone between the browser and server can read and tamper with the traffic.

OAuth, OIDC, DBSC, and related standards already provide building blocks for secure authentication, but standards alone do not make secure methods the norm. HTTPS needed tooling that made encryption easy and a sustained push that made it expected. Machine-to-machine authentication still resembles HTTPS in 2010, with some vendors and enterprises leading the way while long-lived static credentials remain the default for many SaaS vendors and infrastructure providers.

At Vercel, we want to make fast and secure the default across the web, including in our own services and the integrations in our Marketplace. We’ve built OIDC UI, a shadcn/ui registry that gives providers trust-policy forms and token verification code. We’re expanding OIDC support across Vercel and setting new authentication requirements for Marketplace providers.

Long-lived static credentials are insecure

Long-lived static credentials are secrets such as API keys and database passwords that applications keep reusing, often with no expiration. As agents take on more useful work, we give them access to our systems, tools, and data through credentials that can grant permissions far beyond the task at hand.

Those credentials can leak into a code repository or chat, be stolen when a service or dependency is compromised, or be exposed when prompt injection leads an agent to reveal them. However it happens, an attacker can use the credential with the permissions it grants until it expires or is revoked. Recent credential-theft and supply-chain incidents across the industry show why encryption at rest isn’t enough when malicious code can read an application’s credentials in production.

Rotating exposed credentials takes time and coordination across the systems that use them, and mistakes can disrupt production. At Vercel, we’ve previously spent thousands of engineering hours on multiple, very painful key rotations out of an abundance of caution, and we never want to have to do this again.

Better solutions already exist

With OIDC, your application can authenticate without storing a long-lived provider key. A trusted issuer provides a signed, short-lived token identifying the application, and the receiving service verifies that token before deciding what access to grant.

A stolen token stops working when it expires, limiting how long that copy can be used even if the leak goes unnoticed. Your application can obtain fresh credentials programmatically, removing the need to distribute and manually rotate a persistent provider key across the systems that use it.

We’ve been prioritizing OIDC across Vercel so applications can access Blob, AI Gateway, and Sandbox without storing long-lived keys for those services. Our OIDC federation has been generally available since 2024, letting applications running on Vercel exchange Vercel-issued identity tokens for temporary AWS, Google Cloud, and Azure credentials under configured project and environment trust policies. But for developers to stop managing long-lived keys, that support has to extend to all the services their applications depend on.

The rest of the web hasn’t followed

We surveyed more than 1,000 SaaS vendors and found that only 8.4% supported secure authentication methods.

But getting vendors to support secure authentication is only part of the problem. Even when a service offers a secure method, developers often choose a static key because it can be simpler to use. We see three main barriers to broader adoption:

  • Tooling and setup that make secure authentication more complicated than using a static key.

  • Added latency from fetching or exchanging tokens on the request path.

  • Weak incentives for vendors to offer and prioritize secure authentication.

Our goal is to make secure authentication the default on Vercel, while also using our Marketplace to help push more vendors to support it.

Our commitment to a more secure web

We have a responsibility to make this change practical across the services we run, the tools developers use, and the integrations we build with partners.

Make secure authentication easier to use

Using a secure token has to be easier than pasting a key, or developers will keep pasting keys. On Vercel, code retrieves an OIDC token with a function call, and a custom audience specifies the service intended to receive it.

With Vercel Connect, applications and agents use their deployment identity to request provider tokens at runtime, without having to store long-lived provider secrets in environment variables. Once the connector is configured and linked to the project and the user’s account is connected, code can request a token for that user with scopes the provider supports.

We’re also extending OIDC support across the Vercel API and CLI to remove the need for long-lived Vercel tokens in deployment workflows.

OIDC UI for API providers

OIDC UI is a shadcn/ui component registry with a trust-policy configurator and a server-side token verifier. It includes provider forms for Vercel, GitHub, GitLab, Google, Bitbucket, AWS, Azure, and custom OIDC issuers. A provider can let customers configure trust for a particular Vercel project’s production environment, then verify incoming tokens against that policy without building the configuration interface and verification code from scratch.

Reduce the performance cost of secure authentication

A static key in an environment variable is already available when a function runs, so reading it requires no network request. Fetching a token or exchanging it for provider credentials can add network latency, so reducing those calls is part of making secure authentication practical.

Vercel Functions receive a platform-issued token in the request header, which the SDK reads without fetching another. The platform reuses unexpired tokens, while Vercel Connect caches provider tokens in process and refreshes them near expiry. Custom-audience and provider exchanges require network calls.

For example, an application can use the Azure SDK to access Cosmos DB with temporary credentials instead of a database key. With Azure configured to trust the Vercel project and its default token audience, the callback supplies a Vercel OIDC token to ClientAssertionCredential, which exchanges it for the Azure access token used by CosmosClient.

Give providers an incentive to support secure authentication

The Vercel Marketplace offers access to third-party databases, content management systems, observability tools, and more. Our goal is for all of these vendors to support short-lived, identity-based authentication, whether they accept OIDC tokens directly or exchange them for temporary credentials. We’re working to make integrations configure that authentication automatically when developers connect a service, so it does not require a separate setup step.

HTTPS everywhere did not win on ergonomics alone. Chrome put a “Not secure” label on plain HTTP, and then it set deadlines. Now we are setting ours. By November 30, 2026, vendors who do not support OIDC auth from Vercel to their services and use long-lived secrets for authentication will have a similar “Not secure” message on their listing. By January 2027, vendors who do not offer secure auth will be delisted. We are holding the Vercel API and our own native integrations to the same bar.

From static to dynamic

Fifteen years ago, encrypting every request felt like overkill. Today, the padlock is so normal that we only notice when it's missing. Secure authentication between services should become just as routine, so developers can connect the systems they need without storing another long-lived secret. Going from static to dynamic has always been the Vercel mission. It started with pages, and now it’s credentials.

Additional resources

  • OIDC federation covers how deployments get short-lived identity tokens, with guides for AWS, GCP, Azure, and your own API.

  • Custom OIDC token audiences scopes each token to the one service meant to receive it.

  • Vercel Connect requests short-lived, scoped provider tokens at runtime, so code and agents never store credentials.

  • Vercel Connect guides walk through building agents this way, from Slack bots to GitHub agents.

Read more

title: How Interfaze serves 50 million requests a month on Vercel
description:
Interfaze on Vercel

  • 50 million requests a month

  • Backend running on Fluid compute

  • Multiple model providers behind one fallback layer with AI Gateway

Interfaze builds models for deterministic work that general-purpose LLMs handle poorly: document processing, OCR, object detection, web scraping, speech to text, and classification.

As founder Yoeven Khemlani puts it, "Most models aren't deterministic by nature. That's fine when you're drafting an essay. But when a hospital or a legal team needs to process documents, you don't reach for an LLM." Ask an LLM for the total on an invoice and you get a number with no easy way to check where it came from. Interfaze's models return the number along with a bounding box showing where on the page it came from and a confidence score for how sure the model is. Every result can be checked, and the models still take prompts the way an LLM does.

Everything around Interfaze's models runs on Vercel, including the backend. That spans the API serving 50 million requests a month, the sandbox that executes code the model writes, and the routing that keeps data preprocessing running when a third-party model provider goes down.

The backend required no infrastructure work

Interfaze's frontend and backend both run on Vercel. The backend handles every request to Interfaze's API, whether a customer is calling the model or uploading a file. All of it runs as serverless functions in the same codebase as the frontend. When a request needs computation, the model hands the code to Vercel Sandbox, which runs it in isolation. There was no separate infrastructure to set up.

Fluid compute handles the heavy jobs

Scalability was Yoeven's top requirement. The goal is serving the model to millions of users, and Fluid compute scales with traffic on its own. Heavier work runs there too. Vercel's memory and timeout limits are high enough that Interfaze's web scraping, which runs on Puppeteer, works out of the box.

AI Gateway makes model routing reliable at scale

Interfaze pushes large volumes of data cleaning through open source models hosted by third-party providers. A single provider is a weak link. Providers hit rate limits or go down, and when one does, the cleaning stops unless traffic moves somewhere else.

The providers are also not interchangeable. Two of them can claim to host the same open source model and serve it at very different quality.

When a provider fails or throttles, AI Gateway fails requests over to the next provider automatically. It also lets Interfaze choose which provider serves a given model, so the team can run the same workload through each one, see which performs well, and send traffic there.

Workflow SDK runs email sequences over months

Interfaze runs its lifecycle email system on the Workflow SDK, with sends conditioned on product usage. The system tracks which API a customer called, at what volume, and how that compares against their first week. Retries are handled automatically, so one failed step doesn't take down the sequence.

The part Interfaze needed most was durable execution. A workflow can pause a step and pick it back up months later with its state intact, which the team found other systems could not do for long.

Preview deployments carry new model versions to customers

Interfaze runs more than one version of its model at a time, each at its own URL. When an error comes in, the team has to know which version produced the error before they can fix anything. On Vercel every URL is its own deployment with its own logs, so the error is already filed under the version that caused it. There was no separate logging vendor to set up.

Those same preview URLs are how a new model version gets to customers before it ships. The Vercel side of a release builds in about three minutes. Hosting the weights on GPUs is the slow part.

What's next

Interfaze recently released Interfaze 1 Lite, an open-weight version of its model that runs on a single GPU and is served through the same API. Next is a gateway for web search, one API that routes to whichever search provider a developer picks, the way AI Gateway does for models. It launches on the same Vercel backend as everything else.

About Interfaze: Interfaze builds models for deterministic tasks, including OCR, object detection, web scraping, speech to text, and classification. Its customers are engineering teams in legal, healthcare, and finance.

title: How Vercel Agent accesses production safely
description:
An agent working on production systems needs permission to act. A request like “fix this deployment” doesn’t tell you upfront which actions it will take or what access it will need. Grant agents broad access and a mistake can affect unrelated resources. Ask for approval at every step and the user has to approve individual actions before they know how the agent intends to solve the problem. Repeated prompts can turn that review into a habit of clicking approve.

Vercel Agent starts by investigating the problem, then proposes a plan showing what it would do and what access it would need. Approving that plan grants the additional permissions to carry it out, so the user can review the proposed fix before authorizing any changes.

The plan determines the permissions

For a broken production deployment, Vercel Agent might inspect recent deployments and build logs, then compare the failed deployment with the last known-good one. Read-only access lets that investigation run automatically. If it leads to a proposed redeploy, Vercel Agent requests the additional access in a plan the user can review and approve in one decision.

Access is defined by scopes, the named capabilities recognized by the Vercel authorization system. Any plan requesting access beyond the read-only baseline waits for approval as a whole, including any read-only tasks it contains. In this example, the investigation runs under a separate read-only plan before Vercel Agent proposes the redeploy:

Plan

Work

Requested scope

Investigate the failure

Inspect recent deployments and build logs, then compare the failed deployment with the last successful one

read:deployment

Redeploy the last known-good build

Create a deployment

read-write:deployment

A short read-only lookup can run without a plan. For longer investigations, Vercel Agent creates a read-only plan so the user can follow its tasks and progress while it runs automatically.

The plan connects what the user wants done to what Vercel Agent is allowed to do:

  • Intent: The outcome the user asks for.

  • Work: The tasks Vercel Agent proposes to achieve it.

  • Access: The scopes those tasks require.

  • Enforcement: The credentials and API checks that enforce access limits.

Each stored plan records its tasks and progress, with requested scopes attached to each task. The task descriptions explain why access is needed, and the scopes are combined across the plan.

The read-only baseline currently includes every registered scope beginning with read:. Plans need approval when they request access beyond that baseline or include supported external actions, such as opening a GitHub pull request. Read-only operations can still expose sensitive information, so automatic approval does not mean the work is harmless.

Vercel Agent can only use permissions the user already has

Vercel Agent runs as a Vercel App, which the user authorizes to act on their behalf within a team. That authorization is limited by the user’s existing permissions, so approving a plan cannot grant access the user does not have.

The Vercel OAuth service exchanges that authorization for shorter-lived tokens with specific scopes. These scopes define which capabilities the token permits, such as reading deployments or changing project settings. Vercel APIs check the token on each request to enforce those limits.

A user may authorize Vercel Agent for a team with dozens of projects. A redeploy plan requests deployment write access. Editing environment variables, changing domains, and managing team membership each require their own permissions.

Deployment write access is broader than a single redeploy. Naming deployment X in a plan does not, by itself, restrict the token to that deployment. The runtime, the software that coordinates Vercel Agent’s execution, checks that the plan is active before selecting its approved credential. Vercel APIs check each request against that credential’s permissions.

Approval determines which permissions Vercel Agent can use

When a user approves a plan that needs additional Vercel access, its requested scopes are checked again and a token is prepared containing the read-only baseline plus the approved permissions. The runtime, the software that coordinates Vercel Agent’s execution, checks that the plan is active before selecting its approved credential. That credential remains subject to its scopes, team, the user’s permissions, and expiry.

The credential used depends on the work:

Work

Credential

Read-only investigation

A baseline token with read-only scopes

Approved Vercel changes

A token with baseline scopes plus the approved additional scopes

External actions

Credentials and permissions specific to that provider

The model’s instructions tell it when to propose a plan and request approval. If it attempts an operation outside the token’s permissions, Vercel APIs reject the request, even if the model considers the action necessary to complete the task.

A single plan can include Vercel changes and a GitHub pull request. The user reviews both in one plan, while each provider uses separate permissions and credentials. GitHub pull-request access is tied to an owner and repository, so approval to open a pull request in acme/storefront applies to that repository even if the user also has access to acme/payments. Opening a pull request there requires its own approval.

Plans and tokens use the same permission definitions

A proposed plan can request a permission that has been renamed or removed. We initially maintained a separate permission list for Vercel Agent, which could fall out of sync with the OAuth service that issues its tokens. We moved to the same scope definitions so those mismatches could be caught during planning.

At session setup, Vercel Agent loads those definitions from the Vercel scope registry into an in-memory catalog. Fetching the registry requires authorization for the team, while the scope definitions themselves are shared across teams. The catalog supplies the definitions used at three stages:

  • Plan validation: Requested scopes are normalized, and unknown or malformed names are rejected before the plan is stored or presented for approval.

  • Approval: The requested scopes determine whether the plan fits within the read-only baseline or needs additional access.

  • Token preparation: Valid scopes define the credentials for approved work.

For example, a task to update firewall rules might request an outdated scope. The system rejects the proposed plan and returns valid scopes so Vercel Agent can correct it before requesting approval. This catches the mismatch during planning and requires an explicit correction instead of a fallback to broader access.

Fetching the registry adds latency and a service dependency, so Vercel Agent caches the catalog and uses that copy to check stored plans when they are loaded. Those checks reflect the cached definitions until the catalog is refreshed with changes from the registry.

Resuming work requires an active, approved plan

Vercel Agent may receive approval after the original chat request has ended, or lose its connection before carrying out an approved redeploy. The stored plan includes its state, who approved it, and when, alongside its tasks and requested permissions. That record connects the proposed work to the access the user authorized and allows the approval to be checked when work resumes.

Before resuming, the runtime reloads the plan and checks that it is active before selecting a credential with its approved permissions. A stopped plan fails that check, even if its token has time remaining before expiry.

If approval and a request to stop arrive together, the plan can move from waiting for approval to active only if the stop has not already changed its status. The runtime then checks again that the plan is active before using the approved credential.

If the investigation reveals that the current plan needs replacing, Vercel Agent can propose another. A replacement requesting elevated access needs its own approval, giving the user a chance to review the revised work and permissions together.

Where permissions need more precision

As Vercel Agent reached more of the platform, we had to correct access rules for actions that involve multiple resources or have different consequences. Attaching a domain can require both domain and project permissions, while staging a firewall rule and publishing it need different levels of access. Scopes need to capture these distinctions while keeping each plan’s access request manageable.

Matching those scopes to a proposed fix requires care throughout planning:

  • Choosing scopes: Vercel Agent chooses scopes with incomplete information, so it can request too little access and leave a task blocked, or too much and grant more authority than the work needs. Task-level guidance helps it choose, while validation catches invalid scope names. Even a valid scope can grant broader access than necessary.

  • Describing the work: “Redeploy the last successful build” gives the user a concrete action to assess, while scope names alone leave them to work out the consequences. The plan needs to explain the intended change and make clear which limits the token actually enforces.

  • Understanding denials: A denied operation could indicate a missing scope, an incorrect resource, or an operation that should remain blocked. Vercel Agent needs to distinguish those cases before requesting additional permissions.

Even with the right permissions, a redeploy requires judgment about whether the selected commit is safe to ship. That depends on the application, the failure, and the proposed fix. The user needs enough information to assess the choice, and Vercel Agent still has to execute it correctly.

Read-only investigation also needs controls for the information it retrieves, including sensitive project configuration and operational details. We chose a read-only baseline so Vercel Agent can investigate before asking for approval, and that choice needs continued review as scopes and the information they expose change. Other systems may need a narrower baseline. Separate controls must govern how retrieved information is handled and where it can go.

Vercel Agent can make a wrong decision or encounter malicious instructions in content it reads, such as build logs. Scoped credentials limit which operations it can perform in either case, but permitted operations can still cause harm. Plans therefore work alongside sandbox isolation, network policy, secret handling, rate limits, audit logs, and service authorization. Our work on security boundaries in agentic architectures explains the separation between an agent, its credentials, and the code it executes.

From investigation to approved action

Authority stays attached to the work that required it. The runtime selects the approved credential for an active plan, and its scopes define the operations Vercel Agent can perform. With the investigation already done, the user can assess a proposed fix and its requested access together.

Try Vercel Agent to investigate an issue in your project. Review what it finds and, if it proposes a change, assess the plan and requested access before approving it.

title: Virtual models now available on AI Gateway
description:
Virtual models are now available on AI Gateway.

A virtual model is a saved configuration that tells AI Gateway which model and settings to use. Your apps and agents call it with a custom model ID, such as vmc/coding-agent. You can change the model or settings centrally in AI Gateway without redeploying your apps or reconfiguring your agents.

Use virtual models to:

  • Control routing and compliance: Choose providers, configure fallback models, and enforce requirements such as Zero Data Retention.

To create a virtual model, open the Virtual Models page and click Create Virtual Model. Enter a slug, choose the underlying model, configure the settings you want requests to use, and save.

Or create one with the Vercel CLI:
