title: Introducing Vercel CI
description:
Coding agents are opening more pull requests than ever, and each one waits on CI before anyone can review or merge it. Most CI systems run the entire workflow on every push, even a one-line change. The more your agents push, the more time you spend waiting on CI.

Today, we're announcing Vercel CI in Beta. It runs only the tasks affected by your code change, and spins up only the compute those checks need, the same way Fluid compute scales with your traffic.

At Vercel, our CI now keeps up with our coding agents. Time from git push to "CI passed" is 2-6x faster than it was before.

How it works

Vercel CI uses Turborepo to understand your tasks and which ones depend on each other. It reads turbo.json, so if you're already using Turborepo, there's no separate CI config to write.

If you're not on Turborepo yet, add turbo.json and the turbo package. It works in single-package repos too.

Then tag the tasks you want Vercel CI to run.

"tags": ["ci"] is all you need to get started. No workflow YAML to maintain, no drift between your CI config and turbo.json, and Remote Cache is on by default.

When you or your agent push code, Vercel CI determines which tasks need to run based on the change. Tasks whose inputs haven't changed come from cache. The remaining tasks each run on their own machine, powered by Hive, Vercel's compute layer, and start as soon as their dependencies finish.

Vercel CI gives each task the compute it needs and nothing more.

Running your CI on Vercel

To get started, follow the documentation or prompt your agent from your repo:

Once set up, you or your agent can watch and inspect CI through the Vercel dashboard, Vercel CLI, or Vercel MCP. When something fails, go straight to the failing task, see what's blocked behind it, and open its logs, or search across recent runs to see whether a test has been flaky all week.

Vercel CI posts a check to your pull request on GitHub, so your existing branch protection rules can block merges on failure, the same way they do today.

Closing the loop

Vercel CI has already completed nearly 8 million tasks across our own repositories and the private beta, and we're just getting started. We're working to keep shrinking the time between writing code and running it in production.

As we work toward general availability, we plan to add:

  • Advanced observability

  • A vc ci CLI command for distributed execution before pushing code

  • More granular test selection

Vercel CI is available in Beta today on all plans. Read the docs and try it on your repository.

Read more

title: Introducing Virtual Models on AI Gateway
description:
Today, we are introducing Virtual Models on AI Gateway.

Virtual Models are an abstraction of the model string and configurations your apps and developers use. With a single virtual model ID, you can change and update models, configure fallbacks and priority, and enforce Zero Data Retention centrally. The virtual model configuration applies wherever the ID is used.

Assign a virtual model ID to an agent task, and pass it as the model string wherever that task is called. You can then change the model and settings behind the virtual model ID in AI Gateway, and your apps and agents will pick up the new configuration automatically, without code changes or redeploys.

New models use the same virtual model ID

In the last 90 days, 125 new models from more than 10 labs became available on AI Gateway. That adds up to about 10 a week. AI Gateway already makes switching a one-line change. You call any of those models by ID, and AI Gateway routes each request to a healthy provider and can fall back to others when one fails.

That one line still lives in your code, so switching usually means a redeploy.

Virtual Models move model selection and configuration to AI Gateway. You create an ID for a task, like vmc/coding-agent, and then configure the model and the settings it should use:

You can then use that virtual model ID as the model string wherever the task runs:

For coding agents like Claude Code, Codex, and others, connect them with vercel ai-gateway setup, then select your virtual model in each harness's model picker or configuration.

When a different model is available, including one from another provider, edit the virtual model. Every app and agent that calls vmc/coding-agent picks it up within a few minutes, with no code change or deployment needed:

Give each task its own model

An agent task like support ticket triage can run hundreds of times an hour and needs to be cheap. Other tasks, like legal contract review, may only run a few times a day, but require a high level of reasoning.

You can now give each task a purpose-built virtual model and easily evolve that model and configuration over time:

Settings such as fallbacks, Zero Data Retention, and tags stay with the virtual model when you switch models. Provider options apply per provider, so an Anthropic-specific setting stops applying when you point the virtual model at an OpenAI model. Review your provider options whenever you switch providers.

Before you switch a virtual model that serves production traffic, point a second one, like vmc/coding-agent-candidate, at the new model and run your evals against it. If quality drops after the switch, point the original back at the previous model.

Govern which models your team uses and how

Anyone on your team can call a virtual model, and team roles control who can make changes to it. Platform and security teams can centrally govern and test models and settings, while still easily giving teams access to new models as they are released.

Settings on a virtual model win over the same settings in a request, so callers can't override the provider order, fallbacks, or service tier you chose. For example, you can configure the fallback models for vmc/storefront-assistant centrally, and every app using that virtual model ID will use the same failover configuration, even if a request specifies different fallbacks.

If a virtual model requires Zero Data Retention or providers that don't train on request data, those configurations are enforced even if a request explicitly sets zeroDataRetention or disallowPromptTraining to false.

Tags on a virtual model replace any tags sent with the request, so spend lands on the task no matter how each app tags its calls. The Virtual Models page shows requests, spend, and success rate for each task.

Get started

Create a virtual model from your team dashboard or with the Vercel CLI.

About AI Gateway

AI Gateway provides a unified API for calling models, tracking usage and cost, and configuring retries, failover, and performance optimizations for higher-than-provider uptime. It includes built-in custom reporting, Zero Data Retention support, budgets for API keys, routing rules, and more.

AI Gateway reflects provider pricing with no markup and doesn't charge a platform fee on inference, including on Bring Your Own Key (BYOK) requests.

Virtual Models work with every model type on AI Gateway, including image, video, speech, embedding, and realtime models, and with the AI SDK and the OpenAI- and Anthropic-compatible APIs. See the Virtual Models documentation for every setting.

title: Choose the reporting timezone before grouping campaign events
description:
An AI assistant can group an event export by the first ten characters of its timestamp and produce a neat daily table. That table can still use the wrong day boundary.

This small exercise makes the boundary explicit before asking an assistant to summarize a campaign. It counts four fictional event rows, not unique users, qualified leads, or purchases. Nothing connects to an ad account or changes a campaign.

Four timestamps, three possible tables

Save this UTF-8 fixture as events.csv:

event,occurred_at
E01,2026-10-28T20:59:00Z
E02,2026-10-28T21:00:00Z
E03,2026-10-29T00:15:00+03:00
E04,2026-10-29T22:15:00+03:00

The first two timestamps use UTC (Z). The other two include +03:00. For this exercise, the reporting timezone is Europe/Moscow. Choose the timezone specified by your real report; this example does not imply every campaign uses Moscow time.

E01 is one minute before midnight in that timezone. E02 is exactly midnight, so it belongs to the next reporting day. E03 and E04 belong to that next day too.

These are the results of three different grouping rules:

Grouping rule October 28 October 29
First ten characters of each supplied string 2 2
Convert every timestamp to UTC, then take its date 3 1
Convert every timestamp to Europe/Moscow, then take its date 1 3

All three tables count four rows. A total-count check would not reveal the different day boundaries. For the stated reporting contract, the last row is the expected result.

Convert before taking the date

The following complete script uses Python's standard library. Save it as group_events.py beside events.csv:

import csv
import json
from collections import Counter
from datetime import datetime
from pathlib import Path
from zoneinfo import ZoneInfo


REPORT_TZ_NAME = "Europe/Moscow"
REPORT_TZ = ZoneInfo(REPORT_TZ_NAME)


def group_events(rows):
    counts = Counter()
    assignments = []
    for row in rows:
        raw = row["occurred_at"]
        stamp = datetime.fromisoformat(raw.replace("Z", "+00:00"))
        if stamp.utcoffset() is None:
            raise ValueError(row["event"] + ": explicit UTC offset required")
        report_day = stamp.astimezone(REPORT_TZ).date().isoformat()
        counts[report_day] += 1
        assignments.append({"event": row["event"], "report_date": report_day})
    return {
        "report_timezone": REPORT_TZ_NAME,
        "counts": dict(sorted(counts.items())),
        "assignments": assignments,
    }


if __name__ == "__main__":
    try:
        with Path(__file__).with_name("events.csv").open(
            encoding="utf-8", newline=""
        ) as stream:
            report = group_events(list(csv.DictReader(stream)))
    except (ValueError, KeyError) as error:
        print(json.dumps({"error": str(error)}))
        raise SystemExit(2)
    print(json.dumps(report, indent=2))

Run it with:

python3 group_events.py

The output includes the timezone, the counts, and an assignment for each input row:

{
  "report_timezone": "Europe/Moscow",
  "counts": {
    "2026-10-28": 1,
    "2026-10-29": 3
  },
  "assignments": [
    {"event": "E01", "report_date": "2026-10-28"},
    {"event": "E02", "report_date": "2026-10-29"},
    {"event": "E03", "report_date": "2026-10-29"},
    {"event": "E04", "report_date": "2026-10-29"}
  ]
}

The output above uses more compact spacing for the assignment objects; the JSON values are the same as the script's output. Keeping those assignments makes it possible to inspect which event crossed a date boundary instead of comparing totals alone.

The fixture and script were executed locally on Python 3.9.6. The four assignments and the three grouping alternatives in the table were checked. No external language model response was measured in this run; the script provides a reference result for checking one.

zoneinfo requires Python 3.9 or later and available IANA timezone data. It uses the system database or the tzdata package, as described in Python's official zoneinfo documentation. The local run had the required data. A machine without it may raise ZoneInfoNotFoundError; silently replacing the chosen zone with the computer's local timezone would change the contract.

Reject an unspecified offset

Change E03 to this value:

E03,2026-10-29T00:15:00

The timestamp now has no UTC offset. The script stops with exit code 2 and prints:

{"error": "E03: explicit UTC offset required"}

It does not print partial daily counts. Guessing that the value means UTC, Moscow time, or the operator's laptop time would produce a result without a stated source rule. Python distinguishes these naive timestamps from aware timestamps in its datetime documentation.

If the source system documents an offset-free value as belonging to a particular timezone, handle that as a separate input contract. This short example deliberately refuses to infer it.

Check that a different representation preserves the instant

Restore the original fixture. Then replace E02's timestamp with 2026-10-29T00:00:00+03:00.

That is the same instant as 2026-10-28T21:00:00Z. The script must return the same counts and assignments. A program that groups by the string's date would move the row simply because its representation changed.

Both this mutation and the missing-offset mutation were executed locally. One checks an invariant; the other checks a refusal condition.

Use the reference when reviewing an AI summary

Give an assistant the original CSV and a specific instruction:

Count event rows by calendar date in Europe/Moscow.
Require an explicit UTC offset or Z on every timestamp.
Convert each instant to Europe/Moscow before extracting its date.
Do not group by a substring or by the timestamp's original timezone.
If any timestamp has no offset or cannot be parsed, report the error;
do not return partial daily counts and do not guess a timezone.
Return the reporting timezone, daily counts, and each event's assigned date.
Do not infer unique users, leads, purchases, or campaign performance.

Compare the individual assignments as well as the counts. Then repeat the two mutations. A well-written explanation should not conceal a changed grouping rule or an invented offset.

This is a narrowly scoped fixture, not a production analytics pipeline. It assumes the displayed CSV schema and already deduplicated event rows. It does not check export completeness, attribution windows, delayed events, refunds, event definitions, or duplicate identifiers. Those require their own acceptance cases before a daily table can support a business conclusion.

Prepared with an AI agent. The displayed fixture, code, reference values, and two input mutations were checked locally. All event data is synthetic.

title: El límite de Shorts en 0 no basta: cómo quitar los Shorts de YouTube en el iPhone y seguir viendo videos normales (2026)
description:
minulo es una app para iPhone que oculta los Shorts de YouTube mientras los videos normales, las suscripciones y la búsqueda siguen funcionando, y ocultarlos es gratis. La otra forma viene en la propia app de YouTube: el Límite del feed de Shorts puesto en 0. También es gratis, pero un adulto puede descartar el aviso y seguir viendo. (Soy el desarrollador de minulo, Ayumu Kitabayashi, así que tenlo en cuenta al leer.)

Abajo explico cada opción con sus límites, incluidos los de minulo.

1. El Límite del feed de Shorts en 0 (gratis, dentro de YouTube)

Los pasos, según la ayuda de YouTube:

  1. Inicia sesión en la app de YouTube.
  2. Toca la pestaña Tú y luego Configuración.
  3. Toca Gestión del tiempo.
  4. Toca Límite del feed de Shorts y elige 0 en la lista.

El 0 está disponible para todos desde abril de 2026. Al llegar al límite, YouTube muestra un recordatorio. Su ayuda lo explica así: «Se te pedirá que rechaces o ignores el límite que has definido». Es decir, con un toque sigues en el feed.

Lo que conviene saber:

  • Con una cuenta de adulto el límite se puede descartar.
  • Los Shorts siguen apareciendo en Suscripciones y en los enlaces que te mandan.
  • Es solo para la app. La ayuda no describe este ajuste en youtube.com.
  • La ayuda no aclara si el límite afecta a los Shorts de Inicio, de la búsqueda o de las páginas de los canales.

2. Otras opciones de YouTube y del iPhone

Mostrar menos Shorts (⋮ arriba de una fila de Shorts en Inicio). Le dice a YouTube que te muestre menos. Son menos, no ninguno, y YouTube no dice cuánto dura. Se puede deshacer en Mi Actividad.

Desactivar el historial de reproducciones. YouTube quita las recomendaciones de la página de inicio cuando no tienes historial reciente relevante. Su ayuda no dice que esto quite la pestaña Shorts.

Cuenta supervisada para adolescentes. Los padres pueden fijar cuánto tiempo pasa un adolescente deslizando Shorts. Sirve solo para cuentas supervisadas.

Tiempo de uso del iPhone. Puede limitar o bloquear toda la app de YouTube, pero no puede apuntar solo a los Shorts. Si bloqueas YouTube, también te quedas sin videos largos y suscripciones. Apple no documenta una forma de bloquear solo la dirección /shorts en Safari.

Apps y extensiones que ocultan los Shorts. Además de minulo, hay otras como UNDOOMED, Nope y LoomWeb. Nope es una extensión de Safari, así que solo funciona en youtube.com desde Safari, no en la app de YouTube.

3. Ocultar los Shorts con minulo

minulo abre el sitio web de YouTube dentro de la app y oculta lo que tú eliges. No hay ningún aviso que puedas saltarte.

  1. Instala minulo desde el App Store.
  2. En el inicio, toca Agregar un servicio y elige YouTube.
  3. Toca el engranaje junto a YouTube y activa Ocultar la sección de Shorts, Ocultar la pestaña Shorts y Abrir los enlaces de Shorts en el reproductor normal.
  4. Si quieres, oculta también las recomendaciones de Inicio. Las suscripciones, Ver más tarde y la búsqueda se quedan.

Si el problema es que abres la app oficial de YouTube por costumbre, abre la pestaña Bloquear, permite Tiempo de uso y elige YouTube en Apps que bloquear. Cuando intentes abrir YouTube aparece una pantalla de Bloqueado, y el botón Abrir en minulo te lleva a la versión sin Shorts.

Ocultar los Shorts y bloquear la app oficial es gratis. Los horarios por día y hora, los bloqueos de más de 2 horas y el Modo estricto son de minulo Pro (9,99 $ al mes o 39,99 $ al año en EE. UU.).

Lo que minulo no puede hacer

Prefiero dejarlo claro antes de que lo instales:

  • No cambia la app oficial de YouTube. En el iPhone ninguna app puede cambiar lo que muestra otra. Los Shorts solo se ocultan dentro de minulo.
  • El bloqueo gratis dura hasta 2 horas. Cuando termina puedes empezar otro. Ocultar los Shorts no tiene límite de tiempo.
  • Solo iPhone (también hay una versión para Mac que funciona en Safari y Chrome). No hay versión para Android (está en pruebas).
  • Sin notificaciones mientras bloquea. Mientras minulo bloquea la app oficial, sus notificaciones no llegan, y minulo no envía notificaciones propias. Si necesitas los avisos de YouTube, no bloquees la app oficial.
  • Cuando YouTube cambia sus pantallas, algo oculto puede volver a aparecer un tiempo. Las reglas se revisan automáticamente cada semana.
  • Es una app nueva (septiembre de 2026) y todavía tiene pocas valoraciones.

Nota técnica para quien desarrolla

minulo no toca la app de YouTube. Carga la web oficial de cada servicio dentro de la app y oculta las partes elegidas en esa vista. El bloqueo de la app oficial usa Tiempo de uso de Apple: al tocar el icono sale la pantalla de bloqueo del sistema con el botón para abrir minulo. Por eso las limitaciones de arriba son las de iOS y las de la web: lo que la versión web no tiene, minulo tampoco lo tiene.

Resumen

  • Si te basta con un recordatorio: Límite del feed de Shorts en 0, gratis, pero se descarta con un toque.
  • Si quieres dejar de ver YouTube del todo un rato: Tiempo de uso, que bloquea la app entera.
  • Si quieres seguir viendo videos normales sin Shorts: minulo, gratis para ocultarlos.

Todos los métodos, con fuentes: Cómo bloquear los Shorts de YouTube en iPhone

Los nombres de los menús pueden cambiar con las actualizaciones de YouTube y de iOS.

title: Blazar Video Encoder for Generative Video
description:
Lately I've been using video diffusion models and learning more about them. As I was digging around the various codebases I noticed that there were a couple of common approaches to actually encoding the frames that are generated by the diffusion models: mainly use PyAV or shell out to FFmpeg. There's nothing especially wrong with either of these approaches but I think it is possible for us to do a little better. So I (along with my robot friends) built Blazar. You can find the code repo for Blazar here.

Today with PyAV the flow is roughly:

  1. Convert tensor from BF16 or F32 to u8 and reshape to (H, W, C)
  2. D2H transfer
  3. RGB to YUV conversion
  4. (if NVENC) upload to the GPU
  5. Encode

So, I think, this is roughly what we want to do:

  1. Be able to take the native output tensor shape of the model as an input. (B, C, T, H, W) seems to be the common tensor shape but a video encoder will want more like (B, T, H, W, C) or (B, T, C, H, W) (or whatever nv12 is with U' and V' interleaved)
  2. Do a fused YUV + tensor reshape conversion (does that count as a reshape? maybe not) either on GPU or CPU
  3. Encode either using NVENC (or some other HW encoder) or a variety of software encoders
  4. Be relatively easily configurable...
  5. Probably don't get in the way of the Python GIL

So the robot and I landed on a design where most of the work happens in Rust. Backends for YUV conversion and encoding are swappable between hardware and software so that if you would prefer not to use HW for YUV conversion and encoding you don't have to do that. There is a concept of "Calibrations" that are keyed on model and target quality so you can have multiple calibrations with different latency or quality targets and make them configurable by model. These live in human readable TOML files.

import blazar

cals = blazar.Calibrations.load("calibrations/default")
with blazar.Encoder(calibrations=cals, identity={"family": "wan", "version": "2.1",
                                                 "quant": "bf16", "size": "1.3b"},
                    target="balanced", backend="nvenc", codec="h264",
                    output="out.mp4") as stream:
    stream.submit(frame, width=W, height=H, fps=24.0, layout="thwc", range="unit01")
    # or, with device tensors:
    stream.submit(tensor, fps=24.0, range="unit01")

Here's a pretty simple example of using Blazar to encode frames. You can submit them one at a time or as a chunk of video, in which case they'll be mass converted to YUV and then encoded.

Peformance Comparison

This comparison table was done on a Core i7 14700KF with a 4080 Super in WSL. What we are measuring here is a BF16 (1, 3, 121, 1088, 1920) tensor being passed into the encoder pipelines for these scenarios:

  1. Blazar device bf16 (BF16 input tensor, GPU YUV conversion, NVENC)
  2. Blazar device u8 -> CPU YUV Conversion -> NVENC
  3. PyAV device u8 -> CPU YUV Conversion -> NVENC
  4. FFmpeg device u8 -> IPC -> CPU YUV Conversion -> NVENC
path ms/frame fps output vs zero-copy
blazar device bf16 (zero copy) 3.88 258 5.36 MB 1.0×
blazar host u8 6.35 158 5.34 MB 1.6×
pyav h264_nvenc (swscale) 9.37 107 3.79 MB 2.4×
ffmpeg cli h264_nvenc (pipe) 19.81 51 3.43 MB 5.1×

The optimal path is the device bf16 path. Here we feed the tensor directly into a CUDA kernel that simultaneously converts from RGB to YUV and reformats the buffer into the shape NVENC expects (T,C,H,W). On my 4080 Super we're able to hit 258 fps with 1088p tensors from SGLang. If we copy to host as a u8 that drops to 158 fps. Compared to the PyAV or FFmpeg CLI paths this is a fair improvement still.

Arm 1 thread 2 threads 4 threads scaling per-thread at 4
blazar 155.9 fps 383.0 620.8 4.0x 155.2
PyAV 33.7 61.9 63.0 1.9x 15.7

Looking at how Blazar scales with thread count you can see we 4x the throughput with 4x the threads. Really this test was to try to induce some contention in Python's GIL (Global Interpreter Lock) to test its impact on PyAV. You can see it basically caps out at 2x regardless of the number of threads.

The threads here are independent encodes, not breaking individual encodes up into threads which can improve performance at the potential cost of image quality.

Where we're at today

Today the project has support for:

  • Hardware encoders: NVENC (AV1, HEVC, AVC), VideoToolbox (HEVC, AVC)
  • Software encoders: x264, x265, vpx (VP9), svt-av1
  • Opus audio codec is currently supported
  • YUV conversion on GPU or CPU
  • fMP4 or Buffer output
  • Custom configurations

Where I want to take this

I have ideas for the future of the project. I think if we start to see some adoption there will of course be bugs and feature requests. I think that having model-aware and scene-aware encoding might be an interesting feature. I also want to explore using latents to identify regions of interest or use other signals to inform encoding decisions.

Anyway if you are running generative video models please check this project out, I am happy to take any feedback! If you want to contribute that is even better!

title: Windows 11 Slow Startup? 9 Fixes That Actually Speed Up Boot Time
description:
If your Windows 11 PC takes forever to reach the desktop, the culprit is rarely one big thing — it's usually a pile-up of small slowdowns: apps launching at boot, services fighting over your disk, and settings that were never tuned for speed. Here are 9 fixes that actually work, ordered from quickest to deepest.

Fix 1: Turn off unnecessary startup apps

Open Task Manager (Ctrl+Shift+Esc), go to Startup apps, and disable anything you don't need the second you log in — game launchers, updaters, chat apps. Each one steals seconds. Keep only your antivirus.

Fix 2: Enable Fast Startup

Go to Settings > System > Power & battery > "Additional power settings" > "Choose what the power buttons do", and make sure "Turn on fast startup" is checked. This makes shutdown save a system snapshot so boot resumes faster.

Fix 3: Free up disk space

A nearly full drive slows everything down. Open Settings > System > Storage and use Storage Sense to clear temp files, or manually empty Downloads and the Recycle Bin. Aim for at least 10–15% free space.

Fix 4: Update your drivers — especially storage drivers

Outdated NVMe/SATA drivers can stall the boot sequence. Open Device Manager, expand Disk drives and IDE ATA/ATAPI controllers, right-click each, and choose "Update driver". Then check your laptop maker's site for chipset drivers.

Fix 5: Run Startup Repair or SFC

Corrupted system files can drag boot times. Open Terminal (Admin) and run sfc /scannow, then DISM /Online /Cleanup-Image /RestoreHealth. Both are safe and built into Windows.

Fix 6: Delay heavy background services

Some apps (cloud sync, VPNs) can be set to start a minute after login instead of instantly — check each app's settings for a "launch at startup" delay option.

Fix 7: Disable Windows search indexing on old HDDs

If you're still on a spinning hard drive, Settings > Privacy & security > Searching Windows > turn off "Find my files: Classic" indexing, or exclude large folders. On SSDs, skip this — it barely helps.

Fix 8: Update Windows and your BIOS

Pending cumulative updates sometimes include boot-time optimizations. Check Settings > Windows Update, and check your manufacturer's support page for a BIOS update — newer firmware often improves boot initialization.

Fix 9: Do a clean boot to find the slowpoke

Type msconfig, open System Configuration, and on the Services tab check "Hide all Microsoft services" then "Disable all". Restart — if boot is fast now, re-enable services in groups until you find the offender. Then leave it disabled.

A note on HDD vs SSD: if your PC still boots from a mechanical hard drive, no software tweak beats upgrading to an SSD — boot times drop from minutes to seconds. That's the single biggest upgrade you can make.

For the full walkthrough with exact menu paths and screenshots, this step-by-step slow-startup guide walks through each fix in detail.

title: GHSA-JF75-Q64Q-G65R: GHSA-jf75-q64q-g65r: NoSQL Query Manipulation and Partial Authentication Bypass in Waline Server
description:
GHSA-jf75-q64q-g65r: NoSQL Query Manipulation and Partial Authentication Bypass in Waline Server

Vulnerability ID: GHSA-JF75-Q64Q-G65R
CVSS Score: 6.5
Published: 2026-10-28

An improper input validation and NoSQL query construction vulnerability exists in the Waline comment system server (@waline/vercel) version 1.40.3 and earlier. When MongoDB is used as the backend storage engine, the POST /api/token authentication endpoint fails to validate that the user-supplied email parameter is a string. Supplying a JSON object or array operator causes the MongoDB storage adapter to omit the email filter or construct an unintended match-all query, returning all user records and allowing unauthenticated attackers to target the site administrator account directly without knowing the administrator's email address.

TL;DR

Waline versions <= 1.40.3 fail to validate the data type of the email parameter during authentication at POST /api/token. When backed by MongoDB, passing a non-string value (such as a JSON object) causes the query builder to drop the email constraint and execute an empty filter query. Because the login controller selects the first returned record—which corresponds to the primary site administrator—an attacker can perform targeted password guessing or credential stuffing against the administrator account without knowing its email address.

⚠️ Exploit Status: POC

Technical Details

  • Vulnerability ID: GHSA-jf75-q64q-g65r
  • Weakness Class: CWE-287 (Improper Authentication) / CWE-943 (NoSQL Injection)
  • Attack Vector: Network (HTTP POST to /api/token)
  • CVSS v3.1 Score: 6.5 Medium (CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:L/I:L/A:N)
  • Affected Component: @waline/vercel <= 1.40.3 (with MongoDB storage)
  • Patched Version: @waline/vercel 1.41.0
  • Impact: Partial authentication bypass (factor elimination) and targeted admin credential stuffing
  • Exploit Status: Proof-of-Concept (PoC) Publicly Documented

Affected Systems

  • @waline/vercel
  • walinejs/waline (packages/server)
  • @waline/vercel: <= 1.40.3 (Fixed in: 1.41.0)

Code Analysis

Commit: e611aed

Enforce required email and string password validation rules in TokenLogic.postAction() and add integration tests for POST /api/token.

File: packages/server/src/logic/token.js
@@ -35,6 +35,17 @@ module.exports = class TokenLogic extends Base {
    * @apiSuccess (200) {String}  errmsg  return error message if error
    */
   async postAction() {
+    this.rules = {
+      email: {
+        required: true,
+        email: true,
+      },
+      password: {
+        required: true,
+        string: true,
+      },
+    };
+
     await this.useCaptchaCheck();
   }

Exploit Details

  • GitHub Security Advisory: Official advisory containing proof-of-concept explanation demonstrating non-string email parameter handling in MongoDB deployments.

Mitigation Strategies

  • Upgrade @waline/vercel to version 1.41.0 or newer to enforce strict string and email format validation in TokenLogic.
  • Harden the MongoDB storage adapter (parseWhere) to explicitly reject or throw errors when non-string and non-array query values are encountered.
  • Implement Web Application Firewall (WAF) rules to block HTTP POST requests to /api/token containing JSON objects or arrays in the email field.
  • Enable Waline CAPTCHA verification and rate limiting on authentication endpoints to prevent automated credential stuffing.

Remediation Steps:

  1. Update package.json in your Waline deployment repository to specify "@waline/vercel": "^1.41.0".
  2. Run npm install @waline/vercel@^1.41.0 or pnpm update @waline/vercel to fetch the patched release.
  3. Redeploy the Waline server instance on Vercel or your self-hosted Node.js environment.
  4. Verify the fix by sending a test POST request to /api/token with {"email": {"$ne": null}, "password": "test"} and confirming that the server responds with errno: 1001.

References

  • GitHub Advisory Record: GHSA-jf75-q64q-g65r
  • Waline Repository Security Advisory: GHSA-jf75-q64q-g65r
  • Fix Pull Request #3646
  • Fix Commit e611aed4e571c2a86103f5cee48791ca6b460360
  • Reporter Credit Profile (dizconnectz)

Read the full report for GHSA-JF75-Q64Q-G65R on our website for more details including interactive diagrams and full exploit analysis.

title: Raycast, Alfred, Spotlight — and now whatever this is: a launcher with the AI locked inside your Mac
description:
Every launcher race has the same shape. Spotlight ships with the Mac and does 60%. Alfred makes you pay for the other 30%. Raycast gets you to 95% and then puts the AI behind a cloud subscription, because the good models live in a datacenter.

I wanted the last 5% without the datacenter. So HocusFocus is a launcher for macOS 26 with the AI running on-device — Apple's private on-device model, the one that never leaves your Mac. You press Alt Space and type the way you'd talk: "why is the sky blue", "its too loud in here, turn it down a bit", "time in tokyo". Plain English in, actions and answers out.

The boring half still does the boring half well: apps open instantly, math and currency conversions compute inline while you type, clipboard history and notes are one tab away, timers and themes exist because people asked.

A few honest notes for the launcher shoppers:

  • it's macOS 26 Tahoe only. The on-device model needs it, and I'm not shipping a degraded no-AI build for older systems. If you're on 15 or earlier, Raycast or Alfred remain the right answer.
  • no cloud account, no subscription. $5 once, 7-day trial.
  • the site has a little rebuild of the launcher in the browser, so you can type a sum or a conversion and feel the interaction before downloading anything.

If you've been paying monthly for launcher AI that just proxies a cloud model, the calculus here is different: same convenience, the model never leaves the machine, and it costs less than one month of the subscription.

https://www.hocusfocusmac.com/?utm_source=devto&utm_campaign=hocusfocus-launch

Happy to answer anything about the on-device integration or the launcher plumbing.

title: How to Add Controller Support
description:
Controller support means letting players use a gamepad instead of touch. It changes how your game's timing and difficulty work. A touch-only platformer built around split-second taps becomes a different game when a D-pad removes the targeting constraint. Most teams add it without realizing it breaks the core mechanic they designed around.

What controller support actually means

Controller support is a second input layer that runs alongside touch. The game reads from both at the same time. Whichever one the player uses, the game responds.

You are not replacing touch controls. You are adding a parallel path: buttons map to actions, analog sticks map to movement, and the game treats controller input the same way it treats a swipe or a tap.

The work splits into three parts:

  • Input mapping - which buttons do what, and how analog stick movement translates to on-screen motion
  • Dual-input architecture - making sure touch and gamepad can coexist without breaking each other
  • UI adaptation - button prompts, pause menus, and navigation that work with a controller

Mapping buttons is the easy part. The real work is handling two input methods that have different timing, precision, and player expectations. A platformer balanced for swipe gestures feels sluggish with a gamepad unless you adjust movement speed and jump height separately.

This is similar to adding AI to a mobile game - the feature itself is straightforward, but it changes how the core mechanic needs to be tuned.

How dual-input changes your game model

Adding controller support means splitting your input layer into two parallel paths that must arrive at the same outcome. You are not adding a second way to tap the screen.

Touch input is direct. The player taps where they want to go, swipes to attack, or drags to aim. Controller input is indirect. A thumbstick sends continuous position data. A button fires a discrete event. Your game model must normalize both into unified actions.

This architecture affects three parts of your game.

Movement becomes continuous instead of discrete. A touch target is a single coordinate. A thumbstick is a vector that updates every frame. Your character controller must handle both without changing how the game feels.

Difficulty curves need recalibration. A platformer tuned for touch might have tight jump windows or precise landing zones. Controller players clear those obstacles faster because analog input is more precise than a tap. Same level. Easier or harder depending on the input method.

UI flow diverges. Touch players navigate menus by tapping. Controller players expect D-pad navigation and button confirmation. One menu system must serve both, or you maintain two. That decision ripples through every screen in your game.

We saw this clearly in Jungle Jump. The original touch build had pixel-perfect platform edges because tapping is exact. When we added gamepad integration, testers cleared levels in half the expected time. We widened platforms and adjusted enemy timing to rebalance difficulty across both input methods. Same game model. Different tuning.

A harder question appears when touch and controller players compete in the same leaderboard systems. An action game with both input types must either segment leaderboards by input method or accept that controller scores will dominate. Neither choice is wrong, but one has to be made before you ship.

What controller support looks like in a real build

We added controller support to Jungle Jump, a 2D platformer that already worked with touch. Players could tap to jump and swipe to move. Both inputs stayed in the shipped version.

The controller path reads button state every frame and maps it to the same movement functions the touch handler calls. One input model, two entry points. Game logic never checks how the player jumped, only that they did.

Jump height was the hardest part. Touch players commit to a jump on press. Controller players modulate it by holding the button. We capped jump velocity so a held button couldn't reach platforms the level designer placed out of range. That preserved difficulty for controller users without breaking the touch path.

Gamepad integration does not mean reworking the model. Route a second input stream into the same state machine. Test both paths against the same progression curve.

Where teams break the core mechanic

Most teams add controller support after the game is already tuned for touch. You discover that a button-press is faster and more precise than a swipe. Your platformer suddenly becomes trivially easy.

The problem is not the mobile app development itself. Touch controls and gamepad integration operate at different speeds. A jump that required careful timing with a finger now executes instantly with the A button. Enemy patterns balanced around imprecise taps become effortless with analog stick movement.

You cannot bolt controller support onto a touch-tuned game and expect it to feel right. Input mapping changes the difficulty curve.

Teams that ship both inputs well tune twice. They test both paths separately and adjust enemy speed, jump arc, and level pacing so each input feels fair. Balance once and enable both, one version will be broken.

How to tell whether your game needs it

Three signals tell you controller support belongs in your build.

Your game demands precise timing or directional input. Platformers like Jungle Jump need exact jump arcs and fast direction changes. Touch controls work, but a joystick and physical buttons let players execute moves they can already picture. If your core mechanic rewards precision, controller support stops the interface from being the bottleneck.

Your target players already own controllers. Mobile gaming controllers sold well in 2025 and 2026, and a portion of your audience expects to use them. If you are building an action game, a racing title, or anything with real-time combat, a segment of your players will try to connect a controller on day one.

You want to expand beyond mobile. Controller support is the input layer for console and desktop ports. Adding it now means one codebase works across platforms later without rewriting your control scheme from scratch.

The decision comes down to whether the mechanical advantage matters for your game. Touch is already comfortable for many core loops. Controller support adds complexity without clear upside in those cases. Precision unlocks better play in others. Then it belongs in the feature list from the start.

title: LLM Tool Calling in Go: A ReAct-Style Agent Loop with Guardrails and Cost Control
description:
Most of my agent projects in Go share one piece of code: the loop. The model looks at the conversation, decides to call a tool or answer, the program runs the tool, feeds the result back, and repeats. That's the ReAct pattern (reason, act, observe) in its practical form.

I've built this loop several times: in agent-helper, a shared Go library that runs the same chat loop on Gemini or local Ollama models with an installable tool registry; in a Gemini tool-calling assistant for a Jira-style product; in a Clean Architecture ReAct agent that drafts social posts; and in a local voice assistant that uses Ollama tool calling. The happy path is about 40 lines. Most of the engineering is in the guardrails. This post builds a simplified version of that loop with the guardrails included.

Step 1: a provider-agnostic interface

Don't let the agent loop import a specific SDK. Define the minimum it needs:

type Role string

const (
    RoleUser      Role = "user"
    RoleAssistant Role = "assistant"
    RoleTool      Role = "tool"
)

type ToolCall struct {
    ID   string
    Name string
    Args json.RawMessage
}

type Message struct {
    Role       Role
    Content    string
    ToolCalls  []ToolCall // set when the model asks for tools
    ToolCallID string     // set on tool results
}

type Usage struct{ InputTokens, OutputTokens int }

type ChatModel interface {
    Chat(ctx context.Context, msgs []Message, tools []ToolSpec) (Message, Usage, error)
}

Each provider (Gemini, OpenAI-compatible APIs, Ollama) gets a small adapter that converts to and from these types. Switching between a hosted model and a local one then becomes a config change, which is exactly how agent-helper moves the same agent between Gemini and Ollama.

Step 2: a typed tool registry

Tools are plug-ins. The loop shouldn't change when you add one.

type ToolSpec struct {
    Name        string
    Description string
    Schema      json.RawMessage // JSON Schema for the arguments
}

type Tool struct {
    Spec    ToolSpec
    Mutates bool          // changes external state?
    Timeout time.Duration // per-call limit
    Run     func(ctx context.Context, args json.RawMessage) (string, error)
}

type Registry struct{ tools map[string]Tool }

func (r *Registry) Register(t Tool) {
    if r.tools == nil {
        r.tools = map[string]Tool{}
    }
    r.tools[t.Spec.Name] = t
}

func (r *Registry) Specs() []ToolSpec {
    specs := make([]ToolSpec, 0, len(r.tools))
    for _, t := range r.tools {
        specs = append(specs, t.Spec)
    }
    sort.Slice(specs, func(i, j int) bool { return specs[i].Name < specs[j].Name })
    return specs
}

Sorting the specs keeps the prompt stable between calls, which helps reproducibility and, with providers that cache prompt prefixes, cost.

Inside Run, decode arguments strictly into a struct and validate them. The model's JSON is untrusted input:

func decodeArgs[T any](raw json.RawMessage) (T, error) {
    var v T
    dec := json.NewDecoder(bytes.NewReader(raw))
    dec.DisallowUnknownFields()
    if err := dec.Decode(&v); err != nil {
        return v, fmt.Errorf("invalid arguments: %w", err)
    }
    return v, nil
}

Step 3: the loop, with budgets

Here's the core. Every guardrail is explicit:

type Limits struct {
    MaxSteps       int           // model round-trips
    MaxTotalTokens int           // input + output across the run
    MaxRepeats     int           // identical tool calls allowed
    RunTimeout     time.Duration // wall clock for the whole run
}

type Approver func(ctx context.Context, call ToolCall) (bool, error)

type Agent struct {
    Model   ChatModel
    Tools   *Registry
    Limits  Limits
    Approve Approver // nil means write tools are refused
}

var ErrBudget = errors.New("agent budget exhausted")

func (a *Agent) Run(ctx context.Context, msgs []Message) (string, error) {
    ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(ctx, a.Limits.RunTimeout)
    defer cancel()

    used := 0
    seen := map[string]int{}

    for step := 0; step < a.Limits.MaxSteps; step++ {
        reply, usage, err := a.Model.Chat(ctx, msgs, a.Tools.Specs())
        if err != nil {
            return "", fmt.Errorf("step %d: %w", step, err)
        }
        used += usage.InputTokens + usage.OutputTokens
        msgs = append(msgs, reply)

        if len(reply.ToolCalls) == 0 {
            return reply.Content, nil // final answer
        }
        if used > a.Limits.MaxTotalTokens {
            return "", fmt.Errorf("%w: %d tokens", ErrBudget, used)
        }

        for _, call := range reply.ToolCalls {
            key := call.Name + string(call.Args)
            seen[key]++
            var result string
            if seen[key] > a.Limits.MaxRepeats {
                result = "error: you already made this exact call; use the earlier result or try a different approach"
            } else {
                result = a.execute(ctx, call)
            }
            msgs = append(msgs, Message{Role: RoleTool, ToolCallID: call.ID, Content: result})
        }
    }
    return "", fmt.Errorf("%w: max steps (%d)", ErrBudget, a.Limits.MaxSteps)
}

What each guardrail prevents:

  • MaxSteps stops a model that never decides it's done.
  • MaxTotalTokens caps cost per run. Every step resends the whole conversation, so input tokens grow with each round-trip. A ten-step run costs much more than ten times a single call.
  • MaxRepeats catches the common failure where a model calls the same tool with the same arguments again and again.
  • RunTimeout bounds wall-clock time, and because it's a context, it cancels in-flight HTTP calls and tools too.

Step 4: executing tools safely 

func (a *Agent) execute(ctx context.Context, call ToolCall) string {
    tool, ok := a.Tools.tools[call.Name]
    if !ok {
        return fmt.Sprintf("error: unknown tool %q", call.Name)
    }
    if tool.Mutates {
        if a.Approve == nil {
            return "error: this tool changes data and is not allowed in this session"
        }
        ok, err := a.Approve(ctx, call)
        if err != nil || !ok {
            return "error: the user did not approve this action"
        }
    }

    tctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(ctx, tool.Timeout)
    defer cancel()

    out, err := tool.Run(tctx, call.Args)
    if err != nil {
        return "error: " + err.Error()
    }
    const maxResult = 8_000
    if len(out) > maxResult {
        out = out[:maxResult] + "\n[truncated]"
    }
    return out
}

Three details matter here:

  1. Errors go back to the model as text, not up the stack. A model that sees "invalid arguments: unknown field prio" usually fixes the call on the next step. Only infrastructure failures (the model API itself failing) should end the run.
  2. Write tools need approval. The Approver can be a CLI prompt, a Telegram button or a web confirmation. Read tools run freely; anything that sends, deletes or updates waits for a human or a policy check.
  3. Truncate tool output. One tool returning a 2 MB web page will blow your token budget and dilute the model's attention. Cap results, or summarise them before they go back.

Cost control beyond the loop

The loop's budgets are the safety net. These keep costs low in normal operation:

  • Expose fewer tools. Every tool schema is sent on every step. Register only the tools the current task needs.
  • Keep tool results compact. Return the fields the model needs, not whole database rows.
  • Use smaller or local models where possible. With a provider-agnostic interface, routine steps can run on a local Ollama model and harder ones on a hosted model.
  • Log usage per run. Record steps, tokens and tool calls for each run. You can't control a cost you don't measure.

Testing the loop

Because ChatModel is an interface, a scripted fake makes the loop fully testable without network calls:

type scriptedModel struct{ replies []Message; i int }

func (m *scriptedModel) Chat(ctx context.Context, _ []Message, _ []ToolSpec) (Message, Usage, error) {
    r := m.replies[m.i]
    m.i++
    return r, Usage{InputTokens: 100, OutputTokens: 20}, nil
}

Write tests for the boring cases: unknown tool, invalid arguments, repeated call, budget exceeded, write tool without approval. Those are the paths that protect you in production.

Takeaways

The model decides what to try. Your Go code decides what is allowed, how long it may take and how much it may cost. Keep the loop small, keep the tools typed, and make every limit explicit.

Pradip Parmar is a Go backend and AI agent engineer who has worked in Go since 2018. He builds LLM agents with tool calling, MCP servers and RAG systems for businesses, from hosted Gemini and OpenAI-compatible models to fully local Ollama setups. To hire a Go AI agent developer, find him on LinkedIn, Upwork or Contra, and on GitHub.

title: OpenBSD 7.9 を 8.0 へ アップグレード
description:
はじめに

OpenBSD プロジェクトから 2026 年 10 月 20 日に OS の 8.0 がリリースされました 🌷 61 回目のリリースに当たります。

What's New (英語) | Changelog (英語)

本記事で OpenBSD 7.9 を 8.0 にアップグレードする手順を説明します。
各手順はすばらしい 公式ガイド (英語) に基づいています。

チュートリアル

実行するコマンド一式を示しながら、ステップ・バイ・ステップ形式で書いた、アップグレード用のガイドです。

🌷 🐡 🌅

1. アップグレード前準備: 検証とカスタイマイズ

公式のチュートリアルには Before using any upgrade method (私訳: アップグレード方法に関わらずその前に行うこと) セクションが設けられています。

アップグレード方法としては sysupgrade を使うのが、たいていの場合、良い選択になるでしょう。

ディスク空き容量の確認

/usr に 1.1GB 以上の空きがあることが必要です。

$ df -h
Filesystem     Size    Used   Avail Capacity  Mounted on
(...)
/dev/sd0e      7.8G    1.8G    5.5G    26%    /usr

OK のようです :)

現在の利用内容がアップグレード結果に適合することの確認

設定と構文の変更 (英語) と 特別なパッケージ (英語) を確認しましょう。

バックアップ (必要な場合)

適宜、事前にバックアップを取得しておきましょう。

アップグレード内容のカスタマイズ (必要な場合)

2. sysupgrade によるアップグレード

準備は良いですか。

* 注意: 以下のコマンド sysupgrade は、ひとたび実行すると中断はできません。

準備ができたら、以下のコマンドを実行しましょう。実行するのはこれだけです:

$ doas sysupgrade

以下のように出力されるでしょう:

Fetching from https://cdn.openbsd.org/pub/OpenBSD/8.0/amd64/
SHA256.sig   100% |******************************|  2144       00:00
Signature Verified
BUILDINFO    100% |******************************|    54       00:00
Verifying old sets.
INSTALL.amd64 100% |*****************************| 44889       00:00
base80.tgz   100% |******************************|   530 MB    00:18
bsd          100% |******************************| 32494 KB    00:01
bsd.mp       100% |******************************| 32653 KB    00:00
bsd.rd       100% |******************************|  4782 KB    00:00
comp80.tgz   100% |******************************|    99 MB    00:02
game80.tgz   100% |******************************|  2743 KB    00:00
man80.tgz    100% |******************************|  8417 KB    00:00
xbase80.tgz  100% |******************************| 47568 KB    00:01
xfont80.tgz  100% |******************************| 23022 KB    00:00
xserv80.tgz  100% |******************************| 11739 KB    00:00
xshare80.tgz 100% |******************************|  4568 KB    00:00
Verifying sets.
Fetching updated firmware.
fw_update: add none; update intel,vmm
Upgrading.

マシンの再起動とシステムのアップグレードが行われます。ふたたび再起動が行われて、sysmerge が自動で実行されます。それから sshd 等のデーモンが、従来のように起動されます。"Checking for available binary patches..." と出力されて、もし対象が存在すれば "Run syspatch(8) to install:" と表示されるでしょう。

最終的に以下が表示されます:

starting local daemons: cron.
Thu Oct 29 08:40:00 JST 2026

OpenBSD/amd64 ... (ttyC0)

login:

ログインメッセージが表示されています。"OpenBSD 8.0 (GENERIC.MP)" とあります。

3. アップグレード後の操作: sysmerge (必要に応じて)

公式ドキュメントに アップグレード後に行うこと (英語) が書かれています。大いに参考になるでしょう。

In some cases, configuration files cannot be modified automatically. Run

# sysmerge

to check and perform these configuration changes.

ここで言われているのは、手動で sysmerge を実行することが必要な場合もある、ということです。
以下のような conf ファイルを、手動でマージすることが必要な場合もあります。気を付けてください:

  • /etc/login.conf

コマンドを実行しましょう:

$ doas sysmerge

差分がある場合、手動によるマージ が必要になります。

4. syspatch の適用 (スキップ可能)

ここからの 2 つのタスクは、日常的なメンテナンスで、システムをアップデートする時にも実施するものです。

syspatch は重要なコマンドです。OpenBSD から、必要と判明し次第都度、継続的に提供される公式のバイナリ・パッチです。

$ doas syspatch

5. パッケージのアップデート

What's new (英語) セクションがリリースページにありますが、そこの "Ports and packages" (Ports とパッケージ (英語)) に "Some highlights" (注目点 (英語)) が記載されています。例えば、VMM/VMD が今回も更新されています。

次のコマンドはマシンにインストールされているすべてのパッケージをアップデートします:

$ doas pkg_add -u

大量の出力が現れるでしょう。これらは慎重に読む必要があります。終わりの部分は特に、です。そこに重要な変更点や実施すべきアクションが書かれているかもしれません。私の場合、fish をデフォルトのシェルとして使っているのですが、こちらが正常に起動することをいつも確認しています。というのも、かつて Python のアップグレードの影響でクラッシュするようになったことがあるからです 😅

6. 設定と構文の変更

必要に応じて conf を更新して、設定と構文の変更 (英語) に書かれている内容を適用しましょう。

7. 古くなったファイルの削除

ここはシンプルな手順です。公式チュートリアルの 削除すべきファイル (英語) に書かれていることを行うだけです。

今回の対象はありません。

8. 特別なパッケージ

公式チュートリアルの 特別なパッケージ (英語) を確認しましょう。使っているものがあるかもしれません:

  • firefox
  • kea
  • libmaxminddb
  • stalwart-mail

9. 再起動

ゴールが見えて来ました ! 最後に必須では無いですが再起動しておくと良いしれません:

$ doas reboot

おわりに

新しいシステムとあなたが長く楽しい時間を過ごせますように :)

OpenBSD プロジェクトとコミュニティへの深い感謝を込めつつ。

脚注

アップグレードのカスタマイズ方法

ここは参照用であり、標準のアップグレードではスキップできます。

/auto_upgrade.conf をレスポンス・ファイルとして利用できます。
OpenBSD の autoinstall のドキュメントに、次のように書かれています:

If either /auto_install.conf or /auto_upgrade.conf is found on bsd.rd's built-in RAM disk, autoinstall behaves as if the machine is netbooted, but uses the local response file. In case both files exist, /auto_install.conf takes precedence.

(私訳: /auto_install.conf または /auto_upgrade.conf が bsd.rd 内蔵の RAM ディスクに存在する場合、autoinstall は、ネットブートモードで起動されたマシンのように振る舞いますが、ローカルにあるレスポンス・ファイルを使用します。両方のファイルが存在する場合、/auto_install.conf が優先されます。)

/auto_upgrade.conf の完全な内容の一例は次のようなものです:

Location of sets = disk
Pathname to the sets = /home/_sysupgrade/
Set name(s) = -x*
Set name(s) = +xbase*
Set name(s) = -game*
Set name(s) = done
Directory does not contain SHA256.sig. Continue without verification = yes

この場合、xbase を除く x 一式と game が、インストール対象外になります。

それから /upgrade.site を用いた指定も可能です。

sysmerge 差分マージ

まず差分が出力されます。それから以下のようにたずねられます:

  Use 'd' to delete the temporary ./etc/login.conf
  Use 'i' to install the temporary ./etc/login.conf
  Use 'm' to merge the temporary and installed versions
  Use 'v' to view the diff results again

  Default is to leave the temporary file to deal with by hand

How should I deal with this? [Leave it for later]

最初の 3 つは、以下のような挙動になります:

  • d: 現在の (ローカルの) ファイルを保持する。
  • i: sysupgrade が取得した新しいファイルでローカルを上書きする。
  • m: 対話型形式で手動でマージする。

m を入力するとマージモードが立ち上がります。一つ一つの差分について、いずれを採用するのかを確認されるでしょう:

  • l を入力すると左側が採用されます。
  • r は右側です。

その後に、マージ結果ファイルに対して、どの操作を行うのかをたずねられます:

  Use 'e' to edit the merged file
  Use 'i' to install the merged file
  Use 'n' to view a diff between the merged and new files
  Use 'o' to view a diff between the old and merged files
  Use 'r' to re-do the merge
  Use 'v' to view the merged file
  Use 'x' to delete the merged file and go back to previous menu
  Default is to leave the temporary file to deal with by hand

===> How should I deal with the merged file? [Leave it for later]

e を入力すると、エディタが起動されてマージ結果ファイルを編集できるようになります。

i を入力すると、マージ結果ファイルをマシンにインストールします:

===> Merging /etc/login.conf (running cap_mkdb(1), needs a relog)

title: Adding a pause button to an MQL5 Expert Advisor with OnChartEvent
description:
Sooner or later every trader running an Expert Advisor wants to stop it from opening new trades for a while. A news release is coming, the spread looks strange, or they simply want to watch for an hour. The usual options are not great. Removing the EA from the chart also stops it managing the positions it already has. Turning off Algo Trading in the terminal stops every EA on every chart.

A pause button on the chart solves this. It blocks new entries for this EA only, while the EA keeps managing its open positions. This tutorial builds one with OBJ_BUTTON and OnChartEvent(), and makes the paused state survive a restart.

Creating the button 

input long InpMagic = 7310;

const string BTN = "ctb_pause_btn";
bool gPaused = false;

string PauseKey()
{
   // global variable names are limited to 63 characters
   return StringFormat("ctb_paused_%I64d_%s_%I64d",
                       AccountInfoInteger(ACCOUNT_LOGIN), _Symbol, InpMagic);
}

void UpdateButton()
{
   ObjectSetInteger(0, BTN, OBJPROP_STATE, gPaused);
   ObjectSetString(0, BTN, OBJPROP_TEXT, gPaused ? "Resume entries" : "Pause entries");
   ObjectSetInteger(0, BTN, OBJPROP_BGCOLOR, gPaused ? clrOrange : clrSilver);
   ChartRedraw(0);
}

void CreateButton()
{
   if(ObjectFind(0, BTN) < 0)
      ObjectCreate(0, BTN, OBJ_BUTTON, 0, 0, 0);

   ObjectSetInteger(0, BTN, OBJPROP_CORNER, CORNER_RIGHT_UPPER);
   ObjectSetInteger(0, BTN, OBJPROP_XDISTANCE, 150);  // at least the width
   ObjectSetInteger(0, BTN, OBJPROP_YDISTANCE, 30);
   ObjectSetInteger(0, BTN, OBJPROP_XSIZE, 140);
   ObjectSetInteger(0, BTN, OBJPROP_YSIZE, 28);
   ObjectSetInteger(0, BTN, OBJPROP_SELECTABLE, false);
   UpdateButton();
}

Two details matter here.

With CORNER_RIGHT_UPPER the distances are measured from the right edge of the chart to the left edge of the button, so OBJPROP_XDISTANCE has to be at least as large as OBJPROP_XSIZE or the button ends up partly off screen.

The key for the saved state includes the account number, the symbol and the magic number. If the same EA runs on two charts, each copy gets its own pause switch.

Reacting to clicks 

void SetPaused(const bool paused)
{
   gPaused = paused;
   GlobalVariableSet(PauseKey(), paused ? 1.0 : 0.0);
   GlobalVariablesFlush();
   PrintFormat("New entries %s", paused ? "paused" : "resumed");
   UpdateButton();
}

void OnChartEvent(const int id, const long &lparam,
                  const double &dparam, const string &sparam)
{
   if(id == CHARTEVENT_OBJECT_CLICK && sparam == BTN)
   {
      // the terminal has already flipped OBJPROP_STATE for us
      SetPaused((bool)ObjectGetInteger(0, BTN, OBJPROP_STATE));
      return;
   }

   if(id == CHARTEVENT_OBJECT_DELETE && sparam == BTN)
      CreateButton();   // someone deleted it by hand, put it back
}

A button object toggles its own OBJPROP_STATE when clicked, so the handler reads the state instead of keeping a separate toggle. That way the variable and what the trader sees cannot drift apart.

The delete event is not sent by default. You turn it on with ChartSetInteger(0, CHART_EVENT_OBJECT_DELETE, true), which is done in OnInit() below.

Wiring it into the EA 

int OnInit()
{
   ChartSetInteger(0, CHART_EVENT_OBJECT_DELETE, true);

   if(GlobalVariableCheck(PauseKey()))
      gPaused = GlobalVariableGet(PauseKey()) > 0.5;

   CreateButton();
   if(gPaused)
      Print("Starting with new entries paused");
   return INIT_SUCCEEDED;
}

void OnDeinit(const int reason)
{
   ObjectDelete(0, BTN);
}

void OnTick()
{
   ManageOpenPositions();   // stops, trailing, exits: always runs

   if(gPaused)
      return;               // no new entries while paused

   CheckForEntry();
}

ManageOpenPositions() and CheckForEntry() stand for whatever your EA already does. The order inside OnTick() is the important part. Position management runs first and always. The pause only skips the entry logic. A pause button that also stopped trailing stops and exits would be more dangerous than no button at all.

The state is stored in a terminal global variable, so it survives a timeframe change, a change of inputs and a terminal restart. GlobalVariablesFlush() writes it to disk straight away instead of waiting for the terminal to close. Global variables that are not accessed are deleted after four weeks, which is fine for a pause flag.

Deleting the button in OnDeinit() keeps the chart clean when the EA is removed. On a timeframe change OnInit() runs again and recreates it with the saved state.

Testing it

Chart events are not delivered in the Strategy Tester, so try the button on a demo chart.

  1. Attach the EA, click Pause and check the Experts log for the message.
  2. Change the timeframe and confirm the button comes back still paused.
  3. Restart the terminal and check again.
  4. Open a position, pause, and confirm the trailing stop or exit still works while no new trades open.
  5. Delete the button from the object list (Ctrl+B) and confirm it reappears.

A pause switch is a small feature, but it gives the trader a safe middle ground between leaving the EA alone and pulling it off the chart.

title: Activity Monitor shows you a thousand processes. It never tells you which app to blame.
description:
Open Activity Monitor on any Mac that's been alive for a week and sort by memory. You get a wall of Google Chrome Helper (Renderer), Code Helper (Renderer), Safari Web Content, node. A hundred rows, most of them helpers, none of them answering the only question you actually asked: which app is eating my Mac?

The answer is always an app. Chrome launched those helpers. VS Code launched its helpers. But Activity Monitor shows you the process tree flattened, so you do the grouping in your head, process by process, every time.

I kept doing that grouping by hand, so I built an app that does it: HeartbeatMac. Every helper gets folded into the app that launched it. A thousand processes become a hundred apps, one figure each for CPU, memory, energy, disk, network and GPU. If you want the forensics, expand the app and the real process list is right there. Quit or force quit from either level, and it asks before killing anything.

A few things I put in because Activity Monitor annoyed me without them:

  • Live charts per app, not just a snapshot number
  • 30 days of history, so "has my Mac gotten slower since Tuesday" has an answer
  • Alerts when something misbehaves, instead of you babysitting a sorted list
  • A menu bar monitor for the one number you actually check

To be fair to the incumbents: iStat Menus is excellent and deeper than this in most ways, and Stats is free and open source. If you live in those, you may not need this. HeartbeatMac is for the person who opened Activity Monitor this week, got 900 rows of helpers, and closed it.

It's a native app, macOS 15 Sequoia or later. Launch price is $5 once (going to $29 after the first 200 licences, which are going), lifetime updates, 7-day free trial, licence covers 3 Macs.

The site has a live preview with simulated data you can click around, since a web page can't read your Mac and shouldn't:

https://www.heartbeatmac.com/?utm_source=devto&utm_campaign=heartbeat-launch

Happy to answer anything about how the grouping works or what it costs to sample all of this without slowing the Mac down.

title: Solo dev stack: why I build admin systems with full-stack Node.js and a framework with fixed conventions
description:
Some context

I build a lot of admin systems — client work and my own projects. They all share the same traits: tight deadlines, changing requirements, and usually just me on the keyboard.

After years of trial and error, the setup that works best for me is full-stack Node.js + a framework with fixed conventions. Here's why, and what I built around it.

The practical benefits of full-stack Node.js

Not theory — things I actually feel day to day:

One person can carry the whole project. Vue on the frontend, Node on the backend, one language. I write an endpoint and immediately wire up the page for it. No context switching between two languages.

Shared types. With TypeScript on both ends, the API's field types are the same types the frontend uses. Backend changes a field, the frontend build fails and tells you where. No comparing against API docs by hand.

No integration meetings. When you write both ends, you decide what the API looks like. Integration cost is basically zero — anyone who has done frontend/backend coordination knows how much time that saves.

Hiring is easier. If the project grows, half the people who know Vue can pick up Node quickly.

Full-stack alone isn't enough — you need fixed conventions

Node full-stack solves the language problem. But there's another one: every project rebuilds the same plumbing — directory layout, permissions, list pages, menu config. It's roughly the same every time, yet you redesign it every time. It wastes time, and the designs drift, so your own old projects feel foreign six months later.

So I turned my own way of working into Me-Admin — the conventions and common features are already decided:

  • Fixed directory structure and layering; every module looks identical
  • Built-in RBAC (menu / button / API levels), users, roles, menus — ready out of the box
  • The stuff admin panels always need — lists, search, pagination, forms, uploads — already has components and established patterns
  • Mainstream stack: Midway 3 + Sequelize + PostgreSQL on the backend, Vue 3 + Vite + Element Plus + vxeTable on the frontend

The biggest time-saver: define an entity, run two commands, get a whole module.

# Sync the database schema
pnpm exec meadmin sync product

# Generate controller, API, frontend pages, menu permissions
pnpm exec meadmin crud product --menu

Refresh the admin panel and the module is in the menu — full CRUD working. The output is plain source code in your repo, no black boxes. Edit it directly.

meadmin-cn / meadmin

Me-Admin 是一个免费开源的nodejs + vue 全栈一站式中后台解决方案,后端基于medwayjs ,前台基于vue3构建，开箱即用。本项目采用最宽松的MIT协议，最新技术栈，助力你快速创建企业级web中后台项目。

Me-Admin

English | 简体中文

 

全栈一站式解决方案 —— Me-Admin 是一个免费开源的 Node.js + Vue 全栈中后台框架，后端基于 Midway.js 3，前端基于 Vue 3，一键 CRUD、SSR 渲染、权限体系开箱即用。MIT 协议，无加密、无授权限制，可商用。

  • 🌐 官网：https://www.meadmin.cn
  • 📖 文档：https://www.meadmin.cn/aon/doc/
  • 💬 问题反馈：https://github.com/meadmin-cn/meadmin/issues

30 秒生成一个业务模块

定义好 Sequelize 实体之后，只需两条命令：

# 同步数据库结构
pnpm exec meadmin sync exampleDemo

# 一键生成：控制器、接口、前端页面、菜单权限
pnpm exec meadmin crud exampleDemo --menu

meadmin 由 @meadmin/cli 提供命令行入口，统一通过 pnpm exec meadmin <命令> 调用。

刷新后台，菜单已经出现——列表、搜索、分页、增删改查、接口与菜单权限全部就位。生成的都是可读可改的源码，后续业务直接在上面写，没有黑盒。

主要特性

  • 一键 CRUD：命令行一键生成控制器、模型、视图与菜单权限，重复工作交给框架
  • SSR · CSR 混合渲染：前台 SSR 提升 SEO 与首屏速度，后台 CSR 保证交互体验
  • 内置权限系统：RBAC 权限模型开箱即用，菜单、按钮、接口三级管控；支持无限父子级分组与自由授权，管理员可跨组别；动态路由权限方案，支持按钮级权限，前端菜单与接口动态获取两种模式
  • 插件化架构：功能以插件形式自由安装卸载，生态持续扩展，系统保持精简
  • 全 TypeScript：自动生成 TS 类型，前后端契约免维护
  • 组件自动按需引入：自动按需引入 components 下的组件定义，支持自定义引入位置和模式，真正的按需引入

Deadline-driven agile work. Requirement comes in → define the entity → run the commands → the basics are done. All remaining time goes to actual business logic. Requirement changes? Update the entity and regenerate, or just edit the generated code.

title: Powerduck vs Mockoon: OpenAPI Mock Servers
description:
Quick answer: Mockoon is a well-liked desktop tool for designing mock APIs, with strong templating, rule matching, and a CLI for CI. Powerduck is a local-first studio that generates the mock from your OpenAPI contract instead of asking you to hand-build routes. The difference is the source of truth and the drift that follows. Mockoon gives you precise manual control over a standalone mock; Powerduck guarantees the mock matches the contract, the tests, and the docs, and regenerates on save. Pick Mockoon when you want a dedicated, highly customizable mock designer; pick Powerduck when the mock should be derived from the spec and never quietly diverge.

This page compares the two honestly, including the CLI, cloud, and templating, and links to the focused guides. Start with the table, then read the sections that match how your mocks are maintained today.

The two at a glance

Capability Mockoon Powerduck
Primary role Desktop mock designer OpenAPI studio with mock generation
How routes are created Hand-built Generated from the spec
Source of truth The mock file OpenAPI contract
Regenerates on contract change Manual update Yes, on save
Templating Rich dynamic templating OpenAPI examples and responses
CLI / CI CLI, Docker, GitHub Action OpenAPI CLI
Entry price Free desktop; cloud paid Desktop and Hub free
Best for Fine manual control of a mock Spec-synced mocks across the lifecycle

Hand-built routes vs generated mocks

Mockoon is genuinely powerful for designing a mock: you decide every route, status, and response. The cost is that the mock is a separate artifact you maintain, and it drifts the moment the contract changes without anyone noticing. A generated mock starts from the spec, so the routes, parameters, and responses are correct by construction and update on save. The direct comparison is in Mockoon manual routes vs OpenAPI mocks, and the drift problem is in mock drift: Mockoon vs contract mocks.

Templating vs authored examples

Mockoon's templating is one of its strongest features, and it is the right tool when you need bespoke, dynamic responses that are not part of the contract. A spec-driven mock uses the examples and response schemas you already author, so the data the mock returns is the same data the docs show and the tests assert. The tradeoff is in templating: Mockoon vs OpenAPI examples.

CLI, cloud, and where the free tier runs

Both are usable in CI. Mockoon ships a CLI, Docker image, and GitHub Action, and a paid cloud for collaboration; Powerduck runs from the OpenAPI CLI and hosts mocks and docs together on the Hub within plan limits, so the hosted mock is never out of sync with the reference. The CLIs are compared in Mockoon CLI vs Powerduck CLI, and the hosting is in Mockoon cloud vs free Hub mocks.

Stateful scenarios and record-replay

Realistic workflows often need state — a create followed by a list, a token that expires. Mockoon supports scenarios and record-and-replay for exactly this. A spec-driven studio keeps the stateful behavior tied to the contract and the tests, so the same flow the agent exercises is the flow the spec describes. The scenarios are compared in stateful scenarios: Mockoon vs Powerduck, and the alternative to recording traffic is in record and replay vs spec mocks.

Where to go next

Powerduck is the local-first way to keep mocks synced to the contract; Mockoon is a strong dedicated mock designer. See it on the Powerduck homepage. For the wider picture, read the API mocking guide and the OpenAPI guide.

Frequently asked questions

Does Powerduck match Mockoon's templating?

Mockoon has richer bespoke templating for responses that are not part of the contract. Powerduck uses the examples and response schemas you already author, so the mock, docs, and tests share the same data instead of a separate template.

Can I run a generated mock in CI?

Yes. Run it from the OpenAPI CLI or as a container, just as you would with Mockoon's CLI. The difference is that the mock is derived from the spec rather than a separately maintained file.

Which is better when the API changes often?

A generated mock regenerates on save, so it cannot drift from a fast-changing contract. A hand-built mock gives more control but has to be updated by hand each time.

title: The Most Popular Open-Source Voice Cloning Model Can't Be Used Commercially
description:
If you're building a product on open-source text-to-speech, the licence file deserves more of your attention than the demo audio. I learned this the slow way while picking models for a desktop app, and the specifics are worth writing down because the most popular option in the category is also the one you probably can't ship.

The three models worth knowing about.

Kokoro-82M — 82 million parameters, Apache 2.0, eight languages and fifty-four preset voices. It does not clone voices; you pick from its voice list. What it gives you instead is the ability to run on an ordinary CPU without a GPU anywhere in sight, which no other model here manages comfortably. For narration, app prompts, accessibility features, it's the obvious answer and the licence is the most permissive in the group.

XTTS-v2 — Coqui's model, seventeen languages, clones from a roughly six-second reference clip per its own model card. It is, by a distance, the one people search for and the one most tutorials cover. It's also the problem.

Chatterbox — Resemble AI, 500 million parameters, MIT licence, zero-shot cloning from a few seconds of audio. The base model is English only; a separate Multilingual v3 build covers twenty-three languages. Worth knowing before you ship: every output carries Resemble's PerTh watermark, which they describe as surviving MP3 compression and ordinary editing with near-perfect detection. It's inaudible and generated locally — nothing phones home — but it is detectable, and that's a product decision, not a footnote.

The licensing part.

Kokoro is Apache 2.0. Chatterbox is MIT. Both mean what you'd hope: use it, ship it, sell it, tell nobody.

XTTS-v2 is released under the Coqui Public Model License, which restricts use to non-commercial purposes. Not "attribution required", not "under a revenue threshold" — non-commercial. If you're charging for the thing you build, you're outside the licence.

Historically there was a way out: Coqui sold a commercial licence. Coqui Inc. shut down in January 2024. There is no sales team, no licensing portal, no entity to contract with. The commercial option doesn't exist at any price. So the most-downloaded, best-documented, most-searched open-source voice cloning model has no legal path into a paid product, and the reason isn't cost — it's that there's nobody left to ask.

Why this catches people.

Three things stack up. The weights are freely downloadable, which feels like permission. The ecosystem around it — community packages, wrappers, tutorials — is large and none of it leads with the licence. And "open source" does a lot of unearned work in people's heads; plenty of models described that way carry terms that aren't open source in any OSI sense.

What I'd actually do:

  1. Read the LICENSE file in the exact repository you download from, not a summary and not a blog post. Variants, community re-uploads and quantised conversions don't reliably carry the original terms.

  2. Check whether the licensor still exists. A permissive-sounding licence from a dissolved company with no successor is a different risk from the same licence backed by a live entity.

  3. Do this at model-selection time. Swapping an inference engine after you've shipped is a couple of days of work; discovering the problem after you've built a year of marketing around a model's name is a different cost entirely.

  4. Prefer Apache 2.0 or MIT when quality is close — and in this category it genuinely is close now, which wasn't true two years ago.

If you're running local TTS in anything commercial, the five minutes this takes is the cheapest five minutes in your stack.
