title: LeetCode 735 Looks Easy Until the First Collision Isn’t the Last
description:
One tiny chain reaction, a tempting wrong solution, and the O(n) reasoning worth taking into your next interview.

Before you scroll to the Python, try this tiny input in your head.

[4, 7, 3, -9]

Positive numbers move right, negative numbers move left, and the smaller asteroid disappears when two collide. So the 3 loses to -9, which feels like a perfectly reasonable place to finish one iteration.

Except -9 is still moving. It reaches 7 next, then 4, and suddenly the entire answer is [-9].

That is the little trap I like about LeetCode 735, Asteroid Collision. You can understand every rule and still write code that stops one collision too early. Honestly, this is exactly the kind of small problem I want in a practice session, because the mistake is specific enough to fix and the reasoning travels well.

Let’s work through it slowly enough to see the idea, then turn it into a solution you can explain without pointing vaguely at a stack.

First, make sure these two asteroids can actually meet

This is a Medium problem about a row of asteroids. Input order gives their relative positions, the absolute value gives their size, and the sign gives their direction. Every asteroid moves at the same speed.

When two meet, the smaller one disappears. If their sizes match, both disappear. We return the survivors in their original relative order.

Notice how much work that same-speed rule saves us. Two asteroids moving right cannot catch each other, and neither can two moving left. We do not need coordinates, elapsed time or a physics simulation.

Now compare [5, -3] with [-5, 3]. In the first pair, the asteroids move toward each other. In the second, they move apart, so comparing their sizes would already be a mistake.

While scanning from left to right, a collision is possible only when the latest surviving asteroid is positive and the incoming asteroid is negative. Check that relationship before comparing magnitudes.

I prefer drawing those two arrows once before touching the keyboard. It is much easier to catch a direction mistake on paper than inside three nested branches.

Keep the survivors, and look at the nearest one first

Imagine we have processed 4, 7 and 3. They all move right, so our survivors are [4, 7, 3]. When -9 arrives from the right, 3 is the first asteroid in its way.

If 3 disappears, 7 becomes the next one in its way. Removing 7 exposes 4. That access pattern gives us a stack, with the rightmost survivor at the top.

More precisely, after each input asteroid is fully processed, the stack contains the survivors of the prefix we have seen, in their original order, with no unresolved collisions among them.

That last sentence is the promise our code needs to keep. These are survivors so far; future input can still destroy them.

Also, this is not a stack sorted by size. [4, 7, 3] is completely valid, even though its magnitudes rise and fall. Calling every solution with a stack a monotonic-stack solution hides the actual reason we chose it. Here, we need the most recent surviving neighbor.

Stay with -9 until its story is finished

Our incoming asteroid gets its own little piece of state. It stays alive until a larger asteroid destroys it or an equal one destroys both. Popping a smaller neighbor does not finish the incoming asteroid’s turn.

Follow the same -9 through the entire sequence.

  1. Compare 3 with size 9 and remove 3. Keep -9 available for another comparison.

  2. Compare 7 with size 9 and remove 7. The stack now contains only 4.

  3. Compare 4 with size 9 and remove 4. Nothing remains to block -9.

  4. Append -9 once, after the collision loop finishes. The result is [-9].

This explains why a single if statement is not enough. It can resolve the collision with 3 and leave an unresolved collision between 7 and -9. A while loop keeps checking the boundary that each removal exposes.

There are only three outcomes to remember

Once the direction check passes, compare the positive stack top with the magnitude of the incoming negative asteroid.

  • If the top is smaller, pop it and keep the incoming asteroid alive. Another collision may be waiting underneath.

  • If the sizes match, pop the top and mark the incoming asteroid dead. Neither belongs in the result.

  • If the top is larger, leave it alone and mark the incoming asteroid dead. This arrival cannot reach anything farther left.

If the loop finishes with the incoming asteroid still alive, append it. That can happen because the stack is empty, because its top moves left too, or because the incoming asteroid moves right and cannot hit an earlier survivor.

Now the Python has a reason for every branch

I’m keeping the alive flag explicit here because it makes the difference between removing a neighbor and destroying the current asteroid easy to see. Shorter code can wait until the reasoning feels boring in the best possible way.

from typing import List
class Solution:
    def asteroidCollision(self, asteroids: List[int]) -> List[int]:
        survivors = []
        for asteroid in asteroids:
            alive = True
            while (
                alive
                and asteroid < 0
                and survivors
                and survivors[-1] > 0
            ):
                if survivors[-1] < -asteroid:
                    survivors.pop()
                elif survivors[-1] == -asteroid:
                    survivors.pop()
                    alive = False
                else:
                    alive = False
            if alive:
                survivors.append(asteroid)
        return survivors

Inside the loop, asteroid is negative, so -asteroid is its positive magnitude. We are comparing sizes, not deciding that a negative number must be smaller than a positive one.

Python evaluates the and conditions from left to right. The survivors check therefore protects survivors[-1] when the stack is empty.

Equality deserves its own branch. If you only pop the top and forget alive = False, the incoming asteroid gets appended afterward and quietly comes back from the dead. Cute in a movie, deeply unhelpful in an algorithm.

Why this keeps the stack’s promise

Before a new arrival, earlier survivors already have no unresolved collisions with each other. The only new conflict can be between the arrival and the rightmost survivor.

Removing that survivor exposes exactly one new neighbor, so the loop checks again. When the arrival dies, the earlier survivors are still stable. When it survives, the loop has established that it cannot collide with the remaining top, so appending it restores the same promise.

Repeat that for every input asteroid and the final stack contains exactly the survivors we need. We never reorder the input, which matters because position determines who meets whom.

Two loops do not automatically mean O(n²)

This is the explanation I want ready for the follow-up. One incoming asteroid can do a lot of work, but it does that work by permanently removing earlier asteroids.

Across the whole input, each asteroid is appended at most once and popped at most once. Once 3 has disappeared, a later arrival cannot make us pop that same 3 again.

A collision that does not pop anything destroys the incoming asteroid and ends its loop. There is at most one such final comparison per arrival. Equality also ends the loop while removing the top.

So the total work is O(n), including all those repeated collisions. The stack can hold all n asteroids when none collide, giving O(n) extra space. Python list append is amortized constant time, and removing its last element is constant time.

By comparison, repeatedly deleting from the middle of an array can shift many elements on every deletion. A stack lets us do the same local cleanup at the end of the list.

Four tiny cases make the explanation much harder to fake

Before calling the solution finished, hand-trace inputs that force different decisions. Each one should have a reason for existing.

  • [8, -8] becomes []. This checks that equality destroys both asteroids.

  • [-2, -1, 1, 2] stays unchanged. These asteroids either share a direction or move apart.

  • [10, 2, -5] becomes [10]. The incoming -5 removes 2, then loses to 10.

  • [4, 7, 3, -9] becomes [-9]. One arrival has to clear several smaller neighbors before it can be appended.

Then make the chain end in equality with [4, 7, 3, -7]. Remove 3, let 7 and -7 destroy each other, and leave [4]. This catches the version that handles equality correctly in isolation but continues after the incoming asteroid is already gone.

Take the reasoning into your next practice session

Close the implementation and reconstruct it from the stack’s promise. Explain which pair can collide, what each branch removes, and why the same incoming value sometimes needs another turn through the loop.

When that feels comfortable, pick another coding problem and write down what your data structure must keep true before you code. Let the problem determine the structure instead of hunting for a familiar template.

For this one, you should be able to explain why the last survivor matters, why one removal can expose another conflict, and why repeated work can still add up to linear time. Those are useful things to carry beyond an asteroid problem.

My favorite takeaway is that tiny examples can ask surprisingly honest questions. With just four numbers, this one tells you whether your code resolves a single collision or finishes the chain it started.

~ Emily

title: Base64, URL encoding, hashes, UUIDs and Unix timestamps: the one-liners I kept looking up
description:
Every few days I need to Base64 a file, hash a download, or turn an epoch value into a date, and every few days I search for the exact same one-liner. So I finally wrote them down in one place. Copy what you need.

Base64

Where Encode Decode
Linux / macOS base64 file.png base64 -d encoded.txt (-D on older macOS)
PowerShell [Convert]::ToBase64String([IO.File]::ReadAllBytes('file.png')) [Convert]::FromBase64String($s)
Python base64.b64encode(data) base64.b64decode(s)
Browser JS btoa(str) atob(s)
Node.js Buffer.from(str).toString('base64') Buffer.from(s, 'base64')
PHP base64_encode($data) base64_decode($s)

Gotcha: btoa only accepts Latin-1. Text with accents or emoji needs a TextEncoder step first, or it throws.

URL encoding

Language Encode one value Watch out
JavaScript encodeURIComponent(value) encodeURI is for a whole address
Python urllib.parse.quote(value, safe='') quote_plus turns spaces into +
PHP rawurlencode($value) urlencode uses + for spaces
Java URLEncoder.encode(value, "UTF-8") produces +; use %20 inside a path
C# Uri.EscapeDataString(value) HttpUtility.UrlEncode uses +

Gotcha: if you see %2520, the value was encoded twice. Decode once, encode once.

File hashes (checking a download)

System SHA-256 MD5
Windows cmd certutil -hashfile file.iso SHA256 certutil -hashfile file.iso MD5
PowerShell Get-FileHash file.iso -Algorithm SHA256 Get-FileHash file.iso -Algorithm MD5
Linux sha256sum file.iso md5sum file.iso
macOS shasum -a 256 file.iso md5 file.iso
Python hashlib.sha256(data).hexdigest() hashlib.md5(data).hexdigest()

The result is identical everywhere: a hash depends only on the bytes, never on the tool.

UUIDs

Platform One-liner
JavaScript crypto.randomUUID()
Python import uuid; uuid.uuid4()
Java UUID.randomUUID()
C# Guid.NewGuid() (Guid.CreateVersion7() on .NET 9)
PostgreSQL gen_random_uuid() (uuidv7() from PostgreSQL 18)
MySQL UUID() (careful: this is a time-based v1)
Shell uuidgen

Gotcha: for database primary keys, prefer v7. It starts with a millisecond timestamp, so new rows land at the end of the index instead of scattering through it.

Unix timestamps

Where Now Timestamp to date
JavaScript Math.floor(Date.now() / 1000) new Date(ts * 1000)
Python int(time.time()) datetime.fromtimestamp(ts, tz=timezone.utc)
PHP time() date('Y-m-d H:i:s', $ts)
MySQL UNIX_TIMESTAMP() FROM_UNIXTIME(ts)
PostgreSQL EXTRACT(EPOCH FROM now()) to_timestamp(ts)
Shell date +%s date -d @1700000000 (date -r 1700000000 on macOS)
Excel – =A1/86400 + DATE(1970,1,1) (UTC)

Gotcha: 10 digits is seconds, 13 digits is milliseconds. A date in 1970 means you passed milliseconds where seconds were expected, or the other way round.

Discord bonus: <t:1700000000:R> renders as a relative time in every reader's own time zone.

When I don't have a terminal handy, I use the browser versions of these on LogicUtil, a set of free tools that run entirely client-side (nothing is uploaded, no sign-up). Disclosure: I built it. The same tables also live in a GitHub repo: saman-webdev/dev-one-liners. If one of the one-liners above is wrong for your platform, tell me in the comments and I'll fix it.

title: Optimize Service Logic of Your Rust Code by Replacing Arc::clone with Borrowing
description:
In a previous post, I discussed the performance benefits of exposing references rather than cloning data outright. While refining my application logic recently, I realized that this principle applies broadly: eliminating unnecessary clones is one of the easiest ways to clean up general Rust code.

The Arc::clone Trap

Rust beginners often attempt to resolve stubborn borrow checker errors by simply cloning variables and moving them into closures or functions. While move is a fundamental idiom in Rust, excessive cloning should be avoided in production-grade code.

I’ve certainly been guilty of scattering Arc::clone across a codebase just to satisfy the compiler and push a feature across the finish line. The underlying motivation is often a casual approach to Arc.

Arc (Atomic Reference Counted pointer) is a foundational smart pointer for multithreaded Rust. Even though cloning an Arc is far more lightweight than cloning a deep struct, its overhead is non-trivial:

Atomic Operations: Cloning an Arc triggers atomic increment instructions.

Cache Invalidation: These atomic operations cause cache line invalidation across CPU cores.

Contention: High-frequency cloning under heavy concurrency can introduce subtle performance bottlenecks.

Standard borrowing (& or &mut), by contrast, incurs none of these costs.

Conclusion

Aside from scenarios where ownership transfer is strictly required--such as spawning new threads or moving data across async task boundaries—we should look to optimize our Rust architecture by replacing unnecessary Arc::clone calls with proper borrowing. Clean code isn't just about compiling successfully; it's about respecting ownership and memory layout.

title: AI Note Taker for In-Person Meetings: Notes and Follow-Ups
description:
Stay present in the room while AI turns the conversation into meeting notes, decisions, and follow-ups. A practical guide to recording and local transcription.

Originally published on the OneMira Blog. Explore the OneMira C1 AI Voice Recorder — ✨ Local AI · Works Standalone · 🗣️ Speaker ID · Zero Cloud Subscription.

An AI note taker for in-person meetings helps you focus on the conversation and leave with a clear record of decisions and next steps. With OneMira C1, press once to capture the discussion, then use local transcription and built-in AI meeting notes on your Mac or Windows computer. Your phone stays free, and no OneMira subscription is required.

This guide walks through a practical meeting workflow: prepare the recorder, capture the conversation, separate decisions from suggestions, and turn the reviewed notes into a useful follow-up.

What should an AI meeting note contain?

A useful meeting note answers three things: what mattered, what was agreed, and what happens next. Keep the transcript available for context, then organize the recap into these sections:

  • Summary: the purpose of the conversation and the main points discussed.
  • Decisions: what participants actually agreed, including any conditions or unresolved disagreement.
  • Action items: the task, its owner, and its deadline when those were stated.
  • Open questions: anything that still needs an answer or an explicit decision.

For a project discussion, that might mean the chosen approach, the reason for choosing it, and who will check the remaining risk. For a client meeting, it might mean the agreed scope, promised materials, and next conversation. The structure stays useful across different kinds of work.

How do I record an in-person meeting with C1?

Set up OneMira Desktop and pair C1 before the meeting. Complete the required software and model downloads if you plan to use local transcription and AI notes without an internet connection. The setup guide covers installation and pairing.

  1. Agree on recording. Tell participants that you will record to prepare notes and follow your workplace's recording rules.
  2. Check the room. Place C1 where nearby voices can reach it clearly and make a short test from the seats people will use. Its effective pickup range is 5 m; distance alone does not determine the quality of a transcript in a noisy or echoing room.
  3. Press to capture. C1's turntable rotates while recording, providing a visible recording cue. Your phone remains available for other tasks.
  4. Use the conversation on your computer. When connected through Bluetooth or USB-C, OneMira Desktop transcribes locally in real time. If you capture away from the computer, process the conversation locally after reconnecting.

You can use the growing context while a connected meeting is still in progress. For example, ask for the decisions agreed so far before moving to the next agenda item. Check the result with the people in the room when an assignment or decision is unclear.

How do I turn the conversation into a summary and action items?

Use OneMira Desktop's built-in local model to generate meeting notes, then review the names, numbers, decisions, and commitments. A specific instruction gives the draft a more useful structure:

Summarize this meeting. Separate confirmed decisions from proposals and open questions. List each action item with its owner and deadline only when they were stated. Mark missing details as “not specified.” Do not turn a suggestion into an agreement.

How do I use ChatGPT for meeting notes?

Paste a transcript or selected passages into ChatGPT and ask for a summary, decisions, and action items. This copy-and-paste workflow does not require a OneMira integration.

  1. Choose the source text. Copy the relevant conversation from your local OneMira notes. Include speaker labels and timestamps when available.
  2. Ask for structured notes. Paste the text with the prompt above. Ask ChatGPT to flag missing information and point back to the supplied text for each decision or commitment.
  3. Review before sharing. Check names, numbers, owners, and dates against the transcript. Then ask for a short follow-up draft based on the verified notes.

C1 supplies the capture and local transcription; ChatGPT processes the text you send under its own data terms and account limits. For fully offline note generation after setup, use OneMira Desktop's built-in local model instead.

What does a clear action item look like?

Write the commitment precisely enough that someone can act on it. Keep a possible future task separate from an agreed assignment.

Illustrative meeting-note example:

“Let's use the shorter onboarding email. Alex, please send the draft by Thursday. We might add a second email later, but let's look at the replies first.”

  • Decision: use the shorter onboarding email.
  • Action item: Alex will send the draft by Thursday.
  • Open question: whether to add a second email after reviewing replies.

The second email has no agreed owner or deadline. A polished summary should not invent either. This distinction matters when the notes become the basis for someone else's work.

How do I turn meeting notes into a follow-up?

Review the notes, then use the confirmed decisions and action items to prepare a short message for the participants. A simple format is enough:

Summary: [Main outcome of the meeting]
Decisions: [What was agreed]
Next steps: [Task — owner — deadline]
Still open: [Questions requiring a decision]

Keep important context with the note and clarify missing owners or dates before sending. Add the reviewed tasks to the calendar or task tool you already use. Generating an action-item list does not by itself assign work, send a message, or create a reminder.

Make your next meeting easier to follow up

Give the conversation your attention, then turn what was said into a note you can use. C1’s one-press capture works with OneMira Desktop on your Mac or PC for local transcription and included local AI after setup.

No OneMira account or subscription is needed for this local workflow. Choose in Settings whether to keep the original stereo WAV audio for checking a name, number or quotation. Your notes stay editable on your computer. See the desktop requirements and the local AI setup guide.

For a repeatable meeting-note workflow, explore OneMira C1 and current purchase options. See the product walkthrough for setup and an online-meeting example with a ChatGPT summary, or follow the offline AI meeting notes guide to keep generation on your computer.

title: The Physics of AI: Why Your Next Server Needs Liquid Cooling and Heavy Copper
description:
If you follow the tech news, you know that the AI arms race is currently a race for power.

NVIDIA’s latest Blackwell architecture GPUs are pushing power consumption to unprecedented levels—approaching 1,000W per chip, with entire server racks now drawing over 100kW.

As software developers, we usually think of scaling in terms of cloud instances and Kubernetes clusters. But at the physical layer, scaling AI means dealing with extreme thermodynamics. The hardware running your models is hitting the absolute limits of physics.

Here is why AI is forcing a massive shift in server PCB design, and why traditional air cooling and standard copper are no longer enough.

1. The End of Air Cooling: Liquid is the New Normal

For decades, servers were cooled by massive fans pushing air through the chassis. But air has a very low specific heat capacity. It simply cannot carry away the massive heat generated by a 100kW+ AI rack.

This is why tech giants and data centers are rapidly transitioning to Direct-to-Chip (D2C) liquid cooling.

Instead of blowing air, cold plates are mounted directly on top of the hottest components (GPUs and CPUs), and a dielectric or water-based coolant is pumped through them.

The Hardware Challenge: Liquid cooling introduces immense mechanical and chemical stress. The PCB must be highly resistant to moisture and chemical degradation. More importantly, the CTE (Coefficient of Thermal Expansion) of the PCB materials must perfectly match the heavy metal cold plates. If they expand and contract at different rates, the board will warp, and the BGA solder joints under the GPU will crack.

2. Power Delivery: The Heavy Copper Revolution

A GPU drawing 1,000W at sub-1V voltages requires immense current—often exceeding 1,000 Amps.

On standard PCBs, delivering this much current would instantly vaporize the traces. To handle this, AI server boards are shifting to Heavy Copper PCBs (up to 10oz or even 20oz). These aren't just traces; they are physical copper busbars embedded in the board.

The Manufacturing Challenge: Etching 20oz copper is a nightmare. The undercut effect (where etching chemicals eat sideways into the trace) is severe. If a designer routes a 10 mil trace on a heavy copper board without accounting for etching tolerances, it could short out or break during production. This requires highly specialized DFM (Design for Manufacturing) reviews and advanced etching techniques.

3. The Signal Integrity Nightmare: 224G PAM4

To feed data to these monstrous GPUs, networking speeds are jumping from 112G to 224G per lane.

At 224G, signal attenuation through standard FR-4 materials is catastrophic. The data literally dissolves into noise before it reaches the chip.

The Hardware Challenge: This forces the industry to use ultra-low-loss materials (such as M8 or M9 grade laminates) and ultra-smooth copper foils. It also demands extreme precision in impedance control. Even a 5% deviation in trace width or dielectric thickness can destroy signal integrity.

4. The Shift to High-Layer Count HDI

Because the physical distance between the GPU and memory (HBM) must be minimal to reduce latency and power loss, AI server boards are incredibly dense.

Standard boards won't cut it. AI accelerators now use 20 to 30-layer HDI boards (High-Density Interconnect). The BGA pitch is becoming so small that conventional mechanical drills cannot be used. Laser-drilled microvias are mandatory.

The Bottom Line

The AI revolution is not just a software revolution. It is a brutal test of materials science, thermodynamics, and precision manufacturing.

At AnyPCBA, we are seeing this transition firsthand. We support the manufacturing of high-layer HDI, heavy copper (up to 20oz), and high-frequency PCBs for demanding applications. We know that when you are dealing with 100kW racks and 224G signals, a "working" design on a breadboard means nothing without rigorous DFM reviews and precise impedance control.

If you are building hardware for the AI era, or if you need a manufacturing partner that understands the physics behind heavy copper and HDI, let's talk.

At AnyPCBA, we specialize in small-to-medium volume manufacturing of advanced PCBs and PCBA. We hold ISO 13485 and IATF 16949 certifications and are equipped to handle heavy copper, HDI, and rigid-flex boards. Contact us through our website to discuss your high-reliability projects.

What's the biggest physical constraint you've faced when designing hardware for high-performance computing? Share your experience in the comments!

title: Nemotron 3.5 Bolt on one GPU: what the 24 GB covers, the drafter flag and the llama.cpp trap
description:
NVIDIA's Nemotron 3.5 Bolt 74B-A9B 24GB is a 74B agent model that reads text and images. Only about 9B of its parameters (the numbers a model learns in training) work on each token, and a token is roughly a piece of a word. Most are stored at about 2 bits each, so the file is 22.0 GB.

We served it on one A40, a 48 GB data-center card on our cloud, with llama.cpp, the open-source program most people use to run models on one machine. The image reader was on, and so was the drafter, a small helper model that speeds up writing. It used about 27 GB. For one user it wrote 136 tokens a second with the drafter and 70 without.

Three choices matter more than the model: what the 24 GB covers, which llama.cpp you compile, and when the drafter pays off. Every figure sits in our Nemotron 3.5 Bolt deployment write-up with the full measurements.

The 24 GB is a text-only budget for one user

NVIDIA's sum comes to 23.83 GB. That is 22.01 GB for the parameters, 0.87 GB of working memory for roughly 128,000 tokens of conversation, and 0.96 GB for the drafter. The image reader, another 1.68 GB, is deliberately outside the sum.

Two things eat into that margin. First, the unit: a card sold as 24 GB has 24 GiB. Read NVIDIA's figure as decimal and roughly 1.9 GB stays free; read it as GiB and only about 0.2 does. Second, the drafter took close to 2.4 GB on our A40, not 0.96. So a fit on a real 24 GB card stays unproven: we never put Bolt on one.

The recipes NVIDIA publishes for llama.cpp include the image reader, and the smallest of them asks for a 32 GB card. Our 27 GB (25.2 GiB), with the quick-start 98,304 tokens of conversation, counts the image reader too, so it does not check NVIDIA's text-only number. Measure your own server with the drafter on and off, in the unit your card is sold in.

Build the right llama.cpp, and build it in parallel

Bolt needs llama.cpp code from release day, 15 October. Kartik Gulia, an NVIDIA engineer, added the model and its image reader to llama.cpp, and ggerganov merged the change in llama.cpp pull request #30520 that same day. Older builds refuse the file.

We hit exactly that. Our worker (the agent that sets up each GPU machine for InferenceKey) pins a llama.cpp release 1,920 commits older than the merge, so we set v0.7.0 by hand.

Then compiling ate the clock. A fresh machine took 764.8 seconds from request to ready, and 705 of those went into building llama.cpp on 9 CPU cores. Our worker calls cmake --build with no parallel jobs unless CMAKE_BUILD_PARALLEL_LEVEL is set. Even with 12 jobs set by hand, the build was 92% of the wait. On a 31-core machine the same build finished in 2 minutes 41 seconds. A second copy on an already built machine was ready in 15.6 seconds. If first starts matter, count CPU cores, not only the GPU.

The drafter is a server flag, not a request option

Bolt comes with the LiLiCorr drafter, about 1.1B parameters in a 1.0 GB file. The drafter proposes several tokens ahead, Bolt verifies the whole batch in a single step, accepts the run up to its first mismatch and writes that token itself. You turn it on when the server starts:

--spec-draft-hf nvidia/NVIDIA-Nemotron-3.5-Bolt-74B-A9B-24GB-LiLiCorr-GGUF \
--spec-type draft-dflash --spec-draft-n-max 6 --spec-draft-ngl 999

On short and medium prompts it about doubled the speed: over 25 requests the median was 136 tokens a second against 70, with a floor of 110, and 70% of the drafted tokens were accepted. The per-prompt speed and acceptance table shows where it gains most.

Long documents flip the result: the drafter slows prompt reading by about a quarter. A question over a 25,000-token document took 17.5 seconds without the drafter and 21.5 seconds with it. And v0.7.0 has the per-request drafter control compiled out, so the choice is made once per server. Mixed traffic? Benchmark both shapes first.

Two traps outside the model

  • A card can report fine and still be useless. Our first two machines had RTX 5090 cards. nvidia-smi, NVIDIA's status tool, answered, but CUDA, the layer programs use to reach the GPU, failed to start. Our platform still marked the model ready, so we have no 32 GB numbers yet.
  • Hidden reasoning burns time. Bolt thinks before it replies, out of your sight. A one-sentence answer cost 374 tokens of writing time. NVIDIA's model page documents a switch to turn thinking off, and InferenceKey does not forward it yet.

What this does and does not show

The quality numbers are NVIDIA's: Bolt beats Qwen3.6-35B-A3B on most agent benchmarks (Terminal-Bench 2.1: 50.98 against 44.38) and loses on factual recall. NVIDIA's speed table puts it behind Qwen3.6 and Gemma 4. Our side was about 50 requests, one GPU, one request at a time; on a two-tool refund task it called both tools correctly in all 5 runs. We did not test several requests sharing the card, where drafters tend to help less, or vLLM, the data-center server software that is the other route.

NVIDIA built, compressed and released Bolt and its drafter under OpenMDW-1.1, which allows commercial use. Kartik Gulia and ggerganov made llama.cpp able to run it. AI Search's news video pointed us to the family. Our part was wiring it end to end and measuring it. The exact command, per-request timings and worker settings are in the complete Nemotron 3.5 Bolt article on inferencekey.com.

title: Insomnia Collections vs Spec-Generated Requests
description:
Short answer: Authored requests are maintained by hand and reflect what someone saved; generated requests are derived from the contract and reflect the current API. The first is a snapshot; the second is a build output. For a changing API, generation is the only way to stay correct without manual re-sync.

What authored requests guarantee

Exactly the calls someone built, with precise control. They do not guarantee currency, and they miss anything that was never saved.

What generated requests guarantee

Property Authored Generated
Coverage What was saved Declared operations
On API change Manual update On save
Consistency As maintained With the contract
Control Fine Derived

The failure that generation removes

A missing request for a new endpoint, or a stale request for a moved one, is the classic authored-set bug. A generated set reflects the spec, so it cannot be missing a declared operation.

The honest takeaway

Authored requests are the right tool for a small, stable, bespoke set. Once the API grows and changes, generating from the contract is the lower-maintenance, more correct path.

Return to the Powerduck vs Insomnia comparison, or read the API debugging guide.

title: Building a browser where a local LLM clicks and types for you, in Rust
description:
I've been building Ricuicui, a desktop web browser for Mac and Windows with an AI and agents built in. The AI reads the page, clicks, fills in forms and drafts replies while you watch, and it can run entirely on your own machine. Here is how it is put together, and what I learned on the way.

One Rust binary, two rendering engines

Ricuicui is a single program written in Rust. It embeds Servo, the Rust browser engine, to display every site, so there is no Chromium to install next to it.

Next to Servo there is a second, much smaller engine of our own, Cotcotcodet. It does not try to render pixels: it parses pages quickly so the AI can read them, and it runs the page's JavaScript isolated in a separate process. Splitting "showing a page to a human" from "reading a page for an AI" turned out to make the agent both faster and safer.

A local LLM, without Ollama or LM Studio

The local AI uses llama.cpp and models in GGUF format. On a Mac, llama.cpp ships inside the app; on Windows it is downloaded on first use and runs on the graphics card through Vulkan. No separate runtime to install.

Memory decides everything, so the app suggests a model from what you have:

Mac (unified memory) PC (VRAM) Suggested model
8 GB 4 GB Qwen3 0.6B
16 GB 8 GB Qwen3 4B
24 GB 12–16 GB Qwen3 8B
32 GB+ 24 GB+ Qwen3 14B

Any other .gguf file works too (Mistral, DeepSeek…), within the memory available. For the hardest tasks you can switch to an online model (Claude, GPT, Mistral) with your own key, stored in the system keychain.

Letting the model act, without letting it do anything

An agent that can click is only useful if you can trust it. A few rules are enforced by the browser, not by the prompt:

  • the AI asks for your approval before any action that commits you (submitting a form, a purchase, sending a message);
  • it never types a password or a card number: sensitive fields are detected from their type, but also from their placeholder, aria-label or label (PIN, CVV, 2FA codes…);
  • everything it does is shown live, and you can take the wheel at any time.

MCP in both directions

Ricuicui is also an MCP server: it exposes 13 tools locally on 127.0.0.1:7878, so Claude Desktop, Claude Code, Cursor, VS Code or LM Studio can drive the browser while you watch. And it is an MCP client: its own AI can plug into MCP servers (files, memory…) and into A2A agents and webhooks.

Where it stands

Ricuicui is freemium: the base version contains the whole browser, and the Pro licence (EUR 12.90 a year) unlocks the local GPU server. It runs on macOS 11+ (Apple silicon and Intel) and Windows 10/11.

I'd love feedback from people running local models: which sizes are actually usable for agent work on your hardware, and what you would want an AI browser to refuse to do.

→ ricuicui.com

title: Inso CLI vs an OpenAPI CLI
description:
Short answer: The inso CLI runs the client's collections and assertions in CI; an OpenAPI CLI works from the contract and can validate, generate, and verify. The first executes the authored set; the second treats the spec as the source and derives the checks.

What a collection CLI is built for

Running the saved requests and their assertions in a pipeline. It is a reliable runner for a fixed set and is only as current as the collection.

What a spec CLI is built for

Task Collection CLI OpenAPI CLI
Run authored requests Yes Generated
Validate the contract Not its job Yes
Generate surfaces No Docs, mocks, tools
Verify conformance Assertions Schema check

Why the source matters

A spec CLI starts from the artifact that changes with the API, so the checks cannot run against a stale collection. A collection CLI is a runner for a snapshot.

How they fit

Keep the collection CLI for fixed behavioral calls and use the spec CLI for validation and generation. The runner and the source are different concerns.

This is part of the Powerduck vs Insomnia comparison. Finish with collections vs generated.

title: API Mocking in Insomnia vs Powerduck
description:
Short answer: A classic client covers requests and leaves mocking to a separate tool; a studio generates the mock from the same spec as the requests. The first is a request tool; the second keeps the client and the development target in sync by construction.

Why a client needs a mock somewhere

Once the agent or the client needs to develop without a live backend, a mock has to come from another product. That mock is a separate artifact with its own drift.

What a generated mock shares

Property Client + separate mock Studio generated
Mock source Another tool The same spec
Sync Manual On save
Edge cases As built From responses
Drift Common Rare

The failure that shared sources avoid

The client and the mock disagreeing is a silent bug: the request is valid in one place and the mock returns a different shape. A shared spec makes that impossible.

The decision rule

If mocking is a separate concern you are happy to wire, keep it separate. If you want the client and the target to always agree, generate both from one contract.

title: Insomnia vs Powerduck: Pricing and Lock-In
description:
Short answer: Insomnia offers a free local tier and paid plans; Powerduck keeps the desktop and Hub hosting free within plan limits and exports portable static artifacts. The deeper difference is lock-in: a client vault and a platform are harder to leave than a set of generated files.

What the pricing shapes reward

A classic client prices seats and features around the client and its cloud. A local-first studio keeps the work in files and hosts within plan limits, so a larger surface does not push you across a per-seat gate.

The side-by-side

Property Insomnia Powerduck
Local work Free Free
Hosting Paid tiers Hub within plan
Artifacts Client vault Static, portable
Exit cost Export and migrate Plain files

Why lock-in is the real cost

Pricing changes and feature gates are visible. The cost that compounds is the work trapped in a vault or a platform. Portable artifacts keep the decision reversible.

The honest takeaway

Compare the current prices, but weight the exit cost. A tool that exports the work lets you choose again later; a vault does not.

This is part of the Powerduck vs Insomnia comparison. Next, read the mocking comparison.

title: Contract Testing: Insomnia vs Powerduck
description:
Short answer: A client can run assertions on the fields you choose; a contract-first studio verifies the whole response against the schema. The first proves the specific checks you remembered; the second proves there is no undeclared property, missing field, or type drift anywhere.

What assertions cover

They are precise and useful for the fields you decide to check. They are also only as good as the list, so a violation in an unasserted field passes the test.

What contract verification adds

Condition Assertions Contract check
Chosen fields Checked Checked
Undeclared property Missed Flagged
Missing required field Only if listed Flagged
Type drift anywhere Missed Flagged

The failure that matters

A response that passes every written assertion yet violates the contract is the gap. The contract check examines the full response, so it does not depend on a human listing every field.

How to combine them

Keep the behavioral assertions for the flows and add the contract check for conformance. They prove different things and both belong in the pipeline.

This is part of the Powerduck vs Insomnia comparison. Next, read pricing and lock-in.

title: Migrating from Insomnia to OpenAPI
description:
Short answer: Use the existing client collections as evidence of the API and consolidate them into an OpenAPI contract. Then generate the request set from the spec. This is a one-time move that replaces a maintained client vault with a maintained, versioned contract.

What the collections already contain

Paths, methods, bodies, headers, and expected responses — a practical, partial description of the API. They are the fastest way to seed a contract without starting from a blank page.

The migration path

  1. Export the collections and convert the requests into operations.
  2. Add response schemas from real responses and validate the contract.
  3. Generate the request set and compare it to the old collection.
  4. Once aligned, make the spec the source and retire the vault.

What to expect

The first pass will miss responses and edge cases that the collections never captured. Close those gaps against the running API; the resulting contract is more complete than the collection.

The payoff

After the move, the request set is an output. The docs, mocks, and tools share the same source, and the team stops maintaining a separate client artifact.

This is part of the Powerduck vs Insomnia comparison. Next, read contract testing.

title: Insomnia Scratchpad vs a Local-First OpenAPI Studio
description:
Short answer: The scratchpad lets you work without an account, but it is a private vault inside the client. A local-first studio opens the OpenAPI file in your repo, so the work is versioned with the code and not locked in a client vault. Both work offline; only one keeps the file as the source.

What the scratchpad solves

It removes the account requirement for local work, which is a real convenience. The tradeoff is that the work lives in a client vault, a separate artifact from the contract and the repository.

What local-first keeps

Property Scratchpad Local-first studio
No account Yes Yes
Where the work lives Client vault Spec in your repo
Versioned with code No Yes
Portable Via the client Plain files

Why the repo matters

When the contract is in the repo, the requests are generated from it and reviewed with the code. A client vault is a private copy that is not part of the pull request.

The decision rule

Use the scratchpad for a quick, private call. Use a local-first studio when the work should be versioned, reviewed, and kept as the source of truth.

This is part of the Powerduck vs Insomnia comparison. Next, read migrating to OpenAPI.

title: Powerduck vs Insomnia: Which API Client in 2026?

What Insomnia is best at

A comfortable, mature request builder and a solid CLI. It is a natural choice for a developer who wants a classic client and does not need the contract to drive the rest of the lifecycle.

Capability Insomnia Powerduck
Center Client collection OpenAPI contract

title: Powerduck vs Insomnia: API Client and Contract Testing
description:
Quick answer: Insomnia is a polished, long-established API client now under Kong, and it is a comfortable tool for sending requests and running the inso CLI. The reason teams look past it is the same shift that affects every classic client: the work is organized around a client-side collection rather than an OpenAPI contract, and the product has leaned toward accounts and cloud. Powerduck is a local-first, OpenAPI-first studio: it opens the spec in your repo, generates the requests from it, verifies every response against it, and adds mocks and MCP in the same place. Pick Insomnia for a familiar client; pick Powerduck when the contract should own the workflow.

This page compares the two honestly, including the scratchpad, CLI, and pricing, and links to the focused guides. Start with the table, then read the sections that match how you work today.

The two at a glance

Capability Insomnia Powerduck
Primary role API client OpenAPI studio
Center of the workflow Client collections OpenAPI contract
Offline mode Scratchpad / local vault Local files, no account
Requests Authored / imported Generated from paths and tags
Contract verification Not built in Every response checked against the spec
CLI inso CLI OpenAPI CLI
Entry price Free local; paid tiers Desktop and Hub free
Best for A familiar, polished client One contract through the whole lifecycle

The client is comfortable, but the center is the collection

Insomnia's request builder is genuinely good, and the scratchpad and local vault let you work without committing to an account. The structural limitation is that the collection is the artifact you maintain: it is authored, it is separate from the contract, and it drifts when the API changes. A contract-first studio opens the spec and generates the request set, so the two cannot diverge. The headline comparison is in Powerduck vs Insomnia: which API client, and the offline story is in Insomnia scratchpad vs a local-first studio.

Moving from a client to a contract

If you have years of Insomnia collections, the migration is not a rewrite. The durable move is to establish the OpenAPI contract, generate the request set from it, and let the collection become an output rather than an input. A practical path is in migrating from Insomnia to OpenAPI, and the difference between authored and generated requests is in Insomnia collections vs spec-generated requests.

Contract testing is the missing layer

Insomnia can run assertions and tests, and the inso CLI is a solid CI tool, but it is not verifying that a response conforms to the API contract. The failures that hurt are the ones that pass an assertion yet violate the spec: an undeclared property, a missing field, a type change. Powerduck catches those inline against the contract. The comparison is in contract testing: Insomnia vs Powerduck, and the CLIs are compared in inso CLI vs an OpenAPI CLI.

Mocks and the full lifecycle

A classic client covers requests well and leaves the rest — mocks, docs, agent tools — to other products. Powerduck generates a mock from the same spec, so the agent and the client develop against a contract-shaped target instead of a live server. That comparison is in API mocking in Insomnia vs Powerduck.

Pricing and lock-in

Insomnia offers a free local tier and paid individual and team plans; Powerduck keeps the desktop and Hub hosting free within plan limits and exports static artifacts so there is no platform lock-in. The side-by-side is in Insomnia vs Powerduck: pricing and lock-in.

Where to go next

Powerduck is the local-first, OpenAPI-first studio that carries the contract through debug, test, mock, and agent tools; Insomnia is a familiar client. See it on the Powerduck homepage. For the wider picture, read the API debugging guide and the API testing guide.

Frequently asked questions

Can I keep using Insomnia without an account?

The scratchpad and local vault support local work. Powerduck is built local-first from the start, opening the OpenAPI file in your repo with no account and no separate vault.

Does the inso CLI verify responses against OpenAPI?

It can run tests and assertions, but contract verification — proving a response conforms to the schema — is a different check, which Powerduck performs inline against the spec.

Is it worth switching if I only send requests?

If requests are the whole job and you are happy with the client, you can stay. The case for a contract-first studio becomes strong once you also need mocks, docs, tests, and agent tools to stay in sync.

title: How to Connect OneMira Notes to Cursor with MCP
description:
Bring spoken decisions and constraints into Cursor with OneMira MCP. Connect through Desktop settings, check the tools and turn a discussion into your next coding task.

Originally published on the OneMira Blog. Explore the OneMira C1 AI Voice Recorder — ✨ Local AI · Works Standalone · 🗣️ Speaker ID · Zero Cloud Subscription.

Give Cursor the decisions behind the code. Connect OneMira through Desktop’s MCP settings so Cursor can retrieve relevant conversation notes instead of asking you to reconstruct the discussion. Start with a decision recap, an implementation plan or test cases grounded in what the team actually said.

How do you connect OneMira to Cursor?

Use the connection controls in OneMira Desktop. The current OneMira MCP guide documents this path:

  1. Install OneMira Desktop and complete C1 setup on your Mac or PC.
  2. Open Desktop Settings, select MCP and click Connect beside Cursor when it is detected.
  3. In Cursor, review the connection and tool permissions, then confirm that the Mira tools are available.
  4. Ask Cursor to find a non-sensitive note you recognize. Check that the returned content and source match it.

If Cursor is not detected or you need manual configuration, use the current configuration in the linked guide and the executable path for your installation. The local connection does not require a OneMira account; Cursor’s own account, plan and model requirements still apply.



C1's metal side and transparent cover, viewed at desk level.

What can you ask Cursor to do with the conversation?

Start with one useful result. These are example requests, not automatic actions:

  • “Find the discussion about the checkout retry. List the decision, the reason and the unresolved questions, with sources.”
  • “Turn the agreed requirements from this session into an implementation plan. Separate confirmed requirements from your suggestions.”
  • “Draft test cases for the edge cases we discussed. Show me the proposed changes before editing code.”

Read the result against the source notes and review code changes before using them. A transcript supplies context; it does not replace engineering judgment.

Do you need Cursor to use C1?

No. OneMira Desktop includes local transcription and local AI for notes and mind maps on your computer. After the required downloads, that workflow can run offline without a OneMira account or subscription. MCP is an optional way to keep working in a compatible AI tool you already use.

What happens to the notes you share?

The local MCP server returns requested context to Cursor, which may send it to the selected model under Cursor’s and the provider’s terms. Local retrieval does not make that later processing local. Start with a relevant excerpt, review tool permissions and approve changes deliberately. Keep sensitive material out of requests unless you are authorized to share it.

What if the connection is not working?

Check the connection in Desktop settings and the server status in Cursor. For manual setup, verify the executable path and arguments against the current OneMira guide. If tools appear but return no notes, confirm that the recording has synced and try a phrase from a known note.

For CLI users, Cursor’s current reference documents agent mcp list and agent mcp list-tools <identifier>. Use the actual server identifier shown by your configuration. To remove access, disconnect in Desktop settings or remove the server entry in Cursor and confirm it is no longer active. Your local notes remain.

Bring your next discussion into your workflow with C1. For the wider idea, read From Conversation to Context.

title: OpenAPI-First vs Collection-First API Workflows
description:
Short answer: A collection-first workflow maintains requests as the artifact; a contract-first workflow maintains the spec and derives the requests. The first is intuitive and drifts; the second is a discipline and stays correct. For a team that already versions an API, the contract is the durable source.

What collection-first optimizes for

Immediacy: you build a request, save it, and run it. There is no upfront modeling. The cost is that the collection is a separate, authored artifact that must be kept in sync with the API by hand.

What contract-first optimizes for

Property Collection-first Contract-first
Source of truth The collection The spec
Upfront cost Low Modeling
Drift Common Rare
Generated surfaces None Requests, docs, mocks, tools

Why the contract scales

One spec drives every surface, so a change is made once and the requests, docs, mocks, and agent tools all reflect it. A collection-first team makes the same change in several places.

The honest tradeoff

Contract-first asks for discipline and modeling up front. It pays back as the surface grows; for a single, stable endpoint, a collection can be the pragmatic choice.

This is part of the Powerduck vs Hoppscotch comparison. Finish with pricing and limits.

title: API Testing in CI: Hoppscotch vs Powerduck
description:
Short answer: Both can run in CI, but the source of the checks differs. A collection-based runner executes the requests you authored; a spec-first runner derives the checks from the contract and verifies conformance. Use the first to run a fixed set of calls; use the second to prove the responses match the API.

What a collection runner does in CI

It executes the saved requests and their assertions, which is a reliable way to run a known set of checks. It is only as current as the collection, and it verifies the assertions rather than the whole contract.

What a spec-first runner does

Property Collection runner Spec-first
Checks come from Authored requests The contract
Coverage What was saved Declared operations
Conformance Assertions only Full schema check
On spec change Update collection Reflects the spec

The failure that CI should catch

A response that violates the contract but passes the authored assertions is the gap. A spec-first runner checks the full response, so the violation fails the build even if no one wrote an assertion for it.

How to combine them

Run the fixed behavioral calls and the contract checks as two stages. The first proves the flows work; the second proves the responses are valid.

This is part of the Powerduck vs Hoppscotch comparison. Next, read OpenAPI-first vs collection-first.

title: A small Python preflight for background removal: check file limits before upload, check transparency after download
description:
Most of the friction with web-based image tools comes from small mismatches: a PNG that is 23 MB, a poster that is one pixel too wide, a "transparent" file that was saved as JPEG on the way back. None of these are hard problems, but they waste a round trip each time.

This post walks through two short Python scripts that sit next to a background-removal workflow. The first checks a folder of images against the tool's upload limits and fixes what it can. The second inspects the downloaded result and tells you whether it actually has an alpha channel. The limits used here come from the HiDream Background Remover page.

The limits

According to the tool page, an upload must be:

  • JPG, PNG or WEBP
  • up to 5 MB
  • between 256 and 4096 pixels on each side
  • at most 16 million pixels in total

The tool returns an image with a transparent background. The FAQ adds two practical notes: the download format depends on the task result, so check it if you need PNG, and avoid JPEG when exporting transparency, because JPEG has no alpha channel. If you need a white or branded background, the page suggests adding it later in a design editor.

Script 1: preflight.py

The script walks a folder, reports what is wrong with each file, and writes a fixed copy into ready/ when a fix is possible. Fixing means two things: scaling down until both the side limit and the pixel limit are met, and re-encoding as JPEG with decreasing quality until the file fits under 5 MB. Uploads can be JPEG because the transparency is created by the tool, not by your input.

"""Check and fix images before uploading them to a background remover.
Limits (from the tool page): JPG/PNG/WEBP, <= 5 MB,
each side 256-4096 px, <= 16 million pixels."""
import io, sys
from pathlib import Path
from PIL import Image

MAX_BYTES = 5 * 1024 * 1024
MIN_SIDE, MAX_SIDE, MAX_PIXELS = 256, 4096, 16_000_000
FORMATS = {"JPEG", "PNG", "WEBP"}

def problems(path: Path) -> list[str]:
    out = []
    with Image.open(path) as im:
        w, h = im.size
        if im.format not in FORMATS:
            out.append(f"format {im.format}")
        if min(w, h) < MIN_SIDE:
            out.append(f"short side {min(w, h)} < {MIN_SIDE}")
        if max(w, h) > MAX_SIDE:
            out.append(f"long side {max(w, h)} > {MAX_SIDE}")
        if w * h > MAX_PIXELS:
            out.append(f"{w * h:,} px > {MAX_PIXELS:,}")
    if path.stat().st_size > MAX_BYTES:
        out.append(f"{path.stat().st_size / 1e6:.1f} MB > 5 MB")
    return out

def fix(path: Path, outdir: Path) -> Path:
    with Image.open(path) as im:
        im = im.convert("RGB")
        w, h = im.size
        scale = min(1.0, MAX_SIDE / max(w, h), (MAX_PIXELS / (w * h)) ** 0.5)
        if scale < 1.0:
            im = im.resize((int(w * scale), int(h * scale)), Image.LANCZOS)
        quality = 92
        while True:
            buf = io.BytesIO()
            im.save(buf, "JPEG", quality=quality)
            if buf.tell() <= MAX_BYTES or quality <= 60:
                break
            quality -= 8
    out = outdir / (path.stem + "_upload.jpg")
    out.write_bytes(buf.getvalue())
    return out

if __name__ == "__main__":
    outdir = Path("ready"); outdir.mkdir(exist_ok=True)
    for p in sorted(Path(sys.argv[1]).iterdir()):
        try:
            issues = problems(p)
        except Exception:
            print(f"SKIP  {p.name}: not an image"); continue
        if not issues:
            print(f"OK    {p.name}"); continue
        fixed = fix(p, outdir)
        left = problems(fixed)
        print(f"FIXED {p.name}: {', '.join(issues)} -> {fixed.name}"
              + (f" (still: {', '.join(left)})" if left else ""))

I ran it on a test folder with five files: a normal product photo, an oversized poster, a tiny icon, a very noisy PNG and a text file.

$ python3 preflight.py in
FIXED icon.png: short side 180 < 256 -> icon_upload.jpg (still: short side 180 < 256)
FIXED noisy.png: 22.9 MB > 5 MB -> noisy_upload.jpg
SKIP  notes.txt: not an image
FIXED poster.png: long side 5000 > 4096, 17,500,000 px > 16,000,000 -> poster_upload.jpg
OK    shoe.jpg

Two details are worth pointing out.

First, the poster broke two rules at once. 5000 × 3500 is over the side limit and over the pixel limit, so the scale factor is the minimum of both constraints. Checking only the long side would have produced a 4096 × 2867 image, which happens to pass, but a nearly square 4000 × 4000 image would pass the side check and still fail the pixel check. Computing both avoids that trap.

Second, the icon cannot be fixed. The script only scales down, and the line ends with (still: ...) so you notice. Upscaling a 180-pixel icon to meet a minimum is possible, but it is a decision about quality you should make on purpose, for example with an image enhancer first, rather than something a script does silently.

Script 2: check_alpha.py

After processing, the page asks you to compare with the original and inspect edges and transparent areas before downloading. A quick numeric check helps before you look closely:

"""After download: does the result really have transparency?"""
import sys
from PIL import Image

for name in sys.argv[1:]:
    with Image.open(name) as im:
        if "A" not in im.getbands():
            print(f"{name}: no alpha channel ({im.mode}) - re-export as PNG/WEBP")
            continue
        a = im.getchannel("A")
        hist = a.histogram()
        total = im.width * im.height
        clear, solid = hist[0] / total, hist[255] / total
        partial = 1 - clear - solid
        print(f"{name}: transparent {clear:.0%}, opaque {solid:.0%}, soft edge {partial:.1%}")

On a test cutout and a flattened JPEG:

$ python3 check_alpha.py cutout.png flat.jpg
cutout.png: transparent 65%, opaque 35%, soft edge 0.0%
flat.jpg: no alpha channel (RGB) - re-export as PNG/WEBP

The "soft edge" share is the fraction of pixels that are neither fully transparent nor fully opaque. My synthetic test circle has hard edges, so it reads 0.0%. A real cutout of hair, fur or glass will show a noticeable soft-edge share, and those are exactly the areas the page tells you to inspect. The FAQ is direct about it: results depend on the source, and hair, glass and fine edges may need manual touch-ups.

Running it on a whole folder

A practical routine: point the preflight at the folder of product shots before a batch, upload everything from ready/ plus the files marked OK, and keep the original files untouched. After downloading the results, run the alpha check on all of them at once:

$ python3 check_alpha.py results/*.png

Anything without an alpha channel is the first thing to fix, usually by downloading again in a format that keeps transparency. Anything with a large soft-edge share goes to the top of the manual review list. The two scripts together take a few seconds and change the order in which you look at files, which is most of the value.

Where this fits

The page lists three typical sources: product photos (check edges and small components), portraits and pets (hair, fur and low-contrast edges), and illustrations or AI images (translucent materials depend on the source). The scripts do not judge any of that. They only remove the boring failures, so the review time goes to the edges.

Summary

  • Check format, size, side length and total pixels together before uploading.
  • Only scale down automatically; flag images that are too small.
  • After download, confirm the alpha channel exists and look at the soft-edge areas by eye.
  • Keep transparency in PNG or WEBP, and add any background color later in your design tool.

title: One instance per user, not per machine: a lock file that survives RDP reconnects
description:
Disclosure: I'm the developer of the app described here, and this post was drafted and published by an AI agent from the project's source code.

Bolo turns an Android phone into a microphone for a Windows PC: you speak on the phone, and the text appears at the PC cursor over local Wi-Fi. The PC side is a small Node.js helper that sits in the tray, listens for the phone, and types.

It runs on an ordinary desktop, but also on a Windows Server that several people use through Remote Desktop at the same time. That second setup broke the single-instance guard twice, in two different ways. This is the guard as it stands now (src/singleInstance.js, 77 lines) and the two mistakes it fixes.

Why a second copy hurts

Two helpers in the same login don't just waste memory. They fight over the UDP port used for LAN discovery, both watch the clipboard, and each one doubles every child process. The phone can end up connected to whichever copy answered first. The symptom report is "it works sometimes".

Mistake 1: one instance per machine

The obvious guard is a machine-wide lock: a named mutex or a lock file in a shared folder. On a multi-user server that is wrong. Each person who logs in needs their own helper, typing into their own session. A machine-wide lock would let the first user's helper run and make everyone else's exit.

So the lock has to be per session. A lock file is enough here, and it is easy to reason about:

const fd = fs.openSync(lockPath, 'wx'); // exclusive create: fails if the file exists
fs.writeSync(fd, String(process.pid));
fs.closeSync(fd);

'wx' is the whole trick: creating the file is atomic, so two copies starting at the same moment cannot both succeed.

Mistake 2: keying the lock on SESSIONNAME

The first per-session version put %SESSIONNAME% into the lock file name. That looks right: on a Remote Desktop login it's something like RDP-Tcp#0.

It isn't stable. SESSIONNAME changes when the user disconnects and reconnects (RDP-Tcp#0 becomes RDP-Tcp#4), while the session itself, and the helper running in it, carries on. A relaunch after a reconnect looked for a lock under the new name, found none, and started a second helper beside the first. We saw exactly that on the server: one user, two helper PIDs, listening on two adjacent ports.

The fix was to key on the user instead:

const sessionKey = (process.env.USERNAME || os.userInfo().username || 'user')
  .replace(/[^A-Za-z0-9_-]/g, '_');
const lockPath = path.join(os.tmpdir(), `bolo-server-${sessionKey}.lock`);

On this server each user has one Windows session, so per-user is per-session. Two details make it robust:

  • os.tmpdir() is already per user, and on a Remote Desktop host it can even resolve to a per-session subfolder. The user name in the file name is belt and braces.
  • Sanitise the name. User names can contain characters you don't want in a file name. Replace them rather than trust them.

If your machines allow one user to have several simultaneous sessions, this key is too coarse; you would want the session id from the OS instead. Pick the key that matches how your machines are actually used, and write that assumption into the code comment, as this file does.

Stale locks: the PID check

A lock file outlives a crash. If the helper died without cleaning up, the next start finds the file and must decide whether its owner is still alive. The file holds the owner's PID, so:

function pidAlive(pid) {
  if (!pid || Number.isNaN(pid)) return false;
  try { process.kill(pid, 0); return true; }   // signal 0: existence check, kills nothing
  catch (e) { return e.code === 'EPERM'; }     // exists, but not ours to signal
}

process.kill(pid, 0) sends no signal; it only checks that the process exists. Note the EPERM branch: a process that exists but belongs to someone else throws EPERM, and that still means "alive". Treating every error as "dead" would let you steal a live lock.

If the holder is alive, the new copy logs one line naming the PID and exits. If not, it deletes the stale file and tries the exclusive create once more. Only once: if a third copy won the race in between, 'wx' fails again and the loop ends without spinning.

Never block startup on the guard itself

Two choices here are about failing open:

  • If creating the lock fails with anything other than EEXIST (a permissions problem, a missing temp folder), the helper logs a warning and starts anyway. A guard that stops the app from running at all is worse than an occasional duplicate.
  • On platforms where this guard isn't needed, it returns true immediately.

And cleanup is tied to the process: the lock is removed on exit, SIGINT and SIGTERM. A hard kill skips those, which is exactly what the PID check is for.

What carries over

  • Decide what "single" means (machine, user, or session) before choosing the lock.
  • Don't key a lock on a value that changes while the thing it protects keeps running. SESSIONNAME is one.
  • Use an atomic exclusive create ('wx') and store the PID inside.
  • process.kill(pid, 0) checks liveness; EPERM means alive.
  • Reclaim stale locks with one retry, not a loop.
  • When the guard itself fails, let the app start.

Bolo is on Google Play (search "Bolo AI"), and the Windows companion is on GitHub releases. The phone and PC talk over your local Wi-Fi.

title: 智慧隧道管理平台
description:

统一接入现场数据，让隧道管理更直观、更高效

01 为什么需要智慧隧道管理平台？
隧道施工与运营管理涉及人员出入、现场作业、环境监测、设备运行和应急处置等多个环节。若各类设备和业务系统分散建设，数据往往需要分别查看，管理人员难以及时掌握整体情况；出现异常后，信息传递、记录查询和后续跟进也容易不够顺畅。
智慧隧道管理平台的作用，是把现场感知设备、通信网络和管理业务连接起来，将分散的数据集中到统一界面。管理人员可按权限查看现场状态、告警信息和历史记录，并根据项目实际需要逐步配置功能，让平台不仅能“看数据”，也能辅助日常管理与问题跟进。
02 智慧隧道管理平台有哪些核心模块？

人员定位与门禁管理 对接人员定位、实名制门禁和车辆出入等设备，辅助查看进出洞记录及洞内人员分布。
安全步距与施工风险 展示安全步距及相关施工风险监测数据，可按项目管理规则配置异常提醒。
环境与设备监测 汇集气体、温湿度等环境数据和相关设备状态，便于查看实时信息、变化趋势及异常记录。
视频监控与智能识别 集中查看重点区域视频；具备相应设备和算法条件时，可按需求接入AI识别功能。
进度管理与工序协同 结合项目施工计划和现场业务数据，辅助跟踪关键工序、进度节点及相关管理任务。
数字孪生与综合大屏 结合隧道模型、里程、设备点位和业务数据进行可视化展示，支持项目集中查看与汇报。
03 平台如何打通现场数据与业务流程？
智慧隧道管理平台可按照“感知采集、网络传输、平台汇总、业务应用”的思路建设。前端可接入人员定位、门禁、视频监控、环境传感器和安全步距监测等设备，平台统一展示相关数据；结合项目需求配置告警规则、记录查询和统计报表。对于已有智慧工地或视频监控平台的项目，可先核对设备协议、接口和网络条件，再确定数据接入范围及实施计划。

• 数据集中看：人员、环境、设备、视频和告警信息统一展示，便于管理人员快速了解现场整体状态。
• 异常及时提醒：监测数据可按项目管理要求配置提醒条件，出现异常时提示相关人员核查处理。
• 记录查询有依据：平台可对已接入的监测数据、告警信息及处理记录进行保存，方便检查、追溯和复盘。
• 功能可以按需组合：根据隧道类型、施工阶段和预算安排分步建设，并为后续业务扩展预留空间。

05 哪些项目适合建设智慧隧道管理平台？
公路与高速公路隧道：可围绕施工安全、人员定位、安全步距、气体监测、视频监控和进度展示等需求进行配置，帮助项目部集中掌握施工现场情况。

选择智慧隧道管理平台时，建议先明确管理对象、使用人员和主要业务流程，再核对设备协议、数据接口、网络覆盖及告警规则。还要关注平台是否方便现场使用，能否提供方案设计、安装调试、操作培训和后续维护。系统建设不只是配置软件或大屏，更要让现场数据稳定接入、责任流程清楚、日常管理真正用得起来。
