title: A JSON state file ended in zeros after an unclean shutdown: quarantine it, then salvage every record you can
description:
Disclosure: I'm the developer of the tool described here, and this post was drafted and published by an AI agent from the project's source code. Relaymote is unofficial; not affiliated with or endorsed by Anthropic.

Relaymote (MIT, Node.js) is a phone remote for Claude Desktop's Code-tab sessions. It keeps its task list in one file, registry.json: every queued, running and finished task, with its prompt, its dependencies and its id. It is the kind of file nobody thinks about until the day JSON.parse throws on it.

That day came after an unclean shutdown. The file had its normal size, but the last stretch of it was NUL bytes. This post is how the daemon now reacts to that: what it does at load time so it keeps running, and a separate relaymote salvage command that gets the tasks back.

What the damage looks like

The writes were already done the textbook way: write a temp file, fsync it, rename it over the real one. That protects against a half-written file from your own process. It does not fully protect you from the machine losing power around the rename, depending on the file system and what had actually reached the disk. The result we saw was a file whose length had been recorded but whose last blocks never arrived, so they read back as zeros.

The useful observation is about where the damage sits. The front of the file is intact. The break is a clean cut somewhere near the end, followed by padding. Almost every record is still there; only the parser gives up, because one bad byte fails the whole document.

Part 1: at load time, quarantine and keep going

The loader must not crash the daemon, and it must not "fix" the file in place. It does three things when parsing fails:

const q = FILE + '.corrupt-' + Date.now();
if (fs.existsSync(FILE)) {
  fs.renameSync(FILE, q);
  process.stderr.write(`registry.json could not be read; moved it to ${q}. Recover its tasks with: relaymote salvage\n`);
}
  1. Rename, never delete. The damaged file is the only copy of those tasks. Moving it aside gives the daemon a clean slate and leaves the evidence untouched.
  2. Say what to do next in the same log line. The person reading it at 2 a.m. should not have to find the docs.
  3. Keep the id counter above the damage. Task ids are t0001, t0002, and so on. If the daemon starts empty with seq = 0, new tasks will reuse ids the salvage will later bring back. So before starting empty, it scans the raw text for every id and the old seq, and starts above the highest: 
let seq = 0;
for (const m of String(raw).matchAll(/"t(\d+)"\s*:|"seq"\s*:\s*(\d+)/g))
  seq = Math.max(seq, Number(m[1] || m[2]) || 0);

A regex over broken JSON is fine here: it only needs to find numbers, not understand structure. And the new floor is saved straight away, not at the next write, so a second crash cannot lose it.

One Windows detail sits in front of all this: a file another process is renaming into place can be briefly locked (EPERM, EBUSY, EACCES). That is not corruption. The loader retries the read a few times with a short back-off before it decides the file is unreadable, so a normal save from another process never gets the registry quarantined.

Part 2: salvage, from cheapest repair to most expensive

salvage(raw) is a pure function (the tests call it directly) that tries three repairs in order and reports which one worked:

1. Trim the padding. Strip trailing NULs and whitespace, then parse. If the cut happened to land after the closing brace, this is all it takes.

2. Close the document after the last complete record. The file is written with JSON.stringify(state, null, 2), so every task object ends with a newline and exactly four spaces before its }. Find the last "\n }," (or failing that "\n }"), cut there, and append the closing braces for tasks and the root:

const cut = s.lastIndexOf('\n    },');
const j = JSON.parse(s.slice(0, cut + '\n    }'.length) + '\n  }\n}');

This leans on your own serializer's indentation, which is a fair thing to lean on: you wrote it, and it is deterministic. Everything before the last complete task comes back; only the task that was being written at the cut is lost. Any fields that came after tasks in the root object are lost too, which is why seq is recomputed from the recovered ids.

3. Scan for individual records. If the damage is in the middle, closing the document will not parse. So find each "tNNNN": {, walk forward counting braces (tracking whether you are inside a string, and escapes inside strings, so a } in a prompt doesn't end the object early), and try JSON.parse on just that slice. A mangled stretch now costs only the records it touched.

If all three fail, it returns null and the command says NOTHING_RECOVERABLE along with the file size and how much of it was padding, which is usually the whole explanation.

Part 3: merge into the live file without clobbering anything

By the time someone runs salvage, the daemon has been running on an empty registry and may have created new tasks. The recovered tasks are merged in, with a few rules:

  • Live tasks keep their ids. A recovered task whose id is taken by a different live task gets the next free id. It is renumbered, never dropped, and the renumbering is printed.
  • Dependencies follow the renumbering. If recovered task t0040 depended on t0039, and t0039 was renumbered, the dependsOn list is rewritten to match.
  • Running it twice is harmless. Each task gets a fingerprint of its creation time and prompt. A recovered task whose fingerprint already exists under any id is counted as "already present", not added again.
  • Each restored task is tagged with the corrupt file it came from, so you can tell restored tasks from new ones later.
  • Dry run by default. Without --apply it only reports: method used, characters, padding, tasks recovered, how many would be added, how many are already present, the renumbering. With --apply it writes the merged registry with the same temp-file, fsync, rename sequence. It never modifies the corrupt file, so you can run it again.

What carries over

  • When a state file fails to parse, move it aside and keep running. Never repair in place, never delete.
  • Keep id counters above anything the damaged file mentions, and persist that floor immediately.
  • Treat a briefly locked file on Windows as "retry", not "corrupt".
  • Order repairs from cheapest to most expensive and report which one worked.
  • Your own serializer's formatting is a legitimate anchor for finding record boundaries.
  • Merges should renumber rather than overwrite, follow references, and be safe to repeat.

Relaymote is MIT-licensed: github.com/ashwarsadh/relaymote. The code is in lib/registry.js and lib/salvage.js. Unofficial; not affiliated with or endorsed by Anthropic.

title: Building a Clean REST API with Node.js and Express
description:
Building REST APIs is one of the most practical skills in backend development. Here’s a clean, minimal approach using Node.js and Express that I use as my starting point for most projects.

Setup
bash
mkdir rest-api && cd rest-api
npm init -y
npm install express

Project Structure
rest-api/
├── server.js
├── routes/
│ └── users.js
└── middleware/
└── errorHandler.js

Test Server
const express = require('express');
const userRoutes = require('./routes/users');
const errorHandler = require('./middleware/errorHandler');

const app = express();
const PORT = process.env.PORT || 3000;

app.use(express.json());
app.use('/api/users', userRoutes);
app.use(errorHandler);

app.listen(PORT, () => {
console.log(Server running on port ${PORT});
});

Routes with Validation
const express = require('express');
const router = express.Router();

let users = [];
let nextId = 1;

router.get('/', (req, res) => {
const { role } = req.query;
const filtered = role
? users.filter(u => u.role === role)
: users;
res.json(filtered);
});

router.get('/:id', (req, res) => {
const user = users.find(u => u.id === parseInt(req.params.id));
if (!user) return res.status(404).json({ error: 'User not found' });
res.json(user);
});

router.post('/', (req, res) => {
const { name, email, role } = req.body;
if (!name || !email) {
return res.status(400).json({ error: 'Name and email are required' });
}
const user = { id: nextId++, name, email, role: role || 'user' };
users.push(user);
res.status(201).json(user);
});

router.put('/:id', (req, res) => {
const user = users.find(u => u.id === parseInt(req.params.id));
if (!user) return res.status(404).json({ error: 'User not found' });
Object.assign(user, req.body);
res.json(user);
});

router.delete('/:id', (req, res) => {
const index = users.findIndex(u => u.id === parseInt(req.params.id));
if (index === -1) return res.status(404).json({ error: 'User not found' });
users.splice(index, 1);
res.status(204).send();
});

module.exports = router;

Error Handling Middleware
const errorHandler = (err, req, res, next) => {
console.error(err.stack);
res.status(err.status || 500).json({
error: err.message || 'Internal server error'
});
};

module.exports = errorHandler;

title: font-display: swap Fixes Invisible Text. It Also Shifts Your Layout.
description:
The ticket said "homepage CLS regressed after the rebrand." Nobody had touched the layout. Nobody had touched the images. The only diff in that deploy was a font swap — the body copy went from a system font to a licensed one, loaded from @font-face.

Lighthouse didn't care that the new font looked better. It saw text that painted in one spot, then jumped, and it scored that jump like it scores a banner ad shoving the article down the page.

The fix everyone reaches for here is font-display: swap. It was already set. That was the problem.

The belief: "swap" is the whole fix

Here's the belief, and it's not wrong, exactly: web fonts load over the network, and by default most browsers render nothing until the font arrives — the flash of invisible text, FOIT. You add font-display: swap to your @font-face rule, the browser paints your fallback font immediately, and swaps in the real font the moment it's ready. No more invisible text. Problem solved. Ship it.

@font-face {
  font-family: "Brand Sans";
  src: url("/fonts/brand-sans.woff2") format("woff2");
  font-display: swap;
}

That line is in a lot of style guides as the answer to font loading. It's treated as a toggle: FOIT off, done.

The crack: swap doesn't hide the font load. It just moves where you feel it.

font-display doesn't control whether the browser substitutes a fallback font — every strategy except block does that. What it controls is the timeline: how long the browser waits invisibly, and how long it's willing to keep showing the fallback before giving up on the real font for that paint. Per the spec, each value defines a block period and a swap period:

  • auto — browser's own default, usually close to block.
  • block — invisible for ~3s, then swap (classic FOIT).
  • swap — essentially no invisible period; show the fallback instantly, swap in whenever the real font lands (FOUT instead).
  • fallback — a brief invisible flash, a short swap window, then it commits to the fallback if the font's still not here.
  • optional — barely waits at all, and won't swap mid-visit on a slow connection; the real font may only show up on the next navigation, once it's cached.

Notice what none of those values promise: that the fallback font and the real font occupy the same pixels. swap guarantees a render happens fast. It says nothing about whether that render holds still when the second one replaces it.

Fonts aren't interchangeable rectangles. Two fonts at the same font-size can have wildly different x-heights, character widths, and line heights — a serif webfont next to Arial as a fallback is a common offender. When the swap happens, every line that used the fallback re-wraps or re-measures against the new metrics. Paragraphs reflow. Buttons that sat right under the headline jump down eight pixels. If that happens after the page has already settled — which, on a flaky connection, it will — it's an unexpected shift, and Cumulative Layout Shift counts every one of those against you.

🎮 Try it yourself

▶️ Open the interactive playground →

Runs right in your browser — poke at it and watch the concept react live.

So you didn't fix the font-loading problem. You moved it from "the user sees nothing" (bad, but at least static) to "the user sees something, then watches it move" (arguably worse, and it's the one Lighthouse actively measures).

Why the belief persists

Because swap usually looks fine in a quick check. If your fallback stack happens to be metrically close to your webfont — two similar sans-serifs, say — the shift is a pixel or two and nobody notices scrolling past it. It only becomes visible, and scoreable, when the fonts diverge more: a wide geometric sans swapped in over Helvetica, or a serif swapped in over system-ui. And most font-loading guides stop at "FOIT vs FOUT," because that's the part you can see with your eyes. CLS is the part a profiler tells you about, days later, in a Core Web Vitals report nobody opens until SEO flags it.

The better mental model: make the fallback lie convincingly

The fix isn't picking a different font-display value — swap was the right call. The fix is making the fallback font's box match the real font's box closely enough that swapping it out doesn't move anything. CSS Fonts Level 4 gives you the descriptors to do exactly that, declared on a second @font-face for your fallback, under its own name:

@font-face {
  font-family: "Brand Sans Fallback";
  src: local("Arial");
  size-adjust: 104%;
  ascent-override: 92%;
  descent-override: 24%;
  line-gap-override: 0%;
}

body {
  font-family: "Brand Sans", "Brand Sans Fallback", sans-serif;
}

size-adjust scales the fallback font's whole metrics uniformly; ascent-override, descent-override, and line-gap-override tune the vertical metrics that drive line-box height independently. Get them close to the webfont's own metrics, and the fallback occupies almost exactly the same footprint — so when the real font swaps in, nothing reflows. The text might still change shape slightly, but the layout holds still, which is what CLS actually measures.

Nobody tunes these four numbers by hand from a font's metadata — that's what tools like Capsize or the automatic fallback generation in next/font exist for. The point isn't to memorize the math; it's to know this is a solved, declarative problem, not a "pick a better font-display value" problem.

Two more pieces worth knowing once you're here:

  • document.fonts.ready is a promise that resolves once the document's font set has finished loading — useful when you're doing something that depends on final text metrics, like measuring a canvas-rendered label, and need to know the swap has already happened.
  • font-display: optional is the right call, not a worse one, for anything where showing a font instantly matters more than showing the font eventually — a above-the-fold hero on a page where first paint speed outranks brand fidelity. It trades "might never show the webfont this visit" for "will never cause a mid-visit shift."

When plain swap is still fine

Don't go tune override descriptors on every @font-face in the project. It's unnecessary when:

  • Your fallback and webfont are metrically close already (most humanist sans-serif webfonts over system-ui shift by a pixel or less).
  • The text is small and short — a button label has little room to reflow even with a metrics mismatch.
  • The font is almost always cached before paint (self-hosted, preloaded, same-origin, repeat visitor) — there's rarely a visible swap to cause a shift in the first place.

Reach for the fallback-matching technique where the shift is visible and the element is large: headlines, hero copy, anything above the fold that Lighthouse measures in its first few seconds.

🧠 Test yourself

Think it clicked? Take the 7-question quiz →

Instant feedback, a hint on every question, and an explanation for each answer — right or wrong.

The lesson

font-display: swap answers "does the user see text immediately?" It was never an answer to "does the page stay still when the real font shows up?" — that's a layout question, and layout questions get layout answers: matched metrics, not a different loading strategy.

Next time CLS regresses right after a font swap and nobody touched the CSS, you'll know exactly where to look. What's the worst "nobody touched the layout" regression you've chased down to a font? I'll start in the comments.

title: Your AI Agent Will Retry. Your Booking System Will Not Notice.
description:
Letting an agent write to a legacy system of record takes an intent log, not a better prompt.

The agent calls create_booking. The legacy API takes 31 seconds and the HTTP client times out. The orchestrator retries the step. The second call succeeds, and the customer now holds two reservations and a confused confirmation email. The prompt was fine. The model was fine. Nothing in the stack knew that the first call had actually gone through.

Every agent pilot we look at passes its demo on read-only tools: search, lookup, summarize. The trouble starts with the first tool that changes state. Booking, order entry, ticket creation, ERP postings. That is the write path, and it needs the same engineering you would give a payment flow.

An agent has three retry layers, and the legacy system sees all of them

The first layer is the HTTP client. Most SDKs retry on connection errors and 5xx responses by default. The second is the orchestrator. Whether you use LangGraph, Temporal, a queue worker, or a loop you wrote yourself, a failed step gets re-run, and a redelivered message gets processed twice. At-least-once delivery is the default contract of nearly every queue you will use.

The third layer is unique to agents. The model reads a timeout or an ambiguous response, decides the action probably failed, and calls the tool again. This retry is not byte-identical to the first. The arguments may differ in small ways: "adults": 2 versus "adults": "two", a date in a different format, an extra optional field. An idempotency key derived from the raw request body will not catch it.

Stripe popularized client-supplied idempotency keys for exactly this problem, and they work well when the downstream system honors them. Many systems of record do not. SOAP interfaces, batch-file ERPs, and older reservation backends often have no idempotency concept at all. Some will happily create a duplicate and return a fresh ID each time.

A timeout is not a failure, and your agent needs to be told that

The most damaging bug in these systems is a tool wrapper that turns a timeout into the string "Error: request failed". The model reads that as a failure and does what a helpful assistant does: it tries again.

The honest state after a timeout is unknown. The request may have been rejected, may still be queued, or may have committed. Treat it as a fourth outcome next to success, rejection, and error. The agent should receive "outcome pending, do not retry" and a reconciler should find out what happened.

We apply the same discipline to our own internal tooling. Our outreach pipeline runs agents that draft and schedule emails, and the sender records a marker per lead and per email step, checked before every send. The agent never decides whether an email already went out. A file on disk does. The mechanism is almost embarrassingly low-tech, and it has survived crashed runs and re-triggered cron jobs because the check lives outside the model. Production systems need the same property with a stronger store behind it.

Put an intent log between the model and the legacy API

The pattern is small. The agent never calls the legacy system directly. It calls a tool wrapper that writes an intent row to Postgres and returns. A separate worker executes intents against the downstream system.

CREATE TABLE tool_intents (
  intent_key   text PRIMARY KEY,
  run_id       uuid NOT NULL,
  tool         text NOT NULL,
  args         jsonb NOT NULL,
  state        text NOT NULL
               CHECK (state IN ('pending','sent','confirmed','rejected','unknown')),
  external_ref text,
  created_at   timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  updated_at   timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
);

The key is computed from business intent, not from the request:

const parsed = BookingArgs.parse(rawArgs);        // zod: "two" becomes 2, dates become ISO
const intentKey = sha256([run.id, 'create_booking', stableStringify(parsed)].join('|'));

const res = await db.query(
  `INSERT INTO tool_intents (intent_key, run_id, tool, args, state)
   VALUES ($1, $2, 'create_booking', $3, 'pending')
   ON CONFLICT (intent_key) DO NOTHING
   RETURNING intent_key`,
  [intentKey, run.id, parsed],
);

if (res.rowCount === 0) return loadPriorResult(intentKey); // same intent, same answer

Schema validation does the normalization work. Once the model's arguments have been coerced into a strict type, two retries that mean the same thing hash to the same key, and the second insert hits the primary key and returns the earlier result. If a run can legitimately perform the same action twice, add the plan step or line item ID to the hash so the two intents differ on purpose.

The worker claims rows with SELECT ... FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED, which lets several workers drain the table without double-claiming. Writing the intent and enqueuing the work is one transaction, which is the transactional outbox pattern. Before it calls the legacy API, it writes the intent key into whatever free-text reference field the system offers. Almost every booking or ERP interface has one.

Reconcile unknowns by reading, never by writing again

When the worker's call times out, the intent moves to unknown. A reconciler job then queries the legacy system for a record carrying that reference. If it finds one, the intent becomes confirmed with the external ID. If nothing appears after a defined window, it becomes rejected and can be retried safely under the same key, because the reconciler has verified that nothing exists.

Meanwhile the agent sees a structured result such as {"status":"pending","intent":"..."}. A model told that a booking is pending will tell the customer it is being processed. A model told that a call failed will try something else.

Split the dangerous tools in two

Give the model hold_booking and confirm_booking instead of one create_booking. A hold carries a TTL and expires on its own, so a wrong hold costs nothing. Confirmation is the irreversible step, and it can sit behind a policy check, an amount threshold, or a human approval click. Our own outreach pipeline works this way: agents draft freely, and a person approves before the first email to a new contact goes out.

This split also gives you a clean place to enforce limits. The model can propose a thousand holds. Only a bounded number can ever become confirmations.

What it takes to build

None of this needs an ML team. It is Postgres, a worker process, schema validation, and a reconciler, which makes it a solid fit for one senior backend engineer working in NestJS or Python and owning the integration boundary. The unglamorous parts, such as the reconciler and the monitoring on unknown intents, decide whether the agent can be trusted with real customers. Teams under funding pressure tend to postpone them until the first duplicate order arrives.

Key Takeaways

  • Agents retry at three layers: HTTP client, orchestrator, and the model itself. Only the first two are visible in your logs.
  • Treat a timeout as unknown, tell the model "pending, do not retry", and resolve the state by reading the downstream system.
  • Derive idempotency keys from validated, normalized business arguments, not from raw request bodies or LLM-generated call IDs.
  • Route every state-changing tool through an intent table in Postgres, with a worker and a reconciler between the model and the system of record.
  • Split irreversible actions into a cheap, expiring hold and a gated confirmation.

title: DPDP Engineering Checklist: 10 Steps to Protect Personal Data
description:
Introduction
India's Digital Personal Data Protection (DPDP) Act, 2023, and the DPDP Rules, 2025, make personal data protection an important consideration for businesses building and operating digital applications.

For engineering teams, preparing for DPDP requirements involves more than updating privacy policies. It requires examining how personal data is collected, processed, stored, accessed, and shared across an application's architecture.

Consider a typical product workflow. A customer enters their phone number into an application. The backend processes the request, an analytics service records the event, and an error-monitoring tool captures request details during debugging. The primary database may be secure, but the same personal information could now exist in several other systems.

This creates an important engineering challenge: protecting personal data throughout its lifecycle, not just where it is originally stored.

Developers, DevOps engineers, security teams, and engineering managers need to understand where personal data flows, which services can access it, how long it is retained, and what happens when a user exercises an applicable data protection right.

A practical DPDP engineering checklist helps teams identify gaps, assign responsibilities, and build appropriate safeguards into everyday development workflows.

This article covers ten areas to review when preparing applications for DPDP requirements, including data mapping, purpose limitation, consent management, PII protection, access control, application logs, deletion workflows, third-party integrations, breach response, and privacy testing.

For a broader overview of how data protection controls fit into application architecture, see Securelytix's guide to DPDP and AI workflows.
The DPDP Engineering Checklist

  1. Map Personal Data Across Your Application You cannot protect personal data effectively without knowing where it goes.

Start by identifying the personal data your application collects, including names, email addresses, phone numbers, identity details, and other information that can identify an individual. Then trace how that information moves between application components and external services.

Engineering checklist:

  • Identify personal data collected by every application and API.
  • Map data flows between frontend services, backend systems, and databases.
  • Identify copies in caches, message queues, analytics platforms, and backups.
  • Document which internal services and third-party vendors can access personal data.
  • Review AI workflows, including prompts, tool calls, and retrieval systems.
  • Maintain an up-to-date data inventory and data flow diagram. These practices help engineering teams understand where personal information is processed and where additional security controls may be necessary.
  • Apply Purpose Limitation and Data Minimisation Collecting more information than a product needs increases the amount of data that must be protected. The DPDP framework addresses processing for lawful purposes and limits personal data processing to what is necessary for the specified purpose.

Engineering checklist:

  • Collect only the personal data required for the intended purpose.
  • Avoid returning unnecessary personal fields from APIs.
  • Remove redundant personal information from event payloads.
  • Review whether analytics systems need identifiable customer data.
  • Define retention periods and implement appropriate deletion processes. For example, an order-status API may only need an order ID and delivery status. Returning the customer's complete address, phone number, and payment details increases exposure without necessarily improving functionality.

Data minimisation should be considered during API design, database modelling, and product development rather than added after deployment.

  1. Build Consent and Privacy Controls Into the Application Consent management should not be limited to a checkbox or banner on the frontend. Where consent is the applicable basis for processing, the backend and connected services must handle consent status and withdrawal appropriately.

Engineering checklist:

  • Present clear privacy notices explaining the purpose of data collection.
  • Record consent and relevant changes in an auditable manner.
  • Connect consent status to systems that process personal data.
  • Implement workflows for withdrawing consent.
  • Support applicable requests for access, correction, erasure, and grievance redressal. Test these controls across APIs, background jobs, and third-party integrations, not just the user interface. A withdrawal option is ineffective if downstream services continue processing data without an applicable legal basis.
  • Protect PII With Appropriate Security Controls Rule 6 of the DPDP Rules, 2025, addresses reasonable security safeguards for protecting personal data. Engineering teams should evaluate security controls according to the sensitivity of the information, the application's architecture, and the risks involved.

Engineering checklist:

  • Encrypt personal data in transit and at rest.
  • Apply masking or redaction when original values are unnecessary.
  • Evaluate tokenization for sensitive fields used across services.
  • Restrict access to encryption keys and systems holding original data.
  • Test safeguards against unauthorised access and data exposure. For example, an internal service may need to identify a customer without receiving their actual phone number. Tokenization can replace the original value with a token while keeping the mapping in a separately protected system.

PII tokenization is one approach to reducing unnecessary exposure of original personal information across application workflows. The original values remain protected in a controlled vault while supported systems can work with tokenized representations.

Important: Tokenization is one possible security measure, not a complete DPDP compliance solution. Its effectiveness depends on implementation, access controls, and protection of the original data.

  1. Enforce Access Control Across Services Personal data should only be accessible to authorised users and services for legitimate purposes. Even a well-protected database can expose information if an API returns unnecessary fields or a service account has excessive privileges.

Engineering checklist:

  • Apply role-based access control (RBAC) or attribute-based access control (ABAC) where appropriate.
  • Follow the principle of least privilege for employees and service accounts.
  • Restrict access to production databases and sensitive endpoints.
  • Secure service-to-service communication.
  • Review permissions regularly and revoke unnecessary access. Access controls should cover internal APIs, cloud infrastructure, data pipelines, and third-party integrations. Review them whenever application responsibilities or system permissions change.

For an example of how tokenization, controlled data access, and auditability can work together, see Securelytix's security architecture.

  1. Prevent Personal Data Leaks Through Logs and AI Workflows Application logs, traces, and monitoring tools can unintentionally collect personal information during routine debugging. AI workflows introduce additional risks when applications send customer details to model providers, external tools, or retrieval systems.

Engineering checklist:

  • Avoid logging raw request bodies containing personal data.
  • Redact sensitive fields before sending events to monitoring platforms.
  • Review information captured in traces and error reports.
  • Minimise personal data included in AI prompts and tool calls.
  • Restrict access to vector databases, cached responses, and conversation histories.
  • Review third-party data retention and deletion practices. Engineering principle: Protect personal data before it reaches a downstream system.

For AI-enabled applications, this means considering the entire request path, from the application backend to model providers, agent tools, logs, and retrieval systems.

A data privacy vault is one architectural approach for keeping original sensitive values separate from the representations used by downstream services.

Shared middleware, API gateways, and reusable data-handling libraries can help enforce these controls consistently across applications.

  1. Establish Data Retention and Deletion Workflows Deleting a record from the primary database does not guarantee that every copy has been removed. Personal data may remain in caches, search indexes, exports, backups, or third-party systems.

Engineering checklist:

  • Define retention periods based on processing purposes and applicable legal obligations.
  • Automate deletion when required conditions are met.
  • Propagate relevant deletion requests to downstream systems.
  • Define how expired data is handled in backups and archives.
  • Maintain appropriate evidence of completed deletion workflows. The DPDP framework addresses erasure subject to applicable legal requirements and exceptions. Engineering teams should therefore design deletion as a coordinated workflow rather than relying on a single database operation.
  • Secure Third-Party Processors and Integrations Modern applications rely on cloud platforms, payment gateways, analytics tools, and external APIs. Sharing personal data with these services creates additional risks that engineering teams must account for.

Under Section 8 of the DPDP Act, a Data Fiduciary remains responsible for compliance with the Act in respect of processing undertaken by it or on its behalf. Engagement of a Data Processor must also be supported by a valid contract.

Engineering checklist:

  • Maintain an inventory of vendors processing personal data.
  • Review vendor security controls and data-handling practices.
  • Ensure relevant contracts address applicable security requirements.
  • Restrict the personal data shared with each integration.
  • Establish processes for vendor incidents and data deletion. Avoid sending complete customer records to third-party services when only a few fields are necessary. Review integrations whenever vendors, data flows, or processing purposes change.
  • Prepare for Personal Data Breaches Even well-designed security controls cannot eliminate every risk. Engineering teams need an incident response process to identify potential breaches, investigate their impact, and coordinate the required notifications.

Engineering checklist:

  • Configure alerts for suspicious access and potential data exposure.
  • Define incident ownership and escalation procedures.
  • Preserve evidence and investigate affected systems and data.
  • Establish procedures for required notifications to affected individuals and the Data Protection Board of India.
  • Conduct incident response simulations to identify gaps. The DPDP Rules, 2025, prescribe personal data breach notification requirements. Engineering teams should map their response procedures to the applicable timelines and requirements rather than relying on informal internal reporting.
  • Integrate Privacy Testing Into the Development Lifecycle Privacy safeguards can break when developers introduce new APIs, features, integrations, or infrastructure changes. A one-time security review cannot account for every future change.

Engineering checklist:

  • Include personal data exposure scenarios in code reviews.
  • Test access controls, masking, and deletion behaviour.
  • Avoid using real personal data in development and testing environments unless appropriately justified and protected.
  • Review data flows before deploying new integrations.
  • Reassess safeguards after significant architectural changes.
  • Incorporate privacy-related tests into CI/CD pipelines where practical. Automated checks can help detect accidental exposure, unauthorised access, and regressions before new code reaches production. Turn the DPDP Engineering Checklist Into Action A checklist becomes useful when each item has an owner, a defined implementation plan, and a way to verify completion.

Begin by mapping personal data flows, then prioritise risks such as excessive collection, uncontrolled access, exposed logs, and unnecessary third-party sharing. Assign responsibilities across application engineering, DevOps, security, and product teams.

Track each control using a simple status:

  • Not Started
  • In Progress
  • Verified Maintain evidence such as data flow diagrams, access reviews, test results, and deletion records.

Revisit the checklist as the application evolves. Privacy protection should be part of the development lifecycle, not a final approval step before release.
Conclusion
Preparing for DPDP compliance requires more than updating privacy policies. Engineering teams need visibility into personal data flows, appropriate security safeguards, controlled access, reliable deletion workflows, and tested incident response procedures.

This DPDP engineering checklist provides a practical starting point for identifying gaps and strengthening application-level data protection. Use it alongside legal and privacy reviews to assess your organisation's obligations under India's DPDP Act, 2023, and DPDP Rules, 2025.

For teams exploring ways to reduce unnecessary exposure of sensitive information across applications, APIs, and AI workflows, Securelytix VaultKey provides a technical approach based on tokenization and secure data vaulting.

Disclaimer: This article provides general engineering guidance, not legal advice or a guarantee of DPDP compliance.

title: Bitrix24 REST API in Practice: Webhooks, Batch Calls and Rate Limits
description:
The Bitrix24 REST API looks simple on day one. You create an inbound webhook, call crm.deal.list, get JSON back and the prototype works. The trouble starts on the first bulk sync, when a few thousand records need to move and the portal answers with QUERY_LIMIT_EXCEEDED, or a week later, when someone notices that deals updated over the weekend never reached the warehouse system.

This post collects what we have learned building exchanges between Bitrix24 and external systems: how the two kinds of webhooks behave, how to use batch without shooting yourself in the foot, how the rate limits actually work, and the handful of field-level quirks that cause silent data corruption.

Two kinds of webhooks, two different jobs

Bitrix24 uses the word "webhook" for two unrelated things.

Inbound webhook. A URL with a secret embedded in it that lets your code call REST methods on behalf of a specific user:

https://yourcompany.bitrix24.kz/rest/1/x7k2abc9def0ghij/crm.deal.get.json?id=42

The 1 is the user ID, the next segment is the secret. Everything this URL does runs with that user's permissions and is limited to the scopes you ticked when creating it (crm, user, task and so on). Two practical consequences:

  • Create a dedicated technical user for integrations. If the webhook belongs to a sales manager who later leaves the company and gets deactivated, the integration dies with their account.
  • Grant the minimum scopes. The URL is a bearer credential. It ends up in logs, environment files and occasionally in screenshots sent to a chat.

Outbound webhook (event handler). Bitrix24 sends a POST to your URL when something happens: ONCRMDEALADD, ONCRMDEALUPDATE, ONCRMCONTACTDELETE and many more. The body is form-encoded, not JSON, and looks roughly like this once parsed:

event=ONCRMDEALUPDATE
data[FIELDS][ID]=1287
ts=1761712345
auth[domain]=yourcompany.bitrix24.kz
auth[application_token]=k4q9...

Notice what is missing: the deal itself. You get an ID and nothing else. Your handler has to call crm.deal.get to find out what changed, which means every event costs at least one API request.

A minimal handler in Python (Flask) that does the right things:

import os
from flask import Flask, request, abort
from queue_client import enqueue  # Redis, RabbitMQ, a DB table, anything durable

app = Flask(__name__)
APP_TOKEN = os.environ["B24_APP_TOKEN"]

@app.post("/b24/events")
def b24_event():
    form = request.form
    if form.get("auth[application_token]") != APP_TOKEN:
        abort(403)

    event = form.get("event")
    entity_id = form.get("data[FIELDS][ID]")
    if not event or not entity_id:
        abort(400)

    enqueue({"event": event, "id": int(entity_id), "ts": form.get("ts")})
    return "", 200

Three rules are baked in here:

  1. Check application_token. The handler URL is public; without the check anyone can push fake events.
  2. Do not call the API inside the handler. Acknowledge fast and queue the work. A slow or failing handler loses events, and Bitrix24 keeps no replay log for you.
  3. Store only the ID. By the time the worker runs, the deal may have changed again, and you want the latest state anyway.

Events are a hint, not a guarantee

Treat outbound events as "something probably changed, go look". Deliveries get lost during your downtime, network blips or a deploy that broke the route. Two mitigations we use together:

  • Offline events. For applications, Bitrix24 can store events on its side; you pull them with event.offline.get and confirm processing. Push becomes pull and survives your downtime.
  • A periodic reconciliation pass. Every N minutes, request entities with DATE_MODIFY after your last checkpoint and run them through the same worker. Cheap, and it catches whatever the event stream dropped.

The echo loop

If your integration writes back to the same entity it listens to, you will create a loop: you update deal 1287, Bitrix24 fires ONCRMDEALUPDATE, your worker fetches it, sees a "change", pushes it to the external system, which pushes a status back, which updates the deal again.

Break it explicitly. Options that work:

  • Compare a hash of the fields you care about with the last hash you synced. If nothing relevant changed, stop.
  • Check MODIFY_BY_ID (or updatedBy in crm.item.*) and ignore changes made by your technical integration user.
  • Write a sync marker into a custom field, but only if the business is fine with an extra field on the card.

The first option is the most robust, because it also filters out updates that touched fields you do not sync.

batch: up to 50 calls in one request

batch takes a set of named commands and executes them on the server in one HTTP round trip. The limit is 50 commands per batch.

import requests

WEBHOOK = "https://yourcompany.bitrix24.kz/rest/1/x7k2abc9def0ghij/"

def call(method, params=None):
    r = requests.post(WEBHOOK + method + ".json", json=params or {}, timeout=30)
    data = r.json()  # read the body even on 503: the error code says which limit you hit
    if "error" in data:
        raise RuntimeError(f"{data['error']}: {data.get('error_description')}")
    return data

cmd = {
    f"d{deal_id}": f"crm.deal.get?id={deal_id}"
    for deal_id in [101, 102, 103]
}
resp = call("batch", {"halt": 0, "cmd": cmd})
results = resp["result"]["result"]        # successful commands
errors = resp["result"]["result_error"]   # failed commands, keyed the same way

Things to know before relying on it:

Check result_error every time. With halt: 0 the batch continues past failures, and the top level of the response looks successful. A batch of 50 updates where 7 failed returns HTTP 200. If you only read result, those 7 are lost silently.

halt: 1 is not a transaction. It stops at the first error, but the commands that already ran are not rolled back. There are no transactions in the REST API. Design updates so that re-running them is safe.

Commands are query strings. Each value in cmd is a URL-encoded string, not JSON. Hand-built strings break on &, = or Cyrillic. Use an encoder for PHP-style nested arrays (fields[TITLE]=..., filter[>ID]=...); plain urlencode on a nested dict gets it wrong.

Results can feed later commands. You can reference an earlier result inside the same batch:

cmd = {
    "contact": "crm.contact.add?fields[NAME]=Aigerim&fields[PHONE][0][VALUE]=%2B77001234567&fields[PHONE][0][VALUE_TYPE]=WORK",
    "deal": "crm.deal.add?fields[TITLE]=Order%20123&fields[CONTACT_ID]=$result[contact]",
}

Handy, but it makes the batch order-dependent and harder to retry. We use it for create-and-link pairs and avoid it everywhere else.

A batch is one request for the rate limiter, but not free. It counts as one hit against the request frequency limit, but every command inside still consumes server execution time, which is limited separately (see below). Fifty heavy list calls with complex filters in one batch can exhaust the time budget faster than fifty simple get calls spread over a minute.

How the rate limits actually work

There are two independent limits, and integrations usually discover them in this order.

1. Request frequency: a leaky bucket

Each portal has a request counter that behaves like a leaky bucket. Requests fill it, and it drains at a fixed rate per second. While the bucket has room, requests go through instantly. When it is full, you get HTTP 503 with error QUERY_LIMIT_EXCEEDED. The common published figures are a drain rate of 2 requests per second with a burst capacity of 50 on standard plans, and higher values on top plans and on-premise installations. Check the current numbers for your plan, they have changed over the years.

A script firing 200 requests in a tight loop gets the first 50 through, then hits errors, and a naive retry loop only adds more requests. The fix is a client-side limiter that mirrors the server's bucket, plus backoff when the server disagrees:

import time, random, threading

class LeakyBucket:
    def __init__(self, rate=2.0, capacity=50):
        self.rate, self.capacity = rate, capacity
        self.level, self.last = 0.0, time.monotonic()
        self.lock = threading.Lock()

    def acquire(self):
        while True:
            with self.lock:
                now = time.monotonic()
                self.level = max(0.0, self.level - (now - self.last) * self.rate)
                self.last = now
                if self.level + 1 <= self.capacity:
                    self.level += 1
                    return
                wait = (self.level + 1 - self.capacity) / self.rate
            time.sleep(wait)

bucket = LeakyBucket(rate=1.8, capacity=40)  # stay below the real limit

def call_limited(method, params=None, attempts=6):
    for attempt in range(attempts):
        bucket.acquire()
        try:
            return call(method, params)
        except RuntimeError as e:
            if "QUERY_LIMIT_EXCEEDED" not in str(e) and "OPERATION_TIME_LIMIT" not in str(e):
                raise
        time.sleep(min(60, 2 ** attempt) + random.random())
    raise RuntimeError(f"{method}: rate limited after {attempts} attempts")

Two details matter. The limiter runs below the real limit, because telephony, marketplace apps and other scripts share the same bucket. And it must be shared across workers: four processes with their own in-memory bucket send four times the allowed rate. Beyond one process, keep the counter in Redis.

2. Execution time per method

Newer versions of the platform also limit how much server time a single method may consume over a sliding window. Responses carry a time block, with fields such as operating and operating_reset_at telling you how much time the method has used. When a method exceeds its budget, it is blocked for a while with OPERATION_TIME_LIMIT, while other methods keep working.

This bites bulk exports. crm.deal.list filtering on a custom field with a large select is expensive, and a loop of them eats the budget. Log the time block during test runs to see which calls are heavy before production does.

Pagination that does not get slower on every page

List methods return 50 records per page with next and total. The obvious loop passes start=0, 50, 100.... On large tables this degrades, because the server still counts and offsets through everything before your page, and it also computes total on every call.

The faster pattern: sort by ID, filter by >ID from the last record you saw, and pass start=-1 to turn off the count.

def iter_deals(select):
    last_id = 0
    while True:
        resp = call_limited("crm.deal.list", {
            "order": {"ID": "ASC"},
            "filter": {">ID": last_id},
            "select": select,
            "start": -1,
        })
        rows = resp["result"]
        if not rows:
            return
        yield from rows
        last_id = int(rows[-1]["ID"])

Each request is now an indexed range scan, and page 2,000 costs the same as page 1. On exports of hundreds of thousands of records this decides whether the job finishes overnight at all.

Always pass select. Without it you get the default field set, which excludes custom UF_CRM_* fields, and you will wonder why they are empty. With ["*", "UF_*"] you get everything, which is expensive. List the fields you need.

Field-level pitfalls

These do not throw errors. They corrupt data quietly.

Multi-fields append by default. PHONE, EMAIL, WEB and IM are arrays of {ID, VALUE, VALUE_TYPE}. If you call crm.contact.update with PHONE: [{"VALUE": "+77001234567"}], the number is added, not replaced. Run that on every sync and a contact collects fifty copies of the same phone. To change a value, pass the existing item's ID; to delete one, pass its ID with an empty VALUE.

Two naming conventions. crm.deal.* uses UPPER_SNAKE (STAGE_ID, ASSIGNED_BY_ID). The newer universal crm.item.* methods with entityTypeId (2 for deals, 3 for contacts, 4 for companies, plus IDs for smart processes) use camelCase (stageId, assignedById) and wrap results in item or items. Mixing them in one codebase leads to fields that are "set" but never saved. Pick one family per entity and stick to it.

Stage IDs depend on the pipeline. In the default pipeline a stage is NEW or WON; in additional pipelines it becomes C3:NEW, C3:WON, where 3 is the category ID. Hardcoding WON works until sales creates a second pipeline.

Dates come with a timezone offset. Values look like 2026-10-29T11:00:00+05:00. Parse them as aware datetimes. Comparing them as strings or stripping the offset produces off-by-hours bugs in checkpoints, which means missed or duplicated records in reconciliation.

List fields store IDs, not labels. A custom enum field returns "45", not "Wholesale". Load the field definitions with crm.deal.userfield.list once and map both ways.

What to log

Log method, entity ID, direction, duration, the time block, the error code and a correlation ID linking event, queue job and API call. Add one alert on the age of the oldest unprocessed job. Integrations rarely crash; they drift until the numbers stop matching a week later.

Checklist

  • Dedicated technical user, minimal webhook scopes
  • Event handler: token check, enqueue, return 200
  • Reconciliation pass by DATE_MODIFY to catch lost events
  • Echo-loop protection by field hash or author check
  • batch with result_error checked on every call
  • Shared client-side limiter below the published rate, backoff on 503
  • >ID pagination with start=-1 and explicit select
  • Multi-fields updated by ID, stage IDs resolved per pipeline
  • Logs with timing data and an alert on queue age

The REST API itself is the same for cloud and on-premise portals; only authorisation and access setup differ, so these patterns carry over. If you would rather hand the exchange to a team that builds queues, retries and monitoring into every project, here is how we approach Bitrix24 REST API integration with warehouse, logistics and banking systems.

  • Also by me: Thinking in Go (2-book series) — Complete Guide to Go Programming + Hexagonal Architecture in Go
  • My project: Hermes IDE | GitHub — an IDE for developers who ship with Claude Code and other AI coding tools
  • Me: xgabriel.com | GitHub

SQLite on a production server stopped being a stunt a while ago. Rails 8 shipped with SQLite-backed adapters for its cache, its job queue and Action Cable, and the Rails team says there are "thousands of installations" of Campfire and Writebook running on SQLite. The SQLite authors themselves say a site with fewer than 100K hits a day should be fine, and call that figure conservative.

Then you add a second worker process. Then a cron job. Then a queue consumer. Four processes write to the same file, and the logs fill with database is locked.

That message is SQLITE_BUSY, and almost every fix you will find online is one of three settings: WAL mode, a busy timeout, or BEGIN IMMEDIATE. Most posts hand you all three at once. This one turns them on one at a time with a script you can run, so you can see which setting removes which failure. The third one matters most, and it is the one people skip.

Why four writers is enough

SQLite allows one writer at a time per database file. That is by design. The docs say most write transactions take milliseconds, so multiple writers can take turns. The question is what a writer does when it is not its turn.

In the default rollback-journal mode (journal_mode=DELETE), the locking model has readers holding SHARED locks, one would-be writer holding a RESERVED lock, and the actual write to the file needing an EXCLUSIVE lock that can only be taken once every SHARED lock is gone. So in this mode, readers block the commit of a writer.

When a connection can't get the lock it needs, SQLite returns SQLITE_BUSY (primary code 5, per the result-code docs). With no busy timeout set, it returns it right away. node:sqlite defaults the timeout to 0 milliseconds. So the first collision is a thrown error.


SQLite lets one writer through at a time. The settings below decide whether the others wait or fail.

The script: four writers, four setups

The script below uses only Node's built-in node:sqlite. The timeout option it relies on was added in Node v22.16.0 and v24.0.0, so use one of those or newer. It forks N child processes. Each runs a read-modify-write transaction in a loop: read a counter, write the counter plus one, commit. That shape (read first, write second) is what most real application code does: check a balance, then debit it; check stock, then reserve it.

// contend.mjs
// usage: node contend.mjs <setup> [writers] [txns]
import { DatabaseSync } from 'node:sqlite';
import { fork } from 'node:child_process';
import { rmSync } from 'node:fs';

const FILE = 'contend.db';
const SETUPS = {
  rollback: { wal: false, timeout: 0, begin: 'BEGIN' },
  wal: { wal: true, timeout: 0, begin: 'BEGIN' },
  'wal-timeout': { wal: true, timeout: 5000, begin: 'BEGIN' },
  'wal-immediate': {
    wal: true, timeout: 5000, begin: 'BEGIN IMMEDIATE',
  },
};

const args = process.argv.slice(2);
const name = args[0] ?? 'rollback';
const setup = SETUPS[name];
if (!setup) throw new Error(`unknown setup: ${name}`);
const WRITERS = Number(args[1] ?? 4);
const TXNS = Number(args[2] ?? 500);

// errcode is the extended code; the low 8 bits are the primary
const isBusy = (err) => (err.errcode & 0xff) === 5;

function writer() {
  const db = new DatabaseSync(FILE, { timeout: setup.timeout });
  const read = db.prepare(
    'SELECT value FROM counter WHERE id = 1');
  const write = db.prepare(
    'UPDATE counter SET value = ? WHERE id = 1');
  let ok = 0, busy = 0, snapshot = 0;
  for (let i = 0; i < TXNS; i++) {
    try {
      db.exec(setup.begin);
      const { value } = read.get();
      write.run(value + 1);
      db.exec('COMMIT');
      ok++;
    } catch (err) {
      if (!isBusy(err)) throw err;
      busy++;
      if (err.errcode === 517) snapshot++;
      try { db.exec('ROLLBACK'); } catch {}
    }
  }
  db.close();
  process.send({ ok, busy, snapshot });
}

function spawn() {
  return new Promise((resolve, reject) => {
    const child = fork(import.meta.filename, args, {
      env: { ...process.env, CONTEND_WORKER: '1' },
    });
    child.once('message', resolve);
    child.once('error', reject);
    child.once('exit', (code) => {
      if (code) reject(new Error(`writer exited ${code}`));
    });
  });
}

async function main() {
  for (const ext of ['', '-wal', '-shm', '-journal']) {
    rmSync(FILE + ext, { force: true });
  }
  const db = new DatabaseSync(FILE);
  if (setup.wal) db.exec('PRAGMA journal_mode = WAL');
  db.exec(`CREATE TABLE counter
    (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, value INTEGER NOT NULL);
    INSERT INTO counter VALUES (1, 0);`);
  db.close();

  const results = await Promise.all(
    Array.from({ length: WRITERS }, spawn));
  const sum = (k) => results.reduce((a, r) => a + r[k], 0);

  const check = new DatabaseSync(FILE);
  const { value } = check
    .prepare('SELECT value FROM counter WHERE id = 1').get();
  check.close();
  console.log({
    setup: name,
    attempted: WRITERS * TXNS,
    committed: sum('ok'),
    busy: sum('busy'),
    busySnapshot: sum('snapshot'),
    counter: value,
  });
}

if (process.env.CONTEND_WORKER === '1') writer();
else await main();

Run it four times:

node contend.mjs rollback
node contend.mjs wal
node contend.mjs wal-timeout
node contend.mjs wal-immediate

The counts depend on disk speed, core count and scheduling, so this post doesn't print numbers. Two lines in the output are there to check your reading of it. counter must equal committed in every setup: SQLite never loses an update, it refuses one. And busySnapshot counts extended code 517, SQLITE_BUSY_SNAPSHOT, which only appears in WAL mode and is the clue to the third setup.

A note on naming: in Node v26.11.0 DatabaseSync was renamed to Database, with the old name kept as a documentation-only deprecated alias. The script uses DatabaseSync so it runs on the 22 and 24 lines too.

What each setup changes

rollback. The default journal, no timeout. Every collision is a thrown SQLITE_BUSY: a writer can't take the RESERVED lock because another writer has it, or can't commit because a reader still holds SHARED. Expect a lot of failures.

wal. WAL mode changes the reader side: "readers do not block writers and a writer does not block readers." Writers append to a separate log, so commits no longer wait for readers. But the same page is plain about the other half: "there can only be one writer at a time." With the timeout still at 0, two writers colliding still means an instant error. WAL mode is persistent once set, which is why the script sets it once in the parent and the children inherit it.

wal-timeout. Now each connection waits up to 5 seconds for a lock instead of failing at once. Node's timeout option is the same thing as PRAGMA busy_timeout. Most guides stop here. Expect busy errors to remain, and expect some of them to be 517.

wal-immediate. Same timeout, but every transaction opens with BEGIN IMMEDIATE. The transaction docs say this "causes the database connection to start a new write immediately, without waiting for a write statement." The result-code docs give the guarantee that matters: BEGIN IMMEDIATE "might itself return SQLITE_BUSY, but if it succeeds, then SQLite guarantees that no subsequent operations on the same database through the next COMMIT will return SQLITE_BUSY." The wait moves to the BEGIN, where the timeout can actually do its job. With transactions this short, you should expect busy to drop to zero.


BEGIN IMMEDIATE asks for the write lock up front, so waiting happens before you have read anything.

Why busy_timeout can't save a deferred transaction

Plain BEGIN is DEFERRED, the default. Nothing is locked until the first statement. If that statement is a SELECT, you get a read transaction, and the docs say a later write "will upgrade the transaction to a write transaction if possible, or return SQLITE_BUSY." The upgrade is not possible "if some other database connection has already modified the database or is already in the process of modifying the database."

Walk through it in WAL mode. Writer A runs BEGIN and reads value = 41. A now has a snapshot of the database as it was at that moment. Writer B commits value = 42. A tries UPDATE ... SET value = 42. If SQLite let that through, B's write would vanish. So A gets SQLITE_BUSY_SNAPSHOT: another connection "has already written to the database and thus invalidated prior reads." Waiting can't fix this. A's snapshot is old, and no amount of sleeping makes it current again. The only way out is to roll back and start over with a fresh read.

The rollback-journal version of the same trap is spelled out in the busy handler docs: "The presence of a busy handler does not guarantee that it will be invoked when there is lock contention." One process holds a read lock and wants to promote it; another holds the reserved lock and needs the readers gone before it can commit. Each waits on the other, so SQLite skips the busy handler and returns SQLITE_BUSY to the reader "hoping that this will induce the first process to release its read lock."

busy_timeout only helps a connection that holds nothing yet. A deferred transaction that has already read is holding something, and BEGIN IMMEDIATE makes it wait before the read.

The settings to copy, and their limits

For a server process writing to SQLite, the combination looks like this:

PRAGMA journal_mode = WAL;     -- once; it persists
PRAGMA busy_timeout = 5000;    -- per connection
PRAGMA synchronous = NORMAL;   -- optional, see below

Then open every transaction that will write with BEGIN IMMEDIATE, including the ones that read first. Read-only transactions can stay deferred. The synchronous = NORMAL line is the pragma docs' own recommendation for WAL: transactions stay atomic, consistent and isolated, but you "lose durability across power lose" (their typo). Decide whether a lost last commit after a power cut is acceptable before you copy it.

Keep transactions short. A busy timeout only holds while the writer ahead of you finishes quickly. If one transaction calls an HTTP API while holding the write lock, every other writer waits with it, and 5 seconds goes fast.

WAL also has a hard constraint: "all processes using a database must be on the same host computer; WAL does not work over a network filesystem," per the WAL docs. And even in WAL mode the same page lists a few rare cases that still return SQLITE_BUSY, such as a connection running recovery after a crash, so keep the error handling.

When the single writer means it's time for Postgres

The SQLite authors give the cutoff themselves. Their checklist says choose a client/server database when "many threads and/or processes need to write the database at the same instant (and they cannot queue up and take turns)," when the data sits across a network from the application, or when it won't fit comfortably in one file. For a write-intensive site, or one "so busy that it requires multiple servers," they say to consider a client/server engine.

Translated into symptoms from the script: if wal-immediate still throws busy errors at your real transaction length, or the time writers spend queued at BEGIN IMMEDIATE becomes a visible share of your request latency, you are past the point where taking turns works. The same applies the day you need a second app server writing to the same data. In PostgreSQL's MVCC, reading never blocks writing and writing never blocks reading, and its locks are per table or per row rather than per file. You pay for it with a server to run.

Until then, run the script with your real transaction body in place of the counter update. If wal-immediate comes back clean, four writers is fine on SQLite.

If this was useful

Picking a data store usually comes down to limits like the one in this post: the single writer, the same-host rule, what a lock costs you when traffic grows. The Database Playbook goes through those trade-offs for SQLite, Postgres, Redis, DynamoDB and the rest, so you can tell before the logs fill up whether you have a configuration problem or need a different store.

title: Why My Retries Made an Outage Worse: Field Notes on Idempotency Keys, Backoff with Jitter, and Circuit Breakers
description:
Headline: Naive retries turn a slow dependency into a self-inflicted outage, because every caller retrying on the same schedule multiplies load on a service that is already failing. The combination that works is a hard per-attempt timeout, exponential backoff with full jitter under a total retry budget, an Idempotency-Key header on every non-idempotent write, and a circuit breaker that stops calling a dependency that is already down.

A background worker I maintain calls a third-party payments API. During a partial outage on their side, requests started taking 30 seconds and then failing. My retry wrapper did exactly what I had told it to do: try again immediately, three times. Throughput collapsed, the queue backed up, and when the dependency started recovering my workers were still hammering it in lockstep. The retries were not helping the recovery; they were part of what was preventing it. These are my notes from rebuilding that call path.

Key takeaways

  • Retry amplification is real arithmetic. Three retries per request means a dependency at its breaking point receives up to four times its normal load at the exact moment it has the least capacity.
  • Only retry failures that are safe to repeat. Connection errors, HTTP 502/503/504, and HTTP 429 are retryable; HTTP 400, 401, 403, and 422 are not, because repeating a request the server understood and rejected will never produce a different answer.
  • An idempotency key is a client-generated unique string sent in the Idempotency-Key header so the server can recognise a retry of a write it already processed and return the original response instead of performing the work twice.
  • Full jitter beats fixed backoff. Sleeping a random duration in [0, base * 2^attempt] spreads a fleet of retrying clients across the window instead of synchronising them into repeated thundering herds.
  • A circuit breaker fails fast on a dependency that is already down, converting a 30-second timeout into an immediate error and giving the dependency room to recover. Per-dependency, never global.

Why do retries make an outage worse instead of better?

Retries multiply load precisely when a dependency has the least capacity to absorb it. A service that normally handles 1,000 requests per second, configured with three retries across every caller, can see 4,000 requests per second the moment it starts failing. The failure causes the load, and the load sustains the failure. This feedback loop is called retry amplification, and it is the single most common way a partial degradation becomes a total outage.

Synchronisation makes it worse. If every worker retries after exactly one second, then two, then four, the whole fleet arrives at the dependency at the same three instants. The recovering service gets a spike, tips over again, and resets everyone's retry clock to the same value — the classic thundering herd. Fixed backoff does not spread load; it schedules a collision.

The third cost is the one I underestimated: retries consume my own capacity too. A worker sitting in a retry sleep is a worker not processing the queue. With no per-attempt timeout, four attempts at 30 seconds each means a single message occupies a worker for two minutes. My throughput fell before the dependency ever fully failed.

Which failures are actually safe to retry?

Retry only when the request either never reached the server or definitely failed without side effects. In practice that means classifying by status code and error type, not by wrapping everything in a generic try/catch.

Retryable: TCP connection errors (ECONNRESET, ECONNREFUSED, ETIMEDOUT), DNS failures, HTTP 502, 503, and 504, and HTTP 429 with the delay taken from the Retry-After header. These indicate the server was unavailable or explicitly asked you to wait.

Not retryable: HTTP 400, 401, 403, 404, and 422. The server received the request, understood it, and rejected it. Retrying a malformed payload produces the same rejection with extra load, and retrying a 401 can trip an authentication provider's own rate limiting.

The genuinely hard case is HTTP 500 and the request timeout. Both are ambiguous: the write may have committed before the response was lost. This is exactly the situation idempotency keys exist to resolve. Without a key, retrying an ambiguous POST /charges risks a duplicate charge, and not retrying it risks losing a legitimate payment. With a key, the ambiguity disappears and the retry is safe.

What is an idempotency key, and how do I implement one server-side?

An idempotency key is a client-generated unique string, typically a UUID v4, sent in the Idempotency-Key HTTP header so that repeating a request produces the original result rather than a second side effect. Stripe popularised the header, and it is now the de facto convention for payment and provisioning APIs.

The critical detail is that the key must be generated once per logical operation, not once per HTTP attempt. Generating a fresh UUID inside the retry loop defeats the entire mechanism, because each attempt then looks like a brand-new operation to the server. I generate the key when the job is enqueued and store it on the job record, so every retry — including a retry after a process crash and restart — reuses the same value.

async function chargeCustomer(job: ChargeJob) {
  return callWithRetry(() =>
    fetch('https://api.example.com/v1/charges', {
      method: 'POST',
      headers: {
        'Content-Type': 'application/json',
        // Generated once when the job row was created, never inside the loop.
        'Idempotency-Key': job.idempotencyKey,
      },
      body: JSON.stringify({ amount: job.amount, customer: job.customerId }),
      signal: AbortSignal.timeout(10_000),
    }),
  );
}

On the receiving side — and I own APIs that other people retry against — the implementation is a table with a unique constraint doing the concurrency control, not application code checking before inserting.

CREATE TABLE idempotency_records (
  key             text PRIMARY KEY,
  request_hash    text NOT NULL,
  status          text NOT NULL,           -- 'in_progress' | 'completed'
  response_status int,
  response_body   jsonb,
  created_at      timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
);

The handler inserts the key with status in_progress inside the same transaction as the business write. A unique-violation error on insert means another attempt is already handling this key: if the stored record is completed, replay response_status and response_body verbatim; if it is still in_progress, return HTTP 409 so the client backs off rather than racing. Relying on a SELECT followed by an INSERT reintroduces the race the key was meant to close, because two concurrent retries can both read "not found".

Store a hash of the request body alongside the key. If the same key arrives with a different payload, that is a client bug, and returning HTTP 422 surfaces it immediately instead of silently replaying an unrelated response. Expire records after a fixed window — 24 hours is a common choice — because keys are a retry-safety mechanism, not permanent storage.

How should I configure backoff, jitter, and timeouts?

Use exponential backoff with full jitter, cap the delay, and bound the whole operation with a deadline. Full jitter means sleeping a uniformly random duration in [0, min(cap, base * 2^attempt)] rather than the deterministic value. The randomness is the point: it decorrelates a fleet of clients so the recovering dependency sees a smooth arrival rate instead of synchronised spikes.

const RETRYABLE_STATUS = new Set([429, 502, 503, 504]);

async function callWithRetry(
  fn: () => Promise<Response>,
  { retries = 3, base = 200, cap = 10_000 } = {},
): Promise<Response> {
  for (let attempt = 0; ; attempt++) {
    const res = await fn().catch((err) => err as Error);

    const isRetryable =
      res instanceof Error
        ? res.name !== 'AbortError'
        : RETRYABLE_STATUS.has(res.status);

    if (!isRetryable) {
      if (res instanceof Error) throw res;
      return res;
    }
    if (attempt >= retries) {
      if (res instanceof Error) throw res;
      return res;
    }

    const retryAfter =
      res instanceof Response ? Number(res.headers.get('retry-after')) * 1000 : NaN;
    const ceiling = Math.min(cap, base * 2 ** attempt);
    const delay = Number.isFinite(retryAfter) && retryAfter > 0
      ? retryAfter                       // honour the server's instruction
      : Math.random() * ceiling;         // full jitter

    await new Promise((r) => setTimeout(r, delay));
  }
}

Three configuration rules I now treat as non-negotiable. First, every attempt gets its own timeout: AbortSignal.timeout(10_000) is one line and it is what stops a hung socket from holding a worker indefinitely. Second, honour Retry-After when the server sends it, because a 429 with an explicit delay is the dependency telling you exactly what it needs. Third, keep retries shallow — two or three — and never retry inside a layer that is itself being retried, or the counts multiply: three retries at each of three layers is 27 requests from one logical call.

Set a deadline for the whole operation, not just a retry count. If the caller is an HTTP request that will time out in 30 seconds anyway, a retry schedule that can run for 60 seconds is pure waste: the client has already given up and the work is discarded.

When does a circuit breaker help, and when is it overkill?

A circuit breaker is a wrapper that tracks recent failures for one dependency and, past a threshold, short-circuits subsequent calls by failing immediately instead of attempting them. It has three states: closed (calls pass through), open (calls fail instantly for a cooldown period), and half-open (a small number of trial calls decide whether to close again or re-open).

The breaker solves a problem retries cannot. When a dependency is fully down, the correct behaviour is to stop calling it — both to let it recover and to stop burning your own latency budget on calls that are certain to fail. A 10-second timeout becomes an instant error, which means your API returns a fast, honest degraded response instead of queueing requests behind dead connections.

Scope the breaker per dependency, and ideally per endpoint group. One global breaker means a broken analytics endpoint can block your checkout calls. Choose thresholds from a failure rate over a rolling window rather than a raw count, so low-traffic services do not trip on two unlucky requests. And make sure the fallback path is genuinely useful: serving stale cached data or queueing the work for later is worth building a breaker for, while an error page you would have shown anyway is not.

Overkill looks like this: a single-instance internal service with predictable traffic, or a dependency whose failures are already rare and fast. A breaker adds state, configuration, and a new way to be wrong — I have seen a misconfigured breaker stay open long after the dependency recovered. Timeouts and bounded retries come first; add the breaker when a dependency has actually demonstrated that it fails hard.

Which mechanism fixes which failure?

These four mechanisms are not alternatives. Each addresses a different failure, and using one without the others leaves a hole.

Mechanism Problem it solves What it does not solve
Per-attempt timeout A hung request holding a worker or connection forever Nothing about whether the work succeeded
Bounded retry with jitter Transient failures; synchronised client herds Duplicate side effects on ambiguous writes
Idempotency key Duplicate writes when a retry follows a lost response Load amplification; a dependency that is fully down
Circuit breaker Wasted calls and latency against a dependency that is down Individual transient blips; correctness of a single write

Ordered by return on effort: add per-attempt timeouts first, because they are one line and they bound your worst case. Add idempotency keys to every non-idempotent write next, because without them you cannot retry ambiguous failures safely at all. Fix the retry schedule with jitter and a budget third. Add breakers last, on the dependencies that have earned one.

FAQ

Q: Can I use a hash of the request body as the idempotency key?

A: No, because two legitimate identical requests — a customer intentionally buying the same item twice — would collide and the second one would be silently swallowed. Generate a UUID per logical operation and store the body hash separately to detect key reuse with a different payload.

Q: Is it safe to retry a GET request without an idempotency key?

A: Yes. GET, HEAD, PUT, and DELETE are defined as idempotent in the HTTP specification, so repeating them produces the same server state. POST and PATCH are the methods that need a key, and a PUT implemented with side effects such as counters needs one in practice too.

Q: How many retries should I configure?

A: Two or three at a single layer. More attempts rarely convert a failure into a success, and retries at multiple nested layers multiply: three retries in an HTTP client wrapped by three retries in a job queue is up to sixteen requests from one logical call.

Q: Does full jitter make retries slower on average?

A: Slightly, for a single client, since the expected delay is half the ceiling rather than the full value. Across a fleet it is faster overall, because decorrelated arrivals let the dependency recover instead of being knocked over by each synchronised wave.

Q: Where should the idempotency key live for a queued background job?

A: On the job record, written when the job is enqueued. Generating it at call time means a crashed and re-delivered job produces a new key, which is exactly the duplicate-write scenario the key was supposed to prevent.
