title: Is Your React App Invisible to ChatGPT? Test What AI Crawlers Actually See
description:
Here's a bug report you'll never get: "ChatGPT says our product doesn't have a free tier."

Nobody files it, because nobody connects the dots. But if your pricing page is a client-rendered React app, there's a decent chance the AI system that answered that question received this:

<!doctype html>
<html>
  <head><title>Pricing | Acme</title></head>
  <body>
    <div id="root"></div>
    <script src="/assets/index-8f3a.js"></script>
  </body>
</html>

Then it filled the gap from somewhere else: an old review, a competitor's comparison page, or a guess.

Why this is worse in 2026 than it was in 2020

Google spent years building a JavaScript rendering pipeline. Googlebot runs your JS (eventually), so client-side rendering became "mostly fine for SEO."

AI systems didn't inherit that pipeline. There are now three kinds of AI fetchers hitting your site:

Type Examples Renders JS?
Training crawlers GPTBot, ClaudeBot, CCBot Generally treated as no. Assume raw HTML.
AI search crawlers OAI-SearchBot, Claude-SearchBot, PerplexityBot Not reliably. Assume raw HTML.
Live user fetches ChatGPT-User, Claude-User, Perplexity-User Varies by product and changes over time. Don't count on it.

Vendors don't publish rendering guarantees, and behaviour changes. The only safe assumption is the one that has always been safe: if it's not in the HTML response, it might not exist.

Google's AI features (AI Overviews, AI Mode) use Google's index, which is rendered, so a CSR site can show up there and still be invisible to ChatGPT. That's exactly the kind of gap that's easy to miss.

Test it: raw vs rendered, side by side

This script fetches a URL twice, once as a plain HTTP request (what a non-rendering crawler gets) and once in headless Chromium (what a browser gets), then compares the text.

npm i playwright cheerio
npx playwright install chromium

// render-gap.mjs
import { chromium } from "playwright";
import * as cheerio from "cheerio";

const url = process.argv[2];
const mustContain = process.argv.slice(3); // phrases that MUST be visible to crawlers

function textOf(html) {
  const $ = cheerio.load(html);
  $("script, style, noscript, template, svg").remove();
  return $("body").text().replace(/\s+/g, " ").trim();
}

// 1. Raw HTML, as a non-rendering crawler would see it
const rawRes = await fetch(url, {
  headers: { "User-Agent": "Mozilla/5.0 (compatible; OAI-SearchBot/1.0; +https://openai.com/searchbot)" },
});
const raw = await rawRes.text();

// 2. Rendered DOM after JavaScript
const browser = await chromium.launch();
const page = await browser.newPage();
await page.goto(url, { waitUntil: "networkidle" });
const rendered = await page.content();
await browser.close();

const rawText = textOf(raw);
const renderedText = textOf(rendered);
const ratio = rawText.length / Math.max(renderedText.length, 1);

console.log(`Status (raw fetch):  ${rawRes.status}`);
console.log(`Raw text:            ${rawText.length.toLocaleString()} chars`);
console.log(`Rendered text:       ${renderedText.length.toLocaleString()} chars`);
console.log(`Raw / rendered:      ${(ratio * 100).toFixed(0)}%`);

const $raw = cheerio.load(raw);
console.log(`<title> in raw:      ${$raw("title").text() || "MISSING"}`);
console.log(`meta description:    ${$raw('meta[name="description"]').attr("content") ? "yes" : "MISSING"}`);
console.log(`<h1> in raw:         ${$raw("h1").first().text().trim() || "MISSING"}`);
console.log(`JSON-LD in raw:      ${$raw('script[type="application/ld+json"]').length} block(s)`);

for (const phrase of mustContain) {
  const inRaw = rawText.toLowerCase().includes(phrase.toLowerCase());
  console.log(`${inRaw ? "✅" : "❌"} "${phrase}" ${inRaw ? "is" : "is NOT"} in the raw HTML`);
}

if (ratio < 0.5) {
  console.log("\n⚠️  Less than half of the visible text exists without JavaScript.");
  process.exitCode = 1;
}

node render-gap.mjs https://your-site.com/pricing "Free plan" "per seat" "SOC 2"

Status (raw fetch):  200
Raw text:            142 chars
Rendered text:       6,418 chars
Raw / rendered:      2%
<title> in raw:      Pricing | Acme
meta description:    MISSING
<h1> in raw:         MISSING
JSON-LD in raw:      0 block(s)
❌ "Free plan" is NOT in the raw HTML
❌ "per seat" is NOT in the raw HTML
❌ "SOC 2" is NOT in the raw HTML

⚠️  Less than half of the visible text exists without JavaScript.

The mustContain phrases are the important part. Pick the facts you'd be upset to see an AI get wrong (price, free tier, integrations, compliance) and make them a test.

Also check the status code. If the raw fetch with an AI user agent returns 403 or a challenge page while your browser gets 200, your problem is the CDN or WAF, not rendering. Look at your bot-management rules before changing any code.

The fixes, by framework

Next.js (App Router)

Server Components render on the server by default, so most App Router pages are already fine. The usual culprits:

// ❌ Whole page opted into client rendering, data fetched in useEffect
"use client";
export default function Pricing() {
  const [plans, setPlans] = useState([]);
  useEffect(() => { fetch("/api/plans").then(r => r.json()).then(setPlans); }, []);
  return <PlanTable plans={plans} />;
}

// ✅ Server Component fetches data; only the interactive toggle is a client component
import { BillingToggle } from "./billing-toggle"; // "use client" inside

export const revalidate = 3600; // static, refreshed hourly

export default async function Pricing() {
  const plans = await getPlans();
  return (
    <main>
      <h1>Pricing</h1>
      <BillingToggle />
      <PlanTable plans={plans} />
    </main>
  );
}

Also watch for dynamic(() => import(...), { ssr: false }) around content (it's fine for widgets, not for text), and for content that only appears inside tabs or accordions that mount on click. Render it all and hide it with CSS instead.

Vite + React SPA

You have three options, from least to most work:

  1. Prerender the routes that matter at build time (marketing pages, docs, pricing), for example with vite-plugin-prerender or a small Playwright script that saves rendered HTML for a list of routes into dist/.
  2. Move the marketing site to a static-first framework (Astro, Next.js static export) and keep the SPA for the logged-in app at app.example.com.
  3. Adopt SSR (React Router framework mode, TanStack Start) if most of the product is public content.

For most teams, option 2 is the right answer: the app doesn't need to be crawlable, and the marketing site does.

Astro, Eleventy, Hugo

Static by default. Just be careful with client-only islands (client:only) that contain content rather than interactivity.

What about dynamic rendering?

Serving prerendered HTML only to bots (the old "dynamic rendering" pattern) still works technically, but Google describes it as a workaround, not a recommended solution. It also creates two versions of every page that can drift apart, and serving different content to bots is the definition of cloaking. Prefer SSR or static generation, which give everyone the same HTML.

Put the check in CI

Run the script against a preview deployment on every PR that touches marketing or docs routes:

# .github/workflows/render-gap.yml
name: Crawlability
on: pull_request
jobs:
  render-gap:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with: { node-version: 22 }
      - run: npm ci && npx playwright install --with-deps chromium
      # PREVIEW_URL comes from your deploy provider's preview step
      - run: node scripts/render-gap.mjs "$PREVIEW_URL/pricing" "Free plan" "per seat"
      - run: node scripts/render-gap.mjs "$PREVIEW_URL/docs/quickstart" "npm install"

That one check would have caught every "the AI said we don't have X" problem I've seen.

Beyond rendering

Server-side rendering gets your content into the HTML. Whether AI crawlers can reach it at all also depends on robots.txt, your CDN's bot rules, rate limits and status codes, and whether the page is indexed in Google and Bing. Vista AI's page audit checks those things together with the raw-vs-rendered gap for a URL. If you'd rather script it yourself, the render-gap.mjs above plus a robots.txt check covers the most common failures.

Run the script on your pricing page and share the raw/rendered percentage in the comments. Bonus points if it's under 10%.

Next in the series: How AI assistants decide which dev tool to recommend.

title: Marketing Automation: The Content Calendar Feature
description:
Feature Spotlight: Content Calendar

DoAide Pulse is built around the idea that developers should be able to ship code and let the platform handle promotion. The core of that promise is the content calendar – a declarative schedule that tells the system when and where to publish AI‑generated copy. The calendar solves a common problem: keeping a consistent publishing cadence across multiple channels without manual intervention. This is where marketing automation pays off in practice.

The Problem

Indie developers and small teams often produce a new feature, a bug fix, or a documentation update every few weeks. Translating that work into a marketing asset usually requires a separate workflow: writing a blog post, drafting social copy, and posting it to Dev.to, Bluesky, or a newsletter. This process is time‑consuming, error‑prone, and hard to keep in sync with the code repository. The content calendar centralises that workflow, allowing a single source of truth for all scheduled posts.

How It Works

The calendar is a combination of a database model, a FastAPI endpoint, a Celery worker, and a React UI. The system watches a GitHub repository via webhook events; each push triggers an AI model that drafts a blog post and social snippets. Those drafts are persisted in a ScheduledPost table and appear in the calendar UI.

Database Model (SQLAlchemy) 

# models.py
from sqlalchemy import Column, Integer, String, Text, DateTime
from sqlalchemy.orm import declarative_base

Base = declarative_base()

class ScheduledPost(Base):
    __tablename__ = "scheduled_posts"

    id = Column(Integer, primary_key=True)
    repo_id = Column(String, index=True)
    title = Column(String, nullable=False)
    content = Column(Text, nullable=False)
    publish_at = Column(DateTime, nullable=False)
    platform = Column(String, nullable=False)  # e.g., "devto", "bluesky"
    status = Column(String, default="queued")  # queued, published, failed

The publish_at field is the heart of the calendar – it defines the exact moment the worker will attempt to publish. Getting marketing automation right early saves rework later.

FastAPI Endpoint 

# api.py
from fastapi import APIRouter, Depends, HTTPException
from pydantic import BaseModel, Field
from datetime import datetime
from sqlalchemy.orm import Session

router = APIRouter()

class SchedulePostRequest(BaseModel):
    repo_id: str
    title: str
    content: str
    publish_at: datetime
    platform: str

@router.post("/schedule")
async def schedule_post(
    req: SchedulePostRequest,
    db: Session = Depends(get_db),
):
    post = ScheduledPost(**req.dict())
    db.add(post)
    db.commit()
    # Fire a Celery task to enqueue the publish job
    publish_post.delay(post.id)
    return {"id": post.id, "status": post.status}

The endpoint accepts the draft and desired publish time, stores it, and immediately queues a Celery task.

Celery Worker 

# tasks.py
from celery import Celery
from sqlalchemy.orm import Session
from models import ScheduledPost
from devto_api import publish as devto_publish

celery = Celery("pulse", broker="redis://localhost:6379/0")

@celery.task
def publish_post(post_id: int):
    db: Session = get_session()
    post = db.query(ScheduledPost).get(post_id)
    if not post:
        return

    try:
        if post.platform == "devto":
            devto_publish(post.title, post.content)
        # Additional platform logic can be added here
        post.status = "published"
    except Exception as exc:
        post.status = "failed"
    finally:
        db.commit()

The worker pulls the scheduled post from the queue, calls the platform‑specific API, and updates the status.

Dev.to API Wrapper 

# devto_api.py
import requests

API_URL = "https://dev.to/api/articles"
TOKEN = "<devto-token>"

headers = {"api-key": TOKEN}

def publish(title: str, body: str):
    payload = {
        "article": {
            "title": title,
            "published": True,
            "body_markdown": body,
        }
    }
    r = requests.post(API_URL, json=payload, headers=headers)
    r.raise_for_status()

The wrapper abstracts the HTTP call and ensures a consistent interface for the worker. Good marketing automation keeps the rest of the workflow predictable.

React UI (Vite + Tailwind) 

// ContentCalendar.tsx
import { useState } from "react";

export default function ContentCalendar() {
  const [publishAt, setPublishAt] = useState<string>('');

  return (
    <div className="p-4">
      <label className="block mb-2">Publish At</label>
      <input
        type="datetime-local"
        value={publishAt}
        onChange={e => setPublishAt(e.target.value)}
        className="border rounded p-2 w-full"
      />
    </div>
  );
}

The UI allows developers to pick a date‑time and see all queued posts in a grid. The component is lightweight and can be embedded in any dashboard.

What It Looks Like to Use

  1. Push to GitHub – A commit triggers a webhook that runs the LLM pipeline.
  2. Drafts Appear – The AI outputs a markdown article and social snippets, stored as ScheduledPost records.
  3. Schedule – In the dashboard, the developer selects a publish time and platform.
  4. Publish – At the scheduled time, the Celery worker posts to Dev.to via the wrapper.
  5. Audit Trail – The status field shows queued, published, or failed, allowing quick review.

The entire flow is visible from the UI: a calendar view shows upcoming posts, a table lists past publications, and a log pane displays any worker errors. Because the system uses Redis as a broker and PostgreSQL for persistence, scaling is straightforward – add more workers or spin up a read replica without touching the code.

Why It Matters for Developer Marketing

  • Consistency – A single schedule keeps all channels on the same cadence.
  • Automation – No manual copy‑paste; the worker handles the API call.
  • Transparency – The UI shows real‑time status and logs.
  • Extensibility – Adding a new platform is a matter of adding a branch in the Celery task and a new API wrapper.

The content calendar is a concrete example of how DoAide Pulse turns repository activity into a repeatable marketing pipeline, giving indie developers the tools of a full‑blown marketing automation stack without the overhead.

Related reading

  • Marketing Automation via AI Content Calendar | DoAide Pulse
  • Building a Content Calendar in DoAide Pulse

title: Is There a Dynamics 365 Release Wave 2 in 2026? What to Do Next
description:
Every October, Dynamics 365 teams used to open the same calendar entry: "Review release wave 2." This year, that entry has nothing behind it. There is no Dynamics 365 release wave 2 for 2026, no release plan document, and no neat list of features to read through over a cup of tea.

That does not mean updates have stopped. It means the way you hear about them has changed. If your business runs on Dynamics 365, the safest response is to build your own Dynamics 365 change calendar: a shared schedule that shows what is coming, who checks it, and when it reaches your users.

This guide shows you how.

What Microsoft Changed

For years, Microsoft delivered updates in two release waves. Wave 1 ran from April to September. Wave 2 ran from October to March. A release plan arrived a few weeks ahead of each wave, so admins could read it, test in a sandbox, and brief their teams.

In August 2026, Microsoft announced the end of that model for Dynamics 365, Power Platform and Dataverse. New features now appear on a single roadmap, called the AI at Work roadmap, once Microsoft commits to them. The older Release Planner site is due to retire by 15 November 2026.

In short, updates now arrive as a steady stream instead of two big announcements a year. The software is not changing less. The warning system is simply different.

Why This Matters for Your Business

The old release plan did one useful thing: it forced a conversation. Twice a year, someone had to read the changes and decide what mattered. Without that rhythm, three risks appear.

Missed changes. A new setting or a change in default behaviour can slip in unnoticed, then show up as a complaint from a user.

Surprise clashes. Custom workflows, integrations and reports can break when a feature changes underneath them. A small update can cause a big problem if nobody tested it.

Unplanned training. Staff find new buttons before anyone has explained them, and confidence in the system drops.

Companies that treat the roadmap as a news feed will struggle. Companies that treat it as an input to their own schedule will stay calm.

How to Build Your Own Dynamics 365 Change Calendar

A change calendar is a simple shared schedule. It lists every update that could affect your system, who reviews it, and when it reaches users. Here is a five-step way to build one.

Step 1: Pick an owner

Name one person responsible for watching Microsoft's roadmap. This could be a functional consultant, a system admin or a technology partner. Without a named owner, the calendar becomes everyone's job, and so nobody's job.

Step 2: Set a fixed review rhythm

Replace the old wave review with a regular check. A monthly review works well for most mid-sized teams. Large organisations with many connected systems may prefer every two weeks. Block the time in advance, the same way you once blocked time for release wave 2.

Step 3: Sort every change into three groups

For each item on the roadmap, ask one question: what does this do to us?

  • Act now: it affects live processes, security or compliance.
  • Plan: it is useful, but needs testing or training first.
  • Watch: it is interesting, but no action is needed yet.

This keeps your list short and your meetings useful.

Step 4: Match each change to a testing window

Choose a test environment and a fixed slot for checking changes before they reach your live system. Test your most important processes every time, such as quotes, orders, invoices, approvals and any link to other tools. Write down what you tested and what you found.

Step 5: Add communication and training dates

Every change that affects users needs a short note and, where needed, a quick training session. Put these dates on the calendar next to the technical dates. A new feature only helps if people know it exists and trust it.

A Four-Week Dynamics 365 Change Calendar Template

If you want a starting point, try this four-week loop.

  • Week 1: Review the roadmap and sort new items into act now, plan and watch.
  • Week 2: Test priority items in your test environment and check connected systems.
  • Week 3: Brief business users and update your guides.
  • Week 4: Approve changes for release, then look back at what went well and what did not.

Adjust it to your own size and pace. What matters is that the rhythm repeats, so updates become routine instead of a surprise.

Mistakes to Avoid

  • Waiting for a big announcement. There will not be one. Features will appear one by one, and dates can move.
  • Treating every item as urgent. Most roadmap items will not touch your business this quarter. Sorting is the real skill.
  • Leaving business teams out. Finance, sales and operations know which processes are fragile. Invite them to the monthly review.
  • Skipping the record. Keep a short log of what changed, when, and who approved it. It helps with audits and speeds up fixes when something goes wrong.
  • Trusting old dates. Roadmap timing can shift. Recheck dates at each review and update the calendar.

What This Means for Dynamics 365 Teams

The end of release waves is a good moment to move from reacting to planning. Teams with a clear Dynamics 365 change calendar spend less time on surprises and more time using new features well.

Teams without one will feel every update as a small emergency.

At Dynamics Monk, we help organisations across the UK, UAE, Australia, Singapore and Southeast Asia keep their Dynamics 365 systems steady as Microsoft's update model changes. Whether you need a ready-made change calendar, a testing routine, or ongoing support from certified consultants, we can set it up with you.
