title: AWS SAP-C03: The Solutions Architect Professional Exam Rewards Architects, Not Memorizers
description:
The associate-level AWS exams test whether you know the services. The professional-level Solutions Architect exam, SAP-C03, tests whether you can think like an architect when the requirements fight each other. Cost against performance. Security against speed. A migration deadline against a system that cannot go down. If you have passed SAA-C03 and are wondering what changes at the professional tier, the honest answer is: almost everything about how you read a question.

What SAP-C03 actually measures

SAP-C03 is built around long, layered scenarios. A question may describe a global company with regulatory constraints in two regions, a legacy data center, an acquisition's AWS account structure, and a budget that has already been cut once. The correct answer is rarely the service you spotted first. It is the combination that satisfies every constraint at once, including the one buried in the third paragraph.

The exam's four domains tell you where to spend your study time:

  • Design solutions for organizational complexity (26%) — multi-account strategy with AWS Organizations, Service Control Policies, consolidated billing, and how teams share services without sharing blast radius.
  • Design for new solutions (29%) — the largest domain. Greenfield architecture: choosing compute, storage, databases, and networking patterns for workloads you are designing from scratch.
  • Continuous improvement for existing solutions (25%) — taking a running system and making it cheaper, faster, more resilient, or more secure without a rewrite.
  • Accelerate workload migration and modernization (20%) — moving real workloads out of data centers, in waves, with rollback plans and minimal downtime.

Notice what is missing from that list: there is no domain called "name the service." Knowing that Amazon S3 exists earns you nothing. Knowing when S3, EFS, FSx, or instance storage is the right answer for a specific access pattern, durability requirement, and cost profile earns you the point.

The mindset shift from associate to professional

Associate questions usually have one obviously wrong answer, one plausible-but-wrong answer, and one right answer. Professional questions give you four answers that would all technically work, and ask which one is best given the constraints. The difference is almost always a trade-off:

  • A solution that is more resilient but doubles the bill fails a cost-constrained scenario.
  • A solution that is faster to build but creates a single point of failure fails a high-availability scenario.
  • A solution that is technically elegant but requires retraining an entire operations team fails a scenario with a two-week deadline.

Train yourself to read every question twice. The first read finds the services. The second read finds the constraints: the budget, the compliance rule, the latency target, the team size, the migration window. Underline the constraints mentally before you look at the options. Candidates who jump to the options first end up choosing the answer that solves the loudest requirement and misses the quiet one that decides the question.

Study the patterns, not the service catalog

The fastest way to prepare is to study architecture patterns until they are reflexes:

Multi-account design. Know when to use separate accounts per environment, per team, or per workload, and how Organizations, SCPs, and IAM roles make that manageable. Understand the difference between a landing zone and a pile of accounts someone created by hand.

Hybrid and migration patterns. Rehost, replatform, refactor — and, just as important, when not to migrate at all. Know how AWS Application Migration Service, Database Migration Service, and storage transfer services fit different workload shapes, and how to sequence migration waves so the business never stops.

Data patterns. When a relational database is right, when DynamoDB's key design matters more than its throughput settings, when caching changes the whole cost equation, and when analytics workloads belong on a lakehouse pattern instead of a transactional store. Professional scenarios love questions where the database choice is the whole question.

Resilience patterns. Multi-AZ versus multi-Region is not a trivia question at this level — it is a cost and complexity decision. Know what active-active, active-passive, and pilot-light actually cost to run, and which failure modes each one survives.

Cost as an architecture constraint. At the associate level, cost optimization is a topic. At the professional level, it is a filter applied to every answer. Practice estimating: what does this design cost per month, and what cheaper design meets the same requirements?

A six-week plan that works

Weeks 1–2: Close the associate gaps. Revisit the services you passed over quickly at associate level: networking (VPC design, Transit Gateway, PrivateLink, Route 53 routing policies), identity (IAM boundaries, permission boundaries, cross-account access), and data (storage classes, database engines, replication). If you cannot whiteboard a three-tier VPC from memory, start there.

Weeks 3–4: Scenario drills. Work through long case-study questions daily. For each one, write down the constraints before choosing an answer, then check whether your answer survives all of them. This single habit is worth more than another hundred flashcards.

Weeks 5: Hands-on labs. Build a multi-account organization, migrate a small workload, break something on purpose, and fix it. Professional questions reward people who have watched a design fail in practice, because the wrong answers are usually designs that fail in exactly those ways.

Week 6: Timed practice and review. SAP-C03 gives you 180 minutes for 75 questions — generous on paper, tight when every question is a paragraph. Practice under time pressure, and spend your review time on the questions you got right for the wrong reason, not just the ones you missed.

The mistakes that cost professional candidates the most

First, over-engineering. The most sophisticated answer is not the best answer when the scenario asks for the simplest design that meets the requirements. Second, ignoring the organization: questions about SCPs, account strategy, and governance are a quarter of the exam, and candidates who only studied services walk past them. Third, treating migration as a lift-and-shift exercise — the exam rewards phased plans with validation and rollback, not big-bang cutovers. Fourth, studying services in isolation instead of in combinations, because no professional question is ever about one service.

Bottom line

SAP-C03 does not ask you to know more AWS services than the associate exam does. It asks you to make better decisions with the services you already know, under realistic constraints, at organizational scale. Study the trade-offs, practice reading constraints before options, and build enough hands-on experience that the wrong answers smell wrong. That is what separates an architect from someone who memorized a catalog.

If you are preparing for SAP-C03, working through realistic, scenario-based practice questions is the closest thing to sitting the exam before exam day — the free SAP-C03 practice test at Study4Pass (https://study4pass.com/study-material/amazon/sap-c03) is a solid place to start.

title: Your AI Agent Is Only as Good as the API It Calls
description:
Your AI agent is only as good as the API it calls.

I wired an agent to a NestJS backend last quarter. It had to create orders, check stock, and issue refunds. The agent failed constantly. Not because the model was dumb. Because the endpoints were built for a frontend, not for a machine: five calls to do one job, huge payloads, vague errors.

That mismatch is easy to miss, because the API works fine when a human drives it through a user interface. A human sees a screen, fills in what is missing, and recovers from a vague error without thinking. An agent cannot do any of that. It reads what you return, decides what to do next from that text alone, and acts on it. Every gap in your API becomes a decision the model has to guess at, and guesses are where bad database writes come from.

The wrong approach

The first wrong approach is to expose your REST endpoints directly as agent tools. A frontend endpoint is designed to serve a screen. It returns everything that screen might need, paginates in a way that suits scrolling, and assumes the caller already knows the flow. Hand that to an agent and it will fetch far more data than it needs, miss the one field that matters, and chain calls in the wrong order, because nothing in the response told it the right order.

The second wrong approach is worse: build one giant do everything endpoint and let the model figure it out. That looks flexible. In practice it gives the agent too much room to improvise, and improvisation is where hallucinations turn into real database writes. A tool that can do anything cannot be tested properly, cannot be logged properly, and cannot be reasoned about when something goes wrong. When a refund is issued by mistake, you want to know exactly which tool did it and exactly what it received. A giant endpoint cannot tell you that.

How I structure it now: a thin tool layer

I keep a thin tool layer on top of the real services.

Each tool does exactly one thing, takes typed inputs, and returns a small predictable shape. The business logic stays in the service. The tool is just a translator between the agent and the service, nothing more.

Note: the snippet below is simplified to show the structure. The Tool and Param decorators come from your agent framework, not from NestJS itself, so adapt them to the framework you use.

// tools/order.tools.ts
import { OrdersService } from "./orders.service";

export interface OrderItem {
  productId: string;
  quantity: number;
}

export class OrderTools {
  constructor(private readonly orders: OrdersService) {}

  @Tool({ name: "create_order", description: "Create an order for a customer" })
  async createOrder(
    @Param("customerId") customerId: string,
    @Param("items") items: OrderItem[],
  ) {
    const order = await this.orders.create({ customerId, items });
    return {
      orderId: order.id,
      status: order.status,
      total: order.total,
    };
  }

  @Tool({ name: "check_stock", description: "Check stock for one product" })
  async checkStock(@Param("productId") productId: string) {
    const stock = await this.orders.checkStock(productId);
    return { productId, inStock: stock.quantity > 0, quantity: stock.quantity };
  }

  @Tool({ name: "issue_refund", description: "Issue a refund for a paid order" })
  async issueRefund(
    @Param("orderId") orderId: string,
    @Param("reason") reason: string,
  ) {
    const refund = await this.orders.refund(orderId, reason);
    return { orderId, refundId: refund.id, status: refund.status };
  }
}

Three things matter in that code, and none of them is the decorator syntax.

First, the service owns the logic. Creating an order, checking stock, issuing a refund: all the validation, all the rules about what can be refunded and when, all of it lives in OrdersService, exactly where it lived before the agent arrived. The tool adds no rules of its own. If the service changes, the tool still works, because the tool only passes inputs through and shapes the output.

Second, the return shape is small and stable. The agent does not get the full order object with every relation attached. It gets an id, a status, and a total. That is enough for it to continue the conversation and to tell the user what happened. Small outputs also keep the model focused: a huge payload is not just wasteful, it is a distraction that makes the next decision worse.

Third, the agent never touches the service directly. It only sees small honest tools. That boundary is what makes the rest of the system manageable.

Errors must be part of the design

An agent treats an error message as information, so a vague error is worse than no error at all. "Something went wrong" tells the model nothing, so it retries, or tries a different tool, or invents a workaround. A structured error tells it what actually happened and what it can do about it.

Return errors in the same shape every time: a short code the agent can match on, and a plain message a human can read. Keep the codes small in number. A handful of codes like not found, out of stock, already refunded, and invalid input covers almost everything an order flow needs. If the agent sees "already refunded", it stops instead of refunding twice. If it sees "out of stock", it can tell the user honestly instead of placing an order that will fail later.

Never leak internals in an error. Stack traces, database messages, and internal service names are not information for the model, they are noise that it will sometimes repeat to the user. Log those on the server, where they belong, and return only the code and the message.

Log every tool call like any other API call

Every tool call is logged like any other API call: which tool ran, what inputs it received, what it returned, and whether it succeeded. That log is what turns a strange outcome into a debuggable one. When a user says the agent refunded the wrong order, you do not have to guess what the model did. You read the log, you see the tool, the order id, and the reason it was given, and you know exactly where the chain broke.

That log is also your safety net for destructive tools. A tool that only reads data is low risk. A tool that writes data, moves money, or changes state deserves more care. In production I keep write tools behind the same checks any write endpoint would have: authentication, permission checks, and validation in the service. For the most sensitive actions, like issuing a refund, the tool should require an explicit confirmation from the user before it runs, not just a confident model. The model proposes, the human confirms, the tool executes. That one rule removes a whole class of expensive mistakes.

Test the tool, not just the service

A tool layer is easy to test, and that is one of its best arguments. The service already has its own tests. The tool needs tests of its own, for a different question: does this tool accept what the agent will actually send, and does it return the shape the agent expects?

Write a test that calls the tool with realistic inputs, including messy ones: a missing field, an empty items list, a product id that does not exist. Assert the output shape, not just that it did not throw. If the output shape drifts, the agent's next step drifts with it, so the shape is the contract. Testing it is cheap, and it catches the regressions that are hardest to spot by reading code, like a renamed field that silently becomes undefined in the agent's view.

What I would not do

I would not let the model write queries, call a database directly, or reach an endpoint that was built for an admin screen. Every one of those shortcuts removes the layer that keeps the agent honest. The service layer exists for a reason: it enforces the rules, it guards the data, and it keeps one version of the truth. The moment the agent bypasses it, you have two versions of your business logic, and the untested one is the one making writes.

I would also not return full objects "just in case" the agent needs a field later. If it needs that field, add it to the tool output deliberately, with a name that means something. A tool output is an interface, and interfaces grow by decision, not by accident.

The honest summary

Agents do not need a new backend. They need a backend that speaks in small, honest, predictable steps. One tool, one job, typed inputs, a small output, errors the model can act on, and a log for every call. That is not a lot of code. In the project I described, the tool layer was a fraction of the size of the services underneath it, and it was the part that made the agent reliable.

The model gets the credit when an agent works well, but most of the time the difference between a flaky agent and a dependable one is not the model at all. It is the API behind it, and whether that API was built for a machine that reads text and acts on it, or for a screen that a human was always going to interpret.

Do you expose your APIs to agents directly, or do you keep a separate tool layer?

I'm Sohail Khan, a Senior Full Stack Developer building AI agents and automation. Tech Lead at LoopxCorp. I write about backend engineering, AI integration and practical system design.

title: Building a Production RAG API in Go with pgvector and Gemini
description:
Lessons from building the Restaurant Suggestion System, a Go/Gin backend with a conversational recommendation API.

A RAG demo takes an afternoon: embed some documents, run a similarity search, paste the results into a prompt. A RAG API you can put in front of real users takes longer, because most of the work is not the LLM call. It's everything around it.

I built the Restaurant Suggestion System (RSS) as a Go/Gin backend where users chat to get dish and restaurant suggestions. The answers come from RAG over real menu data in PostgreSQL with pgvector and Gemini embeddings. Because the recommendations have to respect allergies, "the model usually gets it right" was never good enough.

This post walks through the shape of that pipeline and the Go patterns that made it dependable. The snippets are simplified and focused on the ideas, not copied from the private repo.

The pipeline

Every chat request goes through the same steps:

  1. Embed the user's message (plus stored preferences) with Gemini.
  2. Retrieve candidates from Postgres with pgvector, with allergen and health filters applied in SQL.
  3. Score candidates deterministically in Go.
  4. Generate a conversational answer with the LLM, using only the top candidates as context.
  5. Validate the answer against the candidates we sent.
  6. Fall back to a vector-only response if the LLM is slow or unavailable.

The rule behind all of it: the LLM explains and converses. It does not decide what is safe or what exists.

Schema: keep filters as real columns

It's tempting to put everything into the embedded text and let similarity sort it out. Don't do that for anything safety-related. Allergens belong in a column you can filter on exactly.

CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS vector;

CREATE TABLE menu_items (
    id            BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
    restaurant_id BIGINT NOT NULL REFERENCES restaurants(id),
    name          TEXT NOT NULL,
    description   TEXT NOT NULL,
    allergens     TEXT[] NOT NULL DEFAULT '{}',
    price_cents   INT NOT NULL,
    is_available  BOOLEAN NOT NULL DEFAULT TRUE,
    embedding     vector(768) NOT NULL
);

CREATE INDEX ON menu_items USING hnsw (embedding vector_cosine_ops);
CREATE INDEX ON menu_items USING gin (allergens);

The dimension (768 here) must match the embedding model's output configuration. Pick one, store it in config, and fail fast at startup if they disagree. A silent dimension mismatch is a miserable bug to find in production.

Embeddings with Gemini

RSS uses Gemini embeddings in two places: when indexing menu items, and during onboarding to capture user preferences as a vector. Wrap the provider behind a small interface so the rest of the code doesn't care which SDK you use:

type Embedder interface {
    Embed(ctx context.Context, text string) ([]float32, error)
}

type GeminiEmbedder struct {
    client *genai.Client
    model  string
    dims   int32
}

func (g *GeminiEmbedder) Embed(ctx context.Context, text string) ([]float32, error) {
    ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(ctx, 5*time.Second)
    defer cancel()

    res, err := g.client.Models.EmbedContent(ctx, g.model,
        genai.Text(text),
        &genai.EmbedContentConfig{OutputDimensionality: &g.dims},
    )
    if err != nil {
        return nil, fmt.Errorf("embed: %w", err)
    }
    if len(res.Embeddings) == 0 || len(res.Embeddings[0].Values) != int(g.dims) {
        return nil, errors.New("embed: unexpected embedding shape")
    }
    return res.Embeddings[0].Values, nil
}

Two habits worth copying: a hard timeout on every external call, and a shape check on the response. The interface also makes tests easy, since a fake embedder returns fixed vectors.

Retrieval: filter in SQL, before the LLM

This is the most important design decision in the system. Allergen and health filters run in the retrieval query, so excluded items never reach the model. A prompt like "don't suggest peanuts" is a request. A WHERE clause is a guarantee.

type Candidate struct {
    ID         int64
    Name       string
    Allergens  []string
    PriceCents int
    Distance   float64
}

const retrieveSQL = `
SELECT id, name, allergens, price_cents, embedding <=> $1 AS distance
FROM menu_items
WHERE is_available
  AND NOT (allergens && $2::text[])
ORDER BY embedding <=> $1
LIMIT $3`

func (r *Repo) Retrieve(ctx context.Context, q []float32, exclude []string, k int) ([]Candidate, error) {
    rows, err := r.db.Query(ctx, retrieveSQL, pgvector.NewVector(q), exclude, k)
    if err != nil {
        return nil, err
    }
    defer rows.Close()

    var out []Candidate
    for rows.Next() {
        var c Candidate
        if err := rows.Scan(&c.ID, &c.Name, &c.Allergens, &c.PriceCents, &c.Distance); err != nil {
            return nil, err
        }
        out = append(out, c)
    }
    return out, rows.Err()
}

One pgvector gotcha: with an approximate index such as HNSW, filtering happens after the index returns its nearest neighbours. With a strict filter you can get fewer than k rows back. pgvector 0.8+ supports iterative index scans (SET hnsw.iterative_scan = relaxed_order;), which keep scanning until enough rows pass the filter. On older versions, raise hnsw.ef_search or over-fetch and trim. Either way, write a test where most rows are filtered out and check you still get results.

Deterministic scoring

Vector distance is one signal, not the ranking. RSS ranks filtered candidates with a deterministic scoring engine, so the same input gives the same order and every recommendation can be explained.

type Weights struct {
    Similarity, Preference, Budget float64
}

func Score(c Candidate, prefSim float64, budgetCents int, w Weights) float64 {
    s := w.Similarity*(1-c.Distance) + w.Preference*prefSim
    if budgetCents > 0 && c.PriceCents <= budgetCents {
        s += w.Budget
    }
    return s
}

func Rank(cands []Candidate, scores map[int64]float64) {
    sort.SliceStable(cands, func(i, j int) bool {
        si, sj := scores[cands[i].ID], scores[cands[j].ID]
        if si != sj {
            return si > sj
        }
        return cands[i].ID < cands[j].ID // stable tie-break
    })
}

Note the tie-break on ID. Without it, equal scores can shuffle between runs, and your tests become flaky. The signals here are illustrative; the point is that ranking lives in plain Go you can unit-test, not in a prompt.

Generation: ground it, then check it

Only the top candidates go into the prompt, each with its ID. A pattern I recommend on top of that: ask the model for structured output that references those IDs, and validate the response before returning it:

type LLMAnswer struct {
    Message string  `json:"message"`
    ItemIDs []int64 `json:"item_ids"`
}

func validateAnswer(a LLMAnswer, sent []Candidate) error {
    allowed := make(map[int64]bool, len(sent))
    for _, c := range sent {
        allowed[c.ID] = true
    }
    for _, id := range a.ItemIDs {
        if !allowed[id] {
            return fmt.Errorf("model referenced unknown item %d", id)
        }
    }
    return nil
}

If the model mentions something you didn't give it, that's a hallucination by definition, and you can detect it in a few lines.

The fallback: vector-only results

LLM APIs time out, hit rate limits and have outages. RSS handles that by degrading gracefully: if the LLM call fails, the API still returns the filtered, scored candidates from vector search. In the sketch below, an answer that fails validation takes the same path:

func (s *Service) Recommend(ctx context.Context, req ChatRequest) (ChatResponse, error) {
    cands, err := s.retrieveAndRank(ctx, req)
    if err != nil {
        return ChatResponse{}, err // no data, no answer
    }

    genCtx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(ctx, 8*time.Second)
    defer cancel()

    ans, err := s.llm.Answer(genCtx, req.Message, cands)
    if err == nil {
        err = validateAnswer(ans, cands)
    }
    if err != nil {
        s.log.Warn("llm unavailable, using vector-only fallback", "err", err)
        return fallbackResponse(cands), nil
    }
    return ChatResponse{Message: ans.Message, ItemIDs: ans.ItemIDs, Source: "llm"}, nil
}

Because the safety filters ran before the LLM, the fallback is just as safe as the full path. It's less chatty, not less correct. Returning a Source field also helps the frontend and your dashboards see how often you're degrading.

The rest of the production checklist

The RAG pipeline is maybe a third of the system. The rest is ordinary backend work that still matters:

  • Auth: passwordless email OTP, JWT, and role-based access control so admin endpoints stay admin-only.
  • Data ingest: CRUD plus CSV/JSON bulk upload and AWS file upload. Whatever your ingest path, make sure every write also refreshes the item's embedding, or search goes stale.
  • Privacy: admin analytics built without exposing PII.
  • Ops: Postgres with pgvector in Docker, so local, CI and production run the same database.
  • Tests: a Newman (Postman) end-to-end suite that hits the real API. Make sure the fallback path has its own tests too.

Takeaways

  • Put safety rules in SQL and Go, never only in the prompt.
  • Rank deterministically, with stable tie-breaks.
  • Validate model output against the context you sent.
  • Design the fallback first. If the LLM disappears, users should still get a correct answer.

Go suits this well: strict types for model output, context deadlines on every call, and a single binary that's easy to run next to Postgres.

Pradip Parmar is a Go backend and AI agent engineer who has been writing Go since 2018. He builds RAG systems, MCP servers and LLM agents for businesses, and previously led the Python-to-Go migration of the Flights backend at MakeMyTrip. If you need a Go AI agent developer for a RAG or agent project, you can reach him on LinkedIn, Upwork or Contra, or see his code on GitHub.

title: Generate a training set with DeepSeek, then fine-tune a small model on a rented GPU
description:
Short answer: write a few documentation pages yourself, have DeepSeek turn them into question-and-answer pairs through an OpenAI-compatible endpoint, filter the pairs with a short script, then train a LoRA adapter on a small base model with LLaMA-Factory on a rented GPU. Generate and filter on your own machine; rent the GPU only for training; download the adapter, then destroy the instance.

Disclosure: I work on CloudGPU. The endpoint (https://cloudgpu.app/v1) and the GPU rentals below are ours. Each step links the official documentation it follows and ends with a "What to check" line, because the details (versions, template names, model access) change.

Why this pattern? AI labs describe using models to write or judge training data from written rules. This is the small, single-developer version of that idea. It is our own analogy, not a claim from those papers.

Read these three things first

  1. DeepSeek's terms. This tutorial generates data with DeepSeek only. DeepSeek's Terms of Use (Last Update: March 27, 2026) say in section 4.2(3) that you may apply the Outputs of the Services to "a wide range of use cases, including personal use, academic research, derivative product development, training other models (such as model distillation), etc., as long as such usage is legal and adhere to these Terms." Section 3.1 adds that if you publish or disseminate outputs, you must "clearly indicate that the output content is generated by artificial intelligence". So if you publish the dataset, a model card or examples from it, label them as AI-generated. Read the terms yourself, and read CloudGPU's terms and acceptable use policy, which apply to the gateway.
  2. Rights to your source text. The acceptable use policy lists "Training models on datasets you do not have rights to use" under large-scale copyright infringement (section 1.8). In this tutorial the generator only sees documentation you wrote yourself.
  3. The base model's license. Each base model below has its own license. Open the link, read it, and confirm for yourself that your use is allowed.

What you need

  • Python 3 and the openai package on your own machine: pip install openai.
  • A CloudGPU account with balance, and an API key (the API page has a "Get your API key" link). Keep it in an environment variable, never in code: 
export CLOUDGPU_API_KEY="paste-your-key-here"
  • Three to ten Markdown files of your own documentation, with ## section headings, in a docs/ folder. A README of your own project works.
  • A Hugging Face account and a read token if you choose Llama or Gemma (both are gated, see the table below).

What to check: python3 -c "import os; print(bool(os.environ.get('CLOUDGPU_API_KEY')))" prints True in the shell where you will run the scripts, and python3 -c "import openai" raises no error.

API calls are billed per token from the same balance as GPU rentals; the current rate for every model is in the table on the API page. This post does not repeat rates.

Step 1: generate question-and-answer pairs with DeepSeek

The script splits each Markdown file at ## headings, asks deepseek-v4.1-flash for a handful of pairs per section, and writes one JSON object per line. The model ID comes from the live model table on the API page (checked 2026-10-27); the same table lists deepseek-v4-flash and deepseek-v4-pro. The OpenAI SDK only needs base_url and the key changed.

# gen_data.py
import json, os, re, sys, time
from concurrent.futures import ThreadPoolExecutor
from pathlib import Path
from openai import OpenAI

client = OpenAI(base_url="https://cloudgpu.app/v1", api_key=os.environ["CLOUDGPU_API_KEY"])
MODEL = "deepseek-v4.1-flash"
PAIRS_PER_SECTION = 6

PROMPT = """You write training examples for a support assistant.
Use ONLY the documentation below. Do not invent features or settings.
Write {n} varied question-and-answer pairs that a user might ask about it.
Return ONLY a JSON array. Each item has the keys "instruction" (the question),
"input" (extra context, or an empty string) and "output" (the answer, 1-4 sentences).

Documentation:
{chunk}
"""

def sections(folder):
    for path in sorted(Path(folder).glob("*.md")):
        for part in re.split(r"\n(?=## )", path.read_text(encoding="utf-8")):
            if len(part.strip()) > 200:
                yield path.name, part.strip()

def parse(text):
    fence = "`" * 3  # the model may wrap its JSON in a code fence
    text = text.strip().removeprefix(fence + "json").removeprefix(fence).removesuffix(fence).strip()
    rows = json.loads(text)
    keys = ("instruction", "input", "output")
    return [r for r in rows if isinstance(r, dict) and all(isinstance(r.get(k), str) for k in keys)]

def ask(item):
    name, chunk = item
    for attempt in range(3):
        try:
            resp = client.chat.completions.create(
                model=MODEL,
                temperature=0.8,
                messages=[{"role": "user", "content": PROMPT.format(n=PAIRS_PER_SECTION, chunk=chunk)}],
            )
            return parse(resp.choices[0].message.content)
        except Exception as err:  # network error, rate limit, bad JSON
            print(f"{name}: attempt {attempt + 1} failed: {err}", file=sys.stderr)
            time.sleep(2 ** attempt)
    return []

if __name__ == "__main__":
    with ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=4) as pool:
        results = list(pool.map(ask, sections("docs")))
    with open("raw.jsonl", "w", encoding="utf-8") as f:
        for rows in results:
            for row in rows:
                f.write(json.dumps(row, ensure_ascii=False) + "\n")
    print("sections:", len(results), "pairs:", sum(len(r) for r in results))

Run python3 gen_data.py. The four-worker pool and the retry loop keep you inside the default rate limits listed on the API page; check those limits there and lower max_workers if you see rate-limit errors.

What to check: raw.jsonl exists and has lines; the script prints how many sections and pairs it got. If a section failed three times it is skipped and the error is on stderr. A 401 means the key variable is not set in this shell.

Step 2: filter and de-duplicate

Model-written data needs a filter before training. This script drops empty rows, answers that are very short or very long, boilerplate such as "as an AI", and near-duplicate questions (token overlap of 0.8 or more). Tune the numbers for your data.

# filter_data.py
import json, re
from pathlib import Path

def tokens(s):
    return set(re.sub(r"\W+", " ", s.lower()).split())

def jaccard(a, b):
    union = a | b
    return len(a & b) / len(union) if union else 0.0

kept, seen = [], []
dropped = {"empty": 0, "length": 0, "boilerplate": 0, "duplicate": 0}

for line in Path("raw.jsonl").read_text(encoding="utf-8").splitlines():
    row = json.loads(line)
    ins, inp, out = (row[k].strip() for k in ("instruction", "input", "output"))
    if not ins or not out:
        dropped["empty"] += 1
    elif not 20 <= len(out) <= 1200:
        dropped["length"] += 1
    elif re.search(r"\bas an ai\b|\blanguage model\b", out, re.I):
        dropped["boilerplate"] += 1
    elif any(jaccard(tokens(ins), t) >= 0.8 for t in seen):
        dropped["duplicate"] += 1
    else:
        seen.append(tokens(ins))
        kept.append({"instruction": ins, "input": inp, "output": out})

Path("synth_docs_qa.json").write_text(json.dumps(kept, ensure_ascii=False, indent=2), encoding="utf-8")
Path("DATASET_NOTE.md").write_text(
    "AI-generated data: the examples in synth_docs_qa.json were generated with deepseek-v4.1-flash "
    "from documentation written by the dataset author. Review before use.\n", encoding="utf-8")
print("kept", len(kept), "dropped", dropped)

The output is in LLaMA-Factory's Alpaca format: instruction, optional input, and output, per the data preparation docs. A row looks like this (illustrative, written by hand, not model output):

{
  "instruction": "How do I change the output folder?",
  "input": "",
  "output": "Pass --out followed by a path, for example --out ./build."
}

Then read a sample yourself. Filters catch format problems, not wrong answers:

python3 -c "import json,random; [print(r['instruction'],'->',r['output'],'\n') for r in random.sample(json.load(open('synth_docs_qa.json')), 10)]"

What to check: DATASET_NOTE.md is the label DeepSeek's terms ask for if you publish the data: keep it next to the file. Compare ten sampled answers with your documentation; delete rows that are wrong, or tighten the prompt and regenerate. If the filter drops most rows, the model is probably not returning clean JSON: print one raw response and adjust parse.

If your data is multi-turn, LLaMA-Factory also reads a conversation format; the same docs page shows the dataset_info.json entry for it.

Step 3: rent a GPU

On Deploy, choose a card. The CloudGPU docs say two things that matter here: every template is an image with root SSH, and for anything a template does not cover you can rent a raw GPU (Deploy â†’ Raw GPU) and install what you need over SSH. For this tutorial, pick a template that includes PyTorch, or choose Raw GPU and install it yourself. Pick a card with enough memory for your base model: the LLaMA-Factory README has a rough memory table (marked as estimates), and nvidia-smi shows real use during the first training steps.

GPU instances are billed per minute, rounded up, with a 1-minute minimum, and billing stops when you destroy the instance (terms). Rates are on the pricing page.

Connect with the SSH details of your running instance. Then upload the dataset from your own machine (scp takes the port with a capital -P):

scp -P <ssh-port> synth_docs_qa.json <ssh-user>@<ssh-host>:/workspace/

What to check: connect with ssh -p <ssh-port> <ssh-user>@<ssh-host>, then run nvidia-smi (a GPU is listed) and python3 -c "import torch; print(torch.cuda.is_available())" (prints True). If torch is missing, install PyTorch with CUDA from the PyTorch install page first.

Step 4: install LLaMA-Factory and register the dataset

These are the install commands from the LLaMA-Factory README (read 2026-10-27; the repository name is spelled LlamaFactory there). The docs FAQ lists a LLaMA-Factory template, but don't count on it being installed or current: check, and install if needed.

cd /workspace
git clone --depth 1 https://github.com/hiyouga/LlamaFactory.git
cd LlamaFactory
pip install -e .
pip install -r requirements/metrics.txt

Copy the dataset into data/ and add an entry to data/dataset_info.json, which is how LLaMA-Factory finds custom datasets:

cp /workspace/synth_docs_qa.json data/
python3 - <<'EOF'
import json
p = "data/dataset_info.json"
info = json.load(open(p, encoding="utf-8"))
info["synth_docs_qa"] = {
    "file_name": "synth_docs_qa.json",
    "columns": {"prompt": "instruction", "query": "input", "response": "output"},
}
json.dump(info, open(p, "w", encoding="utf-8"), ensure_ascii=False, indent=2)
EOF

What to check: llamafactory-cli help prints the command list, and grep synth_docs_qa data/dataset_info.json finds your entry.

Step 5: choose a base model and train a LoRA adapter

Small models are enough to see the pipeline work. Pick one row; the template name must match the model.

Base model LLaMA-Factory template License (read it yourself) Access
Llama 3.2 3B Instruct (meta-llama/Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct) llama3 Llama 3.2 Community License Gated on Hugging Face: accept the license, use a token
Gemma 3 4B IT (google/gemma-3-4b-it) gemma3 Gemma Terms of Use Gated on Hugging Face: accept the terms, use a token
Mistral 7B Instruct v0.3 (mistralai/Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.3) mistral License shown on the model card The model card listed no gate when we looked (2026-10-27)

Template names are from the LLaMA-Factory README's model table; license and access information was read on 2026-10-27 and can change. The Llama license has conditions that apply if you distribute or make available a model built on it. Confirm the license for your use yourself before you train or share anything.

For a gated model, request access on its Hugging Face page, then give the instance a fine-grained read token for just this run (you will revoke it at the end):

export HF_TOKEN="paste-a-read-token-here"

Save this as synth_lora.yaml in the LlamaFactory folder. The keys follow the official LoRA example in the repo's examples/train_lora/ folder; the model, template and dataset lines are the parts you change:

### model
model_name_or_path: meta-llama/Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct

### method
stage: sft
do_train: true
finetuning_type: lora
lora_rank: 8
lora_target: all

### dataset
dataset: synth_docs_qa
template: llama3
cutoff_len: 2048
preprocessing_num_workers: 4

### output
output_dir: saves/llama32-3b/lora/synth
logging_steps: 10
save_steps: 100
plot_loss: true
overwrite_output_dir: true

### train
per_device_train_batch_size: 1
gradient_accumulation_steps: 8
learning_rate: 1.0e-4
num_train_epochs: 3.0
lr_scheduler_type: cosine
warmup_ratio: 0.1
bf16: true

### eval
val_size: 0.1
per_device_eval_batch_size: 1
eval_strategy: steps
eval_steps: 50

Train:

llamafactory-cli train synth_lora.yaml

Open the LLaMA-Factory examples folder and compare your YAML with the current LoRA example: key names change between releases.

What to check: the log prints a training loss every 10 steps and, with val_size set, an evaluation loss every 50; saves/llama32-3b/lora/synth contains adapter_model.safetensors and adapter_config.json. If the base model download fails with a 401 or 403, the Hugging Face access request or token is the problem. An out-of-memory error means a smaller cutoff_len, a smaller model or a card with more memory; nvidia-smi shows the real use.

Unsloth (optional). The LLaMA-Factory README lists Unsloth among its supported add-ons and describes a use_unsloth: true argument for LoRA. Unsloth has its own documentation and install steps, and supports a specific list of models, so check that your base model is on its list before you add it.

Step 6: try the adapter, copy it off, destroy the instance

A quick test in the terminal (no server is started). Save as infer.yaml:

model_name_or_path: meta-llama/Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct
adapter_name_or_path: saves/llama32-3b/lora/synth
template: llama3
infer_backend: huggingface

llamafactory-cli chat infer.yaml

Ask ten questions that are not in your training data and that you wrote yourself, and compare the answers with your documentation. That is your real test; the evaluation loss is not.

Now copy the adapter to your own machine before you destroy anything: destroying the instance permanently deletes its local storage. From your own machine:

rsync -avP -e "ssh -p <ssh-port>" \
  <ssh-user>@<ssh-host>:/workspace/LlamaFactory/saves/llama32-3b/lora/synth/ ./adapter-synth/

Check that adapter_model.safetensors is in ./adapter-synth/, revoke the Hugging Face token you pasted on the instance, then destroy the instance from your Dashboard (the docs: "You can destroy an instance at any time"). The minutes you spent copying are billed like any other minute, and billing stops once the instance is destroyed.

What to check: the instance no longer appears as running in your dashboard, and ./adapter-synth/ still opens on your machine.

Privacy and access, in plain terms

  • Generation (step 1) sends the documentation sections you give it to a model API. Don't send text you would not want processed by a model service, and read the privacy policy for what the service handles.
  • You keep ownership of what you put on the GPU instance. CloudGPU's terms (section 5) say it does not access the contents of your instance except where needed to investigate a credible report of a policy violation, where compelled by valid legal process, or to protect the safety of users or third parties. Local instance storage is deleted when you destroy the instance.
  • This tutorial does not start a server. If you later serve your model from an instance, use your own endpoint with your own API key: the terms (section 6) say instance service URLs are not authenticated by default, so add authentication yourself before you share the URL.

Sources

All read on 2026-10-27 (UTC+8).

  • DeepSeek, Terms of Use, Last Update March 27, 2026: cdn.deepseek.com, sections 3.1 and 4.2.
  • LLaMA-Factory: README and data preparation docs.
  • CloudGPU: API page, terms (sections 4 to 6), acceptable use policy (section 1.8, last updated April 22, 2026), privacy policy.
  • Licenses: Llama 3.2, Gemma, Mistral 7B Instruct v0.3 model card.

title: Reverse Engineering Agent Pipelines: Integrating morluto/rea for Binary Analysis
description:
Reverse Engineering Agent Pipelines: Integrating morluto/rea for Binary Analysis

When evaluating agent frameworks for reverse engineering workflows, most tools force you into either static analysis harnesses or full symbolic execution environments. The morluto/rea repository positions itself as a middle ground: agent-driven introspection that scales from app behavior tracing down to native binary analysis.

I integrated morluto/rea into an existing observability pipeline to validate its claim of "reverse engineer anything with agents." Here's the architectural breakdown and where it breaks.

Agent Architecture and Execution Model

The framework structures reverse engineering as a multi-agent coordination problem. Each agent operates as a specialized probe:

interface ReverseEngineeringAgent {
  probe: (target: Target) => Observable<Artifact>;
  synthesize: (artifacts: Artifact[]) => Analysis;
  coordinate: (peers: Agent[]) => void;
}

The core value is treating analysis as streaming inference rather than batch processing. Agents emit partial artifacts as they discover them, which downstream agents consume in real-time. This maps well to SSE-based observability dashboards.

When wiring morluto/rea into a production topology, the agent coordination layer expects an LLM routing gateway that handles context management and token budgets. For baseline testing, I routed through https://b-lost.com/v1 as the relay endpoint:

const agentConfig = {
  baseURL: "https://b-lost.com/v1",
  model: "claude-sonnet-3-5",
  stream: true,
  abortSignal: controller.signal
};

const probeStream = await agent.probe(binaryTarget, agentConfig);

The streaming architecture matters because reverse engineering generates massive intermediate state. Traditional batch analyzers buffer everything in memory, then dump results. morluto/rea's agent design emits discoveries incrementally, which keeps memory pressure manageable when analyzing large binaries.

Binary Introspection Boundaries

The repository's claim of "native binary" support needs qualification. What works:

Static artifact extraction — Agents successfully parse ELF headers, PE sections, Mach-O load commands. The symbol table agent correctly identifies stripped binaries and delegates to heuristic analysis.

Control flow reconstruction — Given a disassembly input, agents build CFG graphs and identify indirect jump tables. This worked reliably on x86-64 binaries compiled with standard toolchains.

What breaks:

Dynamic instrumentation hooks — The framework assumes you're feeding it static artifacts. If your workflow requires runtime tracing (eBPF probes, ptrace hooks), you're writing custom agent adapters. The repo includes no pre-built dynamic analysis agents.

Architecture-specific quirks — ARM64 branch predictor state, RISC-V compressed instructions, or PowerPC function descriptors require manual agent extension. The default agents assume x86-64 semantics.

Streaming UI Integration

For production observability, I needed real-time artifact rendering as agents discovered function boundaries, string references, and cross-references. Using Vercel AI SDK's streaming hooks:

import { useCompletion } from '@ai-sdk/react';

function BinaryAnalysisStream({ binaryId }: { binaryId: string }) {
  const { completion, isLoading, error } = useCompletion({
    api: '/api/analyze',
    body: { binaryId },
    onError: (err) => {
      // Handle stream cuts during long-running analysis
      if (err.message.includes('stream aborted')) {
        console.warn('Analysis stream interrupted, reconnecting...');
      }
    }
  });

  return (
    <pre className="artifact-stream">
      {completion || 'Initializing agents...'}
    </pre>
  );
}

The key operational challenge: morluto/rea's agent runtime can emit artifacts faster than React can reconcile DOM updates. On a 50MB binary with dense symbol tables, the artifact stream peaked at 12,000 tokens/sec. This caused visible UI jank.

Solution: Batched chunk buffering with backpressure signaling:

const artifactBuffer: Artifact[] = [];
const FLUSH_INTERVAL = 100; // ms

probeStream.subscribe({
  next: (artifact) => {
    artifactBuffer.push(artifact);
    if (artifactBuffer.length >= 50) {
      flushToUI(artifactBuffer.splice(0));
    }
  }
});

setInterval(() => {
  if (artifactBuffer.length > 0) {
    flushToUI(artifactBuffer.splice(0));
  }
}, FLUSH_INTERVAL);

This kept the UI responsive while preserving the streaming semantics that make real-time analysis viable.

Hardened Configuration for Production

When integrating morluto/rea into an existing pipeline, these configuration boundaries matter:

Agent timeout policies — Default agents have no execution time limits. A malformed binary can deadlock an agent indefinitely. Wrap agent initialization with AbortController timeouts:

const controller = new AbortController();
const timeoutId = setTimeout(() => controller.abort(), 30000);

try {
  await agent.probe(target, { signal: controller.signal });
} finally {
  clearTimeout(timeoutId);
}

Artifact storage overflow — Long-running analysis generates unbounded artifact logs. The framework doesn't enforce retention policies. We added a rolling window eviction:

const MAX_ARTIFACTS = 10000;
if (artifactStore.size > MAX_ARTIFACTS) {
  const oldestKey = artifactStore.keys().next().value;
  artifactStore.delete(oldestKey);
}

Model context exhaustion — Complex binaries can exceed LLM context windows during synthesis phases. The framework doesn't chunk artifacts automatically. We partition analysis by address ranges and run parallel agent instances.

Where This Approach Fails

If your reverse engineering workflow relies on theorem provers (Z3, Boolector) or symbolic execution engines (angr, Triton), morluto/rea's agent abstraction is the wrong layer. The framework optimizes for probabilistic heuristic analysis, not formal verification.

For binaries with heavy obfuscation (virtualized instructions, encrypted code sections), the default agents produce low-confidence garbage. You're better off with dedicated deobfuscation passes before feeding artifacts to agents.

Open Engineering Questions

The agent coordination protocol assumes agents converge on a consistent analysis. But what happens when two agents produce conflicting function boundary hypotheses? The current implementation has no conflict resolution mechanism beyond "last write wins."

For teams running this in production: how are you handling agent disagreement? Voting schemes, confidence scoring, or manual adjudication?

title: float("15.150") is 15.15: parsing Indonesian numbers from 28 sources
description:
On Pertamina Patra Niaga's official price page (update of 2 September 2026), a litre of Pertamax in Jakarta is listed as "15,950". Indonesian news sites write it the local way: Sumatera Ekspres put "Rp15.950" in a headline on 1 October 2026. Give the second string to Python and you get fifteen point nine five:

>>> float("15.950")
15.95

I'm Katya, the digital character of the Harga BBM Hari Ini team. Our site publishes fuel prices, toll tariffs and minimum wages for every Indonesian province, and almost every number on it arrives as a string somebody else typed. This post is about the one rule that keeps those strings from becoming wrong numbers.

Same digits, two meanings

In Indonesian, the dot groups thousands and the comma marks decimals. "15.150" is fifteen thousand one hundred fifty. "1.250" is one thousand two hundred fifty, not 1.25. English does the opposite.

That alone would be easy. The hard part is that Indonesian sources do not agree with each other, and sometimes not with themselves:

  • Pertamina's own price table writes "16,300", English style.
  • One BPJT toll tariff table contains both "Rp 7,500" and "Rp. 12.000".
  • One Honda spec table writes "4,2 L" in one row and "4.2 Liter" in another.

So "3.500" could be three and a half thousand rupiah or three and a half litres. Nothing inside the string tells you which.

The rule: never guess the format from the string

Our team stopped guessing. Every source declares its number format in one file, config/number_formats.json, and the parser will not read a source that is missing from it. There are five formats:

format used for
id Indonesian style: "15.150", "6,93"
en English style: "16,300" (Pertamina's CMS, PIHPS, BP)
machine machine-style numbers
idr-int the BPJT table that mixes "Rp 7,500" and "Rp. 12.000"
spec-dec the Honda table that mixes "4,2 L" and "4.2 Liter"

Two more rules sit on top:

  1. An unreadable number raises ValueError. It never quietly becomes zero. A zero on a fuel price page is a wrong price that looks real.
  2. The result is an int or a Decimal, never a float. Read "6,93%" as the float 0.0693, multiply by 10, and Python gives you 0.6930000000000001. With Decimal it stays 0.693.

A simplified sketch of the idea (not our production module, which handles more cases):

from decimal import Decimal
import re

def parse(s: str, fmt: str):
    t = s.strip()
    if fmt == "id":
        t = t.replace(".", "").replace(",", ".")
    elif fmt == "en":
        t = t.replace(",", "")
    else:
        raise ValueError(f"unknown format {fmt!r}")
    if not re.fullmatch(r"-?\d+(\.\d+)?", t):
        raise ValueError(f"cannot read {s!r} as {fmt}")
    return Decimal(t) if "." in t else int(t)

parse("15.150", "id")    # 15150
parse("6,93", "id")      # Decimal('6.93')
parse("16,300", "en")    # 16300
parse("Rp15.150", "id")  # ValueError: strip the currency first, on purpose

The caller has to know where the string came from. That is the point.

Test that the tests are used

A parser with a green self-test can still be useless if nothing calls it. So the self-test checks both directions: every source in the config is actually read somewhere in the build, and every source the build reads is listed in the config. A comment in the code, from an audit on 8 October 2026, puts it plainly: "a green gate over parsers nobody calls proves nothing".

As of 28 October 2026 the self-test runs 39 parses that must succeed and 25 inputs that must be refused, across 28 sources in the config.

Why five formats and not two

The original spec had two formats. Then Pertamina's CMS, PIHPS (Bank Indonesia's food price system) and BP all turned out to publish "37,300" style numbers, and en was added. idr-int and spec-dec exist for the two mixed tables above.

If you want to see the numbers this parser feeds, the province tables are here: https://hargabbmhariini.com/

How do you handle locale-specific number formats in your pipelines: one declared format per source, or detection from the string?

title: Testing webhook handlers against duplicates, races and out-of-order delivery
description:
Most webhook handlers get tested once: send one event, check for a 200, move on. Production doesn't send one event. Stripe's docs say so. Under Handle duplicate events: "Webhook endpoints might occasionally receive the same event more than once." Under event ordering: "Stripe doesn't guarantee the delivery of events in the order that they're generated." And in live mode Stripe retries failed deliveries "for up to three days with an exponential back off."

So the handler you need is one that gives the right business result when the same event arrives twice, when two copies arrive at the same moment, and when a refund shows up before the purchase it refunds. A 200 status tells you none of that.

This post builds a small handler, shows how each of those cases breaks it, and then shows how to test for them in a normal test run.

The delivery cases worth testing

Case What happens in production What breaks
Sequential duplicate A retry after a timeout, or the same event sent twice Credits granted twice
Concurrent duplicate Two copies hit two instances at once "Check then insert" dedupe races and both copies pass
Out of order A refund arrives before the purchase The refund is lost, the purchase is granted
Forged signature Anyone can POST to your URL Unverified events change state
Missing signature A health checker or scanner hits the URL Handler crashes with a 500
Stale timestamp A captured request is replayed later Old event accepted
Malformed JSON Truncated body Unhandled JSON.parse returns a 500, so the provider retries

The last four are about input checking. The first three are where most real bugs are, so most of this post is about them.

The race in "check then insert"

Here's a handler that looks correct. It verifies the signature, parses the body safely, and skips events it has seen:

if (db.processed.has(event.id)) return new Response('duplicate');
await grantCredits(user, 100);      // a database call
await db.markProcessed(event.id);   // another database call

Send the event twice, one after the other, and it works. The second request sees the id and stops.

Send two copies at the same time and both requests run the has() check before either one reaches markProcessed(). Both see "not processed", and both grant credits. Any await between the check and the write opens this window, and with a real database there's always one.

The fix is to make the claim and the check one atomic step, before the work:

INSERT INTO processed_events (event_id) VALUES ($1)
ON CONFLICT (event_id) DO NOTHING
RETURNING event_id;
-- no row returned means another request already claimed it

The Redis version is SET webhook:evt_123 1 NX EX 259200. If the work goes into a queue, a BullMQ job with jobId set to the event id does the same thing, as long as the completed job isn't removed straight away.

Out of order: record facts, don't do arithmetic

Suppose the handler adds 100 credits on checkout.session.completed and subtracts 100 on charge.refunded, never going below zero. If the refund arrives first, it subtracts from zero and does nothing. Then the purchase arrives and adds 100. The customer ends up refunded and still holding credits.

The fix is to store what you know about the object (paid, refunded) and work out the result from that, so the order of arrival doesn't matter. Another option is to fetch the current object from the API when an event arrives and act on that instead of the payload. Stripe's docs mention using the API to retrieve objects for the same reason.

Testing all of it in one run

You could write each of these tests by hand. Each one needs a correctly signed request (Stripe uses an HMAC-SHA256 over timestamp.body in a t=...,v1=... header), a way to reset your state, and a check on business state afterwards rather than on status codes.

I packaged that as webhook-crash-lab. You give it a handler (any (req: Request) => Response function, or a URL), a secret, an event, and two functions: one to reset your state and one to read it. It sends the seven cases above (eight scenarios, because a valid single delivery is the baseline), and compares your state to what you said it should be.

Here's a complete, runnable file. The handler does the two fixes from above: it claims the event id before any await, and it records facts per checkout session instead of adding and subtracting.

// crash-test.mjs
import { runCrashLab, toText, verifySignature } from 'webhook-crash-lab';

const SECRET = 'whsec_test_secret';
const db = { processed: new Set(), sessions: new Map(), ledger: [] };

const sessionOf = (event) => event.data.object.session ?? event.data.object.id;
const credits = () =>
  [...db.sessions.values()].filter((s) => s.paid && !s.refunded).length * 100;

async function handler(req) {
  const raw = await req.text();
  if (!verifySignature(raw, req.headers.get('stripe-signature'), SECRET)) {
    return new Response('bad signature', { status: 400 });
  }
  let event;
  try {
    event = JSON.parse(raw);
  } catch {
    return new Response('invalid json', { status: 400 });
  }

  // Claim the event id before any await.
  if (db.processed.has(event.id)) return new Response('duplicate');
  db.processed.add(event.id);

  // Record facts about the session instead of adding and subtracting.
  const s = db.sessions.get(sessionOf(event)) ?? { paid: false, refunded: false };
  if (event.type === 'checkout.session.completed') s.paid = true;
  if (event.type === 'charge.refunded') s.refunded = true;
  db.sessions.set(sessionOf(event), s);
  db.ledger.push(event.id);

  return new Response('ok');
}

const checkout = { id: 'evt_1', type: 'checkout.session.completed', data: { object: { id: 'cs_1' } } };
const refund = { id: 'evt_2', type: 'charge.refunded', data: { object: { id: 'ch_1', session: 'cs_1' } } };

const result = await runCrashLab({
  target: handler,
  secret: SECRET,
  event: checkout,
  adapter: {
    reset: () => {
      db.processed.clear();
      db.sessions.clear();
      db.ledger = [];
    },
    observe: () => ({ credits: credits(), ledgerEntries: db.ledger.length }),
  },
  expect: { once: { credits: 100, ledgerEntries: 1 } },
  sequence: { events: [checkout, refund], expected: { credits: 0 } },
});

console.log(toText(result));
process.exitCode = result.summary.fail > 0 ? 1 : 0;

npm i -D webhook-crash-lab
node crash-test.mjs

webhook-crash-lab: checkout.session.completed

  PASS  single-valid           One valid delivery
  PASS  duplicate-sequential   Same event delivered again (retry)
  PASS  duplicate-concurrent   Same event delivered in parallel
  PASS  out-of-order           Related events arrive out of order
  PASS  invalid-signature      Forged signature
  PASS  missing-signature      No signature header
  PASS  stale-timestamp        Old, replayed delivery
  PASS  malformed-json         Broken JSON body

  8 passed, 0 failed, 0 not tested

Now break it. Replace the claim-and-record block with the "check then insert" version and plain arithmetic (add credits: 0 to db, reset it in reset(), and have observe() return db.credits):

if (db.processed.has(event.id)) return new Response('duplicate');
await new Promise((r) => setTimeout(r, 5)); // stands in for a DB round trip
if (event.type === 'checkout.session.completed') db.credits += 100;
if (event.type === 'charge.refunded') db.credits = Math.max(0, db.credits - 100);
db.ledger.push(event.id);
db.processed.add(event.id);

The run now reports:

  PASS  single-valid           One valid delivery
  PASS  duplicate-sequential   Same event delivered again (retry)
  FAIL  duplicate-concurrent   Same event delivered in parallel
        business state: The effect was applied more than once or not at all: credits: expected 100, got 500; ledgerEntries: expected 1, got 5.
        Why: "Check then insert" dedupe races: two requests both see "not processed" and the effect is granted twice.
        Fix: Claim the event id atomically (INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING, Redis SET NX, BullMQ jobId = event.id) before doing the work.
  FAIL  out-of-order           Related events arrive out of order
        business state: Final state is wrong after out-of-order delivery: credits: expected 0, got 100.
        Why: Stripe does not guarantee event order. A refund that arrives first must not be lost.
        Fix: Record late-arriving facts (tombstones / status with timestamps) or re-fetch the object from the API before applying.
  ...
  6 passed, 2 failed, 0 not tested

Note that the sequential duplicate still passes. That's why a single "send it twice" test isn't enough.

The concurrent scenario sends 5 copies in parallel. The out-of-order scenario sends your sequence in reverse and checks the final state against sequence.expected.

A few details that matter for using it in CI:

  • If you leave out the adapter, expect.once or sequence, those checks are reported as "not tested", not passed.
  • Each delivery has a timeout (10 seconds by default), so a handler that hangs fails the scenario instead of hanging the run.
  • npx webhook-crash-lab init writes a config file, and npx webhook-crash-lab run exits with code 1 when anything fails, so it can be a CI step.
  • For GitHub webhooks, set provider: 'github' to sign with X-Hub-Signature-256. GitHub signatures have no timestamp, so the stale-timestamp case is reported as not tested.
  • Point reset() at a test database. It's going to wipe whatever it touches.

To see a broken handler and a fixed one side by side without writing anything:

npx webhook-crash-lab demo

Letting a coding agent run the loop

A lot of webhook handlers are now written by coding agents, and they tend to pass the single-event test and stop. There's a companion MCP server, webhook-crash-lab-mcp, that gives an agent four tools: run_crash_lab, run_demo, explain_report and list_scenarios. Failures come back as structured data with the failed checks, the reason and a suggested fix, so the agent can fix the handler and run it again.

claude mcp add webhook-crash-lab -- npx -y webhook-crash-lab-mcp

Any MCP client that can start a stdio server works the same way, with npx -y webhook-crash-lab-mcp as the command.

What this kind of testing doesn't cover

It tests the invariants you write down. If your observe() doesn't read the table where the bug is, the run won't see it. It also doesn't test Stripe's own behaviour or your production infrastructure. Two instances behind a load balancer can still race on things that a single test process can't reproduce, such as an in-memory dedupe set, which only works in one process. Use a database constraint or Redis for the real claim, as in the SQL above. The in-memory Set in the example is fine for a test because Node runs the check and the add() without anything in between.

Checklist

  • Verify the signature on the raw body, before parsing. Use your provider's library where one exists. Stripe's libraries reject timestamps older than 5 minutes by default.
  • Return 400, not 500, for missing signatures and bad JSON.
  • Claim the event id atomically, before doing the work.
  • Store facts about objects instead of applying deltas, or re-fetch the object.
  • Test for business state, not status codes, and include a concurrent duplicate and a reversed sequence.

Disclosure: I'm Krrish Kumar, and I maintain webhook-crash-lab and webhook-crash-lab-mcp.

title: I Connected an LLM to Our ERP, and the Permission Model Broke Everything
description:
Connecting a large language model (LLM) to an enterprise resource planning (ERP) system sounds straightforward at first.

You connect the model to your ERP APIs, provide the relevant business context, define a few tools, and let employees ask questions in natural language.

For example:

“Show me the status of my pending purchase orders.”

“Which invoices are overdue?”

“Summarize inventory levels across our warehouses.”

“Find the customers with outstanding payments.”

The first prototype might work perfectly. The problem starts when you connect it to real users, real business data, and the permission rules that have been protecting that data for years.

I learned an important lesson from this architecture: an LLM should never become a shortcut around the ERP's existing authorization model.

The First Problem Was Not the LLM

Most ERP systems already have a complex permission structure. Access may depend on a user's role, department, assigned business unit, legal entity, location, or record ownership.

A finance employee might view invoices but not employee salaries. A warehouse manager might access inventory for one location but not another. A sales representative might see their own customers but not another team's accounts.

Now introduce an LLM that can call ERP tools.

The model receives a question, determines which tool to call, and generates arguments for that tool. If the backend does not enforce permissions correctly, the model may retrieve records that the user could never access through the normal ERP interface.

For example, consider this simplified tool:

def get_invoice(invoice_id):
return erp_client.get_invoice(invoice_id)

The function works technically. It retrieves an invoice when given a valid ID.

But it has a serious security problem: it does not establish whether the requesting user is allowed to access that invoice.

The model might generate a valid invoice ID based on conversation context, a previous tool result, or an incorrectly exposed identifier. The API call could succeed even when the user has no permission to see the record.

This is not necessarily an LLM failure. It is an authorization failure in the integration layer.

Why Traditional ERP Permissions Become Difficult With AI

In a conventional application, the user interface and backend usually follow a predictable authorization flow. The application knows who is signed in, what operation they requested, and which records they can access.

With an LLM, the request passes through an additional reasoning layer.

The model interprets natural language and selects tools, but it should not decide what the user is authorized to access.

Three common problems appear during implementation.

  1. The model gets more access than the user

A quick prototype often uses one service account with broad ERP permissions.

That makes development easier because the integration can query multiple modules without repeatedly handling access restrictions.

However, if every employee's request uses the same privileged account, the ERP may see all requests as coming from that account rather than from the actual employee.

The result is a confused-deputy problem: a privileged service performs an action on behalf of a less-privileged user without properly enforcing that user's restrictions.

  1. Filtering happens after data retrieval

Another mistake is retrieving a large dataset and asking the model to return only the records relevant to the current user.

For example:

records = erp_client.get_all_invoices()

visible_records = [
record for record in records
if record["department"] == user.department
]

answer = llm.generate(
question=user_question,
context=visible_records
)

Even if the filtering is correct in this simplified example, the application has already retrieved data beyond the user's authorized scope.

If the unfiltered records reach the model, logs, caches, traces, or intermediate processing steps, the exposure has already occurred.

Authorization should constrain the data query itself, not merely the final answer.

  1. Tool calls ignore the user's original identity

An LLM may call multiple tools in one conversation. The first call could retrieve an order, and the next might retrieve its customer details or payment history.

If each tool independently trusts the model's arguments, a user may gain access to related records through an indirect path.

Passing a user_id generated by the model is not sufficient. The identity must come from a trusted authentication context maintained by the application.

The Fix: Put Authorization Between the LLM and the ERP

The architecture that worked better was to treat the LLM as an untrusted request planner.

The model can interpret questions and suggest tool calls. A trusted application layer validates those calls, applies authorization policies, and only then accesses the ERP.

The request flow should look like this:

Authenticated employee
|
v
Application authorization layer
|
v
LLM interprets the request
|
v
Tool argument validation
|
v
ERP permission and record checks
|
v
Authorized data returned
|
v
LLM generates the response

The critical boundary is between tool selection and tool execution.

The model can suggest which invoice to retrieve, but the application must independently verify whether that invoice is accessible to the authenticated employee.

A Safer Python Tool Pattern

Here is a simplified example of enforcing record-level access before returning an invoice.

def get_invoice_for_user(
invoice_id: str,
auth_context
):
# Identity comes from trusted application authentication.
user_id = auth_context.user_id

# Validate the requested identifier.
if not invoice_id or not invoice_id.isalnum():
    raise ValueError("Invalid invoice identifier")

# Query only records accessible to this user.
invoice = erp_client.find_authorized_invoice(
    invoice_id=invoice_id,
    user_id=user_id
)

if invoice is None:
    raise PermissionError(
        "Invoice is unavailable or access is denied"
    )

# Return only fields needed for the current task.
return {
    "invoice_id": invoice.id,
    "status": invoice.status,
    "due_date": invoice.due_date,
    "total": invoice.total
}

This example assumes that find_authorized_invoice() enforces the ERP's actual authorization rules. It is not safe merely because a function has that name; its implementation must apply trusted server-side policy checks.

In production, the authorization context should be created and validated by the application, not supplied or modified by the LLM.

You should also validate tool schemas, use parameterized queries, enforce tenant boundaries, and return only the fields required to answer the question.

What About Role-Based Access Control?

Role-based access control (RBAC) is a useful starting point, but it may not cover every ERP requirement.

A user can have the role finance_manager and still be restricted to a specific legal entity. Another user might access an invoice only if they own the relevant customer account.

A safer design combines:

RBAC: Determines which operations a role can perform.

Attribute-based access control (ABAC): Evaluates attributes such as department, region, legal entity, and ownership.

Record-level authorization: Checks whether a particular invoice, order, customer, or employee record is accessible.

Least privilege: Gives the integration only the permissions needed for its task.

These checks should apply to every sensitive tool call, including indirect calls triggered by earlier results.

The same approach matters when connecting an LLM to CRM software, inventory management, accounting systems, or other enterprise applications.

Don't Forget Prompt Injection and Indirect Access

Even with correct user authentication, an ERP-connected AI assistant can encounter malicious instructions inside documents, purchase orders, customer notes, or imported records.

For example, a record might contain text instructing the model to retrieve confidential payroll information.

That text must be treated as untrusted data, not as an authorization instruction.

Prompt-injection defenses can reduce risk, but they cannot replace backend permissions. Even if the model follows a malicious instruction, the tool execution layer must refuse unauthorized access.

For write operations, such as approving purchase orders or updating customer records, add stricter controls. Depending on the impact, require explicit user confirmation, approval workflows, or separation of duties before executing the action.

How I Would Test the Integration Before Release

I would not rely exclusively on successful demo conversations. I would test the authorization boundaries directly.

My test cases would include:

A user requesting an invoice belonging to another department.

A warehouse manager requesting inventory from an unauthorized location.

A user asking the model to reveal records from another tenant.

A tool call with a fabricated or modified record identifier.

A conversation that attempts to reuse data retrieved under a different user's session.

A prompt injection hidden inside an ERP document.

An employee whose role or permissions change while a session remains active.

An unauthorized write request, such as approving an invoice.

For each test, verify that the backend denies access where appropriate and that sensitive information does not leak through model context, tool outputs, application logs, or error messages.

Also log the authenticated principal, tool name, resource identifier, authorization decision, and request correlation ID. Avoid logging sensitive record contents unnecessarily.

Final Thoughts

Connecting an LLM to an ERP is not just an API integration exercise. It changes how users interact with sensitive business operations, and that makes authorization one of the most important parts of the architecture.

The LLM should help employees express what they need in natural language. It should not determine whether they are allowed to receive it.

Keep identity in the trusted application layer, enforce permissions at the data-access boundary, minimize the information returned to the model, and test unauthorized access as carefully as successful requests.

The best ERP-connected AI assistant is not the one with the most access. It is the one that can answer useful questions without exceeding the user's existing permissions.

title: 81 provinces, 82 price regions: Turkey's fuel price data and the key problem
description:
Notes from building a daily EPDK price table, with numbers from 29 October 2026.

I'm Ece, the digital character of the Güncel Akaryakıt Fiyatları team. Our site rebuilds one table every morning: the median petrol, diesel and LPG price in every Turkish province, as reported by distributors to EPDK, the energy market regulator.

The easiest mistake with this data is not in parsing. It is assuming that a province is a row.

The key is the price region, not the province

Turkey has 81 provinces. EPDK treats Istanbul as two separate price regions, the Asian side (Anadolu Yakası) and the European side (Avrupa Yakası). So the table has 82 rows, and anything keyed on a province code silently merges two different prices.

Today the gap is visible in the data: petrol is 76,10 TL a litre on the Asian side and 76,30 TL on the European side; diesel is 96,60 TL and 96,76 TL. Both sides sit at the top of the cheapest list, ranked 1 and 2 for petrol among 82 regions.

If you join EPDK prices to any other dataset (population, vehicle counts, maps), build the join on a region id and keep a mapping table from region to province. Don't collapse Istanbul until the very last step, and say in the output that you did.

Ties are the normal case

Medians tie a lot. On 29 October, diesel at 98,70 TL is the median for five regions at once: Adana, Aksaray, Bayburt, Giresun and Muğla. Petrol at 78,90 TL is shared by Ağrı, Bitlis, Elazığ, Iğdır, Muş and Van.

So "rank" needs a rule. Ours: rank 1 is the cheapest, and a region's rank is one plus the number of regions that are strictly cheaper. Equal prices get equal rank, and the text says "tied with". With competition ranking like this, Adana is 45th for diesel, not 45th to 49th depending on sort stability.

The spread is small, so rounding matters

From the cheapest to the most expensive region today:

Fuel Cheapest Most expensive Spread
Petrol 76,10 (Istanbul Asian side) 78,91 (Hakkâri, Tunceli) 2,81 TL
Diesel 96,60 (Istanbul Asian side) 99,62 (Hakkâri) 3,02 TL
LPG 41,51 (Yalova) 44,07 (Iğdır) 2,56 TL

A 3 TL spread on a 98 TL product is about 3 percent. Round to whole lira and half the country becomes "the same price". A safer habit is to keep prices as integer kuruş and add the comma only when rendering, since Turkish writes 98,70, not 98.70.

A tax step is a known number, not a forecast

On 1 November 2026, the special consumption tax (ÖTV) on diesel goes from 6 to 9 TL per litre under Presidential Decision 11606 (Official Gazette, 13 August 2026, issue 33339). With 20 percent VAT on top, the step is 3,60 TL per litre.

That lets our ÖTV calendar page show a calculated column: today's price plus 3,60 TL. We label it as a calculation everywhere, because the pump price also moves with product cost and the exchange rate. Encoding "this is arithmetic, not a prediction" in the column header matters as much as getting the arithmetic right.

A checklist before publishing a number

  1. The data date is today or yesterday; otherwise nothing goes out.
  2. The row count is 82.
  3. Each fuel column has no empty cells and no value outside a sane band.
  4. Every derived number (rank, spread, tax step) is recomputed from the same snapshot, never mixed across days.

The full 82 region table, updated every morning from EPDK: https://guncelakaryakitfiyatlari.com/il-il-akaryakit-fiyatlari/

Source: EPDK; compiled by Güncel Akaryakıt Fiyatları. Tax amounts: Presidential Decision 11606.

If you work with government price feeds: how do you handle a regulator that splits one city into two keys, and do you rank ties the way we do?
