title: asyncio.gather() Still Takes 2.5 Seconds? Find the Blocking Call with Debug Mode
description:
You wrapped five calls in asyncio.gather(), expecting them to finish in about the time of the slowest one. Instead the total is the sum of all five, exactly as if you had written a plain for loop.

gather() is almost never the problem. Something inside one of your coroutines is blocking the event loop: a call that does real waiting without ever handing control back with await. While it runs, no other task can make progress, so your "concurrent" code quietly turns sequential.

Here is how to prove it in a minute, find the exact culprit, and fix it.

The 10-line reproduction 

import asyncio, time

async def fetch_blocking(i):
    time.sleep(0.5)          # looks harmless, freezes the whole loop
    return i

async def fetch_ok(i):
    await asyncio.to_thread(time.sleep, 0.5)   # waits in a worker thread
    return i

async def main():
    t = time.perf_counter()
    await asyncio.gather(*(fetch_blocking(i) for i in range(5)))
    print(f"blocking: {time.perf_counter() - t:.2f}s")

    t = time.perf_counter()
    await asyncio.gather(*(fetch_ok(i) for i in range(5)))
    print(f"to_thread: {time.perf_counter() - t:.2f}s")

asyncio.run(main())

On Python 3.13 this prints:

blocking: 2.50s
to_thread: 0.51s

Same gather(), same five tasks. The only difference is whether the waiting happens on the event loop thread or off it. In real code time.sleep is rarely the offender. It is usually requests.get(), a sync database driver, open().read() on a big file, subprocess.run(), or a CPU-heavy loop such as parsing a large JSON payload.

Step 1: Turn on asyncio debug mode

You don't need a profiler to find the blocker. asyncio has a built-in detector: in debug mode it logs every step of a task that holds the loop longer than loop.slow_callback_duration (100 ms by default).

Enable it any one of these ways:

asyncio.run(main(), debug=True)

PYTHONASYNCIODEBUG=1 python app.py
# or
python -X dev app.py

Make sure warnings from the asyncio logger are visible (for a quick script, logging.basicConfig(level=logging.DEBUG) is enough). Running the example above with debug=True prints one line per offending step:

WARNING:asyncio:Executing <Task finished name='Task-2' coro=<fetch_blocking() done, defined at demo.py:4> result=0 created at .../asyncio/tasks.py:748> took 0.500 seconds

That line tells you the coroutine name (fetch_blocking), the file and line where it is defined, and how long it froze the loop. Five of those lines, each about 0.5 s, add up to your mysterious 2.5 s.

If your real blockers are shorter, lower the threshold so they show up:

async def main():
    asyncio.get_running_loop().slow_callback_duration = 0.02  # 20 ms
    ...

Debug mode adds overhead, so use it locally or in staging, not as a permanent production setting.

Step 2: Narrow it down inside the coroutine

The warning points at a coroutine, not a line. If that coroutine is long, time the suspect calls directly:

t = time.perf_counter()
resp = client.get(url)          # suspect
print("get took", time.perf_counter() - t)

The rule of thumb: any call that waits on the network, disk, or a subprocess and is not preceded by await is a blocker. So is any pure-Python loop that runs for more than a few milliseconds.

Step 3: Pick the right fix

What blocks Fix
time.sleep(n) await asyncio.sleep(n)
requests an async client such as httpx.AsyncClient or aiohttp
sync DB driver (psycopg2, pymysql) an async driver (asyncpg, aiomysql, SQLAlchemy's async engine), or wrap calls in asyncio.to_thread
a sync library with no async version await asyncio.to_thread(func, *args) (Python 3.9+)
CPU-heavy work (big parsing, hashing, image work) a process pool via loop.run_in_executor(ProcessPoolExecutor(), func, arg)

asyncio.to_thread is the quickest unblock for I/O-bound sync code, but remember it runs in a thread pool. Because of the GIL, threads will not speed up pure-Python CPU work, which is why that row goes to a process pool instead.

The FastAPI version of this bug

This shows up constantly in FastAPI, and it is sneaky because the "fix" people try first makes it worse.

@app.get("/report")
async def report():
    data = requests.get(UPSTREAM).json()   # blocks the event loop
    return data

With async def, FastAPI runs the endpoint on the event loop. The blocking requests.get() freezes every other request the worker is handling, so under load one slow upstream makes the whole service look dead.

You have two honest options:

  1. Keep it sync. Declare it as plain def report():. FastAPI then runs it in a thread pool, and the blocking call only ties up one worker thread.
  2. Go fully async. Keep async def and use an async client with await: 
@app.get("/report")
async def report():
    async with httpx.AsyncClient(timeout=10) as client:
        r = await client.get(UPSTREAM)
    return r.json()

What you should not do is mix them: async def plus a sync client is the worst of both. If you are still deciding between frameworks for this kind of service, I compared the trade-offs in FastAPI vs Flask: which is better in 2026.

Once it's unblocked: limit concurrency

When the loop is free, gather() fires everything at once, and 500 simultaneous requests can trip rate limits or exhaust a connection pool. Cap it with a semaphore:

sem = asyncio.Semaphore(10)

async def fetch(client, url):
    async with sem:
        r = await client.get(url)
        return r.status_code

async def main(urls):
    async with httpx.AsyncClient(timeout=10) as client:
        return await asyncio.gather(*(fetch(client, u) for u in urls))

On Python 3.11+ you can use asyncio.TaskGroup instead of gather() when you want one failing task to cancel the rest.

Quick checklist

  • Total time equals the sum of the tasks? Something is blocking the loop.
  • Run with asyncio.run(main(), debug=True) or PYTHONASYNCIODEBUG=1 and read the Executing <Task ...> took X seconds warnings.
  • Lower slow_callback_duration if the blockers are short.
  • Swap sync clients for async ones, or wrap them in asyncio.to_thread.
  • Send CPU-heavy work to a process pool.
  • In FastAPI, never put a blocking call inside async def.

If you're newer to async/await and want the fundamentals first (coroutines, create_task, timeouts and cancellation), there's a beginner walkthrough in this Python asyncio tutorial with examples. And when you're debugging the API payloads themselves, the free browser tools on Blogs World, like the JSON formatter, help you inspect responses without pasting them into random sites.

title: Q&A over internal documents: make the system say "not in the docs"
description:
An assistant that answers questions about your documents will be wrong sometimes. What destroys trust is not the wrong answer, it is the confident wrong answer to a question the documents never covered. So the first design question is not "how good is retrieval?" but "when does the system refuse?"

Here is a small demo that treats refusal as a first-class result. The data is public and the numbers are test numbers, not a client result.

What the demo does

One function, KB.answer(question), returns three things: the best passage as the citation, a confidence that it really holds the answer, and a decision: cite it, or refuse.

It deliberately returns the passage, not a generated sentence. Generating prose on top of a cited passage is the step that needs a language model; the part that decides whether to answer at all does not.

  • Data: SQuAD 2.0 dev (Wikipedia, CC BY-SA 4.0), 35 articles. Wikipedia stands in for a company's documentation.
  • Retrieval: BM25.
  • Decision: a small model over retrieval features: the top score, its margin over the runner-up, IDF-weighted coverage of the question's terms, and the share of terms the passage doesn't know.
  • Threshold: tuned on separate articles for a 95% precision target.
  • No LLM, no GPU.

Evaluating without leaking

Articles are split into a tuning set and a test set. A third of the test articles are deliberately left out of the knowledge base, and their questions must be refused. Without that group you only measure how well the system answers questions it was built for, which is the easy case.

Results (test KB: 406 passages, 4,904 questions)

Case Result
Question about a topic NOT in the base refused correctly in 96.1%
Answerable question: right passage in top-3 87.8% (top-1: 75.3%)
Answerable question: cited with confidence 61.2% of questions, 93.2% of those cited point to the right passage
Answerable plus out-of-base, overall 42.5% cited, 90.4% of cited are correct

The refusal rate on out-of-base questions is the number I would put in an acceptance document. It says the system stays quiet when it has nothing.

Honest limits

  • The target was 95% precision. On the test articles the cited answers reached 93% (answerable only) and 90% (with out-of-base questions mixed in). The threshold is a sampled estimate, and a pilot re-tunes it on the client's own documents and questions.
  • Questions that are close to a document but not answered by it (SQuAD's "unanswerable" ones) are refused only 39% of the time. Lexical signals cannot see that difference. This is where a reranker or an LLM belongs in a real build, and I report the number instead of hiding it.
  • Wikipedia is not your wiki. Expect to measure again on real material.

Takeaways

  1. Give refusal its own metric and its own test set.
  2. Always include questions about things that are not in the base.
  3. Return the citation, so a person can verify in one click.
  4. Report the failure mode you have not solved.

title: Stop paying monthly for email validation — self-host the core in one Python file
description:
Email-validation APIs (Abstract, ZeroBounce, Hunter) charge $20–100/mo and cap your volume. But the core of what they sell is not magic — it's three checks you can run yourself for free.

The three checks that catch ~95% of bad emails

  1. Syntax — a sane regex (don't over-engineer RFC 5322).
  2. Deliverability — does the domain have MX records? No MX = mail can't be delivered. You can resolve MX over DNS-over-HTTPS (Cloudflare/Google) with no library and no API key.
  3. Disposable + role detection — reject mailinator.com et al, and flag admin@ / info@ / support@. 
import json, urllib.request, urllib.parse
def has_mx(domain):
    u="https://cloudflare-dns.com/dns-query?"+urllib.parse.urlencode({"name":domain,"type":"MX"})
    r=urllib.request.Request(u,headers={"accept":"application/dns-json"})
    d=json.loads(urllib.request.urlopen(r,timeout=4).read())
    return any(a.get("type")==15 for a in d.get("Answer",[]))

Wrap those three into a score + verdict and you've replaced a monthly bill with a file you own. No per-request cost, unlimited volume.

I packaged the full version (syntax + MX-via-DoH + disposable/role + a tiny HTTP server you can deploy anywhere) here for $5: https://bottiezim.gumroad.com/l/awhjh — or just take the snippet above, it genuinely works.

title: PostgreSQL 19 Release Candidate: What Shipped, What Was Cut, How to Upgrade
description:
Originally published at muhammadmoiz.dev.

PostgreSQL 19 is not out yet. The first release candidate shipped on October 15, 2026, and the project now plans general availability for November 19, 2026, later than many teams expected. Several headline features announced in the June beta were pulled before the RC, so if you planned an upgrade around them, this guide covers what actually made the cut, what changes under your feet, and how to get ready.

Where the release stands right now

The PostgreSQL 19 timeline this year has been longer than usual. Here are the dates that matter, all from the project's own announcements:

Milestone Date
Beta 1 June 4, 2026
Beta 4 (features removed) September 24, 2026
Release Candidate 1 October 15, 2026
RC 2 and minor updates for supported versions November 12, 2026 (planned)
PostgreSQL 14 end of life November 12, 2026
PostgreSQL 19 general availability November 19, 2026 (planned)

The RC 1 announcement explains that the release team chose to fold a large batch of fixes into version 19 before calling it final, which is why a second release candidate is on the calendar. The GA date can still move if a serious issue turns up.

Why so many late fixes? According to a DEV Community write-up that collects the public discussion, long-time committer Peter Eisentraut wrote on October 9 that LLM-assisted code review was at least partly responsible for the wave of reverts, because it surfaced defects in already-committed features much faster than before. The same write-up notes that some community members pushed back, saying a large share of AI-reported bugs turned out not to be real. Either way, the practical result for you is the same: a smaller, more conservative release.

What was cut from PostgreSQL 19

If you read the Beta 1 announcement and got excited, check this list before you plan anything. The official Beta 4 announcement says these were removed so they can be reconsidered for a later major version:

  • SQL/PGQ property graph queries (graph-style queries in standard SQL)
  • Turning data checksums on or off while the cluster is online
  • Temporal UPDATE and DELETE using FOR PORTION OF
  • ALTER TABLE ... MERGE PARTITIONS and SPLIT PARTITIONS
  • pg_get_role_ddl(), pg_get_tablespace_ddl() and pg_get_database_ddl()

GROUP BY ALL, which appeared in the Beta 1 highlights, is also missing from the current release notes. So if a blog post or tutorial shows any of these as "new in Postgres 19", treat it as outdated.

What did make it in

The good news is that a lot of useful work survived. Based on the RC-era release notes, these are the changes most app developers will notice:

Photo: Domaintechnik on Unsplash

For application code

  • INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO SELECT ... RETURNING. An upsert can now hand back the row that already existed instead of silently skipping it. That removes a common "insert, and if nothing came back, run a second SELECT" round trip.
  • Faster foreign key checks. The notes list a general performance improvement for foreign key constraint checks.
  • A WAIT command for replicas. A session on a standby can wait until a given WAL position has been written, flushed or replayed. That gives you read-your-writes behaviour when you send writes to the primary and reads to a replica.
  • More jsonpath string methods, including lower(), upper(), replace(), split_part() and the trim family.
  • COPY TO can output JSON, with a FORCE_ARRAY option to produce a single JSON array.
  • Smarter NOTIFY, which now wakes only the backends listening on the relevant channel. Apps that use LISTEN/NOTIFY for real-time features should see less overhead.

Here is the kind of upsert that gets simpler. This is an illustration, not code from the docs:

-- Create a tag if it doesn't exist, and always get its row back
INSERT INTO tags (name)
VALUES ('billing')
ON CONFLICT (name) DO SELECT
RETURNING id, name;

For operations

  • REPACK, a built-in way to rebuild bloated tables, with a CONCURRENTLY option that avoids blocking reads and writes. It shipped with a narrower scope than first planned, and it received many crash and correctness fixes during the betas, so test it on a copy first.
  • Parallel autovacuum via autovacuum_max_parallel_workers, plus a new scoring system for deciding which tables to vacuum first.
  • Automatic I/O worker scaling between the new io_min_workers and io_max_workers settings.
  • pg_plan_advice and pg_stash_advice, new modules for steering and pinning planner decisions.
  • Logical replication of sequences, which makes replication-based online upgrades less fiddly.
  • TLS SNI support through a new pg_hosts.conf file, so one server can present different certificates per hostname.

Breaking changes to check before upgrading

This is the section to read twice. These items come from the migration section and other behaviour changes in the release notes:

  1. JIT is off by default. If you have analytical queries that benefited from JIT compilation, benchmark them and turn it back on explicitly if needed.
  2. RADIUS authentication is gone. The notes describe the UDP-only implementation as unfixably insecure. Move to another method before upgrading.
  3. MD5 password logins now trigger a warning after successful authentication (controlled by md5_password_warnings). It's a nudge to switch to SCRAM.
  4. standard_conforming_strings is always on. Dumps taken from older versions with this setting off will not load correctly into 19.
  5. max_locks_per_transaction defaults to 128 instead of 64, and lock sizing changed. If you tuned this value, the notes say you effectively need to double it to keep the same capacity.
  6. json_array() returns an empty array instead of NULL when there are no rows. Check any code that tests for NULL here.
  7. Default TOAST compression is now lz4 rather than pglz.
  8. vacuumdb --analyze-only now includes partitioned tables when no targets are given.

A quick way to spot settings that matter on your current server:

SELECT name, setting
FROM pg_settings
WHERE name IN (
  'jit',
  'standard_conforming_strings',
  'max_locks_per_transaction',
  'password_encryption',
  'default_toast_compression'
);

And to find roles still using MD5 password hashes (run as a superuser):

SELECT rolname
FROM pg_authid
WHERE rolpassword LIKE 'md5%';

A practical upgrade checklist

Don't run an RC in production: A release candidate is for testing. Wait for the final 19.0 release, and for most teams, for the first minor release after it, before moving production data.

  1. Know your current version. Run SELECT version();. If you're on PostgreSQL 14, that matters more than 19: version 14 stops getting fixes on November 12, 2026. Plan to move to 17 or 18 now, or straight to 19 once it's stable.
  2. Check your provider. Managed services (RDS, Cloud SQL, Supabase, Neon and others) adopt new majors on their own schedules. Look up when they will offer 19 rather than assuming it will be there on day one.
  3. Spin up the RC in a container and restore a recent copy of your database into it. Run your test suite and your slowest real queries.
  4. Work through the breaking-change list above, especially MD5, RADIUS and standard_conforming_strings.
  5. Pick an upgrade method. The project recommends a major-version approach such as pg_upgrade (fast, in place) or pg_dump / pg_restore (slower, cleaner). Logical replication is another option if you need minimal downtime.
  6. Run pg_upgrade --check first against a copy. It reports incompatibilities without changing anything.
  7. Update drivers and ORMs (node-postgres, Prisma, Drizzle, psycopg and so on) in staging, then confirm migrations still run.
  8. Have a rollback plan: a verified backup and a tested restore, not just a backup.

What this means for business and app owners

If you run a SaaS product, an e-commerce store or an internal tool on Postgres, PostgreSQL 19 is not urgent. Nothing in it is a security fix you must rush to apply, and the most eye-catching features were deferred. The more pressing date is November 12: if your database is on version 14, it will stop receiving security patches that day.

A sensible plan for most teams looks like this: get off 14 this quarter, test 19 in staging once it hits GA, and schedule the production upgrade for early 2027 after the first point release. The features that did ship, like ON CONFLICT DO SELECT, replica WAIT and faster foreign key checks, are real quality-of-life wins worth adopting once you're there.

If your app was built quickly, perhaps with an AI builder, and nobody is sure which Postgres version it runs, which auth method it uses, or whether backups restore, that's worth finding out before any upgrade. A production audit covers exactly those questions, and if you need help planning a database move as part of backend work, get in touch.

Sources

  • PostgreSQL 19 Beta 4 Released (postgresql.org)
  • PostgreSQL 19 Beta 1 Released (postgresql.org)
  • PostgreSQL 19 release notes (RC documentation)
  • PostgreSQL versioning policy
  • PostgreSQL 19 Release Date Moved to Nov 19 After AI Review Found Too Many Bugs (DEV Community)

title: ACH Return Codes Explained: Handling R01–R85 in Production Payout Systems
description:
ACH Return Codes Explained: Handling R01–R85 in Production Payout Systems

When a payout fails, the Nacha network doesn't just say "no." It returns a specific code—one of 85 possible R-codes—that tells you why the transfer bounced and what you should do next. Understanding these codes is critical for building reliable payment infrastructure.

The ACH Return Code Landscape

Every ACH return follows the Nacha Operating Rules and is documented in the ACH Return Entries guide. The codes span from R01 (Insufficient Funds) to R85 (Duplicate Entry), and each one signals a different failure mode. Your integration must decode and handle them programmatically, not just log them.

Returns typically arrive 1–2 business days after the original debit entry is transmitted. For same-day ACH, returns come back the same day by 11:00 AM CT.

Common Return Codes You'll Encounter

R01 – Insufficient Funds
The receiver's account doesn't have enough balance to cover the debit. This is temporary and reversible—the receiver might have funds tomorrow. Your retry logic should flag this for a later attempt (24–48 hours), not immediately.

R03 – No Account / Unable to Locate Account
The account number or routing number doesn't exist, or the account was closed. This is permanent. You should:

  • Mark the recipient record as invalid
  • Notify the user immediately
  • Offer an alternate payment method (card, wire, RTP)

R04 – Invalid Account Number Structure
The account number format is invalid (e.g., too many digits, invalid characters). This is a data quality issue on your end. Validate account numbers against Luhn or bank-specific rules before submission.

R10 – Customer Advises Not Authorized
The receiver claims they didn't authorize the debit. This is a dispute and requires manual investigation. Flag it for compliance review; don't retry.

R29 – Corporate Customer Advises Not Authorized
Similar to R10, but for business accounts. Treat as a dispute.

R51 – Debit Initiated Without Authorization
The originating bank rejected the entry because the receiver's bank detected no authorization on file. This often means the receiver needs to re-authorize recurring debits. Send them a re-authorization request.

R82 – Duplicate Entry
You sent the same entry twice (same amount, date, account). Implement idempotency keys in your API to prevent this. If you receive R82, don't retry; investigate why the duplicate was sent.

Building a Return Handler

Here's a minimal pattern for decoding and routing returns:

async function handleACHReturn(returnEntry) {
  const { returnCode, amount, accountId, payoutId } = returnEntry;

  const permanentCodes = ['R03', 'R04', 'R05', 'R07'];
  const temporaryCodes = ['R01', 'R09', 'R16'];
  const disputeCodes = ['R10', 'R29'];

  if (permanentCodes.includes(returnCode)) {
    await markAccountInvalid(accountId);
    await notifyUser(accountId, `Payout failed: ${returnCode}`);
    await suggestAlternateMethod(accountId);
  } else if (temporaryCodes.includes(returnCode)) {
    await scheduleRetry(payoutId, { delayHours: 24, maxAttempts: 3 });
  } else if (disputeCodes.includes(returnCode)) {
    await escalateToCompliance(payoutId, returnCode);
  } else {
    await logUnhandledReturn(payoutId, returnCode);
  }
}

Return Timing & Reconciliation

  • Standard ACH: Returns arrive within 1–2 business days.
  • Same-day ACH: Returns by 11:00 AM CT the same day.
  • Your settlement: Most ACH credits settle T+1, but returns can arrive T+2 or later.

When reconciling, don't assume a payout succeeded until the return window closes. Keep payout status as "pending" for at least 2 business days.

When to Switch Rails

If ACH returns are too frequent for a recipient (e.g., R01 repeated 3 times), consider offering RTP (Real-Time Payments) or Visa Direct. RTP settles in seconds and provides immediate feedback; Visa Direct works for card-linked accounts.

Key Takeaway

Every R-code is actionable data. Build your return handler to classify codes into permanent failures, retryable errors, and disputes. This transforms ACH returns from a support headache into a signal that drives smarter routing decisions and better user experience.

Decoding ACH return codes programmatically? The ACH Return Codes API returns the full Nacha R01–R85 set with plain-language descriptions and handling guidance.

title: How to Export or Back Up Your Railway Database (Postgres, MySQL, MongoDB, Redis) Before You Migrate
description:
Disclosure: this article was drafted with the help of an AI writing assistant. Facts, times and commands were checked against Railway's official status page, blog and docs, and the dump and restore commands were tested on 23 Oct 2026. Originally published on Medium.

Tested pg_dump, mysqldump and mongodump commands, how to restore them, and the mistakes that break aÂ backup.

Last updated: 23 Oct 2026, 8:43 AMÂ IST.

Quick answer: To export a Railway database, turn on Public Access for the database service (Settings, then Networking), copy its public connection URL from the Variables tab, and run the standard dump tool from your own machine: pg_dump for PostgreSQL, mysqldump for MySQL, and mongodump for MongoDB. Railway's built-in volume backups are useful, but they can only be restored into the same Railway project and environment, so they don't replace a dump file you keep yourself.

TL;DR

  • Railway databases are private by default. Public Access creates a TCP proxy and a public URL variable, such as DATABASE_PUBLIC_URL.
  • PostgreSQL: pg_dump in custom format (-F c), restore with pg_restore. Your pg_dump must be the same major version as the server, orÂ newer.
  • MySQL: mysqldump with --single-transaction --routines --triggers.
  • MongoDB: mongodump --archive --gzip, restore with mongorestore.
  • Redis: redis-cli --rdb saves a snapshot file. Restoring it needs a different method (seeÂ below).
  • Rotate the database password after the export if you opened public access only for theÂ backup.

How these commands were checked: On 23 Oct 2026, every dump and restore command below was run on a test machine against local test databases: PostgreSQL 17 (pg_dump 17.11), MariaDB 11.8 (its mysqldump), MongoDB 8.0 with Database Tools 100.19.1, and Redis 8.0. They were not run against a live Railway database, so the Railway-specific parts (variable names, menus, CLI flags) come from Railway's officialÂ docs.

Why back up your Railway databaseÂ now?

After the October 2026 security incident, many developers want a copy of their data outside Railway. Some are planning a move, and some just want a safety net. That is a sensible habit whatever host youÂ use.

Railway's own position is the same. Its PostgreSQL docs say regular backups and monitoring are "essential" for production databases. If you also need to rotate your database password, Railway's guide on rotating PostgreSQL credentials covers that. You can take the backup first and rotate afterwards.

Step 1: Get a connection URL you canÂ reach

Railway databases are private by default. To reach one from your laptop, you have twoÂ options.

Option A: Public Access (TCP proxy). Open the database service, go to Settings, then Networking, and add Public Access. Railway creates a TCP proxy with a host and port that look like shuttle.proxy.rlwy.net:15140, plus a public URL variable:

  • PostgreSQL: DATABASE_PUBLIC_URL
  • MySQL: MYSQL_PUBLIC_URL
  • MongoDB: MONGO_PUBLIC_URL
  • Redis: REDIS_PUBLIC_URL

Railway notes that traffic through the TCP proxy is billed as network egress. Its pricing page lists egress at $0.05 per GB. Keep that in mind for large databases.

Option B: An SSH tunnel with the CLI, no public access needed. The Railway CLI's connect command has a --tunnel-only flag. It opens a local tunnel, prints connection details for external tools, and holds the tunnel open until you press Ctrl+C. The CLI help says it implies --ssh and works without a public domain. Run railway connect Postgres --tunnel-only (use your database service's name), then point the dump tool at the local host and port itÂ prints.

Keep the URL out of your shell history. The connection URL contains the password. In bash you can paste it into a hidden variable instead of typing it into theÂ command:

read -rs DB_URL   # paste the URL, press Enter (nothing is shown)
echo "${#DB_URL} characters stored"

Step 2: Export a Railway PostgreSQL database withÂ pg_dump

First check versions. The PostgreSQL docs say pg_dump can't dump from a server newer than its own major version. It refuses to try. Check your local version with pg_dump --version, and the server version by running SELECT version(); in psql or the Railway Data tab. Install a matching or newer client ifÂ needed.

Then dump in customÂ format:

pg_dump "$DB_URL" -F c -f railway_backup.dump
pg_restore --list railway_backup.dump | head

The second line lists the dump's contents, which is a quick way to confirm the file isn't empty or corrupt. Custom format is compressed and lets pg_restore pick objects later. Render's migrate-from-Railway guide uses the same pg_dumpÂ command.

If you'd rather have a readable SQL file, run this singleÂ line:

pg_dump "$DB_URL" --no-owner --no-acl -f railway_backup.sql

Big database? Use the directory format for parallel jobs. Parallel dumps only work with the directory format. When I tried -j with custom format, pg_dump stopped with "parallel backup only supported by the directory format". ThisÂ works:

pg_dump "$DB_URL" -F d -j 4 -f railway_backup_dir

Restore it (anywhere) 

# custom format
pg_restore --verbose --no-acl --no-owner -d "$TARGET_DB_URL" railway_backup.dump

# directory format, 4 parallel jobs
pg_restore -j 4 --no-owner -d "$TARGET_DB_URL" railway_backup_dir

# plain SQL file
psql "$TARGET_DB_URL" -f railway_backup.sql

The --no-owner and --no-acl flags skip Railway-specific role ownership, which usually doesn't exist on the new server. In my test, a 1,000-row table came back with all 1,000 rows from each of the threeÂ formats.

Step 3: Export a Railway MySQL database with mysqldump

Railway's MySQL service exposes MYSQLHOST, MYSQLPORT, MYSQLUSER, MYSQLPASSWORD and MYSQLDATABASE, plus MYSQL_PUBLIC_URL through the TCP proxy (MySQL docs). mysqldump doesn't accept a URL, so take the host, port, user and database name from MYSQL_PUBLIC_URL (its format is mysql://user:password@host:port/database). Leaving the password off makes mysqldump prompt for it, which keeps it out of yourÂ history.

mysqldump -h PUBLIC_HOST -P PUBLIC_PORT -u USER -p \
  --single-transaction --routines --triggers \
  DATABASE_NAME > railway_mysql.sql

--single-transaction takes a consistent snapshot of InnoDB tables without locking them. --routines and --triggers include stored procedures and triggers. All three are documented in the MySQL 8.4 mysqldump reference.

Restore it with oneÂ line:

mysql -h TARGET_HOST -P TARGET_PORT -u TARGET_USER -p TARGET_DB < railway_mysql.sql

I tested this pair with MariaDB's mysqldump and mysql client, which accept the same flags. If your target is a managed MySQL service, check its import docs for GTID or privilege notes before youÂ restore.

Step 4: Export a Railway MongoDB database with mongodump

Railway's MongoDB service exposes MONGO_URL, plus MONGO_PUBLIC_URL through the TCP proxy (MongoDB docs). You need the free MongoDB Database Tools, which include mongodump and mongorestore.

mongodump --uri "$MONGO_PUBLIC_URL" --archive=railway-mongo.archive --gzip
mongorestore --uri "$TARGET_MONGO_URL" --archive=railway-mongo.archive --gzip

A single gzipped archive file is easier to move around than a folder of BSON files. Add --drop to mongorestore if you want it to replace collections that already exist on theÂ target.

Step 5: Redis on Railway: what you can and can'tÂ export

Railway's Redis service exposes REDIS_URL, plus REDIS_PUBLIC_URL through the TCP proxy (Redis docs). You can save a point-in-time snapshotÂ with:

redis-cli -u "$REDIS_PUBLIC_URL" --rdb railway_redis.rdb

Restoring is the tricky part. Some guides pipe theÂ .rdb file into redis-cli --pipe. When I tested that on 23 Oct 2026, the target Redis rejected it with an "unknown command" error. That's expected, because --pipe expects Redis commands, not a binary RDB snapshot. Realistic options:

  • If Redis only holds cache or queue data, don't migrate it. Let the new Redis startÂ empty.
  • For a small dataset, copy keys with the DUMP and RESTORE commands.
  • For a self-managed Redis, place theÂ .rdb file in its data directory before it starts. Check your host's docs, because managed Redis services handle imports differently.

What about Railway's built-inÂ backups?

Railway has native volume backups for services with a volume, databases included:

  • Schedules: daily (kept 6 days), weekly (kept 27 days) and monthly (kept 89Â days).
  • Manual backups are limited to 50% of the volume's totalÂ size.
  • Backups are billed like volume storage, for their incremental sizeÂ only.
  • Railway lists two caveats: wiping a volume deletes all its backups, and backups can only be restored into the same project and environment.

For Postgres, the CLI can also start an on-demand backup with railway postgres pitr backup create --service postgres --name pre-migration. See Railway's postgres CLI docs for requirements, such as using the official Railway PostgresÂ image.

These are good for quick rollbacks inside Railway. For a migration or an off-platform safety copy, you still want a dump file youÂ control.

Export files and environment variables too

A database dump isn't your whole app. Before anyÂ move:

  • Volume files (uploads, SQLite files): the volume CLI can download them, for example railway volume files download /backup.tarÂ ./backup.tar. A directory works as the remote pathÂ too.
  • Environment variables: railway variable list --kv prints them in KEY=value format. The CLI help says this prints raw values, so save the output only somewhere safe, never in Git. After the incident, rotate secrets rather than copying old values into a newÂ host.
  • Laravel tip: if you use Laravel's storage/app folder on a Railway volume, back that up along with the database, or you'll lose userÂ uploads.

Checklist before you call it backedÂ up

  1. The dump file exists and isn't tiny. Check it with lsÂ -lh.
  2. You restored it once into a scratch database and counted rows in your keyÂ tables.
  3. The file is stored in two places, for example your laptop plus encrypted cloudÂ storage.
  4. If you opened Public Access only for the backup, remove it, and rotate the password with Railway's Regenerate button (see Railway's rotationÂ guide).

FAQ

How do I export my database fromÂ Railway?

Enable Public Access on the database (or use railway connect with --tunnel-only), copy the public connection URL, and run pg_dump, mysqldump or mongodump from yourÂ machine.

Can I download a Railway database backup from the dashboard?

Railway's native backups are restored inside Railway, into the same project and environment. To get a file you can take elsewhere, run a dump tool yourself.

What does "pg_dump: error: aborting because of server version mismatch" mean?

Your local pg_dump is older than the Railway server's major version. Install a matching or newer PostgreSQL client and run itÂ again.

Does exporting through the TCP proxy costÂ money?

Railway bills TCP proxy traffic as network egress, listed at $0.05 per GB on its pricing page. Small databases cost very little; large ones are worth estimating first.

Can I export a whole RailwayÂ project?

There's no single "export everything" file. Export each database, download volume files, save your variable names (then rotate the values), and keep config files like railway.json or railway.toml inÂ Git.

Is it safe to keep my Railway databaseÂ public?

Only while you need it. Railway's own rotation guide says a credential is usable from anywhere through the TCP proxy while Public Access is on. Remove it when you'reÂ done.

Related reading

  • Is Railway down? What the 21â€“22 October 2026 Railway outage means for developers
  • Railway API token not working? Fix "Not Authorized" and "Project Token notÂ found"
  • Railway alternatives in 2026: Render, Fly.io, AWS or Coolify? A fair migration guide
  • Is Railway safe now? What the October 2026 breach means, plus a hosting security checklist

Sources (checked 23 Oct 2026): Railway PostgreSQL, MySQL, MongoDB, Redis, TCP proxy, volume backups, CLI, pricing, PostgreSQL pg_dump docs, MySQL mysqldump docs, Render's Railway migration guide.

title: Modelling a shared inbox: why the message is the primary key, not the conversation
description:
Every shared-inbox implementation starts with a conversations table and ends up regretting it. Here is the model that survives contact with real support traffic.

The problem with conversation-first

A conversation is a derived thing. It is what you get after you decide which messages belong together. If you store conversations as the source of truth, every new channel forces you to write merge logic that mutates the conversation rows — and merges are the one operation that must never lose data.

Messages, by contrast, arrive once and never change. They are the natural primary key.

The model 

-- the immutable fact
messages(id, channel, external_id, direction, sent_at, body, raw)

-- who it came from (may be shared by many messages)
contacts(id, email, phone, name)

-- the derived grouping, rebuildable at any time
threads(id, subject_key, opened_at, closed_at)

-- the link, append-only
thread_messages(thread_id, message_id, added_at, reason)

Three properties matter:

  1. thread_messages is append-only. A merge inserts rows; it never rewrites history. If the merge was wrong, you can split by deleting the link rows — no data lost.
  2. Threads can be rebuilt. Delete every row in threads and you can regenerate them from messages plus your merge rules. That is the test for whether your grouping logic is a projection or a tangle.
  3. reason is stored. "Same contact, 4h window" vs "manual merge by ana" answers the question every support lead eventually asks: why are these two emails in one thread?

Identity is the hard part

The same person writes from ana@company.com, then from a personal address, then from a second work address after a rebrand. Matching on the exact string gives you three contacts and three threads.

A workable compromise:

  • Exact match first (email, phone, then channel-specific ID)
  • Then a domain-and-name heuristic that suggests a merge rather than performing one
  • Never auto-merge across organisations

The suggestion queue is boring, and it is what keeps identity resolution honest: a human confirms the ambiguous cases rather than a regex.

Delivery state belongs to the message, not the conversation

Outbound mail can be queued, sent, delivered, bounced, complained. That lifecycle is per message and per recipient. Storing "the conversation was sent" hides the one case that matters: one of three recipients bounced.

message_delivery(message_id, recipient, state, updated_at, provider_id)

With that table, "did they get it?" is a query instead of a support escalation.

What this buys you

  • Channel integrations become writers of messages, not reimplementations of threading
  • AI summarisation or tagging attaches to messages/threads as a separate table, never mutating the record
  • Deleting a thread is a policy operation (remove link rows + messages), so retention rules become enforceable
  • Migration to a new database is a row copy, not a logic rewrite

The one thing to get right early

Make messages.external_id unique per channel and dedupe on insert. Every provider retries webhooks. Without that constraint you will ship duplicate replies, and duplicate replies are the failure customers remember.

This is the shape we use in Onsites AI — a shared inbox, CRM and light invoicing for teams of three to thirty, self-hostable or cloud. The schema notes above are portable either way.

title: Node.js OAuth Linking: Resolve Social Identity for Existing Users, Avoid Duplicates
description:
A social login should never create a patient profile until the service has resolved the identity against existing records. In a healthtech signup flow, the least complicated reliable rule is: verify the provider assertion, normalize the provider subject, look up an immutable identity key, and only then decide whether to link, sign in, or start a new profile. Put the abuse gate before account creation, but keep the CAPTCHA result separate from identity proof.

Short answer: model a social credential as a unique identity record, not as an email address. In Node.js, the transaction that consumes that record should lock the candidate user, require an authenticated session before linking, and make a second request harmless. Email is useful for discovery and notification; it is a weak basis for silent account merging.

Keep the states explicit.

What page fired at 3am?

The alert I want is not “OAuth callback errors increased.” That is a dashboard-shaped question. I want to know which action fired: did one person receive two patient profiles, did the callback bind an identity twice, or did the signup gate reject legitimate enrollment? Those are different incidents with different reversals.

A useful incident trace starts at the visible failure. A patient signs in with a social account and sees an empty profile, while support can find an older profile under a prior enrollment method. Work backward: the callback accepted an assertion, an email lookup found a possible match, and the application created a new profile before anyone had explicitly authenticated the old one. The missing signal was an account-resolution event before insertion.

That is the instrumentation change I would make first. Emit a structured event for identity.resolution with a decision such as existing_identity, authenticated_link, new_profile, or manual_review; include a request correlation ID and provider subject hash, but never log the raw token. Alert on impossible transitions, such as the same identity key attached to two users, rather than on a noisy count of all callback failures.

False positives matter. A threshold of one duplicate-binding event is appropriate for a uniqueness violation; a threshold of one manual-review decision is not. Page on the former, sample the latter, and retain enough audit data to explain the decision without putting health information in application logs.

How can Node.js link a social identity to an existing user?

An OAuth subject is scoped to an issuer and client, so the durable lookup key is a tuple such as (issuer, subject). OpenID Connect defines the subject identifier as locally unique and never reassigned within the issuer’s context; the exact scope still has to be understood for the provider integration you operate. Treating an email claim as proof that two accounts are the same skips the question that matters: who authenticated the existing account?

The safe resolution states are small. An existing identity signs the user in. A missing identity with an already authenticated local session can be linked after a deliberate confirmation step. A missing identity with a matching email becomes a recovery or review path, not an automatic merge. Otherwise, create a new profile only after the abuse check and the normal consent and enrollment steps pass.

This is where the “find user by email, then attach provider” shortcut becomes dangerous. An attacker who controls a login address, or a provider whose email claim is unverified or mutable, can turn discovery into account takeover. OWASP’s authentication guidance treats account recovery and verification as security boundaries; the implementation should do the same.

The binding transaction should be boring

The database constraint is the final guard, not a substitute for the resolver. Keep one row per external identity, with a unique constraint over the issuer and subject, and make the link operation transactional. The following Go sketch shows the decision boundary without tying it to a commercial SDK; the same sequence can be implemented behind a Node.js route.

Exactly once.

type ExternalIdentity struct {
    Issuer  string
    Subject string
    UserID  string
}

type Resolution string

const (
    ExistingIdentity  Resolution = "existing_identity"
    AuthenticatedLink Resolution = "authenticated_link"
    NewProfile        Resolution = "new_profile"
    ManualReview      Resolution = "manual_review"
)

func ResolveIdentity(ctx context.Context, tx *sql.Tx, issuer, subject string,
    localUserID *string, verifiedEmail *string) (Resolution, string, error) {
    identity, err := findIdentityForUpdate(ctx, tx, issuer, subject)
    if err != nil && !errors.Is(err, sql.ErrNoRows) {
        return "", "", err
    }
    if err == nil {
        return ExistingIdentity, identity.UserID, nil
    }

    if localUserID != nil {
        if err := insertIdentity(ctx, tx, issuer, subject, *localUserID); err != nil {
            return "", "", err
        }
        return AuthenticatedLink, *localUserID, nil
    }

    if verifiedEmail != nil && emailHasPossibleMatch(ctx, tx, *verifiedEmail) {
        return ManualReview, "", nil
    }
    userID, err := insertNewUser(ctx, tx)
    if err != nil {
        return "", "", err
    }
    if err := insertIdentity(ctx, tx, issuer, subject, userID); err != nil {
        return "", "", err
    }
    return NewProfile, userID, nil
}

The important detail is not the language. It is the order and the constraint. findIdentityForUpdate must run inside the same transaction as the insert, and a uniqueness conflict must be handled as a normal concurrent request, followed by a fresh lookup where appropriate. Do not return a new session merely because the provider callback was valid. The callback authenticates the external identity; your application still has to choose the local account.

The trade-off is deliberate: a possible email match can send a person through recovery or support instead of giving an instant login. That adds friction and creates an operational queue, but the alternative is silently merging records that may represent different people. A CAPTCHA can reduce automated enrollment; it cannot resolve that ambiguity.

In a Node.js service, keep provider verification, resolution, persistence, and session issuance as separate functions. That makes it possible to test the resolver with a fake assertion and a real database constraint, rather than mocking the entire callback into a happy-path boolean.

No shortcut survives a retry.

Where does CAPTCHA belong in this flow?

CAPTCHA is an abuse signal. It is not an identity-linking signal. Run the server-side challenge verification before an anonymous request can create a profile or consume an invitation, and bind the result to a short-lived, single-use signup attempt. Do not let a successful challenge authorize linking to an existing patient profile. That step requires a local authenticated session and explicit confirmation.

The decision table is more useful than a clever callback:

Identity lookup Local session Abuse check Action
Found Any Valid request Sign in to the mapped user
Missing Present Valid request Ask for confirmation, then link
Email candidate Absent Valid request Recovery or manual review
Missing Absent Failed or absent Reject before profile creation

A challenge can fail because the request is automated, malformed, expired, or outside the service’s policy. Those outcomes should be observable, but the client should not receive enough detail to turn the endpoint into an account-enumeration oracle. The same restraint applies to “email already exists” messages.

This design is a poor fit when the application needs a regulated, high-assurance identity proof rather than account continuity. In that case, an OAuth subject and a challenge are insufficient evidence; add a separately governed verification process. It is also less convenient for teams that cannot operate transactional storage and audit retention. Those are real boundaries, not reasons to hide the unresolved match.

What should the on-call measure?

Start with invariants, then measure user friction. The hard invariants are one external identity mapped to one local user, one link operation requiring an authenticated local session, and no profile creation after a failed abuse gate. The useful counters are resolution decisions, uniqueness conflicts, recovery starts, challenge failures, and support reversals, each partitioned by flow rather than dumped into one signup rate.

Test the ugly transitions: two callbacks arriving together, a browser retry after a timeout, a provider subject changing because the issuer configuration changed, and a user attempting to link an identity already owned elsewhere. Verify that retries converge on the same local user and that a failed transaction leaves no half-created profile.

I would review the alert by asking one question: what page fired? If the answer is still “the dashboard looked unusual,” the system has not made its failure mode legible.

The design decision is therefore less about selecting an OAuth library and more about refusing to collapse discovery, authentication, abuse prevention, and account mutation into one callback. Resolve first. Link only from a trusted local session. Keep CAPTCHA in its lane. That sequence prevents duplicate patient profiles without making an automated challenge carry a security promise it cannot support.

Further reading

  • OWASP Authentication Cheat Sheet: https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Authentication_Cheat_Sheet.html
  • OpenID Connect Core 1.0, Section 2: https://openid.net/specs/openid-connect-core-1_0.html
  • RFC 6749, The OAuth 2.0 Authorization Framework: https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6749
  • RFC 6819, OAuth 2.0 Threat Model and Security Considerations: https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6819
