title: Node.js API Queue: Multiple Audio Files, Batch Transcribe (and Why Claims Matter)
description:
The least complicated design that survives a real batch is a durable job record plus a worker that claims one recording at a time. The upload request should create work, return a job identifier, and stop there. A worker can then fetch the audio, call the transcription API, persist the text, and emit usage for the tenant. The Node.js part is the HTTP boundary and worker runtime; the important boundary is the claim, not the queue brand.

Short answer: give every audio object a stable content key, put one transcription job behind it, and make the worker's completion operation idempotent. A retry must be allowed to repeat an HTTP request without creating a second transcript or charging the wrong tenant in your own accounting. RFC 9110 describes idempotent methods as requests whose repeated effect is intended to be the same, which is the right mental model for the state transitions here.

This is the shape I use for a B2B SaaS knowledge base that receives recorded customer calls. Each tenant may upload several files, and the resulting text stays private to that tenant before it is indexed for question answering. Cost visibility is a first-class output. A transcript without tenant_id, job_id, and an auditable usage event is incomplete, even if the text looks perfect.

How should an API batch transcribe multiple audio files?

The API accepts metadata and an object reference, rather than holding an HTTP connection open while audio is processed. A row in the application database owns the lifecycle: queued, running, succeeded, or failed. The queue contains a reference to that row. It is a delivery mechanism, not the source of truth.

That distinction matters after a worker disappears between transcription and acknowledgement. A durable record lets another worker decide whether the lease expired, inspect the attempt count, and continue. The storage key is also where tenant isolation becomes concrete: it should be derived from an authenticated tenant identifier, never accepted as an arbitrary path supplied by a client.

For a batch, the client submits many independent jobs. It does not submit one giant task whose partial progress is hidden. One file per job gives the system a useful retry boundary and makes a tenant's usage ledger explainable. If a 42-file upload has three bad recordings, the other 39 should not wait for a human to split the batch again.

Keep the claim small.

The queue is optional.

The failure boundary is not.

The most revealing test is a deliberately boring one: submit the same audio object twice, let one worker finish the remote call, pause it before the database commit, let another worker claim the lease, and then release the paused worker. That sequence contains the ordinary uncertainty of distributed work in miniature. A design that records only the final transcript cannot explain whether the two submissions were duplicates, a requested reprocess, or two tenants holding identical bytes; a design that records the tenant, content digest, profile revision, attempt, lease token, and usage-event key can answer each question without reading worker logs from last Tuesday. I keep those fields beside the job because operational archaeology is slow, and the customer asking about a bill should not need a reconstruction exercise.

There is a trade-off here. A queue-backed worker adds state, leases, and operational work that a synchronous endpoint avoids. It is a poor fit for a tiny internal tool processing one short file at a time; a direct request is easier to debug there. The queue earns its place when uploads can outlive an HTTP request, failures need replay, or tenants need separate visibility.

Here is the core state transition in Python. The same data contract can sit behind a Node.js endpoint and a queue consumer; keeping the example in one small module makes the failure behavior easier to inspect than a framework-specific sample.

from dataclasses import dataclass
from enum import Enum
from typing import Optional


class Status(str, Enum):
    QUEUED = "queued"
    RUNNING = "running"
    SUCCEEDED = "succeeded"
    FAILED = "failed"


@dataclass
class Job:
    job_id: str
    tenant_id: str
    object_key: str
    content_sha256: str
    status: Status = Status.QUEUED
    attempt: int = 0
    transcript: Optional[str] = None
    usage_event_id: Optional[str] = None


def claim(job: Job) -> bool:
    """Return True only when one worker owns the next attempt."""
    if job.status is Status.SUCCEEDED:
        return False
    if job.status is Status.RUNNING:
        return False
    job.status = Status.RUNNING
    job.attempt += 1
    return True


def complete(job: Job, transcript: str, usage_event_id: str) -> None:
    """A repeated completion writes the same result, never a new job."""
    if job.status is Status.SUCCEEDED:
        return
    job.transcript = transcript
    job.usage_event_id = usage_event_id
    job.status = Status.SUCCEEDED

In production, claim and complete are database transactions, not in-memory mutations. The example exposes the invariants: a successful job is terminal, an attempt has an owner, and the usage event has a stable identifier. I prefer making those invariants boring before adding concurrency.

Why can a retry duplicate the result?

A worker usually has at least two external effects: the transcription request and the local write. It may receive the transcript, persist it, then crash before acknowledging the queue message. The queue redelivers the job. If completion means “insert another transcript,” the duplicate is real. If billing means “increment a counter whenever the worker runs,” the tenant's report is wrong even when the database has one visible transcript.

Use a deterministic idempotency key for the application operation. tenant_id + content_sha256 + transcription_profile is a useful starting point, provided a deliberate reprocess can include a new profile version. Enforce uniqueness in storage. A process-local set, a worker flag, or a timestamp check does not protect two workers racing on separate machines.

The transcription provider may have its own retry rules, and those rules are a separate contract. Keep the application job key in your request metadata when the API supports it, then still make your own completion write idempotent. Network timeouts do not tell you whether the remote operation finished. Treat an uncertain response as an uncertain response, not as proof of failure.

There is a small but important ordering choice. Write the transcript and an outbox usage event in one database transaction. A separate publisher can deliver that event to the cost ledger, where usage_event_id is unique. This avoids the split result in which search can see text but the tenant report cannot explain its processing. It also means a ledger consumer can retry safely.

How do tenant costs stay visible in a queue?

Cost visibility starts at enqueue time, not at the monthly report. Put tenant_id, job_id, byte size, duration when known, and the selected transcription profile on the job. Record actual provider usage when returned. If the response does not include a value you can verify, store the missing field explicitly rather than inventing a precise number.

The queue should enforce fairness as a scheduling concern. A tenant that submits 10,000 short clips can otherwise occupy every worker while a smaller tenant waits. A simple per-tenant concurrency limit and a global limit are enough to start. The limit is not a cost model; it is a way to prevent one tenant's burst from hiding everyone else's work.

I keep three quantities separate:

  • accepted work, which answers what entered the system;
  • completed work, which answers what produced usable text;
  • billable usage, which answers what the external transcription operation reported.

They diverge during retries, validation failures, and cancellations. That divergence is operational information. Collapsing them into one processed_files number makes an inexpensive dashboard and an expensive investigation.

For private knowledge bases, attach tenant authorization to every read path as well as every write path. A transcript job that is correctly tagged can still leak data if a later retrieval query filters only by document ID. The index record should carry the tenant boundary, and the retrieval service should require it rather than treating it as optional UI metadata.

What happens when the worker vanishes?

Use a lease with an expiry and an attempt count. Claiming a job records a worker token and a deadline. A worker may renew the lease while handling a long recording, but only the current token may complete it. After expiry, another worker can claim the job. The completion transaction checks that token, or checks that the job is already succeeded with the same idempotency key.

That last check handles the awkward race: worker A finishes after its lease expires, worker B has already claimed the job, and both receive a transcript. Only one completion wins. The loser rereads the job and treats an equivalent successful result as done. A database uniqueness constraint is a better guard than timing luck.

Not every error deserves a retry. An unreadable object, unsupported codec, or authorization failure should become a visible terminal failure with a reason safe for operators. A timeout, temporary upstream response, or worker process exit is a candidate for retry with bounded backoff. Keep the original error class and the latest attempt timestamp; “failed” alone does not tell anyone whether replay is sensible.

I also validate before enqueueing. Check the object exists, belongs to the authenticated tenant, has an allowed media type, and has a bounded size. This is cheaper than discovering the same fact inside a worker, and it keeps poison jobs from consuming concurrency. Validation is not a substitute for checking again in the worker because the object or authorization state may change between requests.

A practical rollout checklist

Start with a fixture set that includes one short recording, one long recording, an empty file, a deliberately unsupported format, and two identical files submitted under different job IDs. Run the same fixture through a notebook first, then through the worker. The notebook is useful for inspecting transcripts; it is not evidence that leases, redelivery, or tenant filtering work.

Test the transitions, not just the happy-path text. Kill a worker after the remote call and before acknowledgement. Deliver the same queue message twice. Let a lease expire while the first worker is still alive. Submit two files from two tenants with the same content hash. The expected result is one transcript per idempotency key, isolated retrieval, and two separately attributed usage events where the accounting contract calls for them.

Watch queue age, attempt count, lease expiry, terminal failure reason, transcript latency, and usage-event lag. Add tenant dimensions carefully: high-cardinality labels can make observability expensive. A log field or queryable event is often more useful than putting every tenant into a metrics label.

Finally, document the replay rule for operators. Replaying a failed validation job should not silently bypass validation. Reprocessing a succeeded job should require an explicit new profile or revision. That single distinction prevents a “retry all” button from turning an incident into duplicate work.

The least complex system remains the right one here: an API creates durable, tenant-owned jobs; a queue wakes workers; a lease controls ownership; a transaction records the transcript and usage event; and an idempotency key makes uncertain delivery survivable. Node.js can implement the HTTP and worker edges cleanly, but no queue library can decide which effects are safe to repeat. That decision belongs in the job contract.

Further reading

  • RFC 9110: HTTP Semantics
  • LangChain ChatOpenAI integration documentation

title: Hono on Prisma Postgres and Compute, What Worked and What Broke
description:
TL;DR

  • I deployed a Hono API on Prisma Postgres and Prisma Compute with three commands, auth login, build and deploy, and I never installed Bun.
  • One bug caught me. In this scaffold, if a route queries the database before the template's /users route does, /users returns a 500 and the log shows DRIVER.ALREADY_CONNECTED.
  • If you're sizing up the stack, Compute is GA, Composer (which declares and deploys Compute apps) is Early Access, and Prisma ORM 8 is still a release candidate at the time of writing. Pin your versions.

I wrote this article for Prisma, who commissioned it. The opinions are mine.

I built a small bookmarks API with Hono, put it on Prisma Postgres and deployed it to Prisma Compute. A coding agent, Gemini CLI, wrote most of the code from a prompt I wrote, and I kept a log of every error and every fix. The repo is public on GitHub, with the code, migrations, README and smoke test.

The app, a Hono bookmarks API with Prisma Postgres

I added six routes. GET /health, plus five for bookmarks (list, get one, create, update, delete). The scaffold adds GET / and GET /users, and /users matters later. A bookmark has an id, a unique URL, a title, optional notes and a createdAt.

I tested with Node 22.22.2, Gemini CLI 0.65.0 (with gemini-3.5-flash-lite selected), Prisma CLI 8.0.0-rc.21, @prisma/orm-postgres 8.0.0-rc.16 and @prisma/composer 0.28.0, in late October 2026. The Prisma packages have moved on since, so the findings apply to those versions. A re-run of the finished repo on Linux (Node and a local Postgres 16) is marked "on Linux" below.

A quick note on what you'd be building on. The Compute FAQ says Compute has been generally available since August 2026. Prisma's 28 August changelog and the Console both label Composer Early Access, and Prisma's docs call ORM 8 a release candidate at the time of writing.

I wrote the agent's rules in one prompt and made it stop after every phase. I ran every command that installed packages, used credentials or deployed to Prisma myself, and I never pasted my database URL into the agent.

Prisma Postgres with Hono, migrations and the direct vs pooled connection string

I created the database in the Console and it was ready in a few minutes. The connection dialog defaults to the pooled host (pooled.db.prisma.io) and tells you to put the string in .env. I came away with two things.

  • I used the direct host (db.prisma.io) for db:init, migrate and local dev. I didn't test the pooled string.
  • The scripts read DATABASE_URL from the shell, not from .env. On Linux, a valid .env file with no shell variable gave CONFIG.DB_CONNECTION_REQUIRED and created nothing. The Prisma Hono guide says the same.

The scaffold generates the first migration, and I generated the second with npm run migration:plan -- --name add-bookmarks. On my own database I ran db:init first (5 operations, the scaffold's tables) and migrate later, which applied the Bookmark migration. On Linux, migrate alone applied both migrations to an empty local database. The difference is that db:init builds tables straight from the contract, while migrate applies the migrations/ folder, which the Compute FAQ says a deploy applies for a Composer postgres() database. Both are safe to run twice (a second migrate says "Already up to date") and both mask credentials in their output. Every run also prints a pg warning that sslmode=require will change meaning in a future version.

Prisma ORM 8 unique constraint error and sqlState 23505

I put the rules in the prompt. Ids match ^[1-9][0-9]*$ and fit an int4, bodies over 10 KB get a 413 before parsing, URLs are stored as new URL(value).href, and the database's unique constraint decides duplicates. Gemini implemented them with a few early mistakes, including a wrong check order on PATCH, any types and a guessed duplicate check.

That guess is the interesting part. Gemini assumed a Postgres unique violation shows up as err.code === "23505". In ORM 8 the top-level code is undefined. I triggered a duplicate on purpose and logged the error. The useful fields, sqlState (23505) and constraint (Bookmark_url_key), sit on a SqlQueryError. The scaffold already ships the answer in .agents/skills/prisma-8/references/debug.md, which says driver errors "carry no dotted code" and to route on sqlState and the constraint metadata. My Phase 4 prompt named four skill files for Gemini to read and this wasn't one of them. I only read it while fact-checking this article.

Five simultaneous identical POSTs gave one 201 and four 409s.

Fixing DRIVER.ALREADY_CONNECTED in a Prisma ORM 8 Hono app

I had an 85-check smoke test ready before the API existed. The first run came back 84 passed, 2 failed. That adds up to 86 results from 85 checks because the script also records a failure for any 5xx response, so one broken route printed two FAIL lines. Both were GET /users, a route that ships with the scaffold.

{"error":"Could not query users yet. Run contract:emit and apply your schema first."}

The schema was fine, and the server log said something else.

Postgres client already connected
code: DRIVER.ALREADY_CONNECTED
fix: Call connect() at most once per client.

Here is what I worked out from the generated db.ts and the bundled dist/server.mjs. The ORM client connects in the background on its first query. The template's /users route goes through a helper that calls db.connect() explicitly. If one of my bookmark routes ran a query first, the background connect had already started and the explicit one threw. My routes queried db directly and never used the helper. This matches Prisma's runtime reference, which says to call connect() before any query or not at all, because a connect() after a query rejects with DRIVER.ALREADY_CONNECTED.

After a clean restart, GET /bookmarks followed by GET /users gave 500, and 500 again five seconds later. That also explains why smoke run 2 passed with no code change. I'd restarted the server, and the script requests /users before any bookmarks route, so the explicit connect ran first. On Linux the same unfixed code passed all 85 checks on a fresh process, and gave 84 passed, 2 failed once a bookmarks request came first.

Gemini's fixes were the weak part. The first matched the error message text and returned quietly, which hides the error. The second put await connectDatabase() at the top of every handler, before validation, so a bad body would need a database connection just to be rejected. I rejected both. The third calls the helper right before the first query in each handler, after validation, and leaves /health alone. After that /bookmarks, /users, /users returned 200, 200, 200 and a full smoke run gave 85 passed.

The Linux re-run also showed that the guide's own example triggers it. With the guide's POST /users route (step 4) added to a copy of the repo, a fresh process gave 201 for POST /users and then 500 twice for GET /users, with DRIVER.ALREADY_CONNECTED in the log. With GET /users first, the same three requests returned 200, 201 and 200. That was a local Postgres 16, not the deployed app, and the guide may have changed since.

The code compiled and my manual checks passed. Only a test run in the right order showed the problem. If you add a route to a Prisma scaffold, hit the template's own routes before and after yours, on a fresh process.

Deploy a Hono API to Prisma Compute

The Composer docs say local dev (prisma dev) isn't supported on Windows. I'm on Windows 10, so I never ran it, even though the scaffold's "next steps" box suggests it. These are the three commands I did run.

npx prisma auth login
npm run build
npx prisma deploy module.ts

All three worked. The Composer limitations page says deploys authenticate only with a service token, with "no browser flow", but the Composer deploying page documents auth login, and that's what I used. The two pages disagree and I couldn't tell which one is current.

I did three deploys.

  • The untouched scaffold took 3m 38s.
  • My bookmarks code took 3m 10s.
  • A redeploy of unchanged code took 50.4s.

Those are single runs from my machine, not a benchmark.

deploy doesn't build, so you run npm run build first. tsdown bundles everything into one dist/server.mjs of about 2 MB. The scaffold defaults to the us-east-1 region, and since I'm in India I changed one line in prisma.config.ts to ap-southeast-1.

The deployed app got its own Prisma Postgres database, and the migrated tables were there without my local DATABASE_URL being set. The deploy plan showed database-migrate (PrismaOrm.Migration) as updated, with no migration name. The Compute FAQ and the Compute limitations page both say the deploy applies your migrations/ to a Composer postgres() database before the service starts. My tables showed up after the deploy, which fits that, but I only know it from the result and not from the deploy output.

Compute runs the app on Bun even though my code is Node-style (@hono/node-server, built with tsdown for Node 22). The service log says starting bun with entrypoint: bootstrap.js. I installed nothing for that. The Composer getting-started page lists Bun as a prerequisite, so keep it in mind if local Node and deployed Bun ever behave differently.

The same 85 checks against the live app ended with 85 passed, 0 failed, 0 skipped. I didn't save the output. My paste and a screenshot show 79 of the 85 PASS lines, no FAIL line, and the final Result line with the totals. I created a bookmark, redeployed unchanged code and fetched it again, and got the same row. The app keeps no data in memory, so that fits the data living in Postgres. I can't say whether the redeploy restarted the app, so I haven't tested that.

prisma service logs app failed right after the deploy with PROJECT.SETUP_REQUIRED, saying the directory wasn't linked to a project. It needs --project bookmarks-api. The log held two lines and no request lines. The Console overview also said "no deploys yet" while the app was live. The CLI had told me it wasn't recording the deploy because the folder had no git commit, so that may be expected, but I didn't check.

Prisma Compute latency from India

These numbers are my own network path to ap-southeast-1, not a benchmark, and the bookmarks table was empty. The idle test sent one request to /health and then one to /bookmarks from the same process, so the second request likely reused the first one's connection and skipped DNS and TLS. I didn't verify that. The 30 warm requests per endpoint came about 70 seconds later.

Test /health /bookmarks
First two requests after about 16 hours idle (estimated) 682.7 ms 363.5 ms
30 warm requests, median 120.8 ms 127.5 ms
30 warm requests, p95 745.7 ms 134.9 ms

Twenty-eight of the 30 warm /health requests took 116.5 to 130.8 ms. Request 1 took 745.7 ms, and with 30 values that is also the p95, so it says little about typical latency. Request 20 took 967.9 ms and I don't know why. Prisma says idle Compute instances resume in milliseconds, but I can't call my idle figure a cold start because DNS, TLS and any wake-up are mixed into it.

npm audit on a Prisma Compute project and its 14 vulnerabilities

npm ci reports 14 vulnerabilities (5 moderate, 9 high). On Linux they traced back to alchemy and an old nested @prisma/dev, plus lodash through a parser package. Also on Linux, a search of dist/server.mjs found no @prisma/dev or lodash, and its only alchemy mentions are three code comments. The app itself uses the top-level hono 4.13.13 and @hono/node-server 2.1.5, which the audit doesn't flag. A bundle search is not a security review. Don't run npm audit fix --force, because it proposes @prisma/composer and @prisma/composer-prisma-cloud 0.6.0 and prisma 7.10.1, a step back from ORM 8.

What worked, and what I'd tell the Prisma team

What worked well. Once I'd signed in with auth login, build and deploy ran without prompts, and the deployed app arrived with its own database. The doc comments in the installed types also say what update and delete return when nothing matches.

What I'd suggest to Prisma. Each of these comes from something I saw.

  • The template's /users error tells you to run contract:emit, but the server log showed DRIVER.ALREADY_CONNECTED. Logging or returning the underlying error would save someone an afternoon. The runtime reference and the scaffold's skill file describe the lazy connect, but the Hono guide I read doesn't, and the template's own helper calls connect() explicitly. The guide's own POST /users example queries db without connecting, so it runs into the same error.
  • The Composer limitations page says deploys use a service token with no browser flow, while the Composer deploying page documents auth login. A note on which is current would settle it.
  • The deploy plan could name the migration it ran.
  • prisma deploy found my project from the folder, but prisma service logs said the directory wasn't linked to one. Sharing that link between the two commands would save a step.
  • The ORM 8 query types live in @prisma/orm-family-sql, not in the package you install, so they took several searches to find.
  • Versions move fast. A couple of days after I scaffolded, the CLI was telling me 8.0.0-rc.27 existed.

Before you copy the repo

  • GET /users is a scaffold route, and it inserts three sample users on its first call.
  • createdAt comes back as Postgres text (2026-10-23 16:33:47.512805+00), not ISO 8601, because the contract uses the scaffold's TimestamptzString type.
  • There's no auth, so anyone with the URL can write to it. Prisma's pricing page gives the Prisma Postgres Free plan 200,000 operations a month, and the Compute FAQ says the Free plan has no backups. I'm not publishing my live URL.
  • A NUL character (\u0000) in title or notes returns 500 instead of 400. A lone surrogate or invalid UTF-8 is stored as the replacement character. These turned up when the repo was probed with odd input on Linux, and the 85 checks don't cover them. They're listed in the README and not fixed.

What I didn't test

I didn't test prisma dev (unsupported on Windows), the pooled connection string, the Prisma MCP server, Bash on Windows or macOS, or how Compute behaves when idle database connections drop. I tested one small API with an empty table, so I can't speak to load or larger projects. The docs changed several times while I worked, so re-check the linked pages before you rely on any of this.

My verdict

I'd use this stack again. Going from a scaffold to a live API with its own Prisma Postgres database took three commands. The one real bug I hit depended on the order my routes and the scaffold's /users route queried the database, and I could trace and fix it. At the time of writing, ORM 8 is still a release candidate and Composer is in Early Access, so before I ran production traffic on it I'd wait for those, and for the docs to agree on auth. The code, README and smoke test are in the repo.

title: Checkout Failure Attribution in 2026: Feature Flag Rollouts with API Control
description:
The best practices for implementing feature flags in Node.js are to use a modular adapter, API-driven evaluation, and a rollout policy tied to checkout telemetry. That gives a healthtech team a controlled rollout while preserving the cost boundary: every failed checkout should tell you which flag state, backend path, and downstream service were involved.

The important design choice is not the toggle itself. It is keeping flag evaluation modular, API-driven, and observable without turning the checkout handler into a vendor SDK boundary. I would keep the flag key, evaluated state, rollout cohort, and request ID beside the failure event. I would also make the default state closed for anything that can charge a patient.

What should the checkout flag own?

Start with one decision record. For example, checkout.payment_authorization.v2 can choose a new authorization path, but it should not decide whether an entire checkout is medically eligible. Eligibility belongs to the domain service; the flag controls a deployable implementation choice.

That separation creates useful invariants:

  • A missing or stale value fails closed for the new payment path.
  • The checkout request records the evaluated key and state before calling the selected implementation.
  • A rollout can be narrowed without changing application code.
  • A failure event carries attribution data that can be grouped by flag state and backend path.

There is a practical edge here. A flag read is a dependency, so a checkout cannot wait forever for it. Cache a last-known decision for a short, explicitly chosen interval, define the emergency default in code, and make the cache policy part of the adapter contract. Do not silently turn a stale flag into a permanent approval.

The event data matters for cost attribution. If the old path calls one payment processor and the new path calls another, flag_key, flag_value, implementation, and provider_request_id let an incident review separate a bad release from a provider-specific failure. Keep patient data out of those dimensions; a flag analysis does not need a name, diagnosis, or full payment payload.

For a concrete review, imagine that a checkout failure rises only for flag_value=true after the cohort expands. The first question is not “which vendor is cheapest?” It is whether the new implementation ran, whether its downstream request was accepted, and whether the failure was recorded once or retried into several events. A stable checkout-attempt identifier, the selected implementation, the flag state, and the downstream request identifier let an engineer join those answers without copying payment details into telemetry. That is the cost boundary I care about: attribute infrastructure and provider work to a controlled path while keeping regulated data out of operational dimensions. The same fields make rollback evidence legible to an auditor who was not in the deployment channel.

How should Node.js feature flags use an API for checkout rollouts?

For Node.js, expose a narrow internal interface even when the provider has a broad API:

import json
import os
import time
from urllib.error import HTTPError, URLError
from urllib.request import Request, urlopen


BASE_URL = os.environ["FLAG_API_BASE_URL"]


def read_flag(key, attempts=4):
    """Read one flag with bounded exponential backoff for rate limiting."""
    url = f"{BASE_URL}/flags/is_enabled/{key}"
    request = Request(
        url,
        headers={"Authorization": f"Bearer {os.environ['INFRAI_API_KEY']}"},
        method="GET",
    )

    for attempt in range(attempts):
        try:
            with urlopen(request, timeout=2) as response:
                if response.status < 200 or response.status >= 300:
                    raise RuntimeError(f"flag lookup failed: HTTP {response.status}")
                return json.load(response)
        except HTTPError as error:
            if error.code != 429 or attempt == attempts - 1:
                detail = error.read().decode("utf-8", errors="replace")
                raise RuntimeError(f"flag lookup failed: HTTP {error.code}: {detail}")
            retry_after = error.headers.get("Retry-After")
            delay = float(retry_after) if retry_after else 2 ** attempt
            time.sleep(delay)
        except URLError as error:
            if attempt == attempts - 1:
                raise RuntimeError(f"flag lookup failed: {error.reason}") from error
            time.sleep(2 ** attempt)


def checkout_path(flag_response):
    """Translate the service response in one adapter-owned place."""
    return flag_response


if __name__ == "__main__":
    print(checkout_path(read_flag("checkout.payment_authorization.v2")))

The example deliberately stops at the adapter boundary. The response contract should be mapped once in the application, then represented as a typed result such as enabled, source, and evaluated_at in Node.js. Do not scatter calls to a provider throughout payment code. The route is the real API path; the application still owns what a true value means for checkout. A 2-second timeout is a policy choice here, not a measured latency claim; set it from the checkout's own deadline budget.

For a write that changes rollout state, use the provider's documented write route and an idempotency key. A retried toggle must not create a second state transition in an administrative workflow. The same discipline applies to failure capture: the event identifier should be stable across a retry, while the checkout's payment attempt remains independently idempotent.

Which option fits a healthtech checkout?

The candidates solve different parts of this problem. A dedicated flag service can provide the control plane; a client library can make evaluation convenient; an API surface can fit teams that already centralize backend calls. Those are different trade-offs from observability, so I would not select a flag product based on toggle ergonomics alone.

Option Useful fit Boundary to verify
LaunchDarkly A dedicated managed flag service for teams that want rollout controls outside the checkout codebase. Confirm how its evaluation, SDK availability, and audit needs fit the runtime and compliance review.
Unleash A flag-management approach with a Node.js client when the team wants a service or library boundary it can operate and integrate. Confirm the operational ownership of the control plane and the behavior when the client cannot refresh.
ConfigCat A managed feature-flag option for teams comparing another hosted control plane and SDK workflow. Validate the data residency, evaluation, and failure-default requirements before production use.
Infrai A plain REST route can fit a backend already consolidating service access behind one key and one bill; its flag surface includes reads, listing, setting, toggling, deletion, and a rollout route. It does not provide change audit logs, evaluation statistics, parent-child dependencies, a recycle bin, or push updates; clients poll, so the application must own freshness and change governance.

That last row is a real boundary, not a footnote. If a compliance team needs a durable who-changed-what record, build that record in the administrative service or choose a control plane that supplies it. Do not infer governance from the existence of a toggle endpoint.

The surrounding observability choice changes the evidence you can gather. Sentry is a natural fit for grouped application errors, Datadog for teams already combining logs, metrics, and infrastructure views, and Grafana for organizations assembling dashboards around their own telemetry backends. None of those names answers the feature-flag control-plane question by itself. They are useful comparison points for failure evidence, not substitutes for a rollout policy.

The same comparison applies to telemetry. A flag service can tell you what was evaluated; it does not automatically prove that a checkout failure was caused by the new path. Emit the decision with the failure event, then query the resulting logs or metrics through your observability layer. The log model should retain a trace ID and span ID where available, but those fields are correlation handles, not a replacement for a distributed span tree.

How do rollout and failure capture meet?

Use a staged sequence: internal staff, a tightly bounded cohort, then a broader cohort only after the failure rate and cost attribution are explainable. A percentage is not a safety policy by itself. For a payment path, define the population, the rollback owner, the maximum stale-cache age, and the signal that stops expansion.

One rule is easy to forget: the flag read is part of the critical path.

The failure record should answer four questions quickly: which checkout attempt failed, which implementation ran, which flag state selected it, and which downstream operation consumed the request. Add the flag state as structured data rather than embedding it in a sentence, because grouping and filtering need stable fields. In practice, I would keep the 4-attempt retry ceiling next to the adapter and review it with the checkout timeout, because a retry that outlives the request is noise with a bill attached.

Do not pretend that polling is push. A client can only learn a changed flag on its next refresh, so the rollout policy needs a propagation interval and a rollback procedure that tolerates that interval. If the workflow needs an alert, the available query API must be polled by a separate monitor; there is no built-in threshold, SMS, phone, or webhook notification route to assume.

Checkout failures also have a quiet cousin: the job that never ran. A flag and a log query cannot prove that a scheduled task fired. Pair the workflow with a heartbeat or external execution monitor when silent failures matter. That keeps the flag system focused on controlled behavior and the monitor focused on liveness.

Rejected design: flags inside the checkout handler

I would reject direct provider calls from every controller and worker. It looks fast in the first pull request, then the same key is read with different defaults, timeout settings, and cache semantics in three places. The eventual failure report says “new path,” but cannot show which evaluator made the decision.

A thin adapter costs a little structure up front. It earns that structure by giving the team one timeout, one default, one retry policy, and one event shape. It also leaves room to replace LaunchDarkly, Unleash, ConfigCat, or a REST-backed service without rewriting payment orchestration. The version matters less than the contract: test the adapter against the selected API before a rollout reaches a real patient checkout.

There is a valid use case for a local library: a low-risk presentation change with no external side effect, where a process-local default is acceptable and rollout governance is simple. That is not the same boundary as a healthtech checkout. Authorization, billing, and patient-facing failure handling deserve explicit defaults and attributable events.

The decision rule is straightforward: choose the option that meets the rollout and compliance boundary, then make its evaluation visible in the failure data. For a team that values one REST interface and centralized backend access, the API-backed option is reasonable. For a team that needs built-in change history, richer evaluation analysis, or push-oriented control, the missing capabilities are decisive and another flag platform is the better fit.

References

  • LaunchDarkly documentation: https://launchdarkly.com/docs/home
  • Unleash documentation: https://docs.getunleash.io/
  • ConfigCat documentation: https://configcat.com/docs/
  • OpenTelemetry logs signal concepts: https://opentelemetry.io/docs/concepts/signals/logs/

title: WhatsApp Cloud API Rate Limits in Practice: Throughput, Pair Rate, Messaging Limits and Error Codes
description:
The WhatsApp Cloud API has four separate limits, and they fail in different ways. Throughput caps how many messages a business number handles per second (80 by default, 20 for coexistence numbers). The pair rate caps how often you can message one customer (about one message every 6 seconds). The messaging limit caps how many customers you can reach outside a 24-hour window in a day, across the whole business portfolio. Quality and spam limits stop sends that look unwanted. Pace every request against the first two, budget the third before you start a campaign, and treat each error code according to which limit it came from: some mean "wait a second", some "wait a day", some "stop".

The snippets are small, self-contained versions of the patterns, and each was run against the cases shown.

The four limits

Limit Scope Default Error when hit
Throughput Business phone number 80 messages/second, 20 for coexistence 130429
Pair rate One business number → one customer 1 message every 6 seconds 131056
Messaging limit Business portfolio, moving 24 hours 250 to unlimited unique customers No dedicated code documented
Marketing per-user limit One customer Adaptive, no fixed number 131049

Throughput is per registered number. Meta's throughput guide says Cloud API "supports up to 80 messages per second (mps) by default", and that the figure is "inclusive of inbound and outbound messages and all message types". Replies coming in use the same budget as campaigns going out, so don't pace your sends at exactly 80. The upgrade to 1,000 mps is automatic, but only for numbers in a portfolio with an unlimited messaging limit that have reached 100,000 or more customers outside a service window in a moving 24 hours, with a quality rating of at least yellow. Coexistence numbers, the ones also used in the WhatsApp Business app, have a fixed 20 mps.

The pair rate is in Meta's rate limits overview: "1 message every 6 seconds to the same WhatsApp user". Short bursts are allowed, but they borrow from future quota, so a burst is followed by a wait. This is the one that bites chatbots and order updates: three messages in a row to one customer, sent as fast as your code can, is a burst.

The messaging limit is the daily cap on reaching customers who haven't messaged you in the last 24 hours. Meta's messaging limits page counts unique customers in a moving 24 hours, and it's shared: limits are "calculated and set at the business portfolio level and are shared by all business phone numbers within a portfolio". The tiers are 250, 2,000, 10,000, 100,000 and unlimited.

The marketing per-user limit is Meta deciding that one customer has had enough marketing for now. The error codes reference describes 131049 as a message "not delivered to maintain healthy ecosystem engagement".

Pace every request, not every batch

Throughput and the pair rate are both about time between requests, so the gate has to sit directly in front of each call to Meta. We learned this from a campaign sender that checked the rate at the start of each batch: the database work inside each batch took a varying time, so the sends at the end of one batch and the start of the next bunched together, and a number allowed 20 per second briefly received about 30. Moving the check to a per-number permit before every request fixed it.

A pacer per business number tracks two things: the next free slot for the number, and the next free slot for each customer.

// Spaces sends for one business number: a messages-per-second budget for the
// number, and a minimum gap between messages to the same customer.
export type PacerOptions = { mps: number; pairGapMs: number };

export const createPacer = ({ mps, pairGapMs }: PacerOptions) => {
  const slotMs = 1000 / mps;
  let nextNumberSlot = 0;
  const nextForRecipient = new Map<string, number>();

  // Returns the earliest time this message may go, and reserves that slot.
  const reserve = (recipient: string, now: number): number => {
    const at = Math.max(now, nextNumberSlot, nextForRecipient.get(recipient) ?? 0);
    nextNumberSlot = at + slotMs;
    nextForRecipient.set(recipient, at + pairGapMs);
    return at;
  };

  // After a 131056, push this customer back without slowing anyone else.
  const deferRecipient = (recipient: string, until: number) => {
    nextForRecipient.set(recipient, Math.max(nextForRecipient.get(recipient) ?? 0, until));
  };

  return { reserve, deferRecipient };
};

With mps: 80, sends to different customers go out 12.5 ms apart. A second message to the same customer waits 6 seconds, while other customers' messages keep flowing past it. Set mps below the real limit to leave room for inbound traffic.

In production, the pacer's state has to be shared by every worker that sends from the number, for example as a Redis key per number. Two workers with their own in-memory pacers send at twice the rate.

Budget the messaging limit before you start

The messaging limit isn't something to discover halfway through a campaign. Count it before you start: how many customers in this send are outside a 24-hour window, and how many of the portfolio's daily slots are already used?

// Meta's messaging limit: unique customers reached outside a customer service
// window, in a moving 24 hours, shared by every number in the business portfolio.
const DAY_MS = 24 * 60 * 60 * 1000;

export const createDailyLimit = (limit: number) => {
  const lastReached = new Map<string, number>();

  const prune = (now: number) => {
    for (const [user, at] of lastReached) if (now - at >= DAY_MS) lastReached.delete(user);
  };

  // A customer already reached in the last 24 hours doesn't use a new slot.
  const tryReach = (user: string, now: number): boolean => {
    prune(now);
    if (!lastReached.has(user) && lastReached.size >= limit) return false;
    lastReached.set(user, now);
    return true;
  };

  const remaining = (now: number) => {
    prune(now);
    return Math.max(0, limit - lastReached.size);
  };

  return { tryReach, remaining };
};

Two details matter. A customer you've already reached in the last 24 hours doesn't use a second slot. And the budget belongs to the portfolio, not the number, so two numbers running campaigns at once draw from the same pool. Only call tryReach for messages sent outside a customer service window; replies inside one don't count.

Your local count is an estimate. Meta's count is the real one, and it reports limit changes in the business_capability_update webhook's max_daily_conversations_per_business field. The reference lists TIER_* strings such as TIER_2K, while its example payload shows a plain number, so parse both. Update your stored limit from that webhook rather than hard-coding it.

Decide by error code

Meta's error reference says to build error handling around the error code, not the HTTP status or the message. Some codes mean "slow down", some mean "this customer, later", and some mean "stop":

// What to do with a failed send, decided by Meta's error code alone.
export type SendDecision =
  | { action: "retry"; afterMs: number }
  | { action: "retry-recipient"; afterMs: number }
  | { action: "hold-recipient"; afterMs: number }
  | { action: "pause-number" }
  | { action: "give-up" };

const SECOND = 1000;
const HOUR = 60 * 60 * SECOND;

// Meta's pair-rate guidance: retry after 4^X seconds, X counting up from 0.
export const backoffMs = (attempt: number, capMs = 15 * 60 * SECOND) => Math.min(4 ** attempt * SECOND, capMs);

export const decide = (code: number, attempt: number): SendDecision => {
  switch (code) {
    case 130429: // throughput reached for this number
    case 131057: // maintenance mode, e.g. a throughput upgrade (about a minute)
    case 80007: // WABA rate limit
    case 4: // app rate limit
      return { action: "retry", afterMs: backoffMs(attempt) };
    case 131056: // too many messages to this one user
      return { action: "retry-recipient", afterMs: backoffMs(attempt) };
    case 131049: // per-user marketing limit; retrying early can extend the hold
      return { action: "hold-recipient", afterMs: 24 * HOUR };
    case 131048: // sending restriction on the number; check its quality first
      return { action: "pause-number" };
    default: // 131026 undeliverable, 130472 experiment, and anything unknown
      return { action: "give-up" };
  }
};

Each choice, and where it comes from:

  • 130429, 80007, 4: retry later. These are throughput and API rate limits. Meta's advice for each is to try again later or send less often; nothing is wrong with the message itself.
  • 131057: retry shortly. The account is in maintenance mode, for example while its throughput is upgraded, which takes up to about a minute.
  • 131056: retry this customer later. Only the one customer is affected. For throttling after a burst, Meta's Cloud API overview says to "retry after 4^X seconds", with X starting at 0 and going up after each failure, which is where backoffMs comes from.
  • 131049: hold this customer for a day. Meta's guidance is to wait at least 24 hours, and resending sooner can extend the hold. Marketing sent inside an open service window doesn't count toward this limit.
  • 131048: pause the number. Meta describes it as "restrictions on how many messages can be sent from this phone number". Pause, and check the number's quality in WhatsApp Manager before sending more.
  • Everything else: give up and record why. 131026, for example, means the message couldn't be delivered, often because the recipient isn't on WhatsApp, hasn't accepted the latest terms, or is on an old app version. Retrying won't change that.

The same codes can arrive two ways: in the response to your send request, or later in a status webhook with status: "failed" and an errors array. Route both through the same decision.

Put it together

One send passes through the pacer, then acts on the result:

import { decide } from "./classify.ts";
import type { createPacer } from "./pacer.ts";

export type Job = { to: string; attempt: number };
export type SendResult = { ok: true } | { ok: false; code: number };

export type Outcome =
  | { status: "sent" }
  | { status: "requeue"; at: number; job: Job }
  | { status: "pause-number" }
  | { status: "failed"; code: number };

// One send through the pacer; the caller owns the queue and acts on the outcome.
export const sendOne = async (
  job: Job,
  pacer: ReturnType<typeof createPacer>,
  clock: { now: () => number; sleepUntil: (t: number) => Promise<void> },
  send: (to: string) => Promise<SendResult>,
): Promise<Outcome> => {
  await clock.sleepUntil(pacer.reserve(job.to, clock.now()));
  const result = await send(job.to);
  if (result.ok) return { status: "sent" };

  const decision = decide(result.code, job.attempt);
  const next = { ...job, attempt: job.attempt + 1 };
  switch (decision.action) {
    case "retry":
      return { status: "requeue", at: clock.now() + decision.afterMs, job: next };
    case "retry-recipient":
    case "hold-recipient": {
      const at = clock.now() + decision.afterMs;
      pacer.deferRecipient(job.to, at);
      return { status: "requeue", at, job: next };
    }
    case "pause-number":
      return { status: "pause-number" };
    case "give-up":
      return { status: "failed", code: result.code };
  }
};

The caller owns the queue: it puts requeued jobs back with their at time, stops the number's queue on pause-number, and records failed with its code so someone can see why a message didn't go. Two rules make the loop safe:

  • Requeue with a time, never in a tight loop. A retry that ignores at turns one rate-limit error into hundreds.
  • Cap the attempts. After a handful of retries, record the failure. A message that fails five times over an hour probably isn't going to succeed on the sixth.

Checklist

  • Pace every request per business number, and leave headroom for inbound traffic.
  • Keep 6 seconds between messages to the same customer.
  • Share the pacer's state across workers.
  • Budget the portfolio's messaging limit before a campaign, and update the tier from webhooks.
  • Decide by error code: retry, defer one customer, hold for a day, pause the number, or give up.
  • Back off with 4^X seconds and cap the attempts.
  • Handle the same codes from send responses and from failed-status webhooks.

title: Memory-Mapped Caching in Go: mmap Mechanics, Page Fault Latency, and the Eviction Boundary Problem
description:
Memory-Mapped Caching in Go: mmap Mechanics, Page Fault Latency, and the Eviction Boundary Problem

Application-layer caches built on map[string][]byte or Redis are the default answer for hot-path read amplification. They work until they don't: GC pressure from large heap allocations, network RTT jitter on Redis reads, or eviction policies that don't align with access patterns. A narrower alternative—memory-mapped files—trades explicit cache management for OS-level page management with zero-copy reads and off-heap storage. The tradeoff surface is poorly understood in Go services. This article works through the mechanics, the failure modes, and where the design boundary sits.

What mmap Actually Gives You

When you call mmap(2) on a file, the kernel maps file-backed pages into the process virtual address space. No data is read from disk at mapping time. Accesses to unmapped pages trigger a minor fault (page already in the OS page cache) or a major fault (page must be read from storage). The kernel manages this transparently. In Go you call into this via syscall.Mmap or the golang.org/x/sys/unix package.

package filecache

import (
    "fmt"
    "os"
    "syscall"
)

type MmapRegion struct {
    data []byte
}

func OpenRegion(path string) (*MmapRegion, error) {
    f, err := os.Open(path)
    if err != nil {
        return nil, fmt.Errorf("open: %w", err)
    }
    defer f.Close()

    fi, err := f.Stat()
    if err != nil {
        return nil, fmt.Errorf("stat: %w", err)
    }
    size := int(fi.Size())
    if size == 0 {
        return nil, fmt.Errorf("empty file")
    }

    data, err := syscall.Mmap(
        int(f.Fd()),
        0,
        size,
        syscall.PROT_READ,
        syscall.MAP_SHARED,
    )
    if err != nil {
        return nil, fmt.Errorf("mmap: %w", err)
    }
    return &MmapRegion{data: data}, nil
}

func (r *MmapRegion) Slice(offset, length int) []byte {
    return r.data[offset : offset+length]
}

func (r *MmapRegion) Close() error {
    return syscall.Munmap(r.data)
}

The slice returned by Slice points into the OS page cache, not the Go heap. The GC does not scan it. Allocation pressure from large in-process caches disappears. The data is accessible to any goroutine without a copy, and reads that hit warm pages are essentially a memcpy from L3 or RAM, not a syscall.

Where Go's Runtime Intersects

The slice header—pointer, length, cap—lives on the Go heap. The backing array does not. This creates a subtle escape problem: if you return a subslice from Slice and the caller stores it in an interface or passes it to json.Unmarshal, Go's escape analysis sees the header escape but not the data region. The GC won't move it (the runtime only moves heap objects in specific contexts, and mmap pages are not heap-managed), but the GC will not help you if a goroutine holds a stale slice into a region you've already Munmap'd. That's a use-after-free.

The correct contract is: the region owns the lifetime; callers borrow slices within a request-scoped duration and never store them beyond that scope. Enforce this structurally, not by convention.

A second interaction: syscall.Mmap causes the Go runtime's cgo signal handling path to activate for SIGBUS. If a file is truncated after mapping, any access to the now-invalid pages generates SIGBUS, which the Go runtime surfaces as a panic with a specific signal message rather than a clean error. Your service crashes. Validate file size before mapping and use atomic file replacement (write to temp, rename(2)) rather than in-place truncation.

Page Fault Latency Budget

The latency model for mmap reads is bimodal:

  • Warm path (page in page cache): ~50–200ns depending on whether the page is in L1/L2/L3 or main memory. This is on par with a Redis pipelined read within the same host and orders of magnitude faster than a cross-AZ Redis call.
  • Cold path (major fault): Kernel must issue an I/O to the underlying block device. On NVMe this is 100–300µs. On EBS gp3 in AWS it is 200µs–2ms depending on burst credit state. On io1/io2 it is more predictable but not fast enough for a 1ms latency budget on the hot path.

If your service has a 5ms P99 latency budget and you are serving a 2GB index file with a working set larger than available memory, major faults will blow that budget unpredictably. The OS will make eviction decisions based on global page reclaim pressure across all processes on the host, not your per-request deadline. This is the eviction boundary problem: you do not control when pages leave the page cache.

You can influence—but not guarantee—residency with madvise(2). MADV_WILLNEED hints the kernel to prefetch pages asynchronously. MADV_SEQUENTIAL adjusts readahead. Neither is a hard reservation.

func Prefetch(data []byte) error {
    _, _, errno := syscall.Syscall(
        syscall.SYS_MADVISE,
        uintptr(unsafe.Pointer(&data[0])),
        uintptr(len(data)),
        syscall.MADV_WILLNEED,
    )
    if errno != 0 {
        return errno
    }
    return nil
}

mlock(2) pins pages in RAM and prevents eviction entirely, but it requires elevated privileges (CAP_IPC_LOCK), consumes locked memory quota (ulimit -l), and prevents the OS from using that memory for anything else. In containers on ECS or EKS, mlock limits are often restrictive or unavailable. Do not rely on it in containerized services without explicit platform configuration.

Operational Failure Modes in Production

Memory overcommit on shared hosts. Kubernetes nodes and ECS hosts run multiple containers. The page cache is shared. When a co-resident service allocates heavily, the kernel's kswapd begins reclaiming pages. Your mmap region, being file-backed, is eligible for eviction without any signal to your process. The next access triggers a major fault, and your latency spikes. This is the same failure mode as noisy neighbor problems on Redis, just lower-level.

File rotation without remap. A common pattern for serving updated index files is to replace the file on disk and expect the mmap to pick up changes. With MAP_SHARED, the mapping reflects the underlying inode. If you replace the file via rename(2) (creating a new inode), the existing mapping continues to point at the old inode's pages. The process keeps serving stale data silently. You must Munmap, open the new file, and remap. During the remap window, you need a fallback read path or the region must be read-locked against concurrent access.

NUMA topology. On multi-socket servers (less common in cloud but present on bare metal or large instance types), page allocation is NUMA-aware. Pages for the mmap region may reside on a remote NUMA node from the goroutine accessing them, adding 50–100ns per access due to cross-socket memory latency. You can observe this via numastat and influence placement with mbind(2), but the window for that optimization is narrow in typical AWS deployments.

Where mmap-Backed Caching Fits

The pattern works well for:

  • Static or slowly rotating read indexes: ML feature stores, precomputed lookup tables, IP geolocation databases, compiled rule sets. Large, mostly read, rotated infrequently. The working set fits in memory on the target instance type.
  • Zero-copy serving of binary blobs: Serving protobuf-encoded records or columnar data segments directly off a file without deserializing into heap structures. Combine with a fixed-offset index structure (array of [offset uint32, length uint32]) for O(1) lookup without malloc.
  • Shared memory between processes on the same host: MAP_SHARED with a named file or POSIX shared memory allows multiple processes to read the same pages without redundant copies. Relevant if you run a sidecar or co-located agent.

It is the wrong tool when:

  • Your cache working set is significantly larger than available RAM and access patterns are not strongly localized.
  • You need fine-grained TTL-based invalidation on individual keys—there is no key abstraction, only byte ranges.
  • You are running on EBS-backed storage with variable I/O latency and cannot tolerate the P99 impact of major faults.
  • You need write visibility—concurrent writers to a MAP_SHARED region require your own synchronization; the OS does not provide it.

Decision Framework

Before adopting mmap as a caching layer, answer these questions:

  1. Does the working set fit in instance memory with headroom? If the ratio of working set to available RAM exceeds ~0.6, major fault rate will be unpredictable under memory pressure. Measure with perf stat -e major-faults or /proc/vmstat under realistic load.
  2. What is the file update frequency? If rotation happens more than once per minute, remap coordination adds complexity that likely exceeds the benefit. A Redis hash or an in-process sync.Map with a TTL wheel is simpler.
  3. Is your latency budget fault-tolerant to P99 spikes? If your SLO is P99 < 2ms and you cannot bound major fault latency via instance type selection and mlock, the design is fragile.
  4. What is the operational context? EKS or ECS with shared node pools increases noisy neighbor risk. A dedicated instance or a memory-optimized instance type (r7g, x2idn) with a reserved memory allocation changes the math.
  5. Can you tolerate the Go lifetime contract? If slice lifetimes are difficult to bound in your codebase—heavy use of goroutines that outlive request context, interfaces that capture byte slices—the use-after-unmap risk may not be worth it.

When all five conditions are favorable, mmap-backed caches eliminate GC pressure, reduce allocator contention, and provide sub-microsecond read latency on warm pages with no network hop. When they are not, the opacity of OS page reclaim will produce latency anomalies that are difficult to attribute without kernel-level profiling tools.

title: GMO Puts a $1 Million Bounty on Its Hackers After Refusing to Pay Ransom
description:
GMO Puts a $1 Million Bounty on Its Hackers After Refusing to Pay Ransom

When criminals breach a company and demand a ransom, most victims face a grim choice: pay up and hope the data disappears, or refuse and brace for leaks. Japan's GMO Internet Group has chosen a third option this week: turn the tables and pay people who help catch the attackers instead.

On October 28, the Japanese internet and fintech giant officially opened a bounty program offering up to US$1 million (roughly 160 million yen) in total rewards for lawfully obtained information that leads to the arrest of — or an international wanted notice for — the perpetrator of the breach of its Onamae.com Desktop Cloud service. The company is seeking tips that connect people, servers, domains, IP addresses, accounts, or cryptocurrency wallets to the attack, the extortion attempt, or the movement of stolen funds.

From cloud desktops to live trading accounts

The incident at the heart of the bounty is unusual in how far the damage reached. Onamae.com Desktop Cloud rents out Windows cloud desktops that traders commonly use to run automated foreign exchange (FX) trading software around the clock. That means the servers didn't just hold customer records — in many cases they held live credentials to brokerage accounts.

GMO first disclosed unauthorized access to the service on October 21, shut the service down the same day, and reported the matter to Japanese police on October 22. Attackers allegedly used trading credentials stored on the rented servers to place unauthorized orders at brokerages, turning a routine-sounding data breach into real-time financial fraud. GMO estimates that around 27,000 servers across all plans could have been at risk, though the company stresses this is the number of potentially affected machines, not a confirmed count of compromised ones.

A ransom demand, and a hard no

According to reporting by TechCrunch and others, the attackers initially emailed GMO on October 21 demanding roughly $50 million (about 8 billion yen). Later statements attributed to the attacker demanded US$1 million with a deadline of noon JST on October 27, threatening to manipulate trading accounts at more than 70 securities and FX firms in Japan and abroad, publish customer information daily at noon, launch ransomware attacks against users' machines, and expose details of GMO's own internal systems.

GMO's response has been unequivocal. The company says it handed all communications with the extortionists over to police cybercrime units and publicly declared it will never give in to the demands. "We are seeking credible information that leads to the identification and arrest of those involved," the company stated on its dedicated bounty portal, which accepts submissions in Japanese, English, and Chinese.

After the deadline passed, material purporting to contain customer personal information began appearing online, and a suspected attacker published what appears to be at least one customer's name and phone number. GMO confirmed on October 27 that information connected to the company and its customers had been published, and on October 28 announced that the domain used for the extortion site had been taken down — while warning that replacement sites could still emerge.

Making customers whole

Alongside the bounty, GMO has moved to compensate affected users. In an October 28 stock exchange filing, the company said it will pay every current user of the service 5,000 yen and cover actual trading losses and fees for any trades it confirms were unauthorized and caused by the breach. It cautioned that it has not yet confirmed how many customers the compensation program will cover, how much information was published, or which trades qualify.

The company has also been collecting customers' devices since October 25 to check for malware, and has urged users to reset passwords for any trading or financial accounts used from the service. Its group CEO wrote in a blog post that internal security researchers had flagged problems with the service before the attack, and that fixes were underway but not deep or fast enough.

Why this case matters

The GMO incident lands in the middle of what some security experts have taken to calling AI's "Black October" — a stretch marked by a sharp rise in AI-accelerated vulnerabilities and attacks. Whatever tools the attackers used, the case highlights a structural risk that is only growing: cloud services that hold live financial credentials turn a single intrusion into direct monetary theft. A breached marketing database is a liability; a breached trading desktop is a loaded weapon.

It also illustrates a shifting stance on extortion. Companies like Kraken have publicly refused ransom demands before, but putting a formal bounty on the attackers' heads — funded at $1 million, coordinated with police, and open to tips worldwide — is a more aggressive posture. Cyber insurance premiums and regulation increasingly discourage paying ransoms, since payment funds future attacks and offers no guarantee data is deleted. Bounty programs flip the incentive: instead of paying criminals, pay the ecosystem that can unmask them.

There are risks to this approach too. Attackers may escalate leaks to punish defiance, and bounties rarely produce arrests when attackers operate from safe jurisdictions. But as a signal of where enterprise incident response may be heading, GMO's move is one of the clearest yet: don't fund the attack — fund the manhunt.

For now, GMO says it will continue working with law enforcement, compensating customers, and pursuing takedowns of any replacement leak sites. The bounty program remains open, and the investigation is ongoing.

title: MySQL or PostgreSQL, Does It Matter to Choose Which?
description:
When we develop a program, or an app, it is important to keep our data on some place. If you learn basic web app programming from Youtube or from other learning platform, you will be guided to choose MySQL as a starter database. MySQL is beginner friendly, easy to use, and versatile when it comes to intermediate level query. But there is other SQL version, which is PostgreSQL. So what is the difference between those two?

What is SQL?

SQL is Structured Query Language. It is a programming language of which we can use to manage MySQL and PostgreSQL. MySQL and PostgreSQL is a database management system. Those two are the places we can store the database, and SQL is the language we can use to access them.

The learning curve of SQL is quite lean. The core concept of the query is simple. But when it comes to complexes database which have tons of tables, it is quite challenging to optimize the syntax of the query. SQL language is quite a lot to explore, but we can grasp the core of SQL quite easy.

For example, the JOIN syntax. There are many kind of JOIN syntax like INNER JOIN or OUTER JOIN which have different purposes, but the concept is the same, to join the columns of the tables. Same as INSERT, UPDATE, and DELETE, quite explanatory each of those syntax for the SQL.

About MySQL and PostgreSQL

MySQL is commonly used with web application, mostly with PHP and Javascript. Web applications store their user data, config data, and application data within MySQL. In PHP, they have mysqli extension which for some PHP installation is enabled by default. It is the interface for the web application to execute SQL Query to MySQL databases. The query which executed then returns output to the web application or changes data in the database.

But when you familiar with enterprise application like ERP or HRIS, you will heard PostgreSQL much more often. PostgreSQL is a database, just like MySQL. They have quite similar query syntax on INSERT, UPDATE, or DELETE, but on some cases like incremental key, upsert, or concatenate, they have different syntax. PostgreSQL much optimized for bigger application for which they have optimized for larger databases and more complex queries.

So That's It? More optimized?

Well, yes basically. PostgreSQL is more optimized to larger and complex databases.

The truth of deciding of which database to choose is based on what exactly the specifications do you need?

If you only need database for simple web application for about 100 users which not concurrently using, it is better to use MySQL. The installation is simple and will fulfill your app's need. MySQL interface on some programming language mostly pre-installed so it won't be too much of a hassle to install your database.

But if you need a more heavy load transaction and computation, most likely because your app used by a lot of concurrent users and maybe you will be using pgvector to use LLMs, you will need PostgreSQL. It is more optimized for larger JOINs for much more relational tables and even can be setup as Vector Database for your LLMs.

The more we know the capacity of those two database system, the better our app will perform.
