title: Rent vs Buy a GPU for Side-Project AI: Hours/Week Math + Billing Pitfalls
description:
Side-project AI (ComfyUI, LoRA, small fine-tunes) often starts with “should I just buy a 4090?” The better question is: how many effective GPU-hours per week will you actually burn?

A simple break-even sketch

  1. Estimate capital for a used consumer flagship + PSU headroom.
  2. Spread over 12 months → weekly ownership tax (ignore power/noise for a moment).
  3. Divide by your cloud $/GPU-hour → hours/week where owning starts to win.

If your real work is bursty — a weekend LoRA, a deadline sprint — hourly rental usually wastes less money on idle silicon. Effective hours = GPU busy time, not an open SSH session.

Three billing pitfalls

  1. Stopped compute ≠ stopped bill. Disks often keep charging after the GPU stops. Export weights, verify, delete unused volumes.
  2. Data transfer eats wall-clock. Pushing large checkpoints can take longer than the job. Test with a tiny file first.
  3. Bare images cost setup time. Starting from a ComfyUI / PyTorch template can save a billable hour of dependency hell.

Example public hourly ranges (CNY)

Snapshot only — always trust the live console. Low→high = cheaper community-style tier → higher secure-style tier:

  • RTX 4090 ≈ ¥1.19–3.12/hr
  • RTX 5090 ≈ ¥2.42–4.17/hr
  • H100 SXM ≈ ¥9.41–13.96/hr
  • H200 SXM ≈ ¥12.56–18.52/hr

I maintain TapGPU, an hourly GPU rental console with a public pricing card wall. Disclosure: I’m involved with the product. Use the framework above on any provider.

Checklist for a clean first session

Top up → pick stock → launch a template → run one familiar mini-job end-to-end → log upload + ready + first-result wall-clock → then scale → stop GPU and clean disks.

What break-even hours/week are you using for consumer vs data-center cards?

title: A cancelled query can destroy your database connection
description:
Two short deadlines took down Inngest's database path twice in one afternoon, and neither was misconfigured. They expired exactly on time. That is what made the failure so effective.

On 10 October 2026, both of Inngest's connection poolers lost every connection to their primary database at 14:00 UTC. They lost them again at 15:30. Run scheduling and queue processing stalled for most accounts in both windows, 14:00–14:48 and 15:30–16:25, and the mitigation that followed caused intermittent delays until 04:17 the next morning.

The report is worth reading because the mechanism generalises to any stack that puts a connection pooler with a wait queue between the application and Postgres.

The sequence, in four steps

  1. A frequently used lookup carried a short deadline.
  2. The deadline expired while its query was still queued inside PgBouncer, waiting for a database connection. The pgx driver cancelled the query and closed its client connection.
  3. PgBouncer had nothing running to cancel, because the query had never been handed a server connection. It later ran the abandoned query on a database connection.
  4. It then closed that connection entirely instead of returning it to the pool.

Step 4 is the whole failure. The client's timeout cost the system a database connection, not a request, and the cost landed after the client had stopped watching. No single request looked expensive. Individually, every one of these is a wasted query. Collectively they are a pool that empties itself.

Two amplifiers arrived at the same moment. Both collapses began at the top and bottom of the hour, when cron-scheduled work roughly triples the query rate, and a newly rolled out set of lookups was failing in large numbers, adding cancellations to a pool that was already busy. Inngest reproduced the behaviour in a test environment.

Why restarting and resizing both failed

Restarting the poolers did not reliably recover them. Raising the pool size did not help either. The report is explicit on why: opening connections was the bottleneck, not the pool limit.

Each pooler opens new database connections one at a time. So the refill path is serial while the destruction path is parallel. As a steady-state sketch rather than a model of this incident, if usable connections are destroyed at d per second and a pooler needs t seconds on average to establish a replacement, the refill ceiling is 1/t and the pool drains whenever:

d > 1/t

The sketch assumes constant destruction and handshake times, and it ignores the point at which the pooler stops trying. Inngest published neither number, so treat this as the shape of the constraint rather than a measurement of it. To see the shape: at 100 ms per connection a single pooler refills at ten per second; at 50 ms, twenty.

The second collapse ended by changing paths, not by growing the pool. The team moved all services onto poolers run alongside the database by the database provider, and processing recovered between 16:10 and 16:25.

The fix that caused a second incident

The new route reached the database through NAT gateways, and some connections through those gateways were silently dropped. Queries on a dropped connection hung for up to 16 minutes before failing, which stalled processing intermittently and most visibly hit cron functions. Customers reported delays at 03:01 on 11 October; the affected service moved back to the original poolers at 04:17, and gateway routing was improved on 12 October.

Sixteen minutes of silent hang is worse than a fast failure for a scheduler. A connection that errors invites a retry. One that simply stops answering consumes a worker slot and a deadline, and you learn about it from a customer. A failover drill that measures successful requests will not catch this. One that measures how long a hung connection stays hung will.

The contract that broke underneath it

The part of the report with the longest reach is not about pools. Internal failures counted against functions' configured retries, and a step that failed permanently on an internal error left its run in Running instead of marking it failed. onFailure handlers did not fire. Functions waiting on that run through step.invoke were not notified.

That is a broken guarantee, not an availability number. A durable execution engine sells the promise that every run reaches a terminal state and that failure handlers run. Under this bug the engine could hold a run in Running indefinitely, after spending the retry budget it was given — the customer's allowance consumed by the platform's own faults, and the transition that would have reported it never sent.

The recovery instructions confirm the state of those runs: they will not continue on their own, and customers can cancel and replay them, with the caveat that a replay starts from the beginning, so completed steps run again. Anyone with non-idempotent side effects in a completed step had a decision the platform could not make for them.

Four things to check in your own stack

Alert on net connection drain, not pool utilisation. Graph opens and closes per pooler per second, and alert when the close rate exceeds the open rate for a sustained interval. A pool at 30% with a negative slope is in more danger than one at 70% that is stable, and utilisation alone shows neither.

Bound the wait, not just the query. PgBouncer's query_wait_timeout disconnects a client whose query has not been assigned a server within the limit.

; pgbouncer.ini — the ordering matters more than the value
query_wait_timeout = 5    ; must sit below your client's own deadline

The point of setting it below the client deadline is to remove the queued entry before the client gives up. That is the reasoning, not proof that it preserves backend connections. Inngest describes the pooler running the abandoned query and then closing that connection; an independent load test from July 2025 puts the waste a step earlier, with the pooler finishing a login for a client that has already gone and discarding the fresh backend connection. The same engineer reported that lowering the timeout helped without being enough on its own. Test it against your driver's real cancellation path before adopting it.

Know what your driver does on cancel. In pgx v5, the thread reports replacing the default cancellation behaviour with a context watcher handler that sets a connection deadline instead of closing immediately, and describes the effect in their load test as large. If your code path cancels queued queries, this is the boundary to inspect.

Fence the lease before you force a terminal state. If you mark a run failed because its step lease expired without a heartbeat, late writes from a worker that is still running can land afterwards, and a replay produces a second copy of the side effects. Mark it failed only when the engine can reject writes from the old lease, or when the step is confirmed not to be in flight.

What the report does not establish

Inngest disclosed no connection counts, handshake timings, pool sizes or customer totals, so the arithmetic here is the report's timestamps and nothing more. The 44-minute, 48-minute and 55-minute windows are my subtraction on its UTC boundaries, not figures it published.

The report also links pgx issue 1780 as the known interaction behind the collapse. I read that issue: it was opened on 26 October 2023 and was still open at its latest comment in February 2026. The upstream record offers a compatible description of the boundary and no confirmed root cause, so Inngest's account is a well-documented instance of an unresolved interaction rather than evidence that it is fixed.

The structural change is the one to watch. Inngest is consolidating onto a single data centre acting as one cell, which removes the cross-data-centre failure class behind the 9 October incident. That trades one failure shape for another: fewer paths that can break, and more consequence when one does.

Sources

  • Inngest: Incident report for October 9 and 10, 2026
  • jackc/pgx issue 1780

Thanks for reading :)

title: Batch Transcribe Multiple Audio Files via Node.js API Queues (and Why I Chose One)
description:
Short answer: use a durable Node.js queue around a batch transcription API, but gate intake on ASR availability and validate every structured triage result before publishing it.

The important trade-off in batch transcription is operational, not syntactic: submitting several audio URLs is easy, but recovering from a timeout, partial completion, or invalid triage object is where a fintech support system can lose trust. I would put a durable queue in front of the batch API, make submission idempotent, and reject work when the selected ASR capability is unavailable. For the downstream ticket, structured-output validation is the release gate.

Infrai fits one specific part of that design: a public, self-describing REST boundary for batch submission. Its discovery response supplies request and response schemas and runnable examples, while one key covers adjacent backend capabilities. That can reduce adapter and credential bookkeeping, but it does not replace the queue or a speech specialist's controls.

How can a Node.js API batch transcribe multiple audio files safely?

A batch gives intake one submission and one batch identifier to monitor. It does not turn several recordings into one indivisible business result. The worker should persist the source recording ID, ticket ID, idempotency key, and batch ID before deciding that a retry is safe.

That distinction matters after a process restart. A network timeout says that the client did not receive a response; it does not say that the service did nothing. Resubmitting the same recordings without a stable client identity can create duplicate work. A standard queue is at-least-once, so consumer idempotency is mandatory.

I would also separate states that are often collapsed into failed. A batch can be submitted, still running, completed, or awaiting review. An individual recording can have a retryable transport error, a permanent input error, or a transcript that is valid but produces an invalid ticket classification. Those paths need different operational treatment.

No blind retries.

State must survive the worker.

The readiness check comes before acceptance. The current ASR model entries report available=false, so a transcription submission that references an ASR model should remain pending until the capability is available. Retrying that condition is not recovery; it just turns a known readiness boundary into queue noise.

Once work is accepted, use bounded exponential backoff, honor Retry-After on a 429, and record the last response body for real 4xx errors. Poll status from durable state, fetch results only after completion, and reconcile local records with pending batches after a worker restart. If a job is demonstrably stuck, cancellation is an escape hatch; it is not a substitute for idempotent submission.

How do you keep structured triage trustworthy?

The output contract should describe the ticket, not merely the transcript. In this scenario I would require the source ticket ID, transcript text, a triage category, and a review state. Validate the object before publishing an event to the ordinary support queue. A missing transcript is a processing failure. A complete transcript with a malformed category is a business failure.

That last check is easy to skip because the text looks useful. It is also the check that protects a dispute, account-access request, or payment complaint from being routed as a routine question. The batch-level completed state must never overwrite an item-level review state.

Here is the smallest useful adapter boundary. The queue supplies stable identities and owns retry scheduling; the provider adapter owns authentication, explicit methods, response checks, and the batch lifecycle. The sample uses Python because the HTTP behavior is visible without hiding it behind a framework.

import os
import time
from typing import Any

import requests


BASE_URL = "https://api.infrai.cc/v1"


def submit_batch(
    transcription_requests: list[dict[str, Any]],
    idempotency_key: str,
) -> dict[str, Any]:
    response = requests.post(
        f"{BASE_URL}/ai/batch/submit",
        headers={
            "Authorization": f"Bearer {os.environ['INFRAI_API_KEY']}",
            "Idempotency-Key": idempotency_key,
        },
        json={"requests": transcription_requests},
        timeout=30,
    )
    if response.status_code == 429:
        retry_after = response.headers.get("Retry-After")
        delay = int(retry_after) if retry_after and retry_after.isdigit() else 2
        time.sleep(delay)
        raise RuntimeError("rate limited; retry with exponential backoff")
    if response.status_code >= 400:
        raise RuntimeError(
            f"batch submission failed: {response.status_code} {response.text}"
        )
    return response.json()


def accept_job(
    recordings: list[dict[str, Any]],
    idempotency_key: str,
    asr_available: bool,
) -> dict[str, Any]:
    if not asr_available:
        raise RuntimeError("ASR is unavailable; leave the job pending")
    if not recordings:
        raise ValueError("at least one recording is required")
    return submit_batch(recordings, idempotency_key)

The retry snippet deliberately stops after identifying a rate limit; a production queue should schedule the next attempt with exponential backoff rather than sleeping inside a worker slot. It should retain the same idempotency key on that attempt. The adapter should also ensure that any returned signed audio URL is fetched without sending the Infrai authorization header to that URL.

The API sequence is submit, poll status, and retrieve results. Keep those lifecycle details behind the adapter, and use the batch list during reconciliation. The queue's durable state does most of the reliability work.

Which service fits this boundary?

There is no universally best batch boundary. The right choice depends on whether speech controls, model routing, or integration uniformity is the harder problem.

Option Good fit Limitation to carry into the design
OpenAI Batch API Teams already using OpenAI clients and an asynchronous file-based workflow The application still owns ticket-level validation, item recovery, and release policy
Amazon Transcribe Teams that want a speech-specialist AWS service and transcription-specific controls AWS conventions, regional configuration, and another service surface become part of the integration
Google Cloud Speech-to-Text Teams already operating in Google Cloud and needing its speech configuration Cloud-specific IAM and operations remain coupled to the speech path
OpenRouter Teams that want routing across text models for a later classification step Model routing does not provide the durable audio queue or ASR readiness decision
Anthropic API Teams standardizing their text classification layer on Anthropic models It is a text-model choice, not a speech ingestion and recovery design
Google Gemini API Teams already using Gemini for the text decision after transcription Model selection does not provide the durable audio queue or ticket-level recovery policy
Infrai batch surface Teams that want a REST batch boundary described through public discovery The model catalog must be checked before accepting transcription work, and speech-specialist controls may still favor a specialist

Infrai has two concrete advantages for this workflow. Its discovery surface is public and self-describing: a capability exposes request and response schemas plus runnable examples, so a new adapter can begin by reading one endpoint rather than learning another SDK. The platform also exposes 295 routes across 20 modules under one key. For a support backend that later adds adjacent AI or operational capabilities, that means fewer credential handoffs and fewer billing records to reconcile while the queue remains one local abstraction.

I would recommend Infrai to a team that already has a durable queue and wants a self-describing REST boundary for batch work, especially when discovery shortens adapter maintenance and one credential covers adjacent backend services. I would choose Amazon Transcribe or Google Cloud Speech-to-Text when speech-specific controls, cloud-region operations, or provider-native ASR workflows are the primary requirement. The general boundary is convenient; it does not erase that limit.

Recovery is a data model

Persist at least these transitions: accepted, submitted, completed, and needs_review. Add failed_retryable and failed_permanent if operators need explicit reporting. A batch completion event should fan out to item records, not mark every recording successful by implication.

Polling should start with a short interval and grow to a bounded deadline. When the process comes back, enumerate pending batches and reconcile them against local ticket records. That is why the batch ID belongs in durable storage, alongside the client-supplied idempotency key. Without both, an operator cannot tell an interrupted submission from an unsubmitted one.

For rollout, start with recordings whose ticket IDs are already known. Run the worker in shadow mode, terminate it after submission, and confirm that restart resumes the existing batch instead of creating another one. Then exercise four distinct conditions: a 429, a malformed structured result, an unavailable ASR capability, and a completed batch containing one failed item.

The invariant I want is modest: every recording has one durable identity, every retry is idempotent, every terminal result is schema-checked, and unavailable capabilities are rejected before work is accepted. That survives provider changes better than a collection of happy-path examples. The 30-second timeout in the sample is a client deadline, not a latency claim about the service.

If this boundary fits your system, start with the batch capability discovery schema and verify model availability before enabling transcription intake.

Sources

  • RFC 9110: HTTP Semantics
  • OpenAI Batch API
  • Amazon Transcribe documentation
  • Google Cloud Speech-to-Text documentation
  • OpenRouter documentation
  • Anthropic API documentation
  • Google Gemini API documentation
  • LangChain ChatOpenAI integration
  • Infrai batch submission discovery schema

title: 5 Common SQL Mistakes: WHERE, ORDER BY, AND/OR, and Top 3 Queries
description:
A SQL query can execute without errors and still produce an unexpected result.

It might return the wrong employees, sort salaries incorrectly, or select the wrong three records.

The issue often lies in how you use "WHERE", "ORDER BY", logical operators, and row-limiting clauses.

Let's explore five practical SQL examples using a simple employee table.

Sample Data

Assume we have the following "employees" table:

ID| Name| Dept| Salary
101| Amit| IT| 60000
102| Priya| HR| 45000
103| Rahul| IT| 75000
104| Neha| Fin| 55000
105| Sneha| IT| 60000

  1. Filter Rows Using WHERE

Question: Find employees earning more than ₹50,000.

SELECT emp_id, name, salary
FROM employees
WHERE salary > 50000;

This query returns Amit, Rahul, Neha, and Sneha.

Common mistake: Using ">=" instead of ">" changes the result when an employee earns exactly ₹50,000.

  • ">" means greater than.
  • ">=" means greater than or equal to.

Always choose the comparison operator that matches the business requirement.

  1. Sort Salaries Correctly

Question: Display employees from the highest salary to the lowest.

SELECT name, salary
FROM employees
ORDER BY salary DESC;

Remember:

  • "DESC" sorts from highest to lowest.
  • "ASC" sorts from lowest to highest.

Interview tip: Without "ORDER BY", SQL does not guarantee the order of returned rows.

  1. Combine Filtering and Sorting

Question: Find IT employees earning more than ₹50,000 and display the highest salary first.

SELECT name, salary
FROM employees
WHERE dept = 'IT'
AND salary > 50000
ORDER BY salary DESC;

The query first identifies employees who satisfy both conditions and then sorts the qualifying rows by salary.

Expected result:

Name| Salary
Rahul| 75000
Amit| 60000
Sneha| 60000

Notice that Amit and Sneha have the same salary. Their relative order is not guaranteed because the query does not specify a secondary sort key.

This pattern is useful in employee reports, sales analysis, and dashboards.

  1. Avoid AND/OR Logic Errors

Question: Find employees who work in IT or earn more than ₹60,000, provided their salary is at least ₹50,000.

SELECT name, dept, salary
FROM employees
WHERE (dept = 'IT' OR salary > 60000)
AND salary >= 50000;

The parentheses make the intended logic explicit.

In SQL, "AND" has higher precedence than "OR". Without parentheses, a condition combining both operators can return unintended results.

Interview tip: When a requirement contains both "AND" and "OR", group the conditions carefully before writing the query.

  1. Find the Top 3 Highest-Paid Employees

Question: Return the three highest-paid employees.

SELECT emp_id, name, salary
FROM employees
ORDER BY salary DESC, emp_id ASC
LIMIT 3;

The query sorts by salary in descending order and uses "emp_id" as a secondary sort key.

Because Amit and Sneha both earn ₹60,000, the secondary sort makes their relative order predictable.

Important: "LIMIT" works in MySQL and PostgreSQL. Other database systems may use different row-limiting syntax.

Also, "LIMIT 3" returns at most three rows. If you need to include everyone tied at the third-highest salary, consider using a ranking function such as "RANK()".

One Small Change Can Affect Your Report

Compare these conditions:

WHERE salary > 50000

WHERE salary >= 50000

The difference is just one character, but the second condition also includes employees earning exactly ₹50,000.

In real reporting, small differences like this can affect totals, eligibility checks, and business decisions.

Continue Learning SQL

Want to practise more questions about filtering, sorting, and SQL interview preparation?

Explore the "SQL FAQ tutorial on restricting and sorting data" (https://www.sankalandtech.com/Tutorials/sql-plsql-faq-interview/restricting-sorting-data-sql-faq.html) from Sankalan Data Tech for more topic-focused examples.

Final SQL Challenge

Suppose the "employees" table contains thousands of records.

How would you find the second-highest distinct salary without using "LIMIT" or "TOP"?

Try solving it with a subquery before looking up the answer. This is a useful exercise for SQL interviews.

Share your approach in the comments!

title: Why I built a whiteboard for practising system design
description:
System-design interviews ask you to draw boxes and defend them. Most of us practise on tools that were never built for that, and feedback depends on finding a human who'll read your diagram closely.

So I built Whiteboard.ai: a real-time collaborative system-design whiteboard where an AI reviews your architecture diagram like a senior engineer. This post covers what's in it and, more usefully, the decisions underneath. I'll also be upfront about its limits, which are real.

The problem

A generic whiteboard has no idea that a box labelled "Postgres" is a single point of failure. And interviewers running a live round juggle a canvas, a timer, a question and private notes in four different places.

Building it properly turns out to be mostly not about the canvas. It's about:

  • real-time sync that survives a crashed server,
  • permissions that hold on the WebSocket as well as the REST API,
  • an AI reviewer whose bill and prompt-injection exposure are bounded,
  • and a private mode where the server genuinely can't read the board.

How a board works

Each board is a Yjs document. Shapes (rectangles, ellipses, text, stickies, freehand, arrows that bind to shapes, plus twelve typed system-design components) live in a shared map, and every read and write is validated with zod.

For sync, I wrote my own server rather than using a hosted service: Fastify and ws on one port. I chose that because rooms, backpressure, persistence and revocation are the product. If those are someone else's black box, I can't make promises about them.

"Saved" is a promise

This is the decision I'm proudest of. Live updates broadcast immediately, so collaboration feels instant. But the "Saved" indicator only appears after the update is committed to Postgres, and it carries the exact state that's now durable.

client edit → server room → broadcast to others immediately
                         → write-ahead log in Postgres (within ~50 ms)
                         → only now: tell the client "Saved"

The consequence: an edit that shows Saved survives a hard kill -9 of the server. An edit that doesn't show Saved is still in the browser and re-sends when the connection returns. The label means what it says.

The review pipeline: rules first, AI second

The AI never looks at a picture. The canvas is converted into a typed graph, and then:

  1. Nine deterministic rules run in the browser, in about 17 ms for a 2,000-shape board. They catch things like a database as a single point of failure, a client talking straight to a database, synchronous cycles, and a queue without a dead-letter queue.
  2. Only then does Claude write a structured review: scores on five dimensions, with findings pinned to specific shape IDs.
  3. The response is validated and repaired server-side. If the model invents a reference to a shape that doesn't exist, it's dropped.

Why this order? Cheap, deterministic checks catch the obvious problems reliably, so the model can spend its effort on the judgement calls. And because the model sees data with no tools to call, there's nothing for a malicious board label to hijack.

Private data and permissions

A few details that taught me how much "permissions" hides:

  • Interview notes and hidden hints are never in the shared document. The candidate is an editor and could rewrite anything inside it. Secrets live only behind role-checked REST routes, and a test records every frame a candidate's socket receives and asserts that no secret appears.
  • Private rooms are end-to-end encrypted. A 256-bit AES-GCM key is generated in the browser and kept in the URL fragment; the server stores and relays ciphertext only.
  • Spend is bounded in code. Quota is checked and reserved in one transaction under a per-user advisory lock, so two parallel requests at quota minus one produce one success and one rejection.

Bugs that taught me things

Real ones from the project's log:

  • Viewers sat on "Saving…" forever. The store stamped a schema version into the document on creation, an update the server rightly rejects from viewers. Fix: stamp it at the first local edit.
  • A removed member could still open the board offline from IndexedDB. Fix: revocation now wipes the local copy, not just the live socket.
  • Analytics would have leaked an encryption key. Page-analytics recorded full URLs including the fragment, which is where a private board's key lives. Fix: a hook strips fragments from every event, with a test.
  • A candidate who joined via share link saw nothing. Found by a browser test, since candidates normally join by link.

Honest limits

I'll repeat what the case study says, because it matters:

  • It is not deployed. It runs locally against a dev Supabase project, so there's no live demo. Load numbers come from one Mac and haven't been re-measured on a staging host.
  • The AI review eval has never been run against a real API key. It's written (15 fixture boards, 16 planted flaws, a 12/15 pass bar), but the prompt's catch rate is unmeasured.
  • Payments are tested with a scripted provider, not yet in real test mode.
  • Private boards can't rotate keys. A removed member stops syncing but may keep the key and old content.
  • The design check only understands palette shapes. Boards drawn with plain rectangles get few findings.

What I'd tell someone building something similar

  1. Decide what you'll promise, then write a test that tries to break each promise.
  2. Put cheap deterministic checks in front of expensive AI ones.
  3. Treat the AI as an untrusted component with a budget.
  4. Write down the limits while you still remember them.

Twelve questions to ask of any system-design diagram

Use these on your own diagrams, or on a friend's. They're the sort of thing the deterministic rules in Whiteboard.ai check automatically, and every one can also be asked by a person.

  1. Where's the single point of failure? What happens if each box goes down?
  2. Where does data live, and who owns it? One writer, or many?
  3. What's synchronous and what's asynchronous? Are there synchronous call cycles?
  4. What happens at 10x the load? Which box saturates first?
  5. What happens when a downstream service is slow, not down? (Slow is often worse than down.)
  6. Is a client talking directly to a database? If so, where are the access rules enforced?
  7. Do queues have a dead-letter path for messages that keep failing?
  8. Where are the retries, and are they idempotent? What happens if a message is delivered twice?
  9. How do you know it's healthy? What metrics and alerts exist?
  10. What's cached, and how does stale data get invalidated?
  11. How does it deploy and roll back?
  12. What's the data model's biggest assumption that might not hold?

Print this list. Asking them out loud, even to yourself, is most of the skill.

How to practise with a partner

A simple 45-minute format:

Minutes Activity
0–5 Partner reads the prompt ("design a URL shortener"). You ask clarifying questions.
5–10 State requirements and rough numbers (users, reads vs writes).
10–25 Draw the design. Narrate every box.
25–40 Partner pokes at failure modes using the twelve questions.
40–45 Both note what to study.

Swap roles next time. Being the interviewer teaches as much as being the candidate.

A worked example

Prompt: a URL shortener.

  • Core: a write path (create short code) and a read path (redirect).
  • Data: a table mapping code → URL.
  • Scale thought: reads vastly outnumber writes, so cache hot codes.
  • Failure thought: if the cache is down, reads fall back to the database. Can the database cope? If not, add a rate limit.
  • A question to ask yourself: how do you generate codes without collisions? (Counter-based, random with retry, or pre-generated pool, each with trade-offs.)

Even this tiny walkthrough uses five of the twelve questions.

Why drawing failure arrows matters

Diagrams of the happy path are easy and nearly useless. The valuable part is what happens when something breaks. A good habit: use a second colour (red) for failure paths, and don't consider the diagram finished until every important box has a red arrow out of it.

What an AI reviewer can and can't do

A tool can reliably catch pattern problems: a database with no replica, a queue with no dead-letter path. It can't know your product's real requirements, your team's skills or your budget. Treat automated feedback as a second pair of eyes that needs your judgement, not as a verdict.

What's your go-to first question when you start a system design? And if you've built real-time sync before, what did you wish you'd known?

title: How index keys affect inputs: compare DOM, row state, and parent state
description:
When the first row is removed from a React list, do input values stay with the remaining rows? With index keys, the result depended on who owned the value.

An uncontrolled input, whose value lived in the DOM, and an input backed by row-local state displayed another row's value. Inputs receiving values from parent state displayed the correct values, but their DOM nodes were still reassigned to different rows.

Narrow the reproduction from existing code

The personal project's schedule creation screen passes the idx from rows.map as each Card key. It removes rows with array filtering and inserts duplicates by combining array slices.

However, its title input is controlled through value={row.title}. The code alone does not show whether input values ever became mixed up in production. The inspected commit was 770de5f. Related history and design material were also checked before extracting row deletion and value ownership into a separate experiment. The application was neither modified nor used to submit data.

Removing the first row shifts index-based identities

The fixture starts with 3 rows: A, B, and C. B is edited to edited-B, then A is removed. Simply reversing the order after editing B would leave B in the middle of a 3-row list, so deletion makes the identity change visible here.

import React, { useState } from 'react';

const initialRows = [
  { id: 'A', title: 'Alpha' },
  { id: 'B', title: 'Beta' },
  { id: 'C', title: 'Gamma' },
];
function Row({ row, mode, update }) {
  const [localTitle, setLocalTitle] = useState(row.title);
  const props = mode === 'uncontrolled'
    ? { defaultValue: row.title }
    : mode === 'local'
      ? { value: localTitle, onChange: event => setLocalTitle(event.target.value) }
      : { value: row.title, onChange: event => update(row.id, event.target.value) };
  return <label data-row={row.id}>{row.id}<input {...props} /></label>;
}
export function KeyExperiment({ keyMode, mode }) {
  const [rows, setRows] = useState(initialRows);
  function update(id, title) {
    setRows(previous => previous.map(row => row.id === id ? { ...row, title } : row));
  }
  return <section>
    <button id="remove-first" onClick={() => setRows(previous => previous.slice(1))}>Remove first</button>
    {rows.map((row, index) => (
      <Row key={keyMode === 'index' ? index : row.id} row={row} mode={mode} update={update} />
    ))}
  </section>;
}

mode is uncontrolled, local, or parent; keyMode is index or id. The local version initializes each row with useState(row.title). The parent version updates the array by row ID.

Before deletion, a WeakMap records each input's DOM node and row ID. After deletion, the test compares values and node origins. This is fixture instrumentation, not access to React's internal keys.

Value owner Key Values displayed for B / C after deletion Original rows of the nodes used for B / C
DOM index Alpha / edited-B A / B
DOM id edited-B / Gamma B / C
Row state index Alpha / edited-B A / B
Row state id edited-B / Gamma B / C
Parent state index edited-B / Gamma A / B
Parent state id edited-B / Gamma B / C

With index keys, B gets key 0 and C gets key 1 after deletion. Those keys previously corresponded to A and B. defaultValue and a row's initial state are not reapplied from scratch for every new row occupying that position.

With ID keys, B remains key B even after moving. Its edited value and DOM node stayed with that row. React's explanation of list keys describes their role in matching items through deletion, insertion, and reordering.

Controlled values do not settle the identity question

In the parent-state version, React passed the new row.title to each input, so the displayed values were correct. The 6 cases therefore do not support a claim that index keys always produce incorrect displayed values.

The WeakMap still identified the reused nodes as coming from A / B. Correct values alone do not prove that row, component, and DOM identities were preserved. The experiment did not measure focus, IME composition, or DatePicker internal state. It therefore does not establish failures in those parts of the real application either.

For a design that adds and removes rows, storing a row ID in the data and keeping it as the key for the row's lifetime expresses the intended identity. Unsaved rows can receive an ID when created, and a duplicate treated as a separate row can receive a new ID. Generating IDs during every render would not provide stable matching. This is a proposed change for the existing screen, not an applied fix.

The tests ran on September 11, 2026, with React and React DOM 19.3.0, Node.js 24.15.0, esbuild 0.28.2, macOS arm64, and Headless Chrome 152. They used a production build without Strict Mode or React Compiler. The minimal code and results for the 6 conditions track displayed values and DOM nodes separately.

title: Redesigning a Halloween guide for people who need a costume tonight
description:
This post was written with AI assistance.

When someone searches for a last-minute Halloween costume, they probably have a practical question: “What can I put together with the clothes and supplies I can get today?”

That question shaped the recent redesign of Halloween Prep, a small static site with Halloween guides. The goal was to make the costume page easier to scan, especially on a phone.

Start with a choice

The last-minute costume guide begins with three outfit ideas: a black cat, a closet pirate, and a silent-film-inspired look.

Each option shows the base clothes and the finishing detail up front. Readers can jump directly to the materials and steps instead of reading through every idea first.

Make the details useful

Each guide has a checklist, numbered steps, and substitutions. The page also acknowledges that “last minute” doesn’t have to mean using only what’s already at home: a headband, cardstock, or tape might be available at a nearby craft, discount, or dollar store. Availability varies by location.

The checklists can be copied or printed, and the layout was adjusted for smaller screens. The costume images are AI-generated illustrations, not photographs of completed outfits. The instructions are editorial suggestions and haven’t yet been hands-on tested.

Keep the page lightweight

The site is built as a static website with JavaScript, HTML, and CSS. The redesign keeps the existing costume-page URL and uses in-page links so readers can move quickly between the overview and each outfit.

There’s still room to improve: real photos and hands-on testing would make the guides more useful. But this iteration gave the page a clearer job—helping someone choose a workable idea and find the next step.

I’d welcome feedback on the mobile layout and how clearly the guide presents each option.

title: Living the design-to-code dream
description:
This flow should sound familiar to any frontend developer: a designer makes a change in Figma, and now we need to propagate it to our code. By nature, that process involves an entire handoff from UX to engineering. As a company matures, it quickly realizes this flow will not scale. When those changes are not aligned in the code right away, we get drift. The UX team ends up sketching UI with updated assets while production screens still show up with old colors, spacing, and typography.

Scaling this process means automating it, and today's design tools do not make that easy out of the box. Off-the-shelf integrations make assumptions about repository structure, token formats, and release workflows that rarely match an existing organizational stack. Most teams end up building a custom bridge of their own.

This note walks through one approach that puts the ideas from design tools, tokens, and implementation into practice. The goal is to satisfy both sides of the handoff: designers stay focused on design without having to learn code, version control, or release mechanics, while engineers still get a reviewable diff, an approval gate, and a versioned package. We will be focusing on tokens here, though the same pattern applies to icons.

The shape of the bridge

There's more than one way to build this bridge. The source of truth for design tokens can sit either in Figma or in Git. With Git as the source, tokens are authored in the repository and Figma consumes them, just like our codebase does. That keeps the repository authoritative, but designers end up editing tokens somewhere other than the canvas. Our example goes the other way and makes Figma the source of truth, because it is friendlier to designers, who keep working in the tool they already know.

With Figma in the driver's seat, the pipeline splits into two halves: a Figma plugin that turns canvas edits into a pull request, and a CI workflow that turns the merged pull request into a versioned package. The repository tracks only a single raw JSON snapshot of the tokens, while all code artifacts are generated on release.

Designer: Figma plugin → Review: Pull request → Automation: CI workflow → Release: Versioned package

The designer publishes from Figma, engineers approve the PR, and the pipeline generates code and releases a version.

Inside the plugin

Our workflow starts when a designer has changes they want to publish. Opening our custom-built Figma plugin shows them their pending changes alongside a simple screen to publish their work.

"Changes" lists what differs from the last release. "Publish" says what kind of release this is and takes an optional note for engineers.

Behind the scenes, the plugin compares the current Figma variables with the token file on main. It does more than list what differs. It tells the designer, in plain language, what kind of release this is:

  • Updated existing values (patch): colors, sizes, or other values changed.
  • Added new tokens (minor): new tokens that didn't exist before.
  • Removed or renamed tokens (major): tokens were deleted or their names changed, which breaks any app that uses them.

The designer adds a note for engineers and presses "Publish". The plugin then commits the snapshot to a branch and opens a pull request, using the note as its description. After publishing, the designer sees where the request stands.

A removed token is called out as a breaking change before anything is sent. After publishing, the designer sees what happens next.

Handling incremental changes

Figma holds a single live state, so two designers never conflict inside it. Git is where conflicts appear, because every publish is a snapshot of that state taken at a different moment, and a newer snapshot already contains everything an older one did.

So the plugin never opens a second pull request. Each publish either opens one or, if one is already open, updates it with the latest snapshot. Two designers publishing on the same afternoon end up in the same pull request, and its diff always compares main with the current state of Figma.

Versioning our package

After a merge, the pipeline compares the token file with the copy at the latest git tag and derives the major, minor, or patch bump from those same rules. When a release mixes them, the highest one wins. It then reads the latest tag, applies the bump, publishes the package, and pushes the next tag.

Because those rules follow the token names applications depend on, a drastic color change is still a patch. How much a change matters visually belongs in the designer's note and in review, while the version number reflects the contract.

What's in the box?

From the single JSON snapshot, the pipeline generates everything applications need, in the formats each implementation prefers:

  • SCSS variables for stylesheets that rely on compile-time values.
  • TypeScript constants for code that needs tokens in JavaScript, exposed in whichever shape suits the consumer.

The pipeline generates CSS custom properties as well, though the compiled options are the better choice. With them, a removed or renamed token breaks the build of any application still using it, which is exactly what a major bump promises. A CSS custom property that no longer exists fails silently at runtime, so the handshake between design and code only sticks when the compiler is in on it. Custom properties still earn their place for runtime theming, such as switching between light and dark modes without recompiling.

Dream come true

With that, we have ourselves a fully automated workflow, taking a change on the canvas all the way to a versioned package. Ours is just one approach among many, of course. The real takeaway is that automating the handoff is key, and doing it well means separating the designer experience from the developer experience. Once we build the bridge that ties them together, the drift between canvas and production disappears.

title: Exorcist: I made the ghosts of legacy Java code explain themselves (and tried to stop them lying)
description:
This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge: Week 4: Ghost in the Machine.

What I Built

Every legacy codebase is haunted. You open a 25-year-old class, there's a catch (Exception e) that returns null, and the person who could explain why left the project in 2004.

Exorcist is a terminal app that summons them back. It reads a Git repository, works out who really wrote each Java class, and lets the ghost of its main author explain the class in first person, confess its sins line by line, and propose a refactoring as a diff. The model is open-weight and runs locally through Ollama, so the code never leaves your machine.

     .-.
    (o o)   E X O R C I S T
    | O \   summon the ghosts of legacy Java code
     \   \  model: qwen2.5-coder:7b, running locally via Ollama
      `~~~'
Command What happens
summon <repo> Lists every Java class with its ghost (the author with the most commits), birth and death dates
possess <Class> The ghost introduces itself from real Git history and explains the class, citing lines
confess The ghost confesses the class's code smells, worst first, each with its lines
exorcise The ghost rewrites its worst sin; you get a unified diff, never a modified file
epitaph An ASCII tombstone with a one-line epitaph

My take on the theme: the "ghost in the machine" is the people inside old code. Git remembers them perfectly (every commit, every date, every line they last touched) and nobody ever asks them anything. Exorcist gives them a voice, and makes them tell the truth.

Demo

I ran it on JUnit 4: 2,521 commits since December 2000. Reading the whole history takes under five seconds:

exorcist:> summon ../junit4
450 Java spirits rest in junit4, longest dead first.

Class                                Spirit      Born        Died        Commits
-----------------------------------  ----------  ----------  ----------  -------
Stub                                 David Saff  2007-09-04  2007-12-07        2
RepeatedTest                         David Saff  2000-12-03  2012-10-04        8
TestSetup                            David Saff  2000-12-03  2012-10-04        6
ComparisonFailure (junit.framework)  egamma      2002-06-22  2012-10-04       14
JUnit4TestAdapterCache               David Saff  2006-02-15  2012-10-04       10

Then I possessed junit.runner.BaseTestRunner: 326 lines, 30 commits, 10 catch blocks. Its ghost is the author with the most commits on the file:

exorcist:> possess junit.runner.BaseTestRunner
Possessing junit.runner.BaseTestRunner (src/main/java/junit/runner/BaseTestRunner.java)
Spirit: egamma | born 2000-12-03 | died 2016-10-15 | 30 commits | 326 lines
The air grows cold... (qwen2.5-coder:7b)

I am egamma, the author with the most commits on this file, having first touched it
on Sunday, December 3, 2000, and last making changes on Sunday, October 24, 2004.
This class, `BaseTestRunner`, is the backbone of JUnit's test runner infrastructure
[...] The `getTest` (line 91) method is a crucial template method [...]

[10 line citations, all inside the file]

That last line is not the model talking. It's Exorcist checking the answer (more on that below). Now the confession:

exorcist[BaseTestRunner]:> confess

1. (lines 95-142) The `getTest()` method is a long method, spanning 48 lines. [...]
2. (lines 110-113) The broad catch block that catches `Exception` (line 110) hides
   what can really go wrong. [...]
3. (lines 237-238) The empty catch block for `IOException` (line 237) and
   `SecurityException` (line 238) is a sin. It silently swallows exceptions [...]
4. (line 166) The use of `System.out.println()` (line 166) instead of a logger is a sin.
5. (lines 293-295) The broad catch block that catches `Exception` (line 293) [...]
6. (lines 117-121) The broad catch block that catches `Exception` (line 117) [...]

I must have been tired.

[12 line citations, all inside the file]

I checked every one against the source. All six are real, on the right lines. Number 5 is my favourite, and it has been in JUnit since 2000:

} catch (Exception IOException) {
    return stack; // return the stack unfiltered
}

An Exception, caught in a variable named IOException.

And the tombstone:

        ________________________________
      .'                                '.
     /                                    \
    |              R . I . P               |
    |                                      |
    |            BaseTestRunner            |
    |             junit.runner             |
    |                                      |
    |              haunted by              |
    |                egamma                |
    |                                      |
    |      2000-12-03  -  2016-10-15       |
    |                                      |
    |   "BaseTestRunner: The guardian of   |
    |         tests, old and new."         |
    |                                      |
    |       30 commits | 10 mourners       |
~~~~|______________________________________|~~~~

Code

MathFe / exorcist

Hacktoberfest 2026 final-week project: summon the ghosts of legacy Java code. A Spring Shell CLI where the Git author of each class explains it, confesses its code smells and proposes refactorings, powered by a local LLM via Ollama.

Exorcist

Summon the ghosts of legacy Java code.

Exorcist is a terminal app that reads a Git repository, finds who wrote each Java class, and lets the ghost of its main author explain the class in first person, confess its sins and propose a refactoring Everything runs locally: the "ghost" is an open-weight model served by Ollama, so your code never leaves your machine.

     .-.
    (o o)   E X O R C I S T
    | O \   summon the ghosts of legacy Java code
     \   \  model: qwen2.5-coder:7b, running locally via Ollama
      `~~~'

The tone is theatrical, but the facts are not. Every claim the ghost makes must cite line numbers, its life story comes only from real commits, and refactorings are shown as a diff. Exorcist never writes to your files.

Requirements

  • JDK 21 or newer

  • Ollama running locally, with a model pulled. The default is qwen2.5-coder:7b…

View on GitHub

Java 21, Spring Boot, Spring Shell, Spring AI (Ollama), JGit and JavaParser. 98 tests, none of which need a model or a network.

How I Built It

The hard part was not the ghost voice. That's one paragraph of system prompt. The hard part was that a 7B model will happily lie, and a tool that explains legacy code with confident lies is worse than no tool. So most of Exorcist is about handing the model facts and checking what comes back.

1. The ghosts come from Git, not from the model. One walk over the history (merges skipped, renames followed) finds who touched each file. Over 25 years people change names and e-mails: JUnit has dsaff <dsaff> and David Saff <saff@google.com>, who only meet through a third identity, dsaff <david@saff.net>. A small union-find merges them, but never through shared placeholder addresses like noreply@github.com, which would merge strangers. git blame tells the ghost which lines other hands wrote last.

2. No line number, no claim. The source goes to the model with line numbers, and every rule in the prompt points back at them. Then every answer is checked: Exorcist counts the citations, flags lines that don't exist and numbered items that cite nothing. That's the [12 line citations, all inside the file] line, in green when it's clean and yellow when it isn't.

3. Sins are found before they're confessed. JavaParser scans the class for empty or broad catch blocks, printStackTrace(), System.out, deep nesting, long methods, public mutable fields, Vector/Hashtable, @Deprecated code and TODOs, each with exact lines. The model gets them as evidence to judge, not as a script to read.

4. The model writes code. Exorcist writes the diff. exorcise doesn't ask the model for a patch, because small models produce broken ones. It picks a sin the static scan confirms, widens it to the smallest complete code that fixes it (the whole try statement, the statement, the method), and asks for REPLACE LINES a-b plus a code block. Exorcist splices it in, fixes the indentation the model forgot, checks that the file still parses, and computes the diff with JGit. Nothing is ever written to disk.

5. Prompts fit a small model's memory. Long files are cut to a window around the lines that matter, and the model is told exactly what it can't see.

Where the ghosts still lie

It would be odd to write about honesty and then hide the failures, so here they are, all from my own test runs.

  • The first confess run invented an IOException in two items (with the right line numbers, wrong content) and repeated one sin twice. Citations keep claims anchored and checkable. They don't make them true.
  • The first exorcise produced a diff that doesn't compile. It deleted the return null after a failure and caught exceptions the try body can never throw. Exorcist only checks that the result parses, and that's the next thing I want to fix: compiling the spliced file against the project's classpath.
  • gemma3:4b was worse. It called a three-line method "bloated", rewrote a whole method into a 13-line slot (Exorcist did catch that one: "the file no longer parses"), and, while blaming lines on other contributors, called a real JUnit maintainer "not a very good programmer". The authors are real people, so the prompt now has a fifth rule: judge the code, never the people. On the rerun, it criticized commits, not their authors.

So treat Exorcist the way you'd treat a séance: entertaining, sometimes eerily accurate, and never something you act on without checking. Every claim comes with the lines you need to check it.

I built it with Claude Code as a pair programmer. Writing the tests found four real bugs in the code we had written together, including one where, with a small prompt window, the model could be asked to rewrite lines it was never shown.

Why open matters here

Your code never leaves your laptop. The code people most need to understand is legacy code inside companies: banks, insurers, government. It's exactly the code you're not allowed to paste into a hosted chatbot. With Ollama and an open-weight model, Exorcist sends the source of your proprietary 2003 billing class nowhere. No API key, no account, no terms of service.

It works with the lights off. Once the model is pulled, Exorcist needs no network at all. I ran every demo above with the repository and the model on the same machine.

It costs nothing per question. A single possess prompt carries a full class, its outline and its Git history: several thousand tokens. Exploring a 450-class codebase that way on a paid API adds up fast. Locally it's just electricity, so you can ask the ghost again, and again.

You choose the brain. Swapping models is one environment variable (EXORCIST_MODEL=gemma3:4b), which is how I found out that model size matters more than I expected for keeping a ghost honest. With a closed API I couldn't have compared them on the same prompts and the same machine in an evening.

Old code deserves to be remembered by the people who wrote it. It shouldn't have to be shipped off to someone else's server for that to happen.

Happy Halloween, and feliz Día de los Muertos. 🕯️

title: How to make Claude Code build new pages that match your existing app
description:
Ask Claude Code to "add a pricing page" to a project that already has ten pages, and you often get a beautiful page that belongs to a different website. New font pairing, a fresh accent color, a hand-rolled button, maybe its own <style> block. On a new project that's great. In an old project it's a clash you now have to undo by hand.

I hit this enough times across my own side projects (a resume builder and a small Next.js app for checking product ideas) that I stopped fixing pages after the fact and started fixing the instructions instead. This post is the loop I use now, with the prompts and grep commands. Nothing here needs a special tool — it's a SKILL.md file plus a habit.

Why it happens

Most frontend/design skills are written to make output distinctive. The official frontend-design skill in anthropics/skills, for example, pushes for bold, non-generic choices. That's the right goal when there is no existing design. But the model reads the skill, not your codebase, so "be distinctive" wins over "look like the page next door".

The fix is to reverse the order: read the project first, write a short summary of its style, build only from what already exists, then check.

Step 1: Give the agent a design source of truth (if you have one)

In my resume builder repo, the root AGENTS.md has a short rule:

Before changing the visual or interaction layer of `resume-tailor/`,
read `resume-tailor/docs/design-system.md` first. Colors, type scale,
radius, buttons, cards, forms, motion, i18n copy and page skeletons
each have exactly one correct way to write them there.

The design doc itself was not written as an ideal. It was written by measuring the existing code: which tokens are defined in globals.css, how often each className appears, which components are actually imported. That surfaced uncomfortable facts — at one point the codebase had 49 different hand-written button styles while the shared components/ui/button.tsx was imported zero times.

A few things that made the doc genuinely useful for an agent, not just for humans:

  • List the theme-aware class names explicitly. e.g. bg-background, text-foreground, bg-card, bg-muted, text-muted-foreground, border-border. "Use tokens" is vague; a list of allowed names isn't.
  • Write down the exceptions and why. Hard-coded palette classes are allowed in exactly three cases (dark sections, data signal colors, the rendered resume paper). Everything else goes through tokens. After one cleanup pass, hard-coded colors went from roughly 2,370 occurrences to 115, all of them in those exception buckets.
  • Record the traps. In that project rounded-xl and rounded-2xl both resolve to 16px because --radius is recalculated, and a gradient-text class silently disappears if you wrap the text in an extra <span>. Those are exactly the details a model gets wrong.

If you don't have a design doc, don't write one first. Step 2 works without it.

Step 2: Make the agent survey before it writes

This is the core of the skill I wrote, match-existing-style. The first section is a reading list, and it says "do not skip":

## 1. Survey before you design (do not skip)

1. Design rules — any DESIGN.md, design-system.md, docs/design*,
   or a design section in AGENTS.md / CLAUDE.md / README.
   If one exists, it wins over everything below.
2. Tokens — CSS variables (:root, @theme), tailwind.config.*,
   theme files. Note the token NAMES, not just values.
3. Component kit — components/ui/* or similar. Which primitives
   exist (Button, Card, Input, Badge, Dialog…) and how they're imported.
4. Two sibling pages — the existing pages closest to what you are
   building. Note container width, section spacing, heading sizes,
   card style, how the hero is built.
5. Copy voice — languages, i18n helper, sentence vs title case.

"Two sibling pages" is the part that does the heavy lifting when there's no documentation. Your existing pages are the design system; the agent just has to open them.

Step 3: Force a style fingerprint before any code

Next, the skill asks for 8–12 lines of summary before touching a file:

## 2. Write a style fingerprint (keep it short)

- Colors: token names for background / surface / text / muted /
  border / primary action.
- Type: font families in use (do not add new ones), heading sizes
  on sibling pages, body size.
- Shape: radius per element type, shadow style, border usage.
- Spacing rhythm: page container, section gaps, card padding.
- Components: which primitives you'll reuse for each part of the page.
- Patterns to copy: one concrete snippet from a sibling page to mirror.
- Copy: language handling and tone.

Two reasons this matters. First, writing it down commits the model to specific token names before it starts generating JSX, which is when drift happens. Second, you can read 10 lines and catch a wrong assumption in seconds, which is far cheaper than reviewing a 400-line page.

Step 4: Build by reuse, with hard "no"s 

## 3. Build by reuse

- Reuse before you write. Use the project's Button/Card/Input.
- Tokens, not values. No raw hex/rgb or arbitrary palette classes
  unless sibling pages do the same thing for the same purpose.
- No new fonts, no new accent colors, no new radius scale,
  no new shadow style.
- Match the page skeleton of the nearest sibling.
- Missing piece? Build it in the project's idiom and say so.
  Do not pull in a new UI library.

The "say so" line is important. When the page genuinely needs something that doesn't exist yet, you want to hear about it in the summary, not discover a new dependency in package.json later.

Step 5: Self-check with grep, not vibes

The last step is mechanical. Run these against the files the agent created:

# raw colors
grep -nE '#[0-9a-fA-F]{3,8}\b|rgb\(|hsl\(' app/new-page/page.tsx

# raw palette classes the sibling pages don't use
grep -nE '\b(bg|text|border)-(slate|gray|zinc|indigo|blue)-[0-9]+' app/new-page/page.tsx

# hand-made buttons instead of the project's Button
grep -n '<button' app/new-page/page.tsx

# new font imports
grep -n 'next/font' app/new-page/page.tsx

Then, if you can render it, screenshot the new page next to a sibling page. A side-by-side picture catches things no grep will: a different hero height, a missing site header, a card that's slightly too round.

Does it actually make a difference?

I ran a small test: same project, same prompt, two subagents in separate git worktrees. One followed the official frontend-design skill, the other followed match-existing-style. Each built the same new page.

Round 1 was the resume builder, which has a design doc. Round 2 was the idea-checking app, which has no design docs at all — only globals.css tokens and components/ui.

Generic design skill match-existing-style
Hard-coded hex colors (round 1 / round 2) 17 / 30 0 / 0
New fonts added 2 / 2 0 / 0
Project token classes used 0 / 0 19 / 34
Own <style> block 1 / 1 0 / 0

In round 2 the generic-skill page also dropped the site's header (logo, language switch, sign-in) entirely, and came in at 499 lines versus 247.

To be fair to the official skill: its page was well made. It was just aiming at a different goal. And this is one run per project, two projects — a small sample. But the direction held even without a design doc, which was the case I was most unsure about.

The short version

If you only take one thing from this, paste something like this before your next UI request:

Before writing any code: read our design rules (if any), our CSS
tokens, components/ui, and the two existing pages most similar to
what I'm asking for. Write a 10-line style fingerprint (token names,
fonts, radius, spacing, components to reuse, one snippet to mirror).
Then build using only those. No new fonts, colors, or button styles.
When done, grep your new files for hex colors, raw palette classes
and <button>, and list every deviation from the existing style.

I'm packaging the full version as a Claude Code skill — the survey/fingerprint/reuse/check loop plus recipes for the pages people add most (forms, settings, data tables, pricing, empty states). It's in early access here if you want it: Match Style.

title: A CSS bug that wasn't CSS
description:
Spent an afternoon on a layout bug that turned out to be a data issue. One list item had an empty string where the backend expected null, and the UI rendered a zero-height element that shifted everything by four pixels.

title: Building Cursor-style inline AI editing in React with Anky UI
description:
A user wants a shorter paragraph. Moving that paragraph into a chat window adds a second workflow: copy the text, switch context, explain the task, copy the answer, paste it back, then remove the conversational preamble.

An inline editor can keep the task in one place: select, rewrite, compare, accept. Anky UI supplies the interaction primitives for that flow. This article walks through how to connect them without giving the model direct ownership of your document.

Repository: https://github.com/ErAnkushPatil/anky-ui

Video walkthrough: https://x.com/ErAnkushP/status/2115629939106230425

Separate the suggestion from the saved text

Treat the model’s response as a proposal. Keep the original text, the in-progress rewrite, and the committed document distinct. That lets a user reject a change and makes network failure recoverable.

Start with the diff primitive:

"use client";

import { useState } from "react";
import { InlineDiff } from "@erankushpatil/anky-ui";

export function ReviewEdit() {
  const [text, setText] = useState("Our team shipped the new onboarding flow this quarter.");
  const [proposal, setProposal] = useState<string | null>(null);

  return (
    <section>
      <p>{text}</p>
      <button onClick={() => setProposal("We shipped a new onboarding flow.")}>
        Preview an example edit
      </button>
      {proposal !== null && (
        <InlineDiff
          originalText={text}
          modifiedText={proposal}
          onAccept={() => {
            setText(proposal);
            setProposal(null);
          }}
          onReject={() => setProposal(null)}
        />
      )}
    </section>
  );
}

This example deliberately uses a fixed proposal so the review and commit behavior can be tried without a backend. The application updates its document only in onAccept. Rendering a diff alone does not replace selected DOM text.

Anchor actions to the selection

SelectionPalette uses floating-ui to position actions next to highlighted text. Its callback gives your application the prompt and selected text:

<SelectionPalette
  containerRef={editorRef}
  actions={[
    { label: "Shorten", prompt: "Make this shorter. Return only the revised text." },
    { label: "Fix grammar", prompt: "Fix grammar. Return only the revised text." },
  ]}
  onSelectPrompt={(prompt, selectedText) => {
    void requestRewrite(prompt, selectedText);
  }}
/>

Here editorRef and requestRewrite belong to your application. Scope the palette to the editor so selecting navigation text elsewhere does not open an editing action. Decide what should happen if the document changes while the request is running; a stale range should not overwrite newer user edits.

Stream into state with a rollback boundary

The state hook captures a snapshot before a stream begins. On failure or abort, it can return to that snapshot.

Use useOptimisticAIState to track the streamed proposal. Its mutateWithStream(source, transformFn) API accepts a response or stream factory and folds chunks into state. Pass the supplied abort signal to your fetch request. Initialize each proposal with the selected original text and an empty modified value, then append incoming chunks to that proposal. Connect currentState and isStreaming to InlineDiff. The application still owns applying accepted text to the document.

Your server route calls the model and returns a UTF-8 text stream or text SSE. Keep provider credentials on the server, and handle unsuccessful HTTP responses before treating their bodies as rewrite text. Provider helpers also decode supported OpenAI, Anthropic, and Vercel AI SDK formats into text tokens.

Keep keyboard controls predictable

The diff supports Cmd/Ctrl+Enter to accept and Escape to reject. Accept is disabled during streaming. GhostInput uses Tab or right arrow at the end of the textarea to accept a continuation, while Escape clears it.

Test these controls alongside the rest of your editor. A shortcut that works in isolation may conflict with a parent dialog, an input method, or an editor command. Rich-text adapters are provided, but the repository explicitly recommends checking them against your editor version.

Try the primitives 

npm i @erankushpatil/anky-ui

For source ownership:

npx anky-ui add selection-palette

The repository also includes a mock-stream playground:

git clone https://github.com/ErAnkushPatil/anky-ui.git
cd anky-ui
pnpm install
pnpm dev:demo

Anky UI supports React 18/19 and Next.js App Router Client Components. Tailwind presets are optional. Start with the included demo, then test cancellation, rapid successive rewrites, selection changes, and accepting an edit after the document has changed.

Disclosure: I’m the author of Anky UI. This article was prepared with ChatGPT using the repository documentation. The code is an illustrative integration example.

title: One small win from caching responses
description:
Added a five-second cache to one expensive endpoint; median latency dropped by more than half. Not a deep insight: it was slow, we cached it, it got faster.

The interesting part was the failure mode. Stale data looked fine in tests and confused everyone in production once an hour. We now return the cache age in a header, which costs nothing and saved a lot of confused debugging.
