title: Three Errors You Actually Hit Connecting Actions to GCP
description:
Conclusion

Workload Identity Federation failures come from the configuration living in three layers. The error text does not tell you which one.

  • GitHub Actions side — does the job have id-token: write?
  • Pool side — does attribute_condition permit the calling repository?
  • Service account side — is the roles/iam.workloadIdentityUser binding still there?

Any of the three missing produces similar text. Without deciding the order of investigation up front you end up poking at permissions at random. Below are the three errors we actually hit, in the order you hit them.

Symptom

1. Unable to acquire impersonation credentials

The first one you meet. The authentication step itself does not pass. There are three candidate causes, and the higher the layer, the cheaper it is to check.

  • The job has no permissions with id-token: write. Entirely on GitHub's side, so look here first
  • You are running from a different repository. The pool's attribute_condition limits the caller via assertion.repository, so forks and other repositories are rejected
  • The roles/iam.workloadIdentityUser binding on the service account was lost to drift. Restore with terraform apply

The third is the awkward one. The code is correct and it still does not work, and it happens unrelated to any recent change. Someone touching IAM by hand puts Terraform's state and the cloud out of sync, and it surfaces in this shape.

2. Permission 'iam.serviceAccounts.getAccessToken' denied

Here impersonation got as far as the entrance and the target service account refused. It looks like a missing grant; in practice it is usually the wrong target.

  • The service account email is wrong. Where plan and deploy accounts are separate, their permission scopes are separate too. Calling the deploy target with plan credentials is refused, correctly
  • The environment name does not match. If Terraform's env_name and the GitHub Environment the workflow references diverge, you end up pointed at the wrong service account

The error only says "no permission". It does not say "wrong target", so start by confirming the email is the one you meant.

3. Provider or pool not found

The pool or provider simply does not exist. Check:

gcloud iam workload-identity-pools providers describe <provider-id> \
  --location=global \
  --workload-identity-pool=<pool-id> \
  --project=<project-id>

If it is absent, terraform apply has not been run. Apply in that environment's directory.

Cause

All three share a root: the chain of trust is stored in three separate places.

GitHub issues an OIDC token per job. The pool receives it and decides, through attribute_condition, which repositories it accepts. What passes becomes a principal, and if that principal appears in the service account's IAM policy, impersonation succeeds.

Those three are managed in different places: the workflow YAML, the Terraform pool definition, and the service account IAM policy. Break any one and the chain breaks, but the break is only ever observable as an authentication error.

The fix

Reading the service account IAM policy directly is the fastest way to see the real state.

gcloud iam service-accounts get-iam-policy \
  <sa-name>@<project-id>.iam.gserviceaccount.com \
  --project=<project-id>

The expected state has a principalSet of this shape in members:

principalSet://iam.googleapis.com/projects/<num>/locations/global/workloadIdentityPools/<pool-id>/attribute.repository/<owner>/<repo>

If the calling repository is not there, no amount of fixing the workflow will help. If it is there, the lower two layers are alive and you go and look at permissions on the GitHub side.

You can cut it off immediately

Because there is no JSON key in the setup, there is nothing to rotate. Instead you can stop impersonation from a repository directly.

gcloud iam service-accounts remove-iam-policy-binding \
  <sa-name>@<project-id>.iam.gserviceaccount.com \
  --role=roles/iam.workloadIdentityUser \
  --member='principalSet://iam.googleapis.com/projects/<num>/locations/global/workloadIdentityPools/<pool-id>/attribute.repository/<owner>/<repo>'

The moment the binding is removed, authentication from that repository stops. There is no key expiry to wait for.

But always update Terraform and open a PR afterwards. Leaving a hand-edited IAM policy drifts the configuration, and the binding you removed reappears the next time someone applies. Pair the stopgap with the code change.

And that drift, surfacing much later, is the first error in this article. A neglected emergency cut-off and an unexplained authentication failure are the same thing from two sides.

Making it less likely to recur

The three layers are not going away. What you can change is fixing the order in which you check them.

Cheapest first: permissions on the GitHub side, then get-iam-policy on the service account, then confirming the pool and provider exist. Following that order, the first is just opening a YAML file and the second is one command — enough to narrow down which of the three layers is broken.

For another case where the error text does not lead to the cause, see terraform's enabled = false cannot tear down an environment, where the error appears in a module other than the one at fault.

Originally published at tech.rebounder.jp.

title: I'm Building My Own PHP Platform, and I've Been Learning a Lot Along the Way
description:
I'm Building My Own PHP Platform, and I've Been Learning a Lot Along the Way

I'm a self-taught developer, and for some time now, I've been working on a project called Domain System.

It started with an idea: what if I could build my own PHP platform, where the main system and its plugins had their own responsibilities and didn't depend too much on each other?

As I kept working on it, the project grew. I had to think about how to organize the code, how plugins should communicate with the core, how to handle errors, and how to avoid breaking something that was already working.

I won't pretend I have all the answers. I'm still learning, making mistakes, and going back to improve things. But that's part of what makes this project interesting to me.

You can find it on GitHub here:

https://github.com/hadelrachid/domain-system

Why I started thinking differently about PHP

When I started thinking about how to organize the project, I became interested in how operating systems separate their essential parts from the applications that run on top of them.

I wondered if I could borrow a little of that idea for a PHP platform.

In Domain System, I try to keep two things separate:

  • The core: The part responsible for things the system needs to work, such as routing, storage, and other shared services.
  • The plugins: The parts that add features to the platform.

The idea is simple: I don't want the core to know all the details of every plugin. I'd rather have them communicate through interfaces, so I can change one part without having to change everything else.

In practice, getting this right is harder than it sounds. You can create interfaces and still end up with code that's too dependent on other classes. That's something I've been learning to pay more attention to as the project develops.

Some things I've been working on

Installing plugins more safely

One thing that made me think carefully was plugin installation.

When you upload a ZIP file, you can't simply assume that every file inside it is safe to extract wherever you want.

So I added a step where uploaded files are checked before they're moved into place. The process includes checks for problems such as path traversal and ZIP Slip.

It's not something I'd describe as a guarantee that every possible attack is prevented. Security takes more than a few checks, and I know this is an area that deserves ongoing attention.

Trying to make problems easier to recover from

Another challenge is dealing with errors without leaving the system in a bad state.

Domain System includes JSON storage, file-locking and atomic-write techniques, diagnostic tools, and a snapshot and rollback feature.

These are attempts to make problems easier to identify and recover from. I know things can still go wrong, but I'd rather build ways to deal with failures than assume they won't happen.

Building my own visual page editor

I've also been working on Flex Builder, a visual editor for creating page layouts and theme components.

One thing I wanted was for the editor preview to behave as closely as possible to the actual website. To help with that, both use the same compilation process.

I've also been working on responsive layouts, so that hiding an element on a smaller screen doesn't leave awkward empty spaces behind.

There are plenty of details to work through in an editor like this, and it's been a good learning experience.

Using AI without losing control of my code

I also use AI coding tools to help me develop the project.

They can be very useful, especially when you're working on a large codebase. But I've learned that getting code that works in isolation isn't the same as getting code that fits the rest of the project.

Sometimes a change can solve one problem while creating another. A new class might work, for example, but introduce dependencies that make future changes harder.

To help avoid this, I've been creating documentation and rules that explain how the project is organized and how new plugins should be built. There's also a command-line tool to generate a basic plugin structure.

I'm still figuring out the best way to use AI without letting the code become difficult to maintain. Documentation helps, but I still need to review the changes and understand what they're doing.

A little about the technology

Domain System is built with PHP 8.2+. It supports MySQL/MariaDB and SQLite through PDO, as well as its own JSON storage option.

I use PHPUnit for automated tests. At the time of writing, the project has 433 tests and more than 2,340 assertions.

Those numbers are useful, but I don't think they tell the whole story. Passing tests are important, and so is checking whether the code is organized in a way that makes sense and can be maintained over time.

I'm sharing it because I'd like to learn from others

This project has taught me that building something is one challenge; keeping it understandable as it grows is another.

I'm not presenting Domain System as a finished solution or claiming that I've found the best way to build a PHP platform. It's a project I'm developing, learning from, and trying to improve.

If you have a moment to look at the code, I'd really appreciate your thoughts.

For example:

  • Does separating the core from the plugins this way make sense to you?
  • How do you keep a PHP project organized as it grows?
  • If you use AI to help write code, how do you make sure the changes still fit your project's design?

I'd be happy to hear suggestions, questions, or even criticism. I'm sharing the project partly because I know other developers may notice things that I haven't.

Here's the repository:

https://github.com/hadelrachid/domain-system

Thanks for taking the time to read this!

title: Building a pricing-first filter for 4,300 AI tools (and what the data looks like)
description:
A few weeks ago I started AIVerse, a directory of AI tools. The premise was simple: every "best AI tools" list I could find was either a paid placement farm or so stale that half the pricing was wrong. So I built the boring version instead — one that treats pricing and category data as something to be maintained, not written once.

This post is about the data side, because that is where the surprises were.

The shape of the data

Current state of the catalogue, pulled today rather than typed from memory:

Pricing model Tools Share
Free 2,198 50.8%
Freemium 1,425 33.0%
Paid 700 16.2%
Total 4,323 across 92 categories

Category concentration is steeper than I expected. Four categories hold a quarter of everything:

  • Video Generators — 294
  • Image Generators — 269
  • Productivity — 253
  • Developer Tools — 247

The remaining 88 categories average about 37 tools each. 708 listings carry a 2026 publish date, which tells you how fast the supply side is still growing.

One number I do not want to hide: only 614 listings have a verification level recorded. "Free" is therefore a claim taken from the vendor page, not something I confirmed by signing up. That gap is exactly the difference between a directory and a database, and it is the thing I am slowly paying down.

The bug that actually mattered

While exporting every listing to check link health, I diffed the websiteUrl field against vendor domains and found 30 rows pointing not at the vendor but at an affiliate redirect:

capcut → capcutaffiliateprogram.pxf.io/9LPy7W

pxf.io is Impact's link domain; partnerlinks.io is another one. The tracking URLs carried a referring sub-ID (?s=...), which means every "Visit website" click on those 30 pages was crediting someone else's affiliate account. Worse, the descriptions on those same rows said things like "You can use CapCut online at capcutaffiliateprogram.pxf.io" — a templated sentence that turned out to be repeated across 2,084 pages of the site.

Three fixes, in order of how much they mattered:

  1. Reject tracking domains at every entry point. There is one shared list, imported by the crawler, the CSV importer and the public submission form. Previously each path had its own validation and they had drifted apart.
  2. Resolve the 30 existing rows by following the redirect chain to the final vendor domain. Four needed manual judgment: one landed on a /fr locale, one self-redirected in a loop, one dead-ended on the tracker, and one pointed at a completely different product page.
  3. Strip the templated sentence at render time, so those pages stopped showing the tracker before the underlying data was cleaned.

How the pipeline works now

  1. Crawl the upstream catalogue.
  2. Reject tracking domains and anything that is not a vendor-owned URL.
  3. Strip boilerplate — four known template markers. Whatever is left under 25 words gets queued for a human instead of being rendered.
  4. Hand-write the top 150 pages by traffic, four facts each: free tier limit, price tiers, two pros, two cons, and who it is for.
  5. Store that hand-written copy in a git-tracked JSON overlay that takes precedence over the crawled description at render time.

Step 5 is the one I would recommend to anyone building the same thing. My first attempt wrote copy straight into the production SQLite database through an admin form. That sounds fine until you notice the deploy hook restores the live database from a backup on every push — so the copy existed only on the server that was about to be overwritten. Content in git gets a diff, a review and a rollback. Content in a production table gets none of those unless you build them yourself.

What is still broken

  • 9 of 150 pages written. The queue orders by traffic, so this is the head of the distribution, but 94% of the hand-written coverage is missing.
  • No affiliate links yet. Zero of 4,323 listings have a commercial link. That is deliberate: I would rather send traffic to the vendor for free than send it to a tracker that does not pay.
  • The traffic numbers are inherited, not measured. They come from the source catalogue. The only numbers I trust are outbound clicks, and the total is 4. Four clicks. That is the real baseline — everything else is a guess.

Why publish this

Because the honest version is more useful than a launch post. If you are building a directory, the tracking-domain contamination and the "content in the production DB" trap will both find you, and they are easier to spot when someone else has already paid for them.

If you want to look at the result: AIVerse, free AI tools

Start with the free filter — 2,198 listings, filterable by category, with the pricing field printed on every card so you can see what the data quality actually looks like. If a listing is wrong, there is a submission form and I fix it.

title: Editing SVG Paths in the Browser: A Practical Guide to the d Attribute
description:
Most SVG icons you download are a single <path> element with a d attribute that looks like line noise: M4 12l5 5L20 6. It is tempting to treat that string as a black box and regenerate the whole file whenever something needs to change. You don't have to. Once you can read the path commands, small fixes — nudging a corner, closing a gap, flipping a curve — take seconds and keep your file clean.

This guide walks through the commands you will actually meet, a workflow for editing them without breaking things, and a few habits that keep paths maintainable.

The commands that matter

The d attribute is a list of drawing instructions. Each instruction is a letter followed by numbers. Uppercase letters use absolute coordinates; lowercase letters are relative to the current point. The full grammar is defined in the W3C SVG 2 paths chapter, but in practice you will mostly see these:

Command Meaning Example
M / m Move the pen without drawing M10 10
L / l Straight line to a point L20 20
H / h, V / v Horizontal or vertical line H40, v8
C / c Cubic Bézier curve (two control points) C20 0 40 0 50 10
Q / q Quadratic Bézier curve (one control point) Q25 0 50 10
A / a Elliptical arc A5 5 0 0 1 20 20
Z / z Close the shape back to the start Z

That checkmark from the intro, M4 12l5 5L20 6, reads as: move to (4, 12), draw a line 5 right and 5 down (relative), then draw a line to the absolute point (20, 6).

A safe editing workflow

Editing paths by hand goes wrong in predictable ways: you change an absolute coordinate inside a run of relative ones, or you drop a number and every following command shifts. A simple routine avoids most of that.

1. Normalise before you edit. Many optimisers compress paths aggressively, writing l5 5-3 2 with implied repeats and no separators. Before editing, expand the path so that every command letter is explicit and each segment sits on its own line. SVG ignores the whitespace, so this is purely for your eyes:

<path d="
  M4 12
  l5 5
  L20 6
" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2"/>

2. Edit with a live preview. You want to see the shape update as you type. A local HTML file with the SVG inlined and a browser auto-reload works fine; so does an in-browser SVG editor that shows the code and the rendered result side by side — the important thing is the instant feedback, not the tool. Change one number at a time and watch which point moves.

3. Know your viewBox. Coordinates only make sense relative to the viewBox. An icon with viewBox="0 0 24 24" has its drawing space running from 0 to 24 on both axes, regardless of how large it is rendered. If a point disappears, check whether you pushed it outside that box.

4. Re-optimise at the end, not the middle. Once the shape looks right, run your optimiser again to shrink the output. Keep the readable version in source control if you expect to edit it again.

Common fixes you can do by hand

Moving a single corner. Find the L or l that ends at that corner and adjust its numbers. If it is relative (l), remember that the next relative segment starts from the new position, so the rest of the shape may shift with it. Converting that one segment to absolute (L) isolates the change.

Closing a visible gap. If a filled shape has a hairline gap or a stroke looks unjoined, the path probably ends near — but not exactly at — its start point. Adding Z closes it properly and gives you a clean line join instead of two caps.

Softening a sharp corner. Replace an L with a Q whose control point sits at the original corner, and whose end point is a little further along the next edge. It is a cheap way to round one corner without redrawing.

Flipping a curve. For a C curve, mirror the two control points across the line between the start and end points. For arcs, toggling the sweep flag (the fifth number in an A command) flips which way the arc bulges.

Debugging tips

  • Temporarily add stroke="red" and fill="none" to see the actual outline rather than the filled shape.
  • Draw small circles at suspicious coordinates: <circle cx="20" cy="6" r="0.5" fill="blue"/>. It is the fastest way to confirm where a point really is.
  • If the shape renders in one browser but not another, look for a missing separator between two negative numbers (10-5 is valid, 10--5 is not).

Keep paths readable for the next person

Paths are code. A few conventions make them far easier to maintain:

  • Keep icons on a consistent grid (24 × 24 is common) so coordinates are comparable between files.
  • Prefer currentColor for fills and strokes so icons inherit text colour instead of hard-coding hex values.
  • Split complex icons into several <path> elements with meaningful id or class names instead of one enormous path.

Learning to read the d attribute takes an afternoon, and it pays back every time you would otherwise reopen a design tool just to move one point. Start with the checkmark, change a number, and watch what happens.

title: The migration I would do differently next time
description:
Moved a table with about twenty million rows last month and learned three things the hard way.

Do the double-write before the backfill, not after. We did it the other way and spent two evenings reconciling.

Measure replication lag before you start, not during. Ours spiked and we had no baseline.

Write the rollback plan first. We had one, sort of, in someone's head. That is not a plan.

title: Performance at Scale: Optimizing Large and High-Volume Forms
description:
• Designing a Form Architecture That Survives Scale
  • Cut re-renders: minimize DOM churn and validation cost
  • Virtualize and cache fields without losing user input
  • Measure what matters: profiling, benchmarking, and CI-friendly tests
  • Practical Application — checklists, hooks, and snippets

Large, high-volume forms die from three predictable things: gratuitous re-renders, synchronous/over-eager validation, and DOM churn from mounting/unmounting fields. Tackle those three and you turn a sluggish 100+ field form into a responsive, resilient data-collection surface.

Large forms show symptoms that feel familiar: typing lag on-device, long commit times in the React Profiler, fields that lose value when scrolled out of a virtual list, autosave hammering the backend with many tiny requests, and brittle tests that flake when fields mount/unmount. Those are the places you focus first because they cost user time, conversions, and developer time to debug.

Designing a Form Architecture That Survives Scale

Treat the form as a data contract first: a single, schema-driven source of truth and small, well-scoped components that only subscribe to what they need.

  • Use a schema-first approach (for example with Zod) so your validation, types, and API contract live in one place rather than scattered through UI code. That makes step-by-step validation and type-safe transforms predictable.
  • Wire the schema into your form layer with a resolver (e.g., zodResolver + React Hook Form) so validation runs where you expect it and can be run on-demand instead of per-keystroke. This keeps runtime validation predictable and composable.
  • For multi-step forms choose one of two patterns:
    • One form instance across all steps, and validate only the active step with targeted triggers; this keeps all data in one place and simplifies final submission.
    • Separate form instances per step and stitch the results together server-side—simpler component isolation but more plumbing for cross-step constraints.

Table: high-level trade-offs

Approach Pros Cons
Uncontrolled inputs + RHF (register) Minimal re-renders, native input performance Integrations with controlled UI libs need Controller adapters.
Controlled (useState / Formik) Easier to reason in component-local state, simpler third-party controlled components Re-renders per keystroke — scales poorly with many fields.
Hybrid (RHF + Controller for specific widgets) Best balance: RHF performance + compatibility with controlled UI components More cognitive overhead; avoid Controller for trivial native inputs.

Important: For large forms prefer uncontrolled-first patterns and only adopt Controller when you must integrate a controlled widget (Material UI, custom select, complex datepickers). Controller isolates re-rendering but has a cost compared to native register.

Example starter (RHF + Zod):

import { useForm } from "react-hook-form";
import { zodResolver } from "@hookform/resolvers/zod";
import { z } from "zod";

const schema = z.object({
  firstName: z.string().min(1),
  age: z.number().int().optional(),
});

const methods = useForm({
  resolver: zodResolver(schema),
  mode: "onBlur",           // validate less aggressively
  shouldUnregister: false, // useful for multi-step UIs
});

Citations: RHF explains its uncontrolled focus and lower re-render surface as a design point ; schema-first docs for zod and parse options are comprehensive ; resolvers project documents the zodResolver pattern .

Cut re-renders: minimize DOM churn and validation cost

The single biggest win for responsiveness is preventing unnecessary re-renders — especially the root form component.

  • Subscribe narrowly. Use useWatch or useFormState to subscribe to only the fields or flags you need. Avoid destructuring the entire formState at the form root (it forces wide re-renders). useWatch will isolate updates to the hook level.
  • Prefer register (uncontrolled) for native inputs. It keeps input state in the DOM and out of React renders; reading values on demand with getValues() is cheap. Use Controller only for components that expose no ref.
  • Validate intentionally:
    • Use mode: "onBlur" or mode: "onSubmit" for large forms — avoid onChange validation on every keystroke. onChange validation creates a lot of computation and re-renders.
    • For heavy or async checks (e.g., calling an availability API), run them on blur or on explicit trigger(fields) rather than during every change. Use safeParse / parseAsync for async schema refinements when required.
  • Use setValue with options to avoid side-effectful re-renders. setValue(name, value, { shouldValidate: false, shouldDirty: true }) gives you control over whether state flags trigger updates.

Practical patterns that reduce re-renders:

  • Move expensive display computations outside the input-render path (memoize summaries, charts).
  • Wrap large static blocks with React.memo.
  • Avoid inline props or inline event handlers that change identity on each render; pass stable callbacks with useCallback.

Short code snippet: isolate dirty indicator with useFormState so the form root doesn’t re-render:

// Child component only re-renders when isDirty changes
function DirtyBadge({ control }: { control: Control }) {
  const { isDirty } = useFormState({ control, name: "isDirty" });
  return <span>{isDirty ? "Unsaved" : "Saved"}</span>;
}

Citations: RHF documents useWatch, useFormState and the cost of onChange validation modes; setValue options allow you to avoid unnecessary re-renders.

Virtualize and cache fields without losing user input

When the number of rows/fields is large (think 100s–1000s), windowing the DOM is necessary — but doing it naively loses uncontrolled input state when rows unmount. Use targeted patterns to keep state consistent.

  • React’s guidance: virtualize long lists to reduce DOM nodes and render cost. Virtualization dramatically reduces the number of DOM nodes React must reconcile.
  • Libraries: use react-window or a headless solution like TanStack Virtual for full control. react-window is battle-tested and lightweight; TanStack Virtual is more feature-rich and headless.
  • With forms, follow RHF’s "working with virtualized lists" advice:
    • Keep the form values in RHF instead of relying on DOM-only state; use shouldUnregister: false so that fields removed from the DOM don’t lose their registered value.
    • Render editors in a pooled/sticky editor when inline editing is required (mount the active editor outside the virtualized list and bind it to the selected row), or persist values to RHF on blur before unmount.
  • Tune overscanCount to avoid excessive mount/unmount churn as the user scrolls; overscan mitigates visual flicker at the cost of a few extra mounted rows.

Example pattern (simplified):

import { FixedSizeList as List } from "react-window";
import { FormProvider, useForm } from "react-hook-form";

function Row({ index, style, data }) {
  // mount/unmount — register/unregister handled by RHF
  return (
    <div style={style}>
      <input {...data.register(`rows.${index}.value`)} />
    </div>
  );
}

function WindowedForm({ items }) {
  const methods = useForm({ defaultValues: { rows: items }, shouldUnregister: false });
  return (
    <FormProvider {...methods}>
      <List itemCount={items.length} itemSize={40} overscanCount={5}>
        {({ index, style }) => <Row index={index} style={style} data={methods} />}
      </List>
    </FormProvider>
  );
}

Citations: React recommends windowing for long lists ; RHF’s advanced usage shows concrete examples for keeping values with virtualized lists and warns about unmount-reset issues ; react-window docs explain overscan and API shape.

Measure what matters: profiling, benchmarking, and CI-friendly tests

You can’t optimize what you don’t measure. Build a small, reproducible benchmark and add it to CI so performance regressions are visible.

  • Developer-time tools:
    • Use React DevTools Profiler and the <Profiler> API to locate slow commits and the components responsible for the work. Actual render commit durations are what you optimize, not render counts alone.
    • Use why-did-you-render during development to find avoidable re-renders; it’s noisy but great for catching ownership/props identity issues before deployment.
  • Lab tests:
    • Run Lighthouse user flows or scripted Lighthouse runs to capture performance during an interactive path (e.g., go → open form → fill first 50 fields). Lighthouse user flows let you measure during interactions, not just page load.
    • Use Playwright (or Puppeteer) to script form work and capture traces. Playwright’s trace viewer records actions, DOM snapshots, and timing so you can correlate a slow keystroke or commit to an exact action.
  • CI-friendly regression tests:
    • Add a small synthetic test that populates N fields and asserts the median keystroke-to-render time stays below a threshold.
    • Capture traces on first failing runs to root-cause regressions quickly.

Example Playwright snippet (tracing + simple fill time):

// playwright-test.js
import { chromium } from "playwright";

(async () => {
  const browser = await chromium.launch();
  const context = await browser.newContext();
  await context.tracing.start({ screenshots: true, snapshots: true });
  const page = await context.newPage();
  await page.goto("http://localhost:3000/huge-form");
  const t0 = performance.now();
  // simulate filling 200 inputs
  for (let i = 0; i < 200; i++) {
    await page.fill(`[data-test="input-${i}"]`, "x".repeat(10));
  }
  const t1 = performance.now();
  console.log("fill time ms:", t1 - t0);
  await context.tracing.stop({ path: "trace.zip" });
  await browser.close();
})();

Citations: The Profiler API docs explain what to measure and how to interpret commits ; Lighthouse user flows document scripting interactions and measuring them in CI ; Playwright tracing docs explain the trace format and viewer.

Practical Application — checklists, hooks, and snippets

This section is a drop-in toolkit: checklists you can run through quickly, and a ready useAutosave hook that follows safe patterns.

Run this quick checklist on any large form:

  • [ ] Use a schema (Zod) that represents the entire data shape.
  • [ ] Configure RHF with resolver and mode: "onBlur" (or "onSubmit") for the big form.
  • [ ] Prefer register for native inputs; use Controller only for controlled UI widgets.
  • [ ] Isolate expensive UI or derived data with React.memo and useMemo.
  • [ ] For long lists: virtualize with react-window or TanStack Virtual and set shouldUnregister: false. Tune overscanCount.
  • [ ] Add synthetic performance tests (Playwright / Lighthouse user flows) to CI.
  • [ ] Implement autosave that debounces, saves only diffs, and falls back to local persistence / background sync when offline.

A robust useAutosave (TypeScript + RHF-friendly)

  • Goals: debounce saves, save only deltas, persist to an offline store when offline, flush on unload, cancel in-flight saves on new changes. 
// useAutosave.ts
import { useEffect, useRef, useCallback } from "react";
import debounce from "lodash.debounce";

type SaveFn<T> = (patch: Partial<T>) => Promise<void>;

export function useAutosave<T extends Record<string, any>>(
  getValues: () => T,
  watchSubscribe: (cb: (data: T) => void) => { unsubscribe: () => void },
  saveFn: SaveFn<T>,
  opts = { wait: 1200, maxWait: 5000 }
) {
  const lastSavedRef = useRef<T | null>(null);
  const inflightRef = useRef<Promise<void> | null>(null);

  // shallow-diff; return object with changed keys
  const diff = (a: T | null, b: T) => {
    if (!a) return b;
    const patch: Partial<T> = {};
    for (const k of Object.keys(b)) {
      if (a[k] !== b[k]) patch[k as keyof T] = b[k];
    }
    return patch;
  };

  const doSave = useCallback(async () => {
    const values = getValues();
    const patch = diff(lastSavedRef.current, values);
    if (!patch || Object.keys(patch).length === 0) return;
    try {
      inflightRef.current = saveFn(patch);
      await inflightRef.current;
      lastSavedRef.current = values;
    } catch (err) {
      // simple backoff would go here; for offline, persist `patch` to IndexedDB/localStorage
      console.error("Autosave failed", err);
    } finally {
      inflightRef.current = null;
    }
  }, [getValues, saveFn]);

  // debounced save to avoid network storms
  const debouncedSaveRef = useRef(debounce(doSave, opts.wait, { maxWait: opts.maxWait })).current;

  useEffect(() => {
    // initialize lastSaved
    lastSavedRef.current = getValues();
    const sub = watchSubscribe(() => {
      debouncedSaveRef();
    });

    const handleUnload = () => {
      // flush synchronously on unload if possible
      debouncedSaveRef.cancel();
      // best-effort: call sync save (not guaranteed)
      void doSave();
    };
    window.addEventListener("beforeunload", handleUnload);
    return () => {
      sub.unsubscribe();
      debouncedSaveRef.cancel();
      window.removeEventListener("beforeunload", handleUnload);
    };
  }, [getValues, watchSubscribe, debouncedSaveRef, doSave]);
}

Integration notes:

  • Use RHF’s watch(callback) subscription (or watch inside a lightweight component) to avoid root re-renders and to feed useAutosave without causing renders.
  • Persist failed patches to IndexedDB and register a Background Sync so service worker flushes them when network returns. MDN documents the Background Sync API and the SyncManager pattern for this use-case.
  • Use lodash.debounce (or an equivalent) to throttle saves and give users a smooth typing experience.

Small snippet: register background sync (service worker):

// in client when offline save to outbox then:
const reg = await navigator.serviceWorker.ready;
await reg.sync.register("outbox-sync");

Citations: use debounce to prevent request storms ; use localStorage / IndexedDB for persistence when network is flaky (Web Storage / IndexedDB docs) ; Background Sync lets the service worker flush queued requests when connectivity returns .

Sources:
React Hook Form — FAQs - Explanation of RHF's uncontrolled-first design and why it reduces re-renders.

Optimizing Performance — React (legacy docs) - React guidance on windowing long lists and avoiding unnecessary reconciliation.

Profiler API – React - How to use the Profiler to measure commit durations and identify hotspots.

React Hook Form — Advanced Usage (Working with virtualized lists) - Concrete example and cautions for using react-window with RHF and how to preserve values.

bvaughn/react-window · GitHub - react-window docs and API (overscan, List/Grid patterns).

TanStack/virtual · GitHub - Headless virtualizer (TanStack Virtual) and usage patterns for complex virtualization.

Zod (colinhacks/zod) · GitHub - Zod schema API (parse, safeParse, parseAsync) and rationale for schema-first validation.

react-hook-form/resolvers · GitHub - Resolver integrations including zodResolver and how to wire schemas into RHF.

Use tools to measure performance — web.dev - Lighthouse, WebPageTest, and RUM guidance for creating measurable performance baselines.

Playwright — Trace Viewer docs - How to record traces, inspect actions, and use tracing in CI to debug performance.

why-did-you-render · GitHub - Dev-time tool to detect avoidable re-renders and ownership reasons.

Web Storage API — Using the Web Storage API (MDN) - Browser storage fundamentals and constraints for localStorage.

Background Synchronization API (MDN) - Using SyncManager and service worker sync registration for offline-first sync.

lodash.debounce — npm - debounce implementation and options for throttling autosave and heavy callbacks.

useForm — React Hook Form docs - useForm options (mode, shouldUnregister, resolver) and guidance on subscription APIs, getValues, setValue, useWatch and useFormState.

Every change you make to render scope, validation timing, or virtualization should be backed by a quick profile: add a Profiler span, measure an action end-to-end with Playwright/Lighthouse, and only then harden it into CI. Performance at scale is a discipline: architect with schema-first validation, subscribe narrowly, and instrument the form so regressions are visible and actionable.

title: Search Results That Jump Back to an Old Query in React: Finding and Fixing the Race
description:
The problem

A developer built a search bar in React. Each time the user types a letter, the component sends a request to the server and shows the results. Most of the time it works. But sometimes the list shows results for an older, shorter search. The box says "react", and the list shows results for "r". Typing slowly hides the bug. Typing fast makes it show up again.

This is a common bug, and it is easy to miss in local testing, because a local server answers almost every request at the same speed.

The root cause

Every keystroke starts a new request. The network does not promise that answers come back in the same order the requests went out. A short query like "r" can match many rows and take longer on the server. A longer query like "react" can come back fast.

So the timeline can look like this:

0 ms     start request for "r"      (slow, 300 ms)
40 ms    start request for "re"     (fast, 20 ms)
60 ms    "re" answers  -> list shows "re" results   (correct)
300 ms   "r" answers   -> list shows "r" results    (wrong, but it was the last setState)

The buggy code calls setState for every answer, so the last answer to arrive wins, not the last question asked:

// Buggy: every response updates state, in arrival order
useEffect(() => {
  if (!query) return;
  fetch(`/api/search?q=${encodeURIComponent(query)}`)
    .then((res) => res.json())
    .then((data) => setResults({ query, items: data.items }));
}, [query]);

The React docs describe this exact case in "You Might Not Need an Effect": the responses for "hell" and "hello" can arrive in either order, and whichever calls setResults() last is what the user sees. They call it a race condition.

The fix

The fix has three parts. Each part solves a different piece, and all three live in the effect's cleanup function, which React runs before the effect runs again and when the component unmounts.

  1. An ignore flag. Each effect run gets its own flag. Cleanup sets it to true, so a late answer from an old run can no longer change state. This is the part that makes the result correct.
  2. An AbortController. Cleanup calls controller.abort(). Per MDN, this can abort a fetch request and the reading of its response body. The aborted fetch rejects with an AbortError, which we treat as normal, not as a failure. This part saves network and server work.
  3. A short debounce. A timer waits until the user pauses before it sends a request. Cleanup clears the timer, so fast typing sends one request instead of five. This part cuts load. It does not fix ordering by itself.

Here is the full hook:

import { useEffect, useState } from 'react';

export function useSearch(query, { fetchImpl = fetch, delayMs = 250 } = {}) {
  const [state, setState] = useState({ status: 'idle', query: '', items: [], error: null });

  useEffect(() => {
    const q = query.trim();
    if (!q) {
      setState({ status: 'idle', query: '', items: [], error: null });
      return;
    }

    const controller = new AbortController();
    let ignore = false;

    const timer = setTimeout(async () => {
      setState((s) => ({ ...s, status: 'loading', error: null }));
      try {
        const res = await fetchImpl(`/api/search?q=${encodeURIComponent(q)}`, {
          signal: controller.signal,
        });
        if (!res.ok) throw new Error(`HTTP ${res.status}`);
        const data = await res.json();
        if (!ignore) setState({ status: 'done', query: q, items: data.items, error: null });
      } catch (err) {
        if (ignore || err.name === 'AbortError') return; // expected, not a real failure
        setState((s) => ({ ...s, status: 'error', error: err }));
      }
    }, delayMs);

    return () => {
      ignore = true;        // late answers from this run can no longer touch state
      clearTimeout(timer);  // a request that has not started yet never starts
      controller.abort();   // a request in flight is cancelled
    };
  }, [query, fetchImpl, delayMs]);

  return state;
}

Use it like this:

function SearchBox() {
  const [query, setQuery] = useState('');
  const { status, query: shownFor, items, error } = useSearch(query);

  return (
    <>
      <input value={query} onChange={(e) => setQuery(e.target.value)} />
      {status === 'loading' && <p>Loading…</p>}
      {status === 'error' && <p>Something went wrong: {error.message}</p>}
      <p>Showing results for: {shownFor}</p>
      <ul>{items.map((item) => <li key={item}>{item}</li>)}</ul>
    </>
  );
}

Two small details matter:

  • Keep the query that produced the results in state next to the items. Then the UI can show which search the list belongs to, and a test can check it.
  • Do not pass a new fetchImpl function on every render, or the effect will re-run each time. Either leave the default, or create the function once outside the component.

Why keep the ignore flag if we already abort?

Abort is best effort. If the response is already done by the time cleanup runs, or if the fetch function you call does not pass the signal along (some wrappers drop it), the old promise can still resolve. The ignore check is a plain, in-memory test, so it works in every one of those cases. The React docs show the ignore flag as the basic fix and say cleanup should "either abort the fetch or ignore its result." We do both.

How we tested it

We ran this on Node 20 with React 19, @testing-library/react, and jsdom. A fake fetch makes one-letter queries slow (300 ms) and longer queries fast (20 ms), and it honors AbortSignal like the real one. Four tests:

test('buggy hook shows results for an old query', async () => {
  const log = []; const f = makeFakeFetch(log);
  const { rerender } = render(h(BuggyBox, { query: 'r', fetchImpl: f }));
  rerender(h(BuggyBox, { query: 're', fetchImpl: f }));
  await act(() => sleep(400));
  assert.equal(screen.getByTestId('out').textContent, 're -> r'); // box says "re", list is for "r"
});

test('fixed hook keeps the newest query and aborts the old one', async () => {
  const log = []; const f = makeFakeFetch(log);
  const { rerender } = render(h(FixedBox, { query: 'r', fetchImpl: f, delayMs: 0 }));
  await act(() => sleep(5));
  rerender(h(FixedBox, { query: 're', fetchImpl: f, delayMs: 0 }));
  await act(() => sleep(400));
  assert.equal(screen.getByTestId('out').textContent, 're -> re');
  assert.ok(log.includes('abort r'));
});

test('debounce: fast typing sends one request', async () => {
  // types r, re, rea, reac, react 30 ms apart with a 100 ms debounce
  assert.deepEqual(log, ['start react', 'finish react']);
});

test('ignore flag still protects when the old request cannot be aborted', async () => {
  // fetch wrapper drops the signal on purpose
  assert.ok(log.includes('finish r'));                               // old answer did arrive
  assert.equal(screen.getByTestId('out').textContent, 're -> re');   // but it was ignored
});

Result: 4 of 4 tests pass. The request logs from the run:

fixed log:    start r, abort r, start re, finish re
debounce log: start react, finish react

The first test proves the bug is real. The other three prove each part of the fix does its own job.

Trade-offs

  • Debounce adds delay. Every search waits for the pause before it starts. A longer delay sends fewer requests but feels slower. A shorter delay feels faster but sends more. Pick a value and measure it with real users.
  • Abort does not undo work. The server may have already run the query. Abort saves bandwidth and frees the browser connection. It does not roll back anything on the server, so never rely on abort for requests that change data.
  • Two requests in development are normal. With Strict Mode, React runs the effect, cleans it up, and runs it again in development. The docs say you will see two fetches in the Network tab, and the cleanup makes the first one harmless. In a production build there is one.
  • A data library may fit better. The React docs point out that caching, server-side fetching, and request waterfalls are still open problems with hand-written effects, and that frameworks and data libraries handle them. If your app already uses one, use its query hooks instead of this hook. If it does not, this hook is a small, clear step, and it is easy to replace later.
  • The ignore flag alone is enough for correctness. If you cannot abort (for example, an SDK that does not accept a signal), the flag still keeps the screen right. You lose only the network savings.

Make sure the stale results are gone

  1. Run the tests. The buggy test should pass (it proves the bug), and the three fixed tests should pass.
  2. Slow the network in the browser. Open DevTools, go to the Network tab, and pick a slow throttling preset. Type a word quickly. You should see older requests marked as cancelled, and only the last one should complete.
  3. Show the source query. Render "Showing results for: …" next to the list, as in the example. Type fast, then compare it with the input. They should always match once loading ends.
  4. Check the console. There should be no errors for aborted requests. If you see AbortError in your error UI, the catch block is not filtering it.

Official sources

  • React docs, You Might Not Need an Effect (section "Fetching data", race conditions and the ignore flag): https://react.dev/learn/you-might-not-need-an-effect
  • React docs, Synchronizing with Effects (section "Fetching data", abort or ignore in cleanup, two fetches in development): https://react.dev/learn/synchronizing-with-effects
  • React docs, useEffect reference (section "Fetching data with Effects"): https://react.dev/reference/react/useEffect
  • MDN, AbortController: abort() method: https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/AbortController/abort
  • MDN, AbortSignal: https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/AbortSignal

title: Two requests, one rule, two rows: fixing the INSERT ... WHERE NOT EXISTS race in PostgreSQL
description:
A rule like "one comment per user per hour" looks easy. You check for a recent row, and you only insert if there is none. It works in every test you write by hand. Then two requests arrive at the same moment, and the rule quietly breaks.

We set up the exact case on PostgreSQL 17.5, made it fail on purpose, and tried four fixes. Every number below comes from those runs.

The question

Someone on r/PostgreSQL asked about this query. The goal was to let a user post only one comment per hour:

INSERT INTO comments (user_id, content)
SELECT :user_id, 'my comment'
WHERE NOT EXISTS (
  SELECT 1 FROM comments
  WHERE user_id = :user_id
    AND created_at > now() - interval '1 hour'
);

They asked a fair question. If two threads run this at the same time, can two comments slip through? People in the thread said yes. We wanted to show why, and what to do about it.

Why it breaks

PostgreSQL's default mode is called Read Committed. The docs say each query in this mode sees a snapshot of the database taken "the instant the query begins to run." It never sees rows that other transactions have not committed yet.

So here is the timeline:

  1. Request A runs the query. It finds no recent comment, so it inserts one. A has not committed yet.
  2. Request B runs the same query. A's new row is not committed, so B cannot see it. B also finds no recent comment, and inserts one.
  3. Both commit. The user now has two comments in the same hour.

Nothing here is a bug in PostgreSQL. The check and the insert are in one statement, but the check only looks at committed data. There is no unique key for the database to defend, so nothing makes B wait.

The test setup

Our test opens two connections. Request A runs its insert and stays open. Request B runs while A is still open. After half a second, A commits. Then we count rows.

CREATE TABLE users (id int PRIMARY KEY);
CREATE TABLE comments (
  id bigserial PRIMARY KEY,
  user_id int NOT NULL REFERENCES users(id),
  content text NOT NULL,
  created_at timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
);

The core of the Python test, using psycopg2:

a, b = psycopg2.connect(DSN), psycopg2.connect(DSN)
fn(a.cursor(), uid, "from request A")   # A is inside its transaction
def second():
    start = time.monotonic()
    fn(b.cursor(), uid, "from request B")  # B runs while A is open
    result["waited"] = time.monotonic() - start
    b.commit()
t = threading.Thread(target=second); t.start()
time.sleep(0.5)
a.commit(); t.join()

The plain query fails just as the thread said:

naive NOT EXISTS       rows=2  B inserted=1  B waited=0.0s

Two rows, and B never waited.

Fix 1: an advisory lock per user

An advisory lock is a lock with a meaning you choose. PostgreSQL does not attach it to any table. pg_advisory_xact_lock holds the lock until the transaction ends, so you never have to free it by hand.

def advisory(cur, uid, txt):
    # Lock first, in its own statement.
    cur.execute("SELECT pg_advisory_xact_lock(42, %s)", (uid,))
    cur.execute(NAIVE, {"uid": uid, "txt": txt})

The 42 is just a number we picked to mean "comment limit." The second number is the user id. So two users never block each other.

The detail that matters: the lock must be its own statement, before the check. In Read Committed, each statement gets a fresh snapshot. B waits on the lock. When A commits, B gets the lock, and its next statement takes a new snapshot that includes A's row.

advisory lock          rows=1  B inserted=0  B waited=0.5s
advisory, 2 users      rows=2  B inserted=1  B waited=0.0s

B waited for A, then saw the row and inserted nothing. A second user was not slowed down at all.

Fix 2: lock the user's row

If you already have a users table, you can lock the user's row instead. SELECT ... FOR UPDATE makes any other transaction that tries to lock the same row wait.

def row_lock(cur, uid, txt):
    cur.execute("SELECT 1 FROM users WHERE id = %s FOR UPDATE", (uid,))
    cur.execute(NAIVE, {"uid": uid, "txt": txt})

FOR UPDATE on users    rows=1  B inserted=0  B waited=0.5s

Same result. This one is easy to read in code review, because the lock is on a real thing. The cost: anything else that locks that user row will wait too.

Fix 3: let the database enforce the rule

Locks only work if every code path takes them. A new script or a second service might skip the lock. A constraint cannot be skipped.

PostgreSQL has exclusion constraints. They say "no two rows may match on these tests." With the btree_gist extension, we can say "same user AND overlapping one-hour windows" is not allowed.

Our first try failed:

ALTER TABLE comments ADD CONSTRAINT x EXCLUDE USING gist
  (user_id WITH =, tstzrange(created_at, created_at + interval '1 hour') WITH &&);
-- ERROR: functions in index expression must be marked IMMUTABLE

Adding an interval to a timestamptz can depend on the time zone setting, so PostgreSQL will not use it in an index. The fix is to store the window as its own column:

CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS btree_gist;
ALTER TABLE comments ADD COLUMN active_window tstzrange NOT NULL;
ALTER TABLE comments ADD CONSTRAINT one_comment_per_hour
  EXCLUDE USING gist (user_id WITH =, active_window WITH &&);

Then insert with ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING, so a blocked comment is skipped and does not throw an error:

INSERT INTO comments (user_id, content, active_window)
VALUES ($1, $2, tstzrange(now(), now() + interval '1 hour'))
ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING;

exclusion constraint   rows=1  B inserted=0  B waited=0.5s
exclusion, 2 users     rows=2  B inserted=1  B waited=0.0s

One thing to check if you copy an answer from the thread. One reply showed an exclusion constraint with only the time range, and no user_id WITH =. That version stops any two users from posting close together. Always put the user column in.

A tstzrange built this way includes its start and leaves out its end. So a comment exactly one hour later does not overlap and is allowed.

Fix 4: SERIALIZABLE, plus a retry

You can also leave the query alone and run both transactions at the SERIALIZABLE level. PostgreSQL watches for reads and writes that could not happen in any one-at-a-time order, and it cancels one of the transactions.

A committed
B commit failed, SQLSTATE 40001 - could not serialize access due to read/write dependencies among transactions
serializable naive: rows = 1

This is correct, but your code must catch 40001 and run the whole transaction again. The PostgreSQL docs say the same thing: apps at this level must be ready to retry.

A trap we found: advisory lock plus REPEATABLE READ

We also ran Fix 1 with both transactions at REPEATABLE READ. It let two rows through:

B committed
repeatable read + advisory: rows = 2

The docs explain why. At REPEATABLE READ, the snapshot is taken at the start of the first statement in the transaction. Here that first statement is the lock call itself. So B's snapshot is fixed before it waits for the lock, and it never sees A's row. Fixes 1 and 2 depend on Read Committed. If your app or framework changes the isolation level, use Fix 3 or Fix 4.

Which one should you pick?

  • Fix 3, the exclusion constraint, if the rule must hold no matter which code writes to the table. It is our first choice.
  • Fix 1 or 2 if the rule is complex, such as "five comments per hour," which a simple constraint cannot express. Keep the default Read Committed level.
  • Fix 4 if your app already runs at SERIALIZABLE and has a retry loop.

In every case, keep the lock or the transaction short. B waits for as long as A holds on.

Docs we read

  • PostgreSQL 17, Transaction Isolation: https://www.postgresql.org/docs/17/transaction-iso.html
  • PostgreSQL 17, Explicit Locking, Advisory Locks: https://www.postgresql.org/docs/17/explicit-locking.html
  • PostgreSQL 17, Advisory Lock Functions: https://www.postgresql.org/docs/17/functions-admin.html
  • PostgreSQL 17, Constraints, Exclusion Constraints: https://www.postgresql.org/docs/17/ddl-constraints.html
  • PostgreSQL 17, INSERT and ON CONFLICT: https://www.postgresql.org/docs/17/sql-insert.html
  • PostgreSQL 17, btree_gist: https://www.postgresql.org/docs/17/btree-gist.html
  • PostgreSQL 17, Range Types: https://www.postgresql.org/docs/17/rangetypes.html
