title: AI UI Tools Skip Design Basics, Leading to Unpolished Products Despite Beginner-Friendly Marketing
description:
Introduction: The Rise of AI in UI Design

The design landscape is shifting. AI-generated UI tools and skill packs are exploding in popularity, marketed as the fast track to polished interfaces. Friends are ditching Figma, skipping prototyping, and heading straight to production, armed with AI "skills" promising instant design prowess. But this shortcut comes at a cost – a cost measured in inconsistency, lack of intentionality, and ultimately, a degraded user experience.

Let’s break down the mechanics of this trend. AI tools, while impressive, are essentially pattern matchers. They analyze existing designs, identify recurring elements (buttons, spacing, color palettes), and generate variations based on prompts. This works well for senior designers who understand the "why" behind these patterns – the principles of hierarchy, visual weight, and user psychology. They can guide the AI, refine its output, and ensure consistency.

For beginners, however, it’s a different story. Feeding an AI terms like "spring easing" or "vertical rhythm" without understanding their underlying principles is like handing a scalpel to someone who’s never dissected a frog. The AI might produce something that looks "design-y," but it lacks the intentionality, the "why" that makes good design truly effective.

The Breakdown: Why AI Shortcuts Fail Beginners

  • Missing the Feedback Loop: Design is iterative. In Figma, you experiment, compare versions side-by-side, and refine based on visual and functional feedback. AI tools often bypass this crucial step. Changes are made directly in code, where every tweak is costly in time and effort. The result? Designs that are "good enough" but rarely great, lacking the polish that comes from multiple iterations.
  • Black Box Decision-Making: AI tools make decisions about spacing, color, and interaction based on patterns, not principles. A beginner might get a visually appealing button, but they won’t understand why it works. When a design element needs adjustment, they’re left prompting the AI again, hoping for a better outcome. This lack of understanding hinders their ability to troubleshoot, adapt, and grow as designers.
  • The Illusion of Mastery: Skill packs and prompt bundles promise "beginner-friendly" design, but they often teach vocabulary without context. Knowing the term "damping" doesn’t mean you understand how it affects user perception of speed and responsiveness. True design knowledge comes from experimentation, from feeling the difference between a jarring transition and a smooth one. AI shortcuts bypass this tactile learning, creating a generation of designers who can parrot design jargon but lack the ability to apply it effectively.

The Long-Term Risk: A Design Landscape Lacking Intentionality

The proliferation of AI-driven design shortcuts poses a significant risk to the craft. If designers rely solely on AI to generate interfaces, we’ll see a homogenization of design, a landscape dominated by generic, uninspired solutions. The nuanced understanding of user needs, the deliberate choices that make a design truly exceptional, will be lost.

Imagine a world where every website feels like it was assembled from a kit, where every interaction lacks the spark of human intention. This is the future we face if we prioritize speed and convenience over the foundational principles of good design.

The Optimal Solution: AI as a Tool, Not a Teacher

AI has immense potential as a design tool, but it should augment, not replace, human creativity and understanding. Here’s the optimal approach:

  • If you’re a beginner: Resist the siren song of AI shortcuts. Learn the fundamentals – typography, color theory, layout principles, user psychology. Experiment in Figma, iterate relentlessly, and develop your design intuition. Once you understand the "why," AI can become a powerful tool for accelerating your workflow, not a crutch.
  • If you’re an experienced designer: Use AI strategically. Leverage its pattern recognition capabilities to generate initial concepts, explore variations, and automate repetitive tasks. But always maintain control over the final design decisions, ensuring they align with your vision and user needs.

Remember, AI is a tool, not a teacher. True design mastery comes from understanding the principles, from the tactile experience of shaping interfaces, and from the relentless pursuit of excellence. Don’t let AI shortcuts rob you of the joy and satisfaction of creating truly great design.

The Learning Bypass: Consequences and Risks

The rise of AI-generated UI design tools and skill packs has introduced a dangerous shortcut in the design process. Marketed as beginner-friendly, these tools promise professional-level results without the need for foundational learning. However, this bypass comes at a steep cost, leading to inconsistent, unpolished products and a generation of designers lacking essential skills. Here’s how the mechanism breaks down:

1. Pattern Matching vs. Principle-Driven Design

AI tools operate as pattern matchers, analyzing existing designs to replicate elements like buttons, spacing, and color palettes based on prompts. While effective for senior designers who use these tools to augment their understanding of principles like hierarchy and visual weight, beginners lack the context to guide or refine AI output. The result? Designs that are visually disjointed, as observed in the source case where landing pages, settings pages, and dashboards feel like separate products due to inconsistent buttons, spacing, and hover effects. The causal chain here is clear: absence of foundational knowledge → reliance on AI patterns → lack of uniformity and intentionality.

2. The Feedback Loop Gap

Traditional design tools like Figma facilitate an iterative refinement process, allowing designers to experiment, compare versions, and polish their work. AI tools, however, bypass this feedback loop, producing "good enough" designs that lack the tactile learning essential for mastery. For instance, adjusting an easing curve by 2px to achieve smoothness is a physical, iterative process that AI cannot replicate. Beginners who skip this step miss out on the muscle memory of design, leading to a superficial understanding of concepts like damping or optical alignment. The risk? Designs that are technically correct but lack soul, as the designer never internalizes the why behind each decision.

3. Black Box Decision-Making

AI tools make decisions based on patterns, not principles. This black box approach creates a critical failure point: when something goes wrong, designers don’t know how to fix it. For example, if a button’s radius or color feels off, the AI’s pattern-based decision provides no insight into the underlying issue. The designer is left to prompt again and hope, rather than troubleshoot with intent. This mechanism of risk formation—pattern reliance → lack of diagnostic ability → repeated subpar outcomes—undermines long-term skill development and product quality.

4. The Illusion of Mastery

Skill packs and prompt bundles often teach jargon without context, creating an illusion of mastery. Beginners memorize terms like "spring easing" or "60-30-10 color rule" without understanding their application. This is akin to learning the words for tools without ever using them. The causal chain here is insidious: memorization of terms → false confidence → application without understanding → subpar design. For example, knowing the term "damping" doesn’t teach you when a bounce feels cheap versus smooth—only hands-on experimentation does.

5. Long-Term Risks: Homogenization and Devaluation

If this trend continues, the design field risks homogenization, as AI-generated patterns dominate over intentional, principle-driven design. Products will lack the nuanced user understanding and intentionality that come from foundational learning. Worse, the craft of design will be devalued, as shortcuts replace skill. The mechanism of this risk is clear: over-reliance on AI → loss of unique design voice → decline in product integrity.

Optimal Solutions: When and How to Use AI

  • For Beginners: Prioritize learning fundamentals like typography, color theory, and user psychology. Use tools like Figma for iterative experimentation. Rule: If you don’t understand the principle, don’t use the AI tool.
  • For Experienced Designers: Leverage AI for pattern recognition, initial concepts, and automation, but retain control over final decisions. Rule: Use AI to augment, not replace, your expertise.

The key insight? AI is a tool, not a teacher. True design mastery requires understanding principles, tactile experience, and a relentless pursuit of excellence. Bypassing this process with AI shortcuts may save time in the short term, but the long-term cost to product quality and designer skill is too high to ignore.

Case Studies: Real-World Implications

1. The Fragmented Product: No Uniformity, No System

A designer I know switched to an AI UI tool, bypassing Figma entirely. The result? A landing page, settings page, and dashboard that feel like three separate products. Buttons vary in shape, spacing is inconsistent, and hover effects differ across pages. The mechanism here is clear: AI tools generate elements based on pattern matching, not a unified design system. Without a human designer enforcing consistency, the AI pulls from disparate sources, creating a Frankenstein product. The risk? Users perceive the product as unprofessional and disjointed, increasing bounce rates.

2. The Memory File Myth: Consistency Without Intentionality

One solution proposed is to use a "memory file" to force consistency. But this is a band-aid fix. The AI decides the button radius, the grey shade, the hover effect—decisions made without understanding why. When a change is needed, the designer is blind. The causal chain is: AI-driven decisions → lack of intentionality → inability to troubleshoot. The memory file doesn’t teach why a design choice works; it just enforces it. The risk? Designers lose the ability to make informed decisions, leading to brittle designs that break under pressure.

3. The Jargon Trap: Memorization Without Mastery

Beginners are buying skill packs that teach terms like "spring easing" and "optical alignment" without context. They memorize the words but don’t understand the mechanics. For example, "damping" isn’t just a term—it’s a physical concept borrowed from mechanics, where a system’s oscillations are reduced over time. Without tactile experience, beginners can’t feel the difference between cheap and smooth transitions. The mechanism here is: memorization → false confidence → misapplication. The risk? Designs that are technically correct but lack soul, failing to engage users emotionally.

4. The Production Code Trap: First Draft Becomes Final Product

Skipping Figma and going straight to production code is a common mistake. Every change in code costs time and resources, so the first AI-generated version often ships as-is. In Figma, designers iterate, placing five versions side by side and refining. The causal chain is: lack of iteration → lack of refinement → subpar final product. The risk? Products that are "good enough" but never great, failing to stand out in a competitive market.

5. The Course Conundrum: Teaching Jargon, Not Principles

Courses marketed as "beginner-friendly" teach design vocabulary to feed into AI tools. But vocabulary without context is useless. For example, the 60-30-10 color rule isn’t just a ratio—it’s a principle derived from how the human eye perceives contrast and hierarchy. Beginners apply the rule without understanding its purpose, leading to visually unbalanced designs. The mechanism is: superficial knowledge → misapplication → poor outcomes. The risk? A generation of designers who can’t think critically, relying on AI to make decisions for them.

6. The Homogenization Risk: Losing the Unique Design Voice

Over-reliance on AI leads to homogenized designs. AI pulls from the same pool of patterns, creating generic interfaces that lack personality. For example, every button generated by the AI might follow the same radius and shadow because it’s the most common pattern in its dataset. The causal chain is: pattern matching → lack of diversity → homogenization. The risk? Products lose their unique voice, failing to differentiate themselves in a crowded market.

Optimal Solutions: When and How to Use AI

AI is a tool, not a teacher. For beginners, prioritize learning fundamentals first. Use Figma to experiment with typography, color theory, and spacing. Only after understanding these principles should AI be introduced as an augmentation tool. For experienced designers, AI can automate repetitive tasks but should never replace critical decision-making. The rule is: if you don’t understand why a design choice works, don’t let AI make it for you. The optimal solution is to use AI for pattern recognition and initial concepts, but retain control over final decisions to ensure alignment with user needs and brand identity.

Professional Judgment: The Future of Design

If this trend continues, the design craft will be devalued. Shortcuts will replace skill, and intentionality will be lost. The mechanism is clear: over-reliance on AI → loss of foundational skills → decline in product integrity. To avoid this, designers must resist the temptation of quick fixes and invest in tactile learning. The key insight is: AI can’t teach you to feel the difference between good and great design—only experience can.

Expert Opinions: Balancing AI and Human Skill

The rise of AI-driven UI tools has sparked a critical debate in the design community. While these tools promise efficiency and accessibility, they often bypass the foundational learning that underpins great design. As a designer who’s witnessed peers trade Figma for AI-generated skill packs, I’ve seen firsthand how this shortcut mentality leads to unpolished, inconsistent products. Here’s the breakdown—mechanism by mechanism—of why this trend is risky and how to balance AI with human skill.

The Mechanism of AI’s Pattern Matching

AI tools operate as pattern matchers, analyzing existing designs to replicate elements like buttons, spacing, and color palettes. This works well for senior designers who use AI as a starting point, refining outputs with their understanding of hierarchy, visual weight, and user psychology. However, for beginners, this process is a black box. Without foundational knowledge, they rely on AI’s pattern-based decisions, leading to designs that are technically correct but visually disjointed.

Causal Chain: Absence of foundational knowledge → reliance on AI patterns → inconsistent, unintentional designs.

The Feedback Loop Gap

Traditional tools like Figma enable iterative refinement, allowing designers to experiment, compare versions, and build muscle memory for concepts like damping or optical alignment. AI, however, produces “good enough” designs without this tactile learning. The result? Beginners miss the deep understanding that comes from moving an element 2px and feeling it “sit right.”

Risk Mechanism: Lack of iteration → lack of muscle memory → inability to internalize design principles.

The Jargon Trap

Skill packs and courses teach terms like “spring easing” or “60-30-10 color rule” without context. Beginners memorize these words but lack the tactile experience to apply them effectively. For example, knowing “damping” doesn’t mean you understand when a bounce feels too stiff or too loose. This illusion of mastery leads to misapplication and emotionally unengaging designs.

Causal Chain: Memorization of terms → false confidence → application without understanding → poor outcomes.

The Production Code Trap

When designers skip prototyping in Figma and go straight to production, every change becomes costly. The first AI-generated output often ships as the final product, lacking the refinement that comes from iteration. This first-draft-as-final approach results in subpar designs that fail to stand out.

Risk Mechanism: Lack of iteration → lack of refinement → subpar final product → failure to differentiate.

Optimal AI Use: Rules for Beginners and Experts

To balance AI and human skill, follow these evidence-backed rules:

  • For Beginners: Prioritize learning fundamentals like typography, color theory, and spacing in Figma. Avoid AI until you understand why a design choice works. Rule: If you don’t understand the principle, don’t let AI make the decision.
  • For Experienced Designers: Use AI for automation of repetitive tasks, not critical decision-making. Retain control over final design choices to ensure alignment with user needs and brand identity.

Professional Judgment: The Future of Design

AI is a tool, not a teacher. Over-reliance on it risks homogenization, as designs become generic and lack a unique voice. The craft of design is devalued when shortcuts replace skill. To avoid this, invest in tactile learning, iterate relentlessly, and retain human judgment in every decision.

Key Insight: AI cannot teach the difference between good and great design—only experience can. If X (you lack foundational knowledge) → use Y (traditional tools and iterative learning) before introducing AI.

Conclusion: Rethinking AI’s Role in Design Education

The rise of AI-driven UI tools and skill packs has created a paradox: they promise to democratize design but risk devaluing it. By bypassing foundational learning, these tools produce technically correct yet emotionally unengaging designs. The mechanism is clear: AI operates as a pattern matcher, not a principle-based designer. It replicates elements like button radii or color palettes without understanding why these choices work. Beginners, lacking tactile experience, memorize jargon like “spring easing” or “60-30-10 color rule” but fail to internalize their causal impact on user experience.

Consider the feedback loop gap: in Figma, designers iterate, building muscle memory for spacing, alignment, and transitions. AI, however, produces “good enough” outputs, skipping this critical process. The result? Designs that are brittle—unable to adapt or troubleshoot when issues arise. For instance, if an AI-generated button lacks visual hierarchy, a beginner cannot diagnose why it fails because the decision was never theirs to make. They’re left prompting the AI again, hoping for a better outcome.

The long-term risk is homogenization. AI draws from common patterns in its dataset, producing generic designs that lack differentiation. This isn’t just an aesthetic issue—it’s a business risk. Products fail to stand out, leading to higher bounce rates and lost user engagement. The mechanism here is straightforward: over-reliance on AI → loss of intentionality → decline in product integrity.

So, how do we fix this? The optimal solution is not to abandon AI but to reposition it as a tool, not a teacher. For beginners, the rule is clear: if you don’t understand why a design choice works, don’t let AI make it. Prioritize learning fundamentals—typography, color theory, spacing—in Figma. Iterate relentlessly. Only introduce AI after you’ve built the muscle memory to refine its output.

For experienced designers, AI can automate repetitive tasks like generating initial layouts or color palettes. But retain control over critical decisions. Use AI for pattern recognition, not as a crutch. The key insight? AI cannot teach the difference between good and great design—only experience and tactile learning can.

In conclusion, AI in design education is a double-edged sword. Used wisely, it augments creativity. Misused, it undermines it. The choice is ours: invest in skill, not shortcuts. Because in design, as in life, the devil is in the details—and AI doesn’t know how to sweat them.

title: The Architecture of Viral Parody: Audio-Driven Sync, Spatial Constraints, and the Death of Complex AI Toolchains
description:
Why modern creators and engineers are abandoning bloated diffusion pipelines in favor of single-purpose, browser-first micro-studios.

If you followed the generative video landscape over the past two years, the consensus was clear: the future belonged to general-purpose, open-ended prompt engines. Developers built increasingly elaborate ComfyUI node graphs, experimented with complex negative prompt weighting, and integrated multi-gigabyte LoRA models to produce short video clips.

Yet as we move through late 2026, real-world consumer behavior has delivered a sharp reality check.

Everyday users, digital creators, and developers don't want to manage local Python virtual environments, configure cloud GPUs, or pay $29-to-$60 monthly subscriptions for tools they use intermittently. Nowhere has this architectural shift been more evident than in the explosive viral spread of the "Outstanding" Tiny Desk meme across TikTok, Instagram Reels, and YouTube Shorts.

When millions of users wanted to place a friend, colleague, or pet behind an intimate acoustic desk belting out soulful R&B vocals, they didn't reach for open-prompt diffusion platforms. They turned to hyper-focused, browser-first micro-studios.

Here is an architectural breakdown of why constrained single-purpose web applications are beating open-prompt giants, how audio-driven synchronization solves the uncanny valley, and why consumer software is returning to frictionless, transaction-based web models.

1. The Open-Prompt Bottleneck: Why Generalist Models Fail at Satire

Satire and comedy operate on extreme precision. In short-form video, humor is born from the tension between an absurd situation and deadpan realism.

When developers attempt to build comedic parody pipelines using general-purpose text-to-video APIs, three fundamental engineering bottlenecks emerge:

A. Environmental Drift and Spatial Hallucination

When an open-ended diffusion model is given a prompt such as "a man singing behind an acoustic wooden desk with bookshelves," it treats every single frame as a stochastic probability field. Across a 10-second sequence, the desk surface warps, background vinyl records turn into indistinct textures, and microphones float through the subject's face.

Comedic satire requires the setting to be indisputable and rock-solid. If the audience notices the background breathing or morphing, the immersion breaks, and the joke fails.

B. Facial Identity Elasticity

Standard video generation pipelines struggle to maintain facial structural landmarks during expressive, high-velocity audio performances. To force a static 2D portrait to sing, generic tools often over-smooth facial textures into waxy plastic or distort the jawline beyond recognition. The humor of a parody depends entirely on recognizing your actual friend or coworker singing—not an anonymous CGI avatar.

C. The Cognitive Friction of Prompt Engineering

Prompt engineering was always a transitional user interface. Forcing an everyday user to guess magic keywords ("photorealistic, 8k, octane render, vintage condenser mic, steady tripod") is an anti-pattern. Great web engineering abstracts prompt mechanics completely away from the user interface.

2. Spatial Constraint as an Architectural Moat

The solution to environmental drift is not larger models or longer prompts; it is radical environmental constraint.

By eliminating spatial freedom and locking the generative canvas into an immutable physical scene, engineering teams can solve the majority of visual artifacts:

┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                   GENERAL DIFFUSION VS CONSTRAINED UX                  │
├────────────────────────────┬───────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ Open-Prompt Pipelines      │ Free-form text input → Unpredictable room │
│                            │ geometry → Frequent facial distortion.    │
├────────────────────────────┼───────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ Constrained Micro-Studios  │ Fixed acoustic staging → 100% focus on    │
│                            │ facial fidelity → Zero background drift.  │
└────────────────────────────┴───────────────────────────────────────────┘

In the case of the Tiny Desk meme, the physical setting is iconic and fixed:

  • An intimate, cluttered wooden desk framed by analog studio monitors;
  • Curated paperbacks and vintage vinyl records in the background;
  • Soft, incandescent warm lighting replicating a real creative office session;
  • A classic retro condenser microphone anchored in the lower-middle third of the frame.

By keeping the background geometry deterministic, the synthesis pipeline can allocate 100% of its computing budget to what actually matters: natural facial preservation and micro-expression timing.

3. Audio-Driven Lip Sync: The Mechanics of Believability

Singing is far more complex than opening and closing a mouth mesh. Believable vocal performance requires phoneme-accurate mouth articulation, throat muscle tension, rhythmic brow movement, and natural eyelid squinting on sustained notes.

Modern micro-studios decouple audio generation from video rendering:

  1. Mastered Audio Anchoring: Rather than generating synthetic audio on the fly, the pipeline anchors the performance to an authentic, high-fidelity acoustic track (such as Charlie Wilson's viral live performance of "Outstanding" from NPR Music).
  2. Audio-to-Phoneme Alignment: The audio spectrum directly drives the temporal deformation of the lips and jaw, ensuring that vowel transitions and consonant stops match the rhythm down to the millisecond.
  3. Identity Landmark Locking: Critical facial identifiers—eye spacing, smile lines, nasal bridge contours, and skin tone—are preserved without the synthetic smoothing typical of generic video filters.

The result is a clip that passes the "10-Second Believability Threshold": viewers instantly recognize their real-life colleague or friend delivering an emotional musical performance with complete sincerity.

4. The Engineering Case Study: Building a Zero-Prompt Web Studio

An illustrative implementation of this architecture is TinyDeskMeme, a specialized browser platform engineered specifically for the viral acoustic desk format.

Instead of building a heavyweight native desktop application or asking users to install mobile apps with predatory permissions, the service is built as a pure, browser-first Tiny Desk meme video generator:

flowchart LR
    A["1. Client-Side Upload\n(1 Portrait from Mobile Camera Roll)"] --> B["2. Format Selection\n(9:16 Vertical for TikTok / 16:9 Landscape)"]
    B --> C["3. Cloud Orchestration\n(Locked desk staging + audio-driven sync)"]
    C --> D["4. Direct MP4 Delivery\n(10s HD video ready in browser, zero app install)"]

Key Architectural Decisions:

  • Zero Client-Side Footprint: Everything runs inside modern mobile and desktop browsers (Safari, Chrome, Firefox). Users never install native apps or manage local software dependencies.
  • No Prompt Syntax Required: Users never write descriptions, configure seed values, or tweak sliders. You upload a clear photo, pick your desired aspect ratio, and the platform delivers the finished video.
  • The $9.99 One-Time Transaction: Rejecting the pervasive SaaS subscription trap ($29/month recurring models with artificial token expirations), platforms like tinydeskmeme.com employ a transparent guest-checkout model. Creators pay $9.99 for a completed video with zero ongoing billing commitments.

5. Architectural Principles for Next-Generation Creative Web Apps

For developers and founders building in the generative media space, the viral trajectory of the Tiny Desk meme offers four critical takeaways:

1. Abstract Away the Prompt

Prompts are a developer debug interface, not a consumer product. If your users have to spend ten minutes learning how to talk to your AI, your product design is incomplete. Constrain the problem space until a single button or upload handles the job.

2. Design for Algorithmic Retention

In short-form video (TikTok, Reels, Shorts), video length is a critical ranking factor. A 10-to-12-second clip is the optimal window: 0–2 seconds to establish the familiar desk setting, 3–7 seconds to introduce the unexpected vocals, and 8–10 seconds to deliver the comedic punch before looping automatically.

3. Respect Creator Time and Privacy

Users are exhausted by mandatory account creation, email verification loops, and forced software downloads just to test a single feature. Delivering immediate utility with clear data privacy and guest checkout builds far greater long-term brand equity than gating experiences behind registration walls.

Conclusion

The evolution of the creative web is moving rapidly from infinite generative complexity to frictionless, dedicated utility.

While large research labs continue building massive world-simulators, the tools that capture cultural mindshare are those that solve one exact creative problem with zero friction. By combining a culturally resonant audio format with locked environmental geometry and a seamless browser interface, single-purpose studios are proving that in modern software design, constraints are the ultimate foundation of creative excellence.

title: Scalable React Project Structure with Vite and Tailwind CSS
description:
Scalable React Project Structure with Vite and Tailwind CSS

Building a React application is easy to start. Keeping it maintainable as it grows is the real challenge.

As new features are added, a project can quickly become difficult to navigate. Components end up in the wrong folders, API requests are scattered across the codebase, and business logic becomes tightly coupled to the UI.

A well-organized React project structure helps developers maintain clean code, reuse components, and scale applications without introducing unnecessary complexity.

In this article, I'll share a practical folder architecture for React applications built with Vite and Tailwind CSS, explain the purpose of each directory, and discuss when to use shared components versus feature-based modules.

1. Why Does React Project Structure Matter?

React doesn't enforce a specific folder structure. This flexibility is useful, but it also means developers need to establish conventions that fit their projects.

Without a clear structure, you may encounter problems such as:

  • A single components/ folder containing dozens of unrelated files.
  • API calls mixed directly into UI components.
  • Custom hooks duplicated across different features.
  • Business logic scattered throughout the application.
  • Difficult refactoring as the codebase grows.

The goal isn't to create as many folders as possible. It's to make the codebase predictable, easy to navigate, and straightforward to maintain.

2. A Scalable React Folder Structure

For a medium-sized application, a feature-based architecture is a practical starting point.

Here's an example:

src/
├── assets/
├── components/
│   ├── ui/
│   │   ├── Button.jsx
│   │   ├── Input.jsx
│   │   └── Modal.jsx
│   └── layout/
│       ├── Navbar.jsx
│       └── Footer.jsx
├── features/
│   ├── auth/
│   │   ├── components/
│   │   ├── hooks/
│   │   └── services/
│   ├── projects/
│   │   ├── components/
│   │   ├── hooks/
│   │   └── services/
│   └── dashboard/
│       ├── components/
│       └── hooks/
├── hooks/
├── services/
│   └── api.js
├── utils/
├── App.jsx
├── main.jsx
└── index.css

This structure separates shared application resources from feature-specific code.

Important: You don't need to create every directory immediately. Start with what your application requires and introduce additional folders when they provide a clear benefit.

3. Understanding the Main Directories

components/ — Reusable UI Components

The components/ directory contains UI elements shared across different parts of the application.

Examples include:

  • Buttons and input fields.
  • Modals and dropdowns.
  • Navigation bars and footers.
  • Reusable loading and error states.

For example, a generic Button component can be used in authentication forms, dashboard actions, and project pages without duplicating its implementation.

A useful rule is to keep shared components independent of specific business features whenever possible.

features/ — Feature-Based Modules

The features/ directory groups related code by functionality rather than by file type.

For example:

features/projects/
├── components/
│   ├── ProjectCard.jsx
│   └── ProjectList.jsx
├── hooks/
│   └── useProjects.js
└── services/
    └── projectService.js

Everything related to the projects feature stays together.

This approach makes it easier to understand a feature, add functionality, and refactor its implementation without searching through unrelated directories.

services/ — API Communication

API configuration should be separated from UI components.

For example, if you're using Axios, you can create a shared API client:

// src/services/api.js
import axios from "axios";

const api = axios.create({
  baseURL: import.meta.env.VITE_API_URL,
  timeout: 10000,
});

export default api;

Then create a service dedicated to project-related requests:

// src/features/projects/services/projectService.js
import api from "../../../services/api";

export async function getProjects() {
  const { data } = await api.get("/projects");
  return data;
}

Your components can now call the appropriate service instead of handling HTTP configuration themselves.

This separation also makes API logic easier to test and maintain.

Security note: Vite exposes variables prefixed with VITE_ to client-side code. Never store private API keys, database credentials, or server-side secrets in these variables.

hooks/ — Custom React Hooks

Custom hooks help extract reusable stateful behavior from components.

Examples include hooks for browser events, media queries, or shared UI behavior.

Keep hooks used across multiple features in the global hooks/ directory. If a hook belongs exclusively to one feature, place it inside that feature's directory.

This keeps related functionality close together.

utils/ — Shared Helper Functions

The utils/ directory contains general-purpose functions that don't belong to a specific feature.

Examples include:

  • Date formatting.
  • String manipulation.
  • Generic data transformations.
  • Reusable formatting helpers.

Avoid turning this directory into a collection of unrelated business logic. If a utility is specific to a feature, keep it near that feature.

4. Shared Components vs. Feature Components

One common architectural question is where a component should live.

Consider a ProjectCard component.

If it's designed specifically for displaying project information and is only used by the projects feature, keep it inside:

features/projects/components/

On the other hand, a generic Button or Modal used across unrelated features belongs in the shared components/ directory.

This distinction helps prevent shared components from becoming tightly coupled to application-specific business logic.

My recommendation: Don't move components into a global directory just because they might be reusable someday. Extract them when a genuine reuse case appears.

5. Where Should State Management Live?

Folder structure and state management should work together.

A practical approach is to choose state management based on the scope of the state:

  • Local state: Use useState or useReducer for state owned by an individual component.
  • Feature state: Keep feature-specific state and related logic close to the feature.
  • Shared application state: Consider Context or Redux Toolkit when multiple parts of the application need coordinated access to the same state.

You don't need Redux just because your application contains several components.

Start with React's built-in tools and introduce additional state management when the application's requirements justify it.

6. Organizing Tailwind CSS

Tailwind CSS works naturally with this architecture.

You can keep utility classes inside component markup and extract repeated UI patterns into reusable components.

For example:

export default function Button({ children, onClick }) {
  return (
    <button
      onClick={onClick}
      className="rounded-lg bg-blue-600 px-4 py-2
                 font-medium text-white
                 transition hover:bg-blue-700"
    >
      {children}
    </button>
  );
}

Instead of duplicating the same button styles throughout your application, you can reuse the component and maintain a consistent design.

For larger projects, consider establishing shared design tokens and consistent component APIs to make the interface easier to maintain.

7. Common Mistakes to Avoid

Even a well-designed folder structure can become difficult to maintain if it's applied without clear principles.

Here are some mistakes worth avoiding:

  1. Overengineering too early: Don't create unnecessary abstractions before you need them.
  2. Mixing unrelated features: Keep feature-specific components and services close to their functionality.
  3. Duplicating API configuration: Use a shared API client when appropriate.
  4. Putting everything in utils/: Keep business logic close to the feature it belongs to.
  5. Making every component global: Promote components to shared directories when there is a real reason to do so.
  6. Treating one structure as universal: The right architecture depends on project size, team conventions, and application requirements.

A good folder structure should reduce cognitive overhead, not increase it.

8. Final Thoughts

A scalable React project structure is about clear boundaries and maintainable code, not the number of folders in your repository.

For smaller applications, a simple structure is often sufficient. As the codebase grows, a feature-based architecture can help organize components, hooks, services, and utilities around real application functionality.

Start simple, keep related code together, and refactor when your current structure begins to slow down development.

If you're building React applications, take some time to review your current folder structure. Small organizational improvements can make a significant difference as your project evolves.

Let's Connect

I'm a Full Stack Developer interested in building maintainable web applications and exploring practical software architecture.

You can explore my portfolio and projects here:

  • Portfolio: https://mostafanagedy.vercel.app/
  • GitHub: https://github.com/mostafanagedy
  • LinkedIn: https://www.linkedin.com/in/mostafa-nagdey/

What's your preferred approach to organizing React applications: feature-based, type-based, or a combination of both? Share your experience in the comments!

title: Moving a side project to Cloud Run: the deploy pipeline I ended up with
description:
I moved a small side project from a single VM to Cloud Run mostly because I was tired of patching the box. This is the deploy pipeline I settled on, not the one I started with.

The first version was too clever

My initial pipeline built the image, pushed it, deployed, and then ran a smoke test. It broke constantly: the smoke test ran before the new revision had any traffic, the rollback was "redeploy the previous image" typed by hand, and I once deployed on a Friday because I wasn't paying attention.

What I have now

A GitHub Actions workflow with three steps:

  1. Build and push the image, tagged with the commit SHA. No latest, ever. If I can't tell exactly what's running, I can't roll back.
  2. Deploy with --no-traffic, which creates a revision without sending it live.
  3. Run the smoke test against the tagged revision URL, then move traffic with a single command.

The important part is step 2. Deploying a revision without traffic means a broken build never serves a single request, and the rollback is just "point traffic back at the previous revision" — one command, no rebuild.

Things that bit me

Cloud Run sets PORT for you. My app had a hardcoded 8080 and worked locally, then failed in production because the platform expected it to read the env var. Now I read process.env.PORT first, with a local default.

Health checks: I used to rely on the TCP check and it was useless. A real HTTP endpoint that checks the dependencies gives you a revision that fails to go healthy, which is far better than one that serves 500s.

Secrets: never in the image. The runtime service account pulls them from Secret Manager at boot, or they're injected as env vars at deploy. I had one accidental commit of a .env file early on and it scared me straight.

What I'd do with more traffic

Traffic splitting by percentage, and maybe a canary step between smoke test and full rollout. For a side project that nobody is paying for, the current version is enough: broken revisions don't get traffic, rollback is one command, and I can deploy from a phone if I have to.

title: Cloud Run cold starts: what I measured and what I changed
description:
We moved a small API to Cloud Run and immediately started getting complaints about the first request of the day being slow. So I spent a week measuring cold starts instead of guessing.

How I measured

Not with synthetic benchmarks, but with the actual requests: the service logs a timestamp on entry, and I recorded the gap between the request arriving at the load balancer and the first line of our handler executing. That includes platform time we can't control, which is the honest number a user experiences.

I ran this for a week, then made one change at a time and watched the same metric.

What moved the needle

Container size was the biggest single factor. Our first image was built from a full node image with dev dependencies, about 900MB. A multi-stage build with a distroless base brought it to under 100MB, and the p50 cold start dropped from roughly 4 seconds to under 2.

Minimum instances made the tail disappear. We set --min-instances=1 on the service that humans actually wait on, and kept zero for the internal batch jobs. The cost difference for a small instance was about the same as one coffee a week, which I'm happy to pay for not getting "is it down?" messages.

Startup work was the sneaky one. We had a config loader that fetched a dozen secrets over the network on boot. Moving those to environment variables configured at deploy time removed almost a second, and made the service start deterministically.

What didn't help

More memory. I tried bumping to a larger instance class and the cold start barely changed. It does help throughput, not startup.

Parallelism settings: they change how many requests an instance handles, not how fast it starts. Worth tuning separately, and only if you have the traffic to justify it.

The current setup

Small multi-stage image, secrets via env vars, min instances of 1 on the user-facing API, zero everywhere else, and an alert when the p95 startup exceeds our old baseline. Nothing clever. The main lesson was that cold starts are mostly a build-and-boot problem, and the platform will only fix the part it owns.

title: What I actually use Cloud Run for (and what I don't)
description:
I've been running small services on Cloud Run for about a year now. Not a big migration story, just the honest list of where it fits and where it doesn't.

What it's genuinely good at

Internal webhooks. We have a handful of integrations that get maybe a hundred requests a day, each spike is unpredictable, and the rest of the time nobody is calling them. Cloud Run scales to zero, so the bill is basically nothing and I don't have to think about a VM.

Scheduled jobs that used to be cron on a box. Cloud Scheduler hitting a Cloud Run service with a shared secret is boring and reliable, which is exactly what I want for a nightly job.

Small internal tools: a form that writes to a sheet, a service that reformats a file and drops it in a bucket. The kind of thing where the code is fifty lines and the deployment used to be a whole afternoon.

What I don't use it for

Anything with a long-running connection. WebSockets are possible but I'd rather not fight with the request timeout and eventual cold starts. If the service needs to hold a connection for minutes, I put it somewhere else.

Stateful things. Cloud Run gives you no guarantees about which instance handles the next request, so anything that needs a local cache or a local file needs to be designed around that from day one. I learned this the hard way with a SQLite experiment that worked perfectly on my laptop and fell apart the moment two instances existed.

GPU workloads. Not the right product, and pretending otherwise is how you end up debugging someone else's scheduler.

The part people skip: cold starts

For low-traffic internal tools, cold starts are the whole story. The first request after idle can take a few seconds, and for a user clicking a form that feels broken. Two fixes that actually helped: keep the container small (multi-stage build, scratch or distroless base), and set a minimum instance count of 1 for anything a human waits on. The second one costs money, but less than you'd think for a small instance.

What I'd tell someone starting

Start with one small service and no min instances. Watch the cold starts for a week, and only then decide what deserves a minimum instance. The default configuration is a reasonable starting point, and most of the tuning advice you read online is for traffic you don't have yet.

title: ANS-C01 Exam Guide: Cost, Format and Study Plan
description:
The AWS Certified Advanced Networking - Specialty (ANS-C01) exam proves you can design, build and troubleshoot complex networks on AWS and connect them to on-premises sites. Plan on 8 to 12 weeks of study if you already work with AWS networking, and longer if you do not. Hands-on labs matter more than reading.

This guide covers what the exam tests, the format, the cost, a weekly plan, common mistakes and what happens after you pass.

What ANS-C01 proves and who should take it

This is a specialty certification. It is not an entry point. It targets people who already design or run networks and now need to do it on AWS.

Good fits include:

  • Network engineers moving from data center or WAN work into cloud.
  • Cloud architects who own hybrid connectivity, DNS and routing.
  • Security engineers who design traffic inspection and segmentation.

AWS has commonly recommended several years of networking experience and some hands-on AWS time before this exam. If you have never built a VPC or read a BGP table, start with a broader cloud path first. Our Cloud Computing and Networking category pages list other options.

Exam format and skills measured

The exam is commonly described as about 65 questions in 170 minutes, with multiple-choice and multiple-response items. Scores are scaled from 100 to 1000, and the passing score is 750. Questions are mostly long scenarios where several answers look reasonable and only one meets every requirement. Check the current figures on the official AWS exam page before you book.

The four domains and their commonly published weights are:

Domain Weight
Network Design 30%
Network Implementation 26%
Network Security, Compliance, and Governance 24%
Network Management and Operation 20%

In practice, these topics carry the exam:

  • Connectivity: Transit Gateway, VPC peering, PrivateLink, Direct Connect, Site-to-Site VPN.
  • Routing: BGP attributes, route propagation, route table priority, Direct Connect gateways and virtual interfaces.
  • DNS: Route 53 public and private zones, Route 53 Resolver endpoints and rules.
  • Edge and delivery: CloudFront, Global Accelerator, load balancer types.
  • Security and visibility: security groups, network ACLs, AWS Network Firewall, VPC Flow Logs, Traffic Mirroring.

Use the official exam guide PDF from AWS as your checklist. If a topic is on it, you should be able to build it and break it.

What the exam costs and what our voucher includes

AWS has commonly listed specialty exams at $300 USD. Confirm the current price on the AWS Certification page, since AWS can change it and taxes may apply.

Item Price
AWS list price (commonly listed) $300 USD
Our ANS-C01 voucher (October 29, 2026) $279.99 USD

One voucher covers one exam attempt. Here is how our store handles delivery and refunds:

  • The voucher code is emailed within 12 hours of payment. It also appears in your account.
  • You can cancel an order for a full refund before delivery.
  • A delivered code is non-refundable unless the test provider rejects it as invalid, already used or expired on first use.
  • In that case, contact support within 14 days with your order number and a screenshot. We replace or refund the code.

Full terms are on our refund policy and delivery policy pages. If you are ready to book, here is the ANS-C01 voucher.

A 10-week study plan with weekly hours

This plan assumes about 8 to 10 hours per week and some AWS experience. Add two to four weeks if networking is new to you.

Week Focus Hours
1 Read the exam guide. VPC fundamentals, subnets, route tables, gateways. Take a baseline practice test. 8
2 Transit Gateway: attachments, route tables, association vs propagation. 9
3 Direct Connect: dedicated vs hosted, private, public and transit VIFs, Direct Connect gateway. 10
4 Site-to-Site VPN, BGP, ECMP, accelerated VPN, backup paths. 10
5 Route 53, Route 53 Resolver, hybrid DNS, split-horizon patterns. 9
6 Load balancers, CloudFront, Global Accelerator, PrivateLink. 9
7 Security groups, NACLs, Network Firewall, centralized inspection designs. 9
8 Monitoring and troubleshooting: Flow Logs, Reachability Analyzer, CloudWatch, Traffic Mirroring. 9
9 Timed practice exams. Review every wrong answer and write down why. 10
10 Weak domains only. Light review. Rest the day before. 6

Pick one domain per week to build in your own account, even if the build is small.

A worked lab: isolate prod and dev behind one Transit Gateway

This scenario shows up in many forms on the exam. You have three VPCs: prod, dev and shared services. Prod and dev must both reach shared services but never each other.

  1. Create one Transit Gateway with default route table association and propagation turned off.
  2. Attach all three VPCs to the Transit Gateway.
  3. Create two Transit Gateway route tables: one for spokes (prod and dev) and one for shared services.
  4. Associate prod and dev attachments with the spoke table. Associate shared services with its own table.
  5. Propagate only the shared services attachment into the spoke table. Propagate prod and dev into the shared table.
  6. Update each VPC's subnet route tables. Add routes to the other VPCs' CIDRs with the Transit Gateway attachment as the target. Without these routes, traffic never reaches the Transit Gateway.

The result is that the Transit Gateway spoke table holds only the shared services route. Prod and dev cannot reach each other through it. Then verify it from the CLI:

aws ec2 describe-transit-gateway-attachments
aws ec2 get-transit-gateway-route-table-associations --transit-gateway-route-table-id tgw-rtb-0example
aws ec2 search-transit-gateway-routes --transit-gateway-route-table-id tgw-rtb-0example --filters Name=type,Values=propagated

The first command lists attachments. The second shows which attachments use each route table. The third shows learned routes. Run the last two against the spoke table and confirm that only the shared services CIDR appears. Replace the example route table ID with your own.

When you finish, delete the Transit Gateway and its attachments. They are billed hourly while they exist.

Common mistakes that cost points

  • Memorizing service names instead of routing logic. Many questions ask which route wins or why traffic is dropped.
  • Skipping hands-on work. Reading about Direct Connect VIF types is not the same as configuring them in a lab or reviewing a real setup.
  • Ignoring DNS. Hybrid DNS with Resolver inbound and outbound endpoints is a frequent weak spot.
  • Missing the cheapest requirement. Scenarios often add cost, latency or resilience constraints. Read the last sentence of each question first.
  • Trusting exam dumps. They are often outdated or wrong, and they can breach exam rules. Use official docs, whitepapers and legitimate practice tests.
  • Not managing time. With long scenarios, flag hard questions and return to them. Aim for roughly two minutes per question on the first pass.

After you pass

AWS certifications are commonly valid for three years, and you recertify by passing the current exam again or a qualifying higher-level one. Check your AWS Certification account for your exact expiry date.

Use the badge to back up real work: a hybrid connectivity redesign, a DNS migration or a centralized inspection project. If you want a security angle next, see our Cybersecurity category. Our Security+ study guide is also useful if you need stronger security fundamentals.

title: 7 UI/UX Mistakes That Make Startup Landing Pages Look Unprofessional
description:
A great product can still lose customers if the landing page is confusing or hard to use.

Here are 7 UI/UX mistakes I see often on startup landing pages:

1. Weak headline
Visitors should understand what you do within 5 seconds.

Fix: Say clearly what your product does and who it helps.

2. Too many fonts and colors

Too many styles make a page feel messy and unprofessional.

Fix: Use one main font and 2–3 consistent colors.

3. No clear call to action

Visitors should not have to guess what to do next.

Fix: Use one strong CTA such as “Start Free” or “Book a Demo.”

4. Poor mobile design

Most visitors will view your page on a phone.

Fix: Test your text size, spacing, images, and buttons on mobile.

5. Cluttered sections

Trying to say everything at once overwhelms visitors.

Fix: Keep one section focused on one message.

6. Low contrast text

Light gray text may look modern, but it can be hard to read.

Fix: Keep important text clear, readable, and high-contrast.

7. No trust signals

People hesitate to sign up when they see no proof.

Fix: Add testimonials, customer logos, reviews, or clear security information.

Quick rule: If a visitor cannot understand your product and next step within 5 seconds, improve the UX before spending more on ads.

I’m a UI/UX designer helping startups and businesses improve landing pages, mobile app screens, and product flows. If you’re building something and want a quick UX perspective, feel free to connect.

title: Logistics Spend Caps and Rate Limiting: Why Attribution Breaks First (and What I Measure)
description:
A logistics platform should treat a provider-enforced spend cap and an application rate limiter as two different failure boundaries. The cap can stop eligible billable work only where the upstream account recognizes the cap; the limiter can slow or reject requests only where our application sees them. Neither one, by itself, can tell us which warehouse, route, or customer caused the balance to fall.

Short answer: use the upstream cap as a last-resort account boundary, and use application rate limiting as a controllable traffic boundary. Put attribution in the metering path between them: record the tenant, operation, provider account, request outcome, and chargeable quantity before aggregating. If the prepaid balance runs out unattended, the missing control is usually an identity and reconciliation decision, not another dashboard.

The incident lesson is about identity, not throttling

I carry a pager, so I distrust a green dashboard that cannot answer a basic question: what page fired, and which account paid for the work? In a logistics workload, one provider account may serve several customers. A burst of route estimates can look ordinary at the application edge while the bill is attributed to one shared credential.

The operational constraint changes the design. We need billing attribution to survive retries, delays, rejections, and upstream policy decisions. A request ID is useful for tracing; it is not a billing identity. A customer ID is useful for attribution; it is not proof that the provider charged that customer. Those are separate claims.

The invariant I use is narrow: every billable attempt gets one immutable metering record, and every aggregate can be traced back to it without trusting the caller to report its own charge. The record should carry a tenant identifier, operation name, provider account or credential class, request identifier, measured quantity, and terminal decision. In the HTTP layer, a local limiter can return 429 Too Many Requests as defined by RFC 6585, but that status still says nothing about a provider-side charge.

That distinction is easy to miss.

Can an API hard spend cap replace application rate limiting?

An API hard spend cap belongs to the billing boundary. Its promise is narrow: after the provider evaluates the cap, eligible activity for that account may be prevented or suspended, subject to its enforcement rules. It cannot normally distinguish two internal tenants sharing that account, repair a missing tenant ID, classify a retry, or explain usage that has not reached the usage feed.

Application rate limiting belongs to the request boundary. A token bucket, concurrency limit, or per-tenant quota can protect a service from bursts using identities we control. It cannot know final provider price from request count alone, account for variable work without metering, or stop a worker that bypasses the edge limiter.

The worker path is where the neat diagram usually breaks.

Boundary Can control Cannot prove
Provider spend cap Eligible billable activity after provider evaluation Which internal tenant caused the charge
Application limiter Arrival rate, concurrency, tenant admission Provider billing outcome or final price
Metering and reconciliation Attribution across attempts An upstream decision it never received

This is the useful comparison. Calling any one of these a universal spend control is the failure mode.

How do I preserve attribution when the balance is low?

I separate admission from accounting. Admission asks whether a request may start. Accounting records what happened, including a rejection. A low-balance mode should be explicit and reversible; it should not be inferred from a timeout, because a timeout says the client did not receive a result, not that the provider did no work.

Here is the smallest useful Go shape. It records the local admission decision without pretending local code is the billing authority:

package spendcontrol

import (
    "context"
    "errors"
    "time"
)

var ErrRateLimited = errors.New("request rejected by local limiter")

type Meter struct {
    TenantID      string
    Operation     string
    ProviderClass string
    RequestID     string
    Quantity      int64
    Decision      string
    ObservedAt    time.Time
}

type Ledger interface {
    Append(context.Context, Meter) error
}

type Admission interface {
    Allow(context.Context, string, string) bool
}

func Admit(ctx context.Context, ledger Ledger, limiter Admission, m Meter) error {
    if !limiter.Allow(ctx, m.TenantID, m.Operation) {
        m.Decision = "rate_limited"
        m.ObservedAt = time.Now().UTC()
        if err := ledger.Append(ctx, m); err != nil {
            return err
        }
        return ErrRateLimited
    }
    m.Decision = "admitted"
    m.ObservedAt = time.Now().UTC()
    return ledger.Append(ctx, m)
}

In production I would also record completion, provider response class, retry number, and the usage event used for reconciliation. The ledger needs an idempotency key so a retry cannot create a second billable-looking event. That key should come from stable business identity, not a timestamp that changes on every attempt.

There is a real trade-off. Recording before the provider call gives stronger evidence of intent; recording only after success gives cleaner evidence of completed work. I prefer both states when the operation has material billing impact. For a cheap, strictly idempotent read, one event may be enough.

Why do budget alerts fail as hard caps?

Budget tooling is useful for detection and forecasting, but an alert is not an enforcement boundary. AWS Budgets documents threshold actions, Google Cloud budgets document alerts and programmatic notifications, and Azure Cost Management budgets document alert conditions and actions. Their boundaries and delays differ, so none should be treated as an instantaneous provider-side stop without verifying the contract.

The practical test is simple: does the control reject the next billable operation, at which boundary, and with what delay or eligibility rules? Then ask whether the resulting event can be attributed to one internal tenant without reconstructing identity from a shared key.

These products are useful evidence of the distinction, not interchangeable recommendations. AWS Budgets can feed an action workflow; Google Cloud budgets expose alerting; Azure Cost Management budgets support budget alerts. The limitation is common: budget observation does not automatically create tenant-level billing isolation. A team that needs that isolation must build or obtain a separate metering boundary.

Secrets management matters because credentials define the provider account boundary. OWASP recommends controlled secret lifecycle practices. A rotated key can still represent the same shared account, and a new key does not create tenant-level billing isolation. Credential hygiene reduces exposure; it does not substitute for attribution.

The decision rule I would ship

Use application rate limiting when the immediate risk is burst behavior, queue growth, or disproportionate tenant concurrency. Key it by tenant and operation, and inventory worker paths that bypass the edge.

Use a provider-side hard cap as the last line of defense against unattended account exhaustion. Treat scope and delay as facts to verify, not assumptions inferred from a dashboard.

Use metering and reconciliation when the requirement is accurate billing attribution. Store who requested the work, which provider account was used, what operation ran, what quantity was observed, and how the event was reconciled.

Test a rejected request, a timeout after upstream acceptance, a retry, a shared credential, and a bypass worker. Compare the internal ledger with the provider usage export. The result should remain explainable when the balance is zero.

References

  • OWASP Secrets Management Cheat Sheet: https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Secrets_Management_Cheat_Sheet.html
  • AWS Budgets documentation: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/cost-management/latest/userguide/budgets-managing-costs.html
  • Google Cloud budgets and budget alerts: https://cloud.google.com/billing/docs/how-to/budgets
  • Microsoft Azure Cost Management budgets: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/cost-management-billing/costs/tutorial-acm-create-budgets
  • RFC 6585, Additional HTTP Status Codes: https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6585

title: Shipping an Arabic Version of Your App: What Your Translator Needs From You
description:
If your product is launching in Saudi Arabia or the wider Gulf, an Arabic version usually ends up on someone's task list as "send the strings to the translator". From the translator's side of the table, most delays and most bad Arabic UI text come from a handful of engineering decisions made before the first string was sent.

Here is what makes Arabic localization go smoothly, written from the translation side but aimed at developers.

1. Plurals: Arabic has six forms, not two

English has one and other. Arabic, according to the Unicode CLDR plural rules, uses six categories: zero, one, two, few, many and other. If your code builds sentences like count + " files", there is no correct Arabic translation for it.

Use ICU MessageFormat (or your framework's equivalent) and let the translator fill in every category:

{count, plural,
  zero {لا توجد ملفات}
  one {ملف واحد}
  two {ملفان}
  few {# ملفات}
  many {# ملفًا}
  other {# ملف}
}

In JavaScript you can see which category the runtime picks for a given number:

const pr = new Intl.PluralRules('ar');
[0, 1, 2, 3, 11, 100].map(n => `${n}: ${pr.select(n)}`);
// "0: zero", "1: one", "2: two", "3: few", "11: many", "100: other"

2. Never concatenate translated fragments

"Welcome, " + name + "! You have " + n + " new messages" forces the translator to translate three disconnected pieces and hope the word order works. Arabic word order and gender agreement often need the whole sentence. Send complete messages with named placeholders ({name}, {count}) and keep them together.

3. Give every string context

"Open" can be a button (a verb: افتح), a status (an adjective: مفتوح) or a shop's opening time. "Save" can be a button or "save 20%". A key like btn.open plus a one-line comment or a screenshot saves a round of questions and prevents the wrong form shipping. Gender matters too: if a string addresses the user directly, tell the translator whether a neutral form is required.

4. Right-to-left is a layout problem, not a translation problem

The translator delivers Arabic text. Whether it reads correctly depends on your markup and CSS:

  • Set dir="rtl" and lang="ar" on the root (or the relevant container), not just text-align: right.
  • Use logical CSS properties (margin-inline-start, padding-inline-end, inset-inline-start) instead of left/right, so the same stylesheet works in both directions.
  • Mirror directional icons (back/forward arrows, progress chevrons), but not icons that represent real objects or brands.
  • Wrap user-generated or mixed-direction values (names, emails, order numbers, Latin product names) in <bdi> or use unicode-bidi: isolate, so a phone number or an English product name inside an Arabic sentence does not scramble the punctuation around it.

5. Let text grow and use a real Arabic font

Arabic UI strings are often similar in length to English but can be noticeably taller and sometimes longer, especially in short labels. Avoid fixed-width buttons and truncated labels. Choose a font with proper Arabic glyphs and test diacritics and line height. Fallback system fonts can look very different on Android, iOS and Windows.

6. Dates, numbers and currency: format with Intl, don't translate

Do not put formatted dates or prices in translation files. Format them at runtime:

new Intl.DateTimeFormat('ar-SA-u-ca-islamic-umalqura', { dateStyle: 'long' }).format(new Date());
// Hijri (Umm al-Qura), e.g. "١٨ جمادى الأولى ١٤٤٨ هـ"

new Intl.DateTimeFormat('ar-SA-u-ca-gregory', { dateStyle: 'long' }).format(new Date());
// Gregorian with Arabic month names, e.g. "٢٩ أكتوبر ٢٠٢٦"

new Intl.NumberFormat('ar-SA', { style: 'currency', currency: 'SAR' }).format(1250);

Set the calendar explicitly with the -u-ca- extension: the default calendar for plain ar-SA is not the same in every browser and runtime version. Decide deliberately which calendar and which digits (Arabic-Indic ٠١٢٣ or Western 0123) your product shows, and apply that consistently. Official and financial documents in Saudi Arabia often carry both Hijri and Gregorian dates.

7. Send files the translator can work with

A structured export (JSON, XLIFF, .po, .strings, or a CSV with key, source, context and max-length columns) is far better than screenshots or a PDF of the UI. Lock placeholders and HTML tags so they cannot be translated by mistake, and include a glossary of product terms that must stay consistent across the app, the website and the help center.

8. Review in the running product

Translation in a spreadsheet is only half the job. Arabic must be reviewed in context: truncation, line breaks, mirrored layouts, and whether the tone fits a Saudi audience. Plan a short in-app review round before launch.

If you need the Arabic side handled professionally, this is the kind of work our website and app localization service covers (page in Arabic).

Disclosure: I work at Googan, a certified translation office in Riyadh (ISO 17100). This post is general guidance, not legal or regulatory advice.
