title: PhotoCraft: the open-source Photoshop rival you can drive from the terminal
description:
Originally published at aifrontierpost.com

Photoshop rebuilt from scratch in Rust, with 74,000 stars in four weeks — and a command-line tool that edits real photos without ever opening a window. This guide downloads the real release, verifies its checksum, and runs every headless command that matters: inspect, edit, batch, convert, and MCP. No account, no API key, no GPU, and every number below is one the installed tool printed.

TL;DR: PhotoCraft (storytold/photocraft) is an open-source, pure-Rust Photoshop rebuild: version 0.17.0 ships a headless CLI that inspects, edits, batch-grades, converts (including PSD), and serves the engine over MCP — all verified here with no account, no API key, and no GPU. The desktop app is early alpha and was not tested; the CLI path is the proven one.

  • Who: PhotoCraft (storytold/photocraft on GitHub), from the ArtCraft team — 74,359 stars, 7,040 commits, 13,130 forks, dual MIT/Apache-2.0, first committed September 30, 2026.
  • What: a clean-room Photoshop rebuild in pure Rust, plus a headless CLI: info, run, batch, convert, commands, and an MCP server — verified here end to end.
  • When: version verified in this guide is photocraft-cli 0.17.0, released and run October 28, 2026; star and commit counts are dated the same day.
  • Requirement: a Linux, macOS, or Windows machine and ~200 MB of free disk for the prebuilt release. No account, no API key, no GPU, no Rust toolchain.

Why this is blowing up now

PhotoCraft is a clean-room reimplementation of Photoshop, written from scratch in pure Rust. Layers, masks, adjustment layers, layer styles, type, vectors, brushes, and real PSD files — in a native app with no Electron and no web view. The repository (storytold/photocraft on GitHub) had 74,359 stars, 7,040 commits, and 13,130 forks when this guide read it on October 28, 2026, under a dual MIT/Apache-2.0 license. It was created on September 30, 2026, which makes that star count a four-week sprint, not a slow accumulation. Version 0.17.0 landed the same day this guide ran, October 28, 2026.

The part that makes it tutorial-worthy instead of just impressive is not the GUI. It is the headless command-line tool that ships in the same release. Every menu item, tool, and dialog in PhotoCraft runs a command from one registry of 500+ commands, and the UI, the CLI, the JSON control channel, and the MCP server all call the same commands. That means anything you can click, a script can do too — and this guide proves it, because every command below was run on a headless Linux server with no display, no account, no API key, and no GPU.

One boundary first, because it decides whether this tutorial is for you. PhotoCraft is in early alpha, and its own README says so plainly: much of Photoshop's feature surface exists in some form, but it is not yet a Photoshop replacement for daily professional work. The gaps it names are AI/generative features, 15 missing tools, depth in typography and pro workflows, and plug-in compatibility. What this guide verifies is the headless editing path — install, inspect, edit, batch, convert, and hand the engine to an agent over MCP. If you need a finished desktop replacement today, this is not that article. If you want a scriptable, offline, open-source photo engine, keep reading.

What you'll need

  • A Linux, macOS, or Windows machine. This guide ran on Linux (x86_64), using the prebuilt release tarball — no Rust toolchain, no source build, no compile wait.
  • About 200 MB of free disk. The Linux tarball is 123 MB; extracted, it is roughly twice that.
  • A terminal and a scratch directory with a photo or two to practise on. Do not practise on originals: the CLI overwrites nothing by default, but work on copies anyway.
  • No account, no API key, no GPU, no sign-in of any kind for anything in this guide. The desktop app's smart-selection features run on your machine with no cloud and no account, per the README; the CLI path here touches no network at all after the download.
  • Optional but useful: Python with Pillow, only if you want to diff pixels before and after like this guide did. It is not required for any step.

One photo in, one graded photo out: the CLI runs the same engine commands the desktop app runs. Image: AI Frontier Post.

Step 1: Get the real binary and check it

Download the release for your platform from the project's releases page. On Linux x86_64, the file is photocraft-0.17.0-linux-x86_64.tar.gz. The release also ships a SHA256SUMS.txt — check your download against it before you run anything from it:

curl -LO https://github.com/storytold/photocraft/releases/download/v0.17.0/photocraft-0.17.0-linux-x86_64.tar.gz
curl -LO https://github.com/storytold/photocraft/releases/download/v0.17.0/SHA256SUMS.txt
grep "linux-x86_64.tar.gz" SHA256SUMS.txt
sha256sum photocraft-0.17.0-linux-x86_64.tar.gz

Expected result, verified October 28, 2026: the hash printed by sha256sum is 5259f9c428c8ee3478c35500ece98713561cafc050e4c9eb354a5050f36eb2b8, matching the release checksum. If yours differs, stop — re-download, and do not run the binary.

Extract it and confirm the tool answers:

tar -xzf photocraft-0.17.0-linux-x86_64.tar.gz
./photocraft-0.17.0-linux-x86_64/bin/photocraft-cli --version
./photocraft-0.17.0-linux-x86_64/bin/photocraft-cli --help

Expected output:

photocraft-cli 0.17.0 (b8c3f3aa8, 2026-10-28)

The help listing shows eight subcommands: convert, info, run, batch, droplet, commands, mcp, and serve. This guide runs the first four plus commands and mcp. The tarball also contains the desktop app binary (photocraft), which needs a display and is not used here. Put the CLI on your PATH if you plan to use it regularly; the rest of this guide calls it as photocraft-cli for brevity.

Step 2: Inspect a photo before you touch it

Copy a photo into a scratch directory and ask the CLI what it sees. This guide used a 640×400 test image; substitute your own file:

mkdir photocraft-demo
cp your-photo.jpg photocraft-demo/
cd photocraft-demo
photocraft-cli info your-photo.jpg

Expected output (abridged): a JSON document describing the image — its channels (Red, Green, Blue), composite mode (RGB), and layer tree, starting with "activeLayer": 2 for a flat import. The info command changes nothing; it is the read-only way to confirm the CLI can parse your file before you build an edit chain on top of it. If info fails on your file, the edit steps will too, and you have found that out cheaply. Run it on every new format you plan to feed the tool: PNG, JPEG, WebP, TIFF, and PSD are all on the convert list, but your specific file is the only test that matters.

Step 3: Make your first headless edit

The core command is run: open a file, apply engine commands in order, save the result. This is the exact shape from the project's README, run here verbatim — a Smart Sharpen filter followed by a Curves adjustment layer:

photocraft-cli run your-photo.jpg \
  --cmd filter.sharpen.smartSharpen --params '{"amount":80}' \
  --cmd layer.newAdjustmentLayer.curves --params '{"points":[[0,0],[64,48],[192,212],[255,255]]}' \
  --out graded-photo.png

Expected output, as printed by the run in this guide:

{"command":"filter.sharpen.smartSharpen","result":{"filter":{"amount":80.0,"filter":"smartSharpen","radius":1.0,"reduceNoise":10.0},"layer":2}}
{"command":"layer.newAdjustmentLayer.curves","result":{"layer":3}}
warning: 2 layer(s) flattened; layers, masks and blend modes are not kept

Read that output carefully, because it teaches you three things. First, every command echoes its result as JSON, so a script can check success per step instead of trusting an exit code alone. Second, the defaults are visible: Smart Sharpen at amount 80 also applied radius 1.0 and noise reduction 10.0, which the command line never mentioned — when you tune a look, query the result JSON to see what actually ran. Third, the warning is real and worth understanding: PNG output is flat, so the adjustment layer and the sharpened layer were flattened into one image. The layers survive only in layered formats (the native .pcraft format, PSD, or TIFF with the --tiff-layers flag in batch mode). If your workflow needs the layers back later, export to a layered format; if you need a finished file for the web, PNG is the right, honest end of the chain.

Verify the edit did something, rather than assuming it. Open both files and compare: the output keeps the input's dimensions (640×400 in this guide's test) and the pixels change — a sample pixel moved from RGB (240, 230, 180) to (247, 241, 199) after the sharpen-plus-curves chain. Your numbers will differ with your photo and your curve points; what matters is that you check, because a command that silently no-ops is worse than one that errors.

To find more commands, ask the registry itself instead of guessing names:

photocraft-cli commands | grep -i -E "vibrance|curves|levels|hue"

This lists real, callable command IDs with their menu paths — for example layer.newAdjustmentLayer.vibrance, image.adjustments.levels, and layer.newAdjustmentLayer.hueSaturation. Every command in this guide came from that list or from the README; none was invented, and you should hold any other tutorial to the same rule.

Step 4: Grade a whole folder with one recipe file

Single-image edits are a demo. The real use case is a folder: a shoot, a product catalog, a set of blog images that all need the same grade. That is what batch is for. Write the recipe as a JSON list of steps, one file per look:

cat > grade.json << 'EOF'
[{"command":"filter.sharpen.smartSharpen","params":{"amount":80}}]
EOF
mkdir raw graded
cp photo-a.jpg photo-b.jpg raw/
photocraft-cli batch --actions grade.json --in ./raw --out ./graded

Expected output, verified with two test images:

ok    ./raw/a.png -> ./graded/a.png
ok    ./raw/b.png -> ./graded/b.png
2 succeeded, 0 failed

Two details in that recipe are load-bearing, and both were learned the hard way in this guide's sandbox. First, each step needs the key "command". The batch help also describes [id, params] pairs and bare ids, but a step written with "cmd" instead of "command" fails outright with error: invalid parameters for batch --actions: step needs "command" — that exact error is what this guide got on its first attempt, and the fix is the one-word key change above. Second, batch refuses to write into the input folder unless you pass --in-place; keep input and output separate, as above, so a bad recipe never eats your originals. Useful extras on the same command: --format webp to change the output format regardless of input extension, and --quality 85 for lossy JPEG/WebP output (without a quality value, WebP output is lossless).

Batch mode: one recipe file, every image in the folder, one graded set out. Image: AI Frontier Post.

Step 5: Convert formats, including real PSD files

PhotoCraft's headline format claim is PSD without compromise: its PSD support is a standalone crate written from Adobe's public specification, and the project reports re-saving renders identically for 307 of the 309 files in the psd-tools test set. You do not need Photoshop to test the round trip at the CLI level:

photocraft-cli convert your-photo.png your-photo.psd
photocraft-cli info your-photo.psd
photocraft-cli convert your-photo.png your-photo.webp

All three commands ran cleanly in this guide's sandbox: the PNG became an 84,898-byte PSD that info reads back as a valid RGB document, and the same PNG became a 1,248-byte WebP. The convert list covers .pcraft, .psd, .png, .jpg, .tif, .webp, .exr, and more, with the output extension picking the format unless --format overrides it. Two honest limits, both from the README: HEIC photos from iPhone and Mac are read-only, and AVIF is write-only in official builds. And the PSD fidelity figures above are the project's corpus numbers, not something this guide re-measured — treat them as the project's claim, verified here only to the extent that a real PSD file was produced and re-read.

Step 6: Let an agent drive the same engine over MCP

The same engine is also an MCP server, which is the step that matters if you want a coding agent to edit images instead of you typing commands. Start it on stdio with explicit read and write roots — an omitted root denies that direction of file access, so grant only the scratch directory:

photocraft-cli mcp --automation-read-root "$PWD" --automation-write-root "$PWD"

Send it a standard MCP handshake (JSON-RPC initialize, then notifications/initialized, then tools/list), and it answers with server info photocraft 0.17.0 and a tool list that includes command_list (discover command ids and parameter docs), command_run and command_batch (edit, one history step per command), doc_open, doc_save, and doc_inspect. Its own instructions say to start with doc_new/doc_open, discover ids with command_list, and save as native .pcraft or export by extension. The ui_* tools (inspect, screenshot) require bridge mode against a running desktop app via --bridge 127.0.0.1:PORT and do not work headless — do not build an agent workflow on them unless the app is open.

What this guide verified for MCP is the handshake and the tool list, not a full agent-driven edit session. Wiring it into your MCP client is the documented next step: point the client at the stdio command above with the two root flags, and the agent gets the same 500+ commands the CLI has, scoped to one folder. That scoping is the point — an agent with an image editor should get a scratch folder, not your photo library.

When to use this vs alternatives

PhotoCraft's CLI is the right shape when your edits are a repeatable recipe: grade every photo from a shoot the same way, convert a folder between formats, or hand a bounded set of commands to an agent. It is the wrong shape when you need one-off creative work with a mouse — that is what the desktop app (or GIMP, or Photoshop) is for — and when your pipeline is already Python, where a Pillow script will beat a subprocess call on simplicity. Against ImageMagick, the difference is the model: ImageMagick is a pixel pipeline, while PhotoCraft is a layered document engine with adjustment layers, masks, and PSD round trips, so a recipe can stay editable instead of baked. Against GIMP's Script-Fu, the difference is friction: no Scheme, no display server, one JSON recipe file, and an MCP surface an agent can call. Against Photoshop Actions, the difference is cost and openness: no subscription, no account, and the whole engine is MIT/Apache-2.0 source you can read. And against writing your own editor: do not. This one already has 1,700+ tests behind it, including compositor oracles that check the CPU and GPU renderers against each other.

What this guide did not verify

  • The desktop GUI: it needs a display, and this guide's sandbox has none. Every GUI claim here (68 tools, brush engine, live adjustment layers) is the project's, not a measured result.
  • A full agent-driven edit over MCP: the handshake and tool list were verified, but no agent session edited an image end to end in this guide.
  • PSD fidelity beyond produce-and-re-read: the 307-of-309 corpus figure is the project's measurement, quoted as such.
  • Smart selection and Select Subject: documented as on-device with no cloud or account, but not exercised headless here.
  • Star, commit, and fork counts move with every release. The figures here (74,359 stars, 7,040 commits, 13,130 forks, version 0.17.0) are dated October 28, 2026; re-run --version and check the repository page before quoting them elsewhere.

The takeaway

PhotoCraft earns its stars the way open-source tools used to: it is a real, working engine with a real, working command line, and it does not ask for your account, your money, or your GPU before it does anything useful. Download one 123 MB tarball, check its hash, and you can inspect, sharpen, curve, batch-grade, convert, and hand the whole thing to an agent — all from a terminal, all offline after the download. The alpha label is honest and the GUI is unproven here, but the headless path is not a promise. It ran. Start with Step 3 on a copy of one photo tonight; if the recipe-file workflow in Step 4 feels like the missing piece in your image pipeline, the rest of the engine is already installed.

Sources

  • PhotoCraft repository page (github.com/storytold/photocraft) — star, commit, fork, license, and creation-date figures; the early-alpha status note.
  • PhotoCraft README — the headless CLI examples, the 500+ command registry, the MCP and control-channel description, the format list, and the HEIC/AVIF limits.
  • PhotoCraft release v0.17.0 (October 28, 2026) — the Linux tarball, the SHA256SUMS.txt checksum, and the per-platform download table.
  • The installed CLI itself, run in this guide: photocraft-cli 0.17.0 — every version string, command result, batch count, conversion, and MCP handshake quoted here came from running it, not from documentation alone.

title: Build Once, Render Anywhere: Generating OG Images and PDFs from JSX/HTML Without a Headless Browser Using Rust-Powered Takumi
description:
Originally published on tamiz.pro.

Generating Open Graph (OG) images and PDFs from JSX or HTML is a common need for dynamic social sharing, reports, and invoices. The typical approach—spinning up a headless browser like Puppeteer or Playwright—is heavy: high memory usage, slow cold starts, and complex orchestration. Takumi offers a radical alternative: a Rust-powered renderer that converts JSX/HTML directly into images and PDFs, without a browser. In this tutorial, you'll learn how to build a reusable rendering service that takes JSX/HTML as input and outputs PNG or PDF, using Takumi's Node.js bindings. You'll see how to set up the environment, write render functions, handle dynamic data, and deploy efficiently. By the end, you'll have a production-ready pattern that cuts rendering latency and resource consumption dramatically.

Table of Contents

  • 1. Why Takumi?
  • 2. Prerequisites
  • 3. Setting Up the Project
  • 4. Core Rendering API
  • 5. Rendering an OG Image from JSX
  • 6. Rendering a PDF from HTML
  • 7. Handling Dynamic Data and Styling
  • 8. Performance and Deployment Considerations
  • 9. Frequently Asked Questions

1. Why Takumi?

Headless browsers are powerful but overkill for static rendering. They consume 200–500 MB of RAM per instance)Skip to content

Takumi is a Rust-based rendering engine that interprets a subset of HTML/CSS and JSX, rasterizing to images or vector PDFs. It's designed for serverless environments and edge functions where cold starts matter. Key benefits:

  • Memory footprint: Under 50 MB per instance, compared to 300+ MB for Chromium.
  • Startup time: ~10ms to initialize, vs 300ms+ for a browser launch.
  • Deterministic output: No layout flakiness; pixel-perfect results.
  • Language agnostic: Use from Node.js, Python, or directly via HTTP.

Takumi does not execute JavaScript. That's a feature: it forces you to precompute dynamic values and pass them as props, resulting in predictable and secure rendering.

2. Prerequisites

  • Node.js 18+ (we'll use the official @takumi-js/core package)
  • npm or yarn
  • Basic familiarity with JSX (we'll use React-like syntax, but Takumi has its own runtime)
  • No need for a browser installation

3. Setting Up the Project

Create a new directory and initialize:

mkdir og-renderer
cd og-renderer
npm init -y
npm install @takumi-js/core

Takumi's Node package wraps the native Rust binary. For serverless, you can also use the standalone HTTP server (we'll cover that later).

Now create a basic index.js file and verify the installation:

const { renderToImage } = require('@takumi-js/core');

console.log('Takumi loaded', typeof renderToImage);

Run it:

node index.js

You should see Takumi loaded function.

4. Core Rendering API

Takumi exposes two primary functions:

  • renderToImage(jsx, options) → returns a Buffer (PNG or JPEG)
  • renderToPdf(html, options) → returns a Buffer (PDF)

Both accept a string of JSX/HTML and an options object for width, height, format, and quality.

The JSX is not compiled by Babel; it's parsed by Takumi's own parser. You can write JSX-like syntax directly in a template literal, or use a .tsx file and compile it to a string before passing.

Options overview

Option Type Default Description
width number 1200 Output width in pixels
height number 630 Output height (for images)
format string 'png' 'png' or 'jpeg'
quality number 90 JPEG quality only
pdf object {} PDF-specific options (page size, margins)

5. Rendering an OG Image from JSX

Let's create a function that takes a title, subtitle, and brand color, and returns a PNG Buffer for an OG image.

Create render-og.js:

const { renderToImage } = require('@takumi-js/core');

function generateOgImage({ title, subtitle, bgColor = '#1a202c', textColor = '#ffffff' }) {
  const jsx = `
    <div style="display: flex; flex-direction: column; justify-content: center; align-items: center; width: 100%; height: 100%; background: ${bgColor}; padding: 40px;">
      <h1 style="font-size: 64px; color: ${textColor}; margin-bottom: 16px;">${title}</h1>
      <p style="font-size: 32px; color: rgba(255,255,255,0.8);">${subtitle}</p>
    </div>
  `;

  return renderToImage(jsx, {
    width: 1200,
    height: 630,
    format: 'png'
  });
}

// Example usage
const fs = require('fs');
const buffer = generateOgImage({
  title: 'Build Once, Render Anywhere',
  subtitle: 'Rust-powered rendering without a browser'
});

fs.writeFileSync('og-image.png', buffer);
console.log('OG image generated');

Run it:

node render-og.js

You should get a clean 1200x630 PNG. Notice we used inline styles—Takumi supports a subset of CSS, including flexbox, which is enough for most layouts.

6. Rendering a PDF from HTML

For PDFs, you can pass HTML (or JSX) and specify PDF options. Here's how to generate a simple invoice PDF:

Create render-pdf.js:

const { renderToPdf } = require('@takumi-js/core');

function generateInvoicePdf({ customerName, amount, invoiceId }) {
  const html = `
    <html>
      <body style="font-family: Arial, sans-serif; padding: 40px;">
        <h1 style="color: #333;">Invoice #${invoiceId}</h1>
        <p>Customer: <strong>${customerName}</strong></p>
        <p>Amount due: <strong>$${amount}</strong></p>
        <p>Thank you for your business!</p>
      </body>
    </html>
  `;

  return renderToPdf(html, {
    pdf: {
      pageSize: 'A4',
      margins: { top: '20mm', bottom: '20mm', left: '20mm', right: '20mm' }
    }
  });
}

const fs = require('fs');
const buffer = generateInvoicePdf({
  customerName: 'Jane Doe',
  amount: '199.99',
  invoiceId: 'INV-2025-001'
});

fs.writeFileSync('invoice.pdf', buffer);
console.log('PDF generated');

Run it:

node render-pdf.js

Open the PDF to see a clean, vector-based document. Takumi's PDF output is vector, meaning text is selectable and sharp at any zoom.

7. Handling Dynamic Data and Styling

In a real application, you'll have dynamic data from a database or API. Since Takumi doesn't run JS, you must precompute values and inject them into the template. Here's a pattern using a template function:

function renderBlogCard(post) {
  const jsx = `
    <div style="display: flex; height: 100%; background: linear-gradient(135deg, #667eea 0%, #764ba2 100%); padding: 40px;">
      <div style="display: flex; flex-direction: column; justify-content: space-between; width: 100%;">
        <div>
          <p style="font-size: 24px; color: rgba(255,255,255,0.8); text-transform: uppercase;">${post.category}</p>
          <h1 style="font-size: 48px; color: white; margin-top: 12px;">${post.title}</h1>
        </div>
        <div style="display: flex; align-items: center;">
          <img src="${post.authorAvatar}" style="width: 48px; height: 48px; border-radius: 50%;" />
          <p style="font-size: 20px; color: white; margin-left: 12px;">${post.author}</p>
        </div>
      </div>
    </div>
  `;
  return jsx;
}

// Usage
const post = {
  category: 'Engineering',
  title: 'Why We Ditched Headless Browsers',
  author: 'Alex Rivera',
  authorAvatar: 'https://example.com/alex.png'
};

renderToImage(renderBlogCard(post), { width: 1200, height: 630 })
  .then(buf => fs.writeFileSync('blog-card.png', buf));

Styling limitations

Takumi supports a useful subset of CSS: flexbox, grid (basic), colors, fonts (system and custom via @font-face), borders, border-radius, box-shadow, and text styling. It does not support position: absolute or complex animations. For most OG images and simple PDFs, this is sufficient.

To use custom fonts, you can embed them as base64 in a <style> tag:

const fontBase64 = '...'; // read from file
const jsx = `
  <style>
    @font-face {
      font-family: 'Inter';
      src: url(data:font/ttf;base64,${fontBase64}) format('truetype');
    }
  </style>
  <div style="font-family: 'Inter', sans-serif;">...</div>
`;

8. Performance and Deployment Considerations

Memory and CPU

Takumi uses a single native thread and is non-blocking in Node. It's ideal for serverless functions (AWS Lambda, Vercel Edge, Cloudflare Workers). You can run it in a warm container and render in under 5ms for a typical OG image.

Caching

Since output is deterministic for given inputs, cache aggressively. Use a key based on the template + data hash:

const crypto = require('crypto');
function cacheKey(data) {
  return crypto.createHash('sha256').update(JSON.stringify(data)).digest('hex');
}
// In a serverless function, use a CDN or in-memory cache.

HTTP server mode

For microservices, Takumi can run as a standalone HTTP server. The Node package includes a serve function:

const { serve } = require('@takumi-js/core');
serve(3000); // starts a REST API

Then POST to /render with JSON body:

{
  "jsx": "<div>Hello</div>",
  "options": { "width": 800, "height": 400, "format": "png" }
}

This decouples rendering from your app's runtime.

Cold start comparison

Approach Cold start Memory per instance Throughput (images/sec)
Puppeteer 300-800ms 300-500 MB ~10
Takumi 10-20ms 40-60 MB ~100

Numbers are indicative; your mileage may vary.

9. Frequently Asked Questions

Can I use Takumi with React components?

Yes, but you need to compile your React component to a string of JSX. You can use renderToString from ReactDOMServer (which outputs HTML) and then pass that HTML to Takumi, or you can use a custom Babel plugin to output JSX text. However, Takumi's JSX parser is not a full React implementation—it only supports declarative elements, not hooks or state. For static content, it works well.

Does Takumi support images from URLs?

Yes, you can use <img src="https://...">. Takumi will fetch the image at render time. Ensure the URL is accessible from your runtime environment. For performance, consider pre-downloading images and using base64 data URIs.

Is Takumi open source?

Takumi is available under a commercial license, but there is a free tier for low-volume usage. Check the official Takumi website for the latest pricing and terms.

By replacing headless browsers with Takumi, you can achieve dramatic improvements in speed and resource usage for static rendering tasks. Start integrating it into your existing stack today—your serverless bill and your users' latency will thank you.

title: Two Requests Edited the Same Order. Optimistic Locking in a Go Repository Adapter
description:
• Book: Hexagonal Architecture in Go
  • Also by me: Pocket Guides for Developers — the 8-book series
  • My project: Hermes IDE | GitHub — an IDE for developers who ship with Claude Code and other AI coding tools
  • Me: xgabriel.com | GitHub

Order o-42 says pending. Five minutes ago the warehouse service marked it shipped, and the API call that did it returned 200 OK. So did the one a support agent made a few milliseconds later to add a delivery note. Both handlers loaded the order, changed one field, and saved the whole row back. The note is there. The shipment is gone from the record, and nobody saw an error.

That is the lost-update bug. Nothing throws and nothing logs. The second save wrote a stale copy of the order over the first, and the database did exactly what it was told.

The fix is old and has a name. Martin Fowler's catalog calls it Optimistic Offline Lock: "Prevents conflicts between concurrent business transactions by detecting a conflict and rolling back the transaction." This post puts each piece of it where it belongs in a Go service built with ports and adapters, so the domain owns the rule and every adapter, real or fake, has to honor it.

The bug, in one UPDATE

Here is the save that causes it. It is the repository method most of us write on day one:

const naiveSave = `
UPDATE orders
   SET status = $2, note = $3
 WHERE id = $1`

Handler A reads {status: pending, note: ""}, sets the status to shipped, saves. Handler B read the same row before A saved, sets the note, and saves {status: pending, note: "leave at door"}. B's pending is the stale value it loaded, and it overwrites A's shipped.

Postgres is behaving as documented. Its default isolation level is Read Committed, and the Postgres docs spell out what a second updater does when it hits a row another transaction just changed: it waits for that transaction to commit, then "the search condition of the command (the WHERE clause) is re-evaluated to see if the updated version of the row still matches the search condition." WHERE id = $1 still matches, so B's write lands. That re-evaluation is also the hook for the fix: add a condition that stops matching once someone else has written.


Both writers read the same row. The second save quietly undoes the first.

Put the version on the aggregate, and the error in the domain

The version is part of the order's state, so it lives on the domain type. The conflict is a business fact ("someone changed this order while you were working on it"), so the error lives in the domain package too. No adapter types leak in.

package order

import (
    "context"
    "errors"
)

var (
    ErrNotFound         = errors.New("order: not found")
    ErrConcurrentUpdate = errors.New("order: concurrent update")
)

type Order struct {
    ID      string
    Status  string
    Note    string
    Version int64
}

// Repository is the port.
//
// Save succeeds only if the stored version equals o.Version.
// On success the stored version becomes o.Version + 1.
// If another write got there first it returns
// ErrConcurrentUpdate. If the order does not exist it
// returns ErrNotFound.
type Repository interface {
    Get(ctx context.Context, id string) (Order, error)
    Save(ctx context.Context, o Order) error
}

The doc comment is the contract. Every adapter you write will be tested against those four rules, which is the whole point of having a port.

The pgx adapter: zero rows affected means you lost

The table needs one extra column:

CREATE TABLE orders (
  id      text   PRIMARY KEY,
  status  text   NOT NULL,
  note    text   NOT NULL DEFAULT '',
  version bigint NOT NULL DEFAULT 1
);

The adapter uses pgx v5. Pool.Exec returns a pgconn.CommandTag, and CommandTag.RowsAffected() tells you how many rows the UPDATE touched.

package postgres

import (
    "context"
    "errors"
    "fmt"

    "github.com/jackc/pgx/v5"
    "github.com/jackc/pgx/v5/pgxpool"

    "example.com/shop/order"
)

type OrderRepo struct{ pool *pgxpool.Pool }

func NewOrderRepo(p *pgxpool.Pool) *OrderRepo {
    return &OrderRepo{pool: p}
}

func (r *OrderRepo) Get(
    ctx context.Context, id string,
) (order.Order, error) {
    var o order.Order
    err := r.pool.QueryRow(ctx, `
        SELECT id, status, note, version
          FROM orders WHERE id = $1`, id,
    ).Scan(&o.ID, &o.Status, &o.Note, &o.Version)
    if errors.Is(err, pgx.ErrNoRows) {
        return order.Order{}, order.ErrNotFound
    }
    if err != nil {
        return order.Order{}, fmt.Errorf("get %s: %w", id, err)
    }
    return o, nil
}

func (r *OrderRepo) Save(
    ctx context.Context, o order.Order,
) error {
    tag, err := r.pool.Exec(ctx, `
        UPDATE orders
           SET status = $3, note = $4,
               version = version + 1
         WHERE id = $1 AND version = $2`,
        o.ID, o.Version, o.Status, o.Note)
    if err != nil {
        return fmt.Errorf("save %s: %w", o.ID, err)
    }
    if tag.RowsAffected() == 1 {
        return nil
    }
    return r.missOrConflict(ctx, o.ID)
}

func (r *OrderRepo) missOrConflict(
    ctx context.Context, id string,
) error {
    var exists bool
    err := r.pool.QueryRow(ctx,
        `SELECT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders WHERE id = $1)`,
        id,
    ).Scan(&exists)
    if err != nil {
        return fmt.Errorf("check %s: %w", id, err)
    }
    if !exists {
        return order.ErrNotFound
    }
    return order.ErrConcurrentUpdate
}

Walk the race again with this UPDATE. A and B both loaded version 1. A's update commits and the row is now version 2. B's update waits on A's row lock, then Postgres re-evaluates WHERE id = $1 AND version = 1 against the new row. It no longer matches, so B updates zero rows and gets ErrConcurrentUpdate instead of a silent overwrite.

The missOrConflict lookup is there because zero rows has two causes, and the port promised to tell them apart. It only runs on the unhappy path, so the common case stays a single round trip. If a deleted order and a conflict mean the same thing to your callers, you can drop it, but then change the port's doc comment too.


The version in the WHERE clause is the gate. A stale copy carries the wrong number and updates nothing.

The in-memory fake honors the same contract

Your use-case tests should not need a database. They also should not run against a fake that is more forgiving than production, because then the tests pass on code that loses updates. The fake implements the same four rules:

package memory

import (
    "context"
    "sync"

    "example.com/shop/order"
)

type OrderRepo struct {
    mu     sync.Mutex
    orders map[string]order.Order
}

func NewOrderRepo(seed ...order.Order) *OrderRepo {
    m := make(map[string]order.Order, len(seed))
    for _, o := range seed {
        m[o.ID] = o
    }
    return &OrderRepo{orders: m}
}

func (r *OrderRepo) Get(
    _ context.Context, id string,
) (order.Order, error) {
    r.mu.Lock()
    defer r.mu.Unlock()
    o, ok := r.orders[id]
    if !ok {
        return order.Order{}, order.ErrNotFound
    }
    return o, nil
}

func (r *OrderRepo) Save(
    _ context.Context, o order.Order,
) error {
    r.mu.Lock()
    defer r.mu.Unlock()
    cur, ok := r.orders[o.ID]
    if !ok {
        return order.ErrNotFound
    }
    if cur.Version != o.Version {
        return order.ErrConcurrentUpdate
    }
    o.Version++
    r.orders[o.ID] = o
    return nil
}

The check and the write happen under one lock, which is the in-memory equivalent of the conditional UPDATE. A fake that compared versions, released the lock, and then wrote would have the same race you are trying to test for.

A use case that retries, a bounded number of times

A conflict is not always a failure. In the opening story, the note and the status don't contradict each other. If B reloads the order and applies its change to the fresh copy, both edits survive. The use case does that, and gives up after a few attempts so a hot row can't spin a request forever:

package app

import (
    "context"
    "errors"

    "example.com/shop/order"
)

const maxAttempts = 3

type Orders struct{ repo order.Repository }

func NewOrders(r order.Repository) *Orders {
    return &Orders{repo: r}
}

func (s *Orders) Update(
    ctx context.Context,
    id string,
    change func(*order.Order) error,
) error {
    var err error
    for range maxAttempts {
        var o order.Order
        o, err = s.repo.Get(ctx, id)
        if err != nil {
            return err
        }
        if err = change(&o); err != nil {
            return err
        }
        err = s.repo.Save(ctx, o)
        if !errors.Is(err, order.ErrConcurrentUpdate) {
            return err
        }
    }
    return err
}

for range maxAttempts needs Go 1.22 or later, which added range over integers. The change function runs again on every attempt, against freshly loaded state, so it must be a pure edit: "set status to shipped," not "set status to whatever the user saw plus one."

Retrying is only right when the change still makes sense on newer data. If a person made a decision by looking at the old version (a price, a stock count), retrying behind their back is its own lost update. Return the conflict to the edge instead. Over HTTP that maps cleanly onto conditional requests: send the version as an ETag, and per MDN's If-Match page, a mismatched precondition gets a 412 Precondition Failed.

One test, both adapters

The contract test takes a constructor, so the fake and the Postgres adapter run the exact same assertions. Both goroutines load the order before either saves, which forces the conflict instead of hoping for it.

package ordertest

import (
    "context"
    "errors"
    "sync"
    "testing"

    "example.com/shop/order"
)

func OneWriterWins(t *testing.T, repo order.Repository) {
    ctx := context.Background()
    a, err := repo.Get(ctx, "o-42")
    if err != nil {
        t.Fatal(err)
    }
    b := a
    a.Status = "shipped"
    b.Note = "leave at door"

    errs := make(chan error, 2)
    var wg sync.WaitGroup
    for _, o := range []order.Order{a, b} {
        wg.Add(1)
        go func() {
            defer wg.Done()
            errs <- repo.Save(ctx, o)
        }()
    }
    wg.Wait()
    close(errs)

    var won, lost int
    for err := range errs {
        switch {
        case err == nil:
            won++
        case errors.Is(err, order.ErrConcurrentUpdate):
            lost++
        default:
            t.Fatalf("unexpected error: %v", err)
        }
    }
    if won != 1 || lost != 1 {
        t.Fatalf("won=%d lost=%d, want 1 and 1", won, lost)
    }
    got, err := repo.Get(ctx, "o-42")
    if err != nil {
        t.Fatal(err)
    }
    if got.Version != a.Version+1 {
        t.Fatalf("version=%d, want %d",
            got.Version, a.Version+1)
    }
}

The goroutine captures o directly, which is safe because Go 1.22 made loop variables per-iteration. Wiring the test up for the fake takes one call:

func TestMemoryOneWriterWins(t *testing.T) {
    seed := order.Order{
        ID: "o-42", Status: "pending", Version: 1,
    }
    ordertest.OneWriterWins(t, memory.NewOrderRepo(seed))
}

The Postgres version does the same against a real pool: read a connection string from an environment variable, t.Skip when it is empty, create the table, insert the seed row, and pass postgres.NewOrderRepo(pool) to OneWriterWins. Run both with go test -race ./...; the race detector will also catch a fake that forgot its mutex.

A second test belongs next to it: fire two Orders.Update calls at the fake concurrently, one setting the status and one setting the note, and assert that the final order has both. That one proves the retry turns the conflict into two surviving edits instead of one.

If this was useful

The version column is the easy part. The design work is deciding that the conflict is a domain error, writing the port's contract down, and making the fake as strict as the database so your fast tests mean something. Hexagonal Architecture in Go is the book I wrote about exactly that layer: where repositories, transactions and adapters sit in a Go service, and how to test each side of the port without a pile of mocks. If you also want the language underneath, The Complete Guide to Go Programming, the companion book in the Thinking in Go series, covers Go itself.
