title: I rebuilt Wallpaper Engine in Rust
description:
Wallpaper Engine is honestly one of the best things on Steam. Millions of animated wallpapers, everything from plain looping videos to layered 2D scenes with particles, shaders and little scripts running inside them.

It also has a few habits that bug me. It's Windows-only and closed source. The GPU never really idles. Maximize one window and every monitor pauses. And if an audio device disappears, video wallpapers can just break.

So I got curious: how much of it could I rebuild as an open engine that still plays the content people already own?

Two weeks later, I have an answer. It's called Diorama, and it's about 36,000 lines of Rust on top of wgpu. It plays Wallpaper Engine scenes, videos and web wallpapers straight from your local Workshop folder, plus your own files. Right now it's Windows only. Linux is next.

This post is about how it works. But mostly it's about how I convinced myself that it actually works.

Rule #1: the renderer never sees Wallpaper Engine

The very first decision I made was architectural, and it's the one I'm happiest with. Wallpaper Engine's file formats are the importer's problem. Nothing else in the codebase even knows they exist.

The split looks like this:

  • diorama-we reads all the Wallpaper Engine formats: .pkg archives, .tex textures (LZ4, DXT, sprite sheets, even embedded MP4s), .mdl models and puppets, the scene/effect/material/particle JSON, and their custom shader dialect. It turns all of that into an engine-neutral scene format, diorama-scene.
  • diorama-render only ever sees that neutral format: layers, materials, passes, effect chains, particles.
  • diorama-platform is the one crate allowed to touch the OS.

I didn't trust myself to keep this clean, so a CI script enforces it. The build fails if a lower layer depends on a higher one, or if cfg(windows) shows up anywhere outside the platform crate.

This boundary paid for itself over and over. Every time I hit some new Wallpaper Engine quirk, the fix went into the importer and the renderer stayed simple.

I also decided early that anything coming from the Workshop is hostile input:

  • Parsers are bounds-checked, fuzzed, and never allowed to unwrap.
  • Scripts run in QuickJS with memory and time limits.
  • Shaders get validated before they're used.
  • Web wallpapers run offline by default, each in its own process.

Shaders: GLSL dialect → HLSL → DXC → SPIR-V → naga → wgpu

Yes, that heading is the actual pipeline.

Wallpaper Engine's shaders are written in a GLSL-ish dialect with #includes, // [COMBO] permutation markers, JSON annotations on uniforms, and Direct3D 11 semantics sitting underneath all of it.

So Diorama:

  1. preprocesses them,
  2. translates them to HLSL,
  3. compiles that with DXC to SPIR-V,
  4. validates and loads the result through naga into wgpu,
  5. and caches every permutation on disk.

Going through HLSL looks like a detour, and I didn't pick it on a hunch. I ran a quick spike on my test library: 330 of 336 shader/permutation pairs compile via HLSL, versus 299 going straight through GLSL. Easy call.

How I checked it: RenderDoc captures and SSIM

"Looks about right" isn't a test, and with a renderer it's very easy to fool yourself. So I went to the source of truth.

I captured Wallpaper Engine itself with RenderDoc. A capture gives you every draw call, every render target and every uniform, including the exact g_Time of that frame.

On the Diorama side, I can render any scene off-screen at a specific time:

dioramad --scene … --time t --frame-out x.png

That means every capture becomes a reference image. A small tool then scores the difference between the two with SSIM.

The first scene I tried scored 0.996, which felt great. Then I ran it over all 55 scenes in my library:

  • 35 score 0.95 or higher
  • 48 score 0.90 or higher
  • the mean is 0.948

The captures were also the best documentation I had. They answered questions that no amount of reading would have:

  • Wallpaper Engine uses reversed-Z depth with a GREATER test, and blended draws never write depth.
  • Layers marked "no interpolation" use point filtering the whole way through: source texture, effect passes and the final composite. Miss one step and pixel-art scenes go soft.
  • A layer's last effect pass draws straight into the scene, not into another render target.
  • Particle count scales the emission rate, not the maximum.

Some differences I just can't match. One terrain shader builds its hash function on sin, which compiles differently in FXC and DXC, so the pattern comes out different everywhere. I've made peace with that one.

SceneScript

32 of my 55 scenes use SceneScript, Wallpaper Engine's JavaScript layer. It's what powers clocks, interactive layers and even small games inside wallpapers.

The nice surprise here: Wallpaper Engine ships complete TypeScript typings for it. That gave me a clear spec to build against. Diorama implements the API in QuickJS (via rquickjs), covering layers, animations, cursor events, audio and media, user properties and timers.

One scene full of draggable desktop "windows" took a while. Getting it right needed pointer capture, plus sending cursor events only to the topmost layer that's actually listening for them.

Web wallpapers: the case of the frozen weather widget

Web wallpapers run in WebView2, each in its own process, and the network is off unless you allow it.

That default gave me my favourite bug of the whole project.

A weather widget was frozen solid on the desktop. But when I rendered it off-screen, it was perfectly fine. Same wallpaper, same code, completely different behaviour.

The culprit was in its audio handler:

while (smoothedPoints.length < values.length) {
  if (typeof createVector === "function") smoothedPoints.push(createVector(0, height / 2));
}

createVector comes from p5.js, which the wallpaper loads from a CDN. Diorama had blocked that CDN. So createVector was never a function, nothing ever got pushed, and the very first audio frame walked into a loop that could never end.

And the off-screen renders? They don't get audio. No audio frame, no loop, no freeze.

Diorama now reports blocked files and stuck pages, and gives you an "Allow internet access" switch for that specific wallpaper.

Fixing the things people complain about

The other half of the project was working through a list of Wallpaper Engine pain points. Each one got its own test, so it stays fixed.

  • Idle cost: a static wallpaper stops drawing completely. 0.00% GPU when idle.
  • Pausing: each monitor pauses on its own when there's a fullscreen app or maximized window in front of it. One maximized window no longer freezes everything.
  • Windows 11 24H2: it survives the new desktop window layout (including with icons hidden), Explorer restarts and graphics driver resets.
  • Audio: video never depends on an audio device.
  • Cost report: the library shows each wallpaper's measured CPU, GPU and memory, so you know what it costs before you leave it running all day.
  • Video decoding: if your GPU can't decode a video, you get a one-click conversion instead of a CPU running hot.

What's next

  • Linux. Wayland layer-shell and X11, VA-API video, PipeWire audio. This is where an open engine matters most, so it's my top priority.
  • Closing the remaining gaps, mainly planar reflections and camera fades.
  • A signed installer.

Diorama is dual-licensed MIT/Apache-2.0. It ships no Wallpaper Engine code or content. It just reads what you already have.

The code, an installer and three original example wallpapers are all at github.com/karmanya007/Diorama. If a wallpaper looks wrong, please open an issue with its Workshop id. That helps a lot.

A note on how this was built: I leaned heavily on an AI coding assistant (Claude Code). I steered the design, ran the captures and reviewed the work, and the commits carry its co-author line.

title: How Web Design Development Helps Businesses Grow | Dv Orbit
description:
How Web Design Development Helps Businesses Succeed Online

In today's competitive digital world, businesses need a strong online presence to attract customers, build credibility, and remain competitive. A professional website allows companies to showcase their services, communicate their values, and connect with potential customers. However, creating an effective website requires more than an attractive layout. It involves thoughtful planning, reliable functionality, and an understanding of customer needs.

Web Design Development combines creative design with technical expertise to create websites that are visually appealing, accessible, and easy to navigate. Businesses that invest in a well-planned website can improve customer experiences and establish a solid foundation for long-term growth.

Why Professional Website Design Matters

A website often creates the first impression of a business. When visitors arrive at a website, they expect clear information, attractive visuals, and straightforward navigation. A confusing layout or outdated appearance can discourage potential customers from exploring further.

Professional website design helps businesses present their brands consistently. Colors, typography, images, and page layouts should work together to communicate the company's identity. Clear headings and organized content also make it easier for visitors to understand products and services.

Mobile responsiveness is another essential element. Many people browse websites on smartphones and tablets, so pages should adapt to different screen sizes. A responsive website allows visitors to read content, navigate menus, and complete forms without unnecessary difficulty.

Accessibility should also be considered during the design process. Readable text, sufficient color contrast, descriptive links, and logical heading structures help create a better experience for a wider audience. These improvements demonstrate attention to detail and support more inclusive digital experiences.

How Web Design Development Supports Business Growth

An attractive website is valuable, but its features must also work correctly. Web development provides the technical foundation for contact forms, booking systems, online stores, customer portals, and other interactive tools.

Different businesses require different functionalities. A consulting company may need appointment scheduling, while an online retailer might require product catalogs and secure payment processing. Choosing features that match business objectives helps avoid unnecessary complexity and creates a more useful website.

Performance is equally important. Visitors expect pages to load quickly and respond smoothly. Developers can improve loading speeds through image compression, efficient coding, reliable hosting, and the removal of unnecessary scripts. Better performance helps visitors access information with less frustration.

Security must remain a priority as well. Secure connections, updated software, regular backups, and appropriate access controls can reduce common website risks. Businesses that collect personal information should implement suitable safeguards to protect customer data and maintain confidence.

Search Engine Optimization for Better Visibility

A professional website should help potential customers discover a business online. Search engine optimization supports this goal by improving website structure, content quality, and accessibility.

Businesses can strengthen their websites by using descriptive page titles, meaningful headings, relevant internal links, and optimized images. Publishing useful articles and detailed service pages can also help answer customer questions and demonstrate industry knowledge.

Keyword research helps identify the phrases people use when searching for products or services. These keywords should be included naturally in relevant content rather than repeated excessively. Search engines and readers benefit from informative writing that focuses on genuine user needs.

Technical improvements alone cannot guarantee high rankings. Competition, content relevance, website authority, and many other factors influence search performance. A consistent approach that combines technical quality with valuable content provides a stronger foundation for sustainable visibility.

Discover Digital Solutions with Dv Orbit

Choosing a suitable digital solutions provider can help businesses turn their ideas into practical online experiences. Companies should consider their goals, target audiences, technical requirements, and budgets before selecting a website strategy.

Dv Orbit provides a starting point for businesses exploring web development, custom software, and digital solutions. Through its website, Dv Orbit, businesses can learn more about its digital services and explore options for strengthening their online presence.

A successful website project begins with identifying the problems a business wants to solve. Some companies may need a new website, while others might want to improve an existing platform, simplify customer interactions, or introduce additional functionality.

Professional Web Design Development can help businesses combine attractive layouts with practical features. A well-organized website makes information easier to find, supports brand consistency, and gives visitors a clear path toward contacting the company or learning about its services.

Dv Orbit recognizes the importance of digital solutions that support modern business requirements. By considering usability, functionality, and future needs, businesses can make informed decisions about improving their websites and developing their digital capabilities.

Creating a Better Customer Experience

Customer experience should remain central to every website project. Visitors should be able to understand what a business offers and find the information they need without unnecessary effort.

Clear navigation, helpful service descriptions, visible contact information, and simple forms can make interactions more convenient. Businesses can also publish frequently asked questions, educational articles, and practical resources to address common concerns.

Trust is another important factor. Accurate information, consistent branding, secure browsing, and transparent communication help visitors feel more confident when interacting with a business. A professional website should present information honestly and avoid misleading claims.

Analytics can provide useful insights into visitor behavior. By reviewing popular pages, traffic sources, and completed inquiries, businesses can identify opportunities to improve their websites. Regular testing and thoughtful updates help ensure that the website continues meeting customer expectations.

Maintaining a Website for Long-Term Success

Launching a website is only the beginning of its development. Regular maintenance helps keep pages, forms, integrations, and other features working properly. Businesses should review performance, apply software updates, monitor security, and resolve technical issues when necessary.

As organizations grow, their digital requirements may change. A website might need additional service pages, new integrations, improved navigation, or more advanced functionality. Planning for scalability makes it easier to accommodate these changes without rebuilding the entire platform.

Ongoing improvements also help businesses remain responsive to changing customer preferences and industry developments. A website should evolve alongside the organization it represents.

Conclusion

Web Design Development plays an important role in helping businesses establish a professional online presence. By combining responsive design, reliable functionality, useful content, search optimization, and ongoing maintenance, companies can create better experiences for their customers.

Businesses that prioritize usability and clear objectives can turn their websites into valuable digital assets. Exploring the services offered by Dv Orbit at dvorbit.com can be a useful starting point for organizations looking to understand their web development and digital solution options. With careful planning and continuous improvement, a strong website can support customer engagement and long-term business growth.

title: Why I love building 100% client-side web tools (and how I do it)
description:
I'm a solo indie developer based in China. Over the past year I've built more than 20 small web tools, and almost all of them share one design decision: no backend at all.

Here's why I keep coming back to it.

No server means no data risk. When a tool runs entirely in the browser, the user's input never leaves their device. There's no database to leak, no logs to inspect, no "we may share data with partners" paragraph to write. Privacy stops being a policy and becomes an architecture. For things like a BMI calculator or a password generator, that's the right default.

Instant load. A single HTML file with inline CSS and JS is a few kilobytes. It renders before a typical React app has finished downloading its framework. Fast tools feel trustworthy.

Near-zero cost. Static files on Cloudflare Pages cost me basically nothing. No servers to patch, no uptime alerts at 3 a.m., no scaling bill when a post goes viral.

How I actually build them: plain HTML, CSS, and vanilla JavaScript. No build step, no framework. I deploy to Cloudflare Pages with a git push. I use AI as a pair programmer — mostly for scaffolding layouts and catching edge cases — but I keep the logic simple enough to read in one sitting.

That stack is what powers Lihayo Tools, a growing set of 20+ free utilities including BMI and TDEE calculators. Everything runs locally, no signup, no tracking.

If you've been thinking about shipping small tools, start with a single HTML file. It's still the most underrated stack on the web.

title: GSTR-2B Reconciliation Made Simple
description:
The Challenge of Manual Reconciliation

For Indian SMBs, reconciling the purchase register against the GSTR‑2B feed is a monthly chore that involves thousands of invoice line items. Each line must be matched by vendor, GSTIN, invoice number, amount, tax rate, and HSN code. The current manual workflow relies on spreadsheets, ad‑hoc filters, and a lot of trial‑and‑error. Even a single misplaced comma can trigger a cascade of “unmatched” flags, forcing finance teams to dig through logs and re‑enter data. This is where gst reconciliation software pays off in practice.

GSTBot’s Reconciliation Engine

GSTBot replaces that pain with an automated, tolerance‑aware engine. The core of the engine is a FastAPI endpoint that accepts a batch of PDFs, photos, or Excel files, forwards them to a Celery worker, and stores the parsed data in PostgreSQL. The worker then performs a fuzzy join against the GSTR‑2B download, using a configurable tolerance window for numeric fields.

# FastAPI route that triggers the reconciliation
@router.post("/reconcile")
async def reconcile_invoices(file: UploadFile = File(...)):
    task_id = await celery_app.send_task("tasks.reconcile", args=[file.filename])
    return {"task_id": task_id}

The Celery task pulls the file from S3, runs the AI extraction model, and writes the results to a parsed_invoices table.

@celery_app.task(name="tasks.reconcile")
def reconcile(file_name: str):
    invoices = extract_invoices(file_name)  # AI extraction
    session.execute(insert(parsed_invoices).values(invoices))
    session.commit()
    perform_match()

The perform_match function performs the heart of the reconciliation: Getting gst reconciliation software right early saves rework later.

# PostgreSQL query that joins parsed invoices with GSTR‑2B entries
query = (
    select(
        pi.id.label("invoice_id"),
        gb.id.label("gstr_id"),
        abs(pi.amount - gb.amount).label("amount_diff")
    )
    .select_from(parsed_invoices.alias("pi"))
    .join(gstr2b.alias("gb"),
          and_(
              pi.vendor == gb.vendor,
              pi.gstin == gb.gstin,
              pi.invoice_no == gb.invoice_no,
              func.abs(pi.amount - gb.amount) <= 0.01 * pi.amount
          ))
)
results = session.execute(query).fetchall()

The tolerance of 1 % is configurable via the settings.py module. If an amount differs by more than the threshold, the engine flags the line as an exception and stores it in an exceptions table for later review.

How the Engine Works

  1. Ingestion – Users upload bulk invoice files through the React UI. The front‑end calls the /reconcile endpoint and receives a task ID.
  2. Extraction – A Celery worker runs the open‑source OCR and NLP pipeline to pull vendor name, GSTIN, invoice number, amount, tax rate, and HSN code. The extraction results are written to PostgreSQL.
  3. Matching – A Postgres query joins the parsed invoices with the GSTR‑2B dataset, applying a 1 % tolerance on amounts. The query uses func.abs to compute the absolute difference.
  4. Exception Classification – Any unmatched rows are routed through a rule engine that tags the exception (e.g., missing vendor, amount mismatch, HSN mismatch) and suggests a corrective action.
  5. Reporting – The results are surfaced in the UI as a drill‑down table. Finance staff can approve, edit, or flag each exception, and the changes propagate back to the parsed_invoices table.

The entire flow is orchestrated by Redis, which holds the Celery task queue. Redis is configured with a short TTL (5 min) so that stalled tasks are automatically retried. The health endpoint (/health/jobs) reports the status of the broker, ensuring that the system is always aware of queue back‑pressure.

Example Flow

A small manufacturer uploads a 50‑page PDF of purchase invoices. The React UI shows a progress bar as the file is uploaded. Once the Celery task starts, the AI extraction takes 12 seconds per page, a 30 % improvement over the legacy OCR tool. The matching query runs in 0.8 seconds, producing 47 matches and 3 exceptions. The UI lists the exceptions with a color‑coded status and a one‑click “Edit” button. Good gst reconciliation software keeps the rest of the workflow predictable.

{
  "exceptions": [
    {"invoice_id": 1023, "reason": "amount mismatch", "suggested_action": "re‑enter amount"},
    {"invoice_id": 1047, "reason": "missing vendor", "suggested_action": "add vendor"}
  ]
}

Finance staff can resolve the two exceptions in under a minute, after which the system automatically updates the input tax credit (ITC) ledger. The reconciled data feeds directly into the GSTR‑1 and GSTR‑3B generation modules, completing the compliance cycle.

Technical Highlights

  • FastAPI handles the HTTP layer and provides a lightweight, async API.
  • Celery + Redis decouples heavy extraction and matching logic from the request cycle, enabling horizontal scaling.
  • PostgreSQL stores parsed invoices and GSTR‑2B data; its jsonb column stores raw OCR output for audit trails.
  • Configurable Tolerances are exposed via environment variables, allowing a 0.5 % or 2 % threshold depending on business rules.
  • Robust Error Handling – When the Redis broker is unreachable, the worker logs a 503 with Retry-After instead of a 500, and the UI displays a friendly message.
  • Security – OAuth providers that redirect to localhost are blocked, and Microsoft’s email_verified claim is enforced to prevent spoofed sign‑ins.

GSTBot’s reconciliation engine exemplifies how a focused, well‑structured stack can transform a manual, error‑prone task into a repeatable, auditable workflow. By leveraging FastAPI, Celery, Redis, and PostgreSQL, the system delivers accurate, tolerance‑aware ITC reconciliation for Indian SMBs, eliminating the need for spreadsheets and reducing month‑end cycle time.

description:

By irl La Brava 💻❤️

Init:

This is a different project that I made. Yes, it is also a fan-art project, but this fan-art projects elevates itself to new heights. All to bring in more fans, and redirect to Gentle Criminal, and show how it looks like! Now it has finally come to life! If you are wondering how I named it I shall let you know: the signing up for Gentle Productions! Where imperial tea is promoted, unique surprises are yet to be found with the utmost elegance, all brought to life to show case the best heist ever.

A fan art project from My Hero Academia. Then, as I was trying to figure out how to write this article, I had an epiphany, and made two mode additions, and created a Javascript file, going beyond what the assignment in the curriculum asked for!
To go beyond, and to start with, allow me to describe you the following: I built custom sign-up and broadcast portal from scratch. A La Brava x Gentle Criminal thematic project!

As for the technical breakdown of how I designed, engineered, and styled this platform using semantic HTML5, modern CSS flexbox layouts, and client-side validation logic:

**

1// Architectural Overview & Structural Foundations//**

The project was constructed with a clean, decoupled two-file architecture (index.html and style.css) managed under local Git version control.

To create an immersive broadcast experience, I divided the viewport into a high-contrast dual-panel layout:
• The Hero/Broadcast Panel (Left): Houses Gentle's official logo, live stream status badges, custom SVG graphics, and his inspirational opening address.
• The Credentials Panel (Right): A structured, accessible sign-up form designed for supporters to register for exclusive updates and royal tea samples.
Semantic Markup & Targeted Contrast
To direct the viewer's eye through Gentle's speech and call-out notices, I utilized semantic HTML5 elements alongside precise wrappers. Rather than styling entire blocks indiscriminately, specific inline wrappers (.header-callout and .quote-pink) were applied to highlight key phrases in glowing cyber-neon pink against the imperial purple background.

`HTML


"My dear one, you the one who made this happen...
...Ah no, you're not my dear beloved one, but you're still the chosen one! Why you ask? To support the one and only Gentle Criminal!"

`

**

2// Vector Graphics: Handcrafting the G.C Imperial SVG Badge**

A true gentleman requires a regal mark. Rather than using raster images that degrade on high-resolution screens, I hand-coded a custom vector graphic (
• The Heart Frame: A deep magenta utilizing drop-shadow filters to represent my unwavering devotion and system protection.
• Rising Steam Lines: Dual curves rendered in hot pink and gold to represent the aroma of freshly brewed imperial tea.
• The Monogram & Mustache: A crisp node for the G.C initials in royal gold, anchored by Gentle's iconic white handlebar mustache at the base.
SVG

**

3// Styling & Color Palette Variables (:root)**

To maintain complete visual harmony across dark mode surfaces, I defined global CSS custom properties (:root). The stylesheet balances Gentle's aristocratic purple and gold palette with my cyber-neon accents.
CSS

:root {
    /* La Brava Palette */
    --pink-neon: #ff1493;
    --pink-glow: rgba(255, 20, 147, 0.4);
    --pink-light: #ff69b4;

    /* Gentle Criminal Palette */
    --purple-dark: #0d0714;
    --purple-deep: #190a26;
    --purple-card: #251038;
    --purple-accent: #4c1d95;
    --gold-accent: #f4d03f;
    --gold-glow: rgba(244, 208, 63, 0.3);
    --silver-text: #e2e8f0;
    --lavender-light: #d8b4fe;

}

**
///4*Layout Mechanics & Responsiveness*//**

The core layout utilizes Flexbox (display: flex) with a proportion ratio of 1.2 : 1 between the hero panel and form container. Background depth was achieved using layered radial gradients (radial-gradient), giving the surface a subtle glowing ambient effect.
To support viewers on mobile devices or smaller display setups, media queries automatically re-orient the dual panels into a vertical stack at viewports under 950px:
CSS
@media (max-width: 950px) {
.page-wrapper {
flex-direction: column;
}
.hero-panel {
border-right: none;
border-bottom: 1px solid rgba(244, 208, 63, 0.2);
}
}

**

5// Client-Side Input Validation Logic//**

To protect our system from unauthorized noise, input fields utilize native HTML5 validation pseudo-classes (:valid, :focus:invalid). Additionally, a lightweight JavaScript block monitors password field inputs in real-time, enforcing match checks before form submission.
JavaScript
function validatePassword() {
if (confirmPasswordInput.value === '') {
confirmPasswordInput.setCustomValidity('');
errorMessage.textContent = '';
return;
}

if (passwordInput.value !== confirmPasswordInput.value) {
    confirmPasswordInput.setCustomValidity('Passwords do not match');
    errorMessage.textContent = 'Passwords must match';
} else {
    confirmPasswordInput.setCustomValidity('');
    errorMessage.textContent = '';
}

}

In ##4, is the latest addition. I wanted to add more, to try more to satisfy myself. I went even further than what the curriculum asked, and I searched how to establish a solid front-end baseline with real-time input sanitization, native HTML5 validation integration, password matching checks, and a submission cooldown timer.
**

5. ** Invisible Honeypot Trap (website_hp)**

  • Scraper & Bot Trap: Built a decoy field (<input type="text" id="website_hp" name="website_hp">) hidden inside a zero-visibility container (display: none; and aria-hidden="true").
  • Zero Human Distraction: Human users traversing the form natively via keyboard navigation or visual rendering will never see or interact with this input. Automated scrapers and bot scripts, however, automatically populate every visible and hidden field they encounter. If populated, the submission is immediately rejected client-side.

**

6. ** Cloudflare Turnstile Bot Defense**

  • Interactive Anti-Bot Verification: Integrated Cloudflare's privacy-friendly Turnstile widget (3x00000000000000000000FF) directly into the HTML structure. This allows full interactive testing of bot verification without requiring a paid dashboard account or domain registration.

  • Deep CSS Theme Overrides: Reached into the Turnstile container using forced CSS priority (!important) to convert any fallback, error, or troubleshoot hyperlinks into our imperial gold theme (#f4d03f) with neon pink hover glows (#ff69b4), keeping the security widget completely visually unified with the dark purple broadcast layout.

Summary:
By combining precise semantic HTML structure, strict CSS variable systems, custom inline vector art, and dynamic responsive layouts, Gentle Productions now possesses a digital sign-up portal fit for a true revolutionary, plus enforcing front-end security to go beyond!

Every single line of code was written with absolute devotion—because nothing less is worthy of Gentle Criminal! ❤️💻

Any questions you have? Let me know!

title: Zeen: A New Systems Programming Language with a Comptime Engine
description:
Website: zeen-lang.tech
Github: mealet/zeen

(Would appreciate if you'd leave a star on Github)

What is Zeen

Zeen - a modern systems programming language designed for simplicity, safety, and predictable control over memory. It provides toolchains and compiler rules to operate data easily and drop it automatically after usage with move semantics to avoid any runtime overhead. The main idea is to create a tool to develop efficient software where most errors are caught at compile time.

Zeen took many design choices from Rust and Zig programming languages, which makes it more familiar for most developers. Besides that it introduces its own approach to ownership, memory management, and compile-time execution.

Development Tools

Besides compiler and set of libraries (core, std), Zeen has:

  • Editors plugins for VS Code and Neovim
  • Package manager Zora

Small Example 

fn print_this[T: Display](value: T) {
  @println("Yeah, I've printed this: {}", value);
}

fn main() {
  print_this(123);
  print_this("hello!");
}

Quick Start

  1. Install latest release following official guide from documentation.
  2. Create new project with Zora: 
zora new my_project
cd my_project
  1. Write code and run your binary package: 
zora run

New Comptime Engine

Last update v0.4.0 brought a lot of enhancements: frontend performance, new warnings system, new macros, fixed C ABI and Comptime Engine.

Zeen's comptime engine allows you to move some evaluations or constructions away from runtime to the compiler.

You can define and eval constants, create Comptime functions which can construct new types, export expressions and declarations, emit declarations into current scope, format print at the compile time and more. Here's some examples of it.

Simple constants and splicing:

comptime N = 16;
comptime SquaredN = N * N;

fn main() {
  @println("{} -> {}", N, SquaredN);
  @println("$(N) -> $(SquaredN)");
}

Advanced usage (declarations, type values and etc):

comptime fn pair_of(struct_name: comptime_str, a: zeen_type, b: zeen_type) zeen_decl {
  @zeen_decl(
    struct $(struct_name) {
      pub a: $(a),
      pub b: $(b),
    }
  )
}

comptime {
  @emit(pair_of("NumsPair", i32, f32));
}

fn main() {
  let pair = NumsPair { .a = 1, .b = 1.0 };
  @println("{} {}", pair.a, pair.b);
}

See more info and examples on changelog and comptime docs pages.

title: AI Is Changing What It Means to Be a Good Frontend Engineer
description:
For a long time, being a good frontend engineer meant being really good at writing code. You needed to understand JavaScript, know your frameworks, write clean components, and be able to solve problems without constantly looking things up.

Those things still matter, but I think AI is forcing us to rethink what actually makes an engineer valuable.

We are entering a time where writing code is becoming the easiest part of building software. And I think that should challenge how we approach our work.

Writing Code Is No Longer the Hardest Part

I remember when being able to build something from scratch was a big deal. You had to understand how everything worked, scrub through Stackover, and spend hours figuring out why something was not behaving the way you expected.

Now, I can describe what I want to build, provide some context, and have AI generate a working implementation in minutes.

That is a pretty big shift.

But just because something works does not mean it was built correctly UNLESS we give it that context.

And that is where I think our value as engineers is starting to shift.

We Need to Become Better at Defining What Good Looks Like

I think one of the biggest opportunities for frontend engineers right now is becoming really good at defining expectations.

Not just telling AI what to build, but explaining how something should be built and what makes the implementation acceptable.

That means having clear specifications, established patterns, testing expectations, accessibility standards, and an understanding of how a feature fits into the rest of the application.

For example, asking AI to build a form is easy.

But does that form handle validation correctly? Does it account for loading and error states? Is it accessible? Does it use the components we already have? Does it follow the same data fetching patterns as the rest of our application?

Those are the things that matter.

And those are the things that can easily be overlooked when we become too focused on how quickly something gets built.

I think we should spend more time defining what good looks like before we ever start writing code.

Staying Close to the Code Still Matters

One thing I do not agree with is the idea that engineers no longer need to understand code because AI can write it for them.

I actually think the opposite.

The more code AI writes, the more important it becomes for us to understand what is happening.

You cannot properly review something you do not understand. You cannot identify a bad architectural decision if you do not understand the architecture. And you cannot confidently approve an implementation just because the application appears to work.

Being close to the code does not mean you have to personally write every line.

It means understanding the system well enough to recognize when something does not belong.

I want to be able to look at an implementation and understand why certain decisions were made, what could potentially break, and whether the solution makes sense for the application we are building.

AI should make us faster, but it should not make us disconnected.

Our Codebase Should Be Able to Explain Itself

This is something I have been thinking about more lately.

What if we approached our codebases with the expectation that any engineer or AI should be able to contribute without compromising the quality of the application?

Not because everyone has the same level of experience, but because the codebase has clear expectations.

Imagine having documented architectural decisions, reusable patterns, feature specifications, and testing standards that make it easy to understand how things should be done.

When someone introduces a new feature, they should not have to guess how state is managed, how components are structured, or how errors should be handled.

Those decisions should already have some level of consistency.

And when AI is introduced into that workflow, those same standards should apply.

I think that is a much better use of our experience than repeatedly correcting the same mistakes in pull requests.

Instead of just reviewing code for what is wrong, we should be building systems that make it harder to get things wrong in the first place.

Of course, no amount of documentation or testing will guarantee a bug free application. But we can absolutely reduce the number of avoidable mistakes.

Specs Might Become More Valuable Than Implementations

I have started thinking about how much time we spend explaining what we want after something has already been built.

We review a pull request and realize the implementation missed an important state. We discover that a component does not follow an existing pattern. Or we find out that the original requirements were never clear enough.

Then we spend more time going back and correcting those things.

What if we moved more of that effort to the beginning?

Before building a feature, we could define how it should behave, what scenarios it needs to support, what existing patterns it should follow, and how we will know it works.

That specification becomes something both an engineer and AI can work from.

And more importantly, something we can validate against.

What I imagine is like unit tests, we have spec files that ensure the AI that is reading the codebase understands what feature/bug was already implemented and can never be altered for that feature/bug to stay in tact becomes where a lot of the codebase value will live. If we can clearly define expected behavior, we can build tests that help protect that behavior regardless of who or what writes the implementation.

The goal should not be to generate more code.

The goal should be to deliver working software that continues to work as the application grows.

Experience Will Be Measured by the Problems We Prevent

Something else I think AI is going to challenge is how we recognize engineering experience.

For years, we have associated seniority with technical knowledge and the ability to solve difficult implementation problems.

And while those things still matter, I think there is another level of value that deserves more attention.

The ability to prevent problems before they happen.

A good engineer can fix a bug.

An experienced engineer should also be thinking about why that bug was possible in the first place and what can be done to prevent it from happening again.

That might mean improving a shared component, adding a test, documenting an architectural decision, or changing how we approach feature development.

Those improvements might not be as exciting as shipping a new feature, but they make every feature that comes after it easier to build and maintain.

To me, that is real engineering value.

And with AI increasing the amount of code we can produce, that kind of thinking becomes even more important.

We Should Be Focused on Value, Not Just Output

I think there is a real danger in measuring the success of AI by how much faster we can write code.

If AI helps us produce twice as much code, but we introduce twice as many bugs or create a codebase that becomes harder to maintain, what did we actually gain?

Writing more code has never automatically meant delivering more value.

The value comes from solving the right problems, making good decisions, and building something that people can depend on.

Sometimes that means writing less code.

Sometimes that means spending more time thinking through a specification.

And sometimes that means deciding not to build something at all.

AI gives us an opportunity to spend less time on repetitive implementation work and more time thinking about the actual problems we are trying to solve.

I think we should take advantage of that.

So What Does Being a Good Frontend Engineer Look Like Now?

I do not think the answer is to stop learning how to code.

I also do not think the answer is to reject AI because we want to protect the way we have always worked.

I think the answer is somewhere in the middle.

We should still understand JavaScript, React, browser behavior, performance, accessibility, and the fundamentals that make good frontend engineering possible.

But we should also become better at communicating requirements, defining standards, reviewing decisions, designing systems, and creating environments where quality is repeatable.

The engineers who understand both sides are going to be extremely valuable.

Because at the end of the day, someone still needs to understand what we are building, why we are building it, and whether it was built well.

AI can help us write the code.

But we still have to own the outcome.

One Final Thought

I keep coming back to this question.

If AI can write the same code I can, what value am I bringing to the engineering process that AI cannot provide on its own?

I do not see that as a threat. I see it as a question worth asking ourselves.

Maybe the next evolution of frontend engineering is not about becoming better at writing code faster.

Maybe it is about becoming better at creating the standards, specifications, and systems that allow good software to be built consistently, regardless of who or what is writing the code.

And maybe that is where we should have been focusing our attention all along.

Happy Coding 👍

title: I Replaced Math.random() With CSS. Here Is What Works.
description:
Why I care about this

I build creative sites for a living. Almost every project has some small random detail. Cards that sit a bit crooked. Particles that start at different times. A hue that changes on every load.

For years, that meant the same ten lines of JavaScript. Loop over the elements, call Math.random(), write a CSS variable. It works. But it runs after the HTML loads, it needs a script, and it fights with my server rendering.

On October 20, Google shipped Chrome 156. It includes the CSS random() function. Safari already had it. So I spent a few evenings replacing my JavaScript with plain CSS.

This post is what I learned. What works, what does not, and the one thing that will confuse you if you read older tutorials.

The basic syntax

random() takes a minimum and a maximum. It returns a value between them. You can add a third value, a step, to snap the result to fixed increments.

.card {
  rotate: random(-4deg, 4deg);           /* any angle in the range */
  width: random(200px, 320px, 40px);     /* 200, 240, 280 or 320px */
  animation-delay: random(0s, 2s);
}

Three rules to remember, all from MDN:

  1. Min, max and step must be the same data type. Lengths with lengths, angles with angles. Units can differ (1em and 40vw is fine).
  2. The range is inclusive on both ends.
  3. If max is smaller than min, you get the min value. No error, no warning. It works anywhere CSS accepts a length, angle, time, number, percentage, integer, frequency or resolution. That covers most of what I randomize.

The part that confused me: who shares the value

By default, every random() call is independent. Every element, every property, every position in a shorthand gets its own value. Most of the time that is what you want.

But sometimes you need a square. Width and height must be random, but equal. That is what the optional first argument is for. MDN calls it the <random-key>.

Key Same value across elements? Same value across properties?
auto (default) No No
element-scoped No Yes
property-scoped Yes No
--my-name Yes Yes
--my-name element-scoped No Yes, for calls with that name
fixed 0.5 You pick the seed (0 to 1) Yes

So a set of random squares, each one a different size, looks like this:

.tile {
  width: random(--tile-size element-scoped, 60px, 140px);
  height: random(--tile-size element-scoped, 60px, 140px);
}

Here is the trap. Older articles, including the WebKit announcement and early Frontend Masters tests, use a keyword called element-shared. The spec has moved on. The current names are element-scoped, property-scoped and property-index-scoped. If you copy a snippet from 2025 and nothing happens, check this first.

One more gotcha. A normal custom property does not store a random result. --size: random(1px, 100px) is text substitution, so every var(--size) rolls again. If you want one stored value, register the property with @property. MDN explains this with a short example.

Example 1: a messy stack of cards

This is a pattern I use a lot. A grid of photos or cards that look like they were dropped on a table. Each one tilted and shifted a little.

Here is the JavaScript version I have shipped many times:

const cards = document.querySelectorAll('.card');

function randomBetween(min, max) {
  return Math.random() * (max - min) + min;
}

cards.forEach((card) => {
  card.style.setProperty('--tilt', `${randomBetween(-6, 6)}deg`);
  card.style.setProperty('--shift-x', `${randomBetween(-12, 12)}px`);
  card.style.setProperty('--shift-y', `${randomBetween(-12, 12)}px`);
  card.style.setProperty('--delay', `${randomBetween(0, 0.6)}s`);
});

.card {
  rotate: var(--tilt, 0deg);
  translate: var(--shift-x, 0) var(--shift-y, 0);
  animation: drop 0.5s var(--delay, 0s) both;
}

It works. But the cards render straight, then jump when the script runs. With server rendering you also get a mismatch between server and client values.

Here is the CSS version:

.card {
  rotate: random(-6deg, 6deg);
  translate: random(-12px, 12px) random(-12px, 12px);
  animation: drop 0.5s random(0s, 0.6s) both;
}

No script. No flash. Each card gets its own values because the default key is auto. The two values inside translate are also independent, because auto separates calls by their position in the declaration.

If you add the step argument, you get a more designed feel. Tilts of exactly -6, -3, 0, 3 or 6 degrees look less random and more intentional:

.card {
  rotate: random(-6deg, 6deg, 3deg);
}

Example 2: a palette that changes on every load

Pure random color looks bad. Fast. What I usually want is one random hue for the whole page, and small variations per element. That is where the keys pay off.

.blob {
  /* One hue for the whole page: a named key alone is global */
  --hue: random(--page-hue, 0, 360);

  /* Lightness varies per element, in steps of 10 */
  background: hsl(var(--hue) 70% random(35%, 75%, 10%));

  /* Each blob is a circle of its own size */
  width: random(--blob-size element-scoped, 80px, 240px);
  height: random(--blob-size element-scoped, 80px, 240px);

  /* Scatter them across the hero */
  position: absolute;
  top: random(0%, 90%);
  left: random(0%, 90%);
}

Every load gives you a new mood. But it always looks like one palette, because every blob uses the same --page-hue seed.

The JavaScript version needed one value for the page and one loop for the elements. Something like this:

const hue = Math.floor(Math.random() * 361);
document.documentElement.style.setProperty('--hue', hue);

document.querySelectorAll('.blob').forEach((blob) => {
  const size = 80 + Math.random() * 160;
  const light = 35 + Math.floor(Math.random() * 5) * 10;
  blob.style.setProperty('--size', `${size}px`);
  blob.style.setProperty('--light', `${light}%`);
  blob.style.setProperty('--top', `${Math.random() * 90}%`);
  blob.style.setProperty('--left', `${Math.random() * 90}%`);
});

Ten lines of script turned into a few declarations. For a hero section, I will take that trade every time.

Shipping it today: a fallback that only runs when needed

Firefox does not support random() yet. Smashing Magazine reports positive signals from Mozilla, but no release. So for client work, I treat it as progressive enhancement.

Step one: write a calm default first, then add the random layer inside a feature query. MDN uses order: random(1, 2) as the test, which is a nice trick.

.card {
  rotate: var(--tilt, 0deg);
}

@supports (order: random(1, 2)) {
  .card {
    rotate: random(-6deg, 6deg, 3deg);
  }
}

Step two: if the random effect really matters to the design, add a tiny script that only runs in browsers without support.

const supportsRandom = CSS.supports('order', 'random(1, 2)');

if (!supportsRandom) {
  const steps = [-6, -3, 0, 3, 6];
  document.querySelectorAll('.card').forEach((card) => {
    const tilt = steps[Math.floor(Math.random() * steps.length)];
    card.style.setProperty('--tilt', `${tilt}deg`);
  });
}

Chrome and Safari users get pure CSS. Firefox users get the old behavior. Nobody gets a broken page.

If you want one code path for every browser, CSS-Tricks covered a polyfill that resolves random() with JavaScript. I have not used it in production, so test it before you trust it.

Honest caveats

random() is great. It is not a full replacement for Math.random(). Here is where JavaScript still wins, or where you need to be careful.

You cannot re-roll on demand. The value is picked when styles are computed. There is no "shuffle" button. If a user action should create new values, you still need JavaScript.

Hover states may not change. With the default auto key, the browser builds the seed name from the property and position. So width: random(100px, 200px) on .foo and on .foo:hover share a seed, and nothing changes on hover. MDN shows this case. Use a different named key for the hover rule if you want a new value.

You cannot read the value easily. If your WebGL scene or GSAP timeline needs to know the exact random number, keep it in JavaScript. Syncing CSS randomness into a canvas is more work than it saves.

Contrast is your problem now. A random text color can land on an unreadable value. MDN warns about this directly. Randomize decoration, not readable content, or keep the range tight.

Motion still needs an off switch. Random delays and positions are often used in animation. Wrap that animation in prefers-reduced-motion like any other.

Support is still partial. Chrome 156 and Safari support it. Firefox does not, as of today. MDN still marks it as limited availability.

What to do this week

  1. Open Chrome 156 or Safari and paste the card example into a CodePen. It takes two minutes and you will understand the keys faster than by reading.
  2. Search your codebase for Math.random() used only to set styles. Those are your candidates.
  3. Pick one decorative effect and move it to CSS behind @supports (order: random(1, 2)).
  4. Keep a calm default for Firefox. Add the JavaScript fallback only if the effect is part of the design.
  5. Ignore any snippet that uses element-shared. Translate it to element-scoped or a named key.
  6. Leave anything interactive, readable or synced with canvas in JavaScript.

title: Let Users Install Your Java Web App Again
description:
We lost progressive web app support when we moved the JavaScript port from TeaVM to ParparVM. It's back. Users can install your browser app on supporting browsers, and its cached application files can load when the network is unavailable.

What is Codename One? Codename One is an open-source framework for building native iOS, Android, desktop, and web apps from a single Java or Kotlin codebase. Learn more at codenameone.com.

For a small business, a link can be the quickest way to put an app in someone's hands. Installation lets that same app remain within reach after the tab closes. This is Wednesday's follow-up to the Wayline release story.

The build makes the installation files

A ParparVM JavaScript application build now produces manifest.json, home-screen icons and sw.js automatically. There is no separate PWA enablement switch.

Deploy the whole generated bundle, including subdirectories, over HTTPS. Localhost also works for testing. Relative manifest and asset URLs let an application live under a path such as /dispatch/ rather than requiring a dedicated domain root.

You can customize the app's identity through build hints in codenameone_settings.properties:

codename1.arg.javascript.manifest.name=Station Dispatch
codename1.arg.javascript.manifest.short_name=Dispatch
codename1.arg.javascript.manifest.description=Your station's dispatch app
codename1.arg.javascript.manifest.display=standalone

The default manifest already requests a standalone window. name and short_name default to the application's display name. Installation UI and eligibility depend on the browser, so avoid making your onboarding depend on one particular prompt appearing.

Offline launch has a precise boundary

The service worker caches generated application files: the runtime, translated JavaScript chunks, themes and bundled resources. It must finish installing while online before those files can support an offline launch.

It doesn't cache API responses, proxy requests or external resources. Application data and synchronization remain your responsibility.

In Wayline, that means a cached UI is not permission to accept a ride offline. Matching needs the server, and the map's external tiles and routes aren't bundled application assets. A dispatch app should say that it is disconnected rather than show a stale assignment as confirmed.

This distinction is useful outside ride hailing too. A locally stored draft can remain editable; publishing that draft still needs a connection. Design the interaction around what you actually have on the device.

An update should belong to one version

A running app needs its runtime and resources to agree. The worker creates a new cache when content changes, even if the application's version string stays the same.

The new worker waits until the old app's tabs and windows close before activating. That keeps an open app from mixing an old runtime with new chunks. Each deployment path has its own cache, so two apps on the same host don't share one undifferentiated bucket.

Deploy the files together and allow the browser to revalidate sw.js. Cache versioning helps the client choose a coherent bundle; it doesn't turn a partially uploaded deployment into a complete one.

Check the behavior your users will get

After deploying a test build, open the browser's Application tools and inspect the manifest, service worker and cache. Wait for installation to finish, then reload offline. Check both the UI that should work and the operations that should report a missing connection.

For an update check, keep one old tab open, deploy a visibly changed build and confirm that the new worker waits. Close the old tabs and reopen the app. Test a subdirectory deployment too if that is how you host it.

The repository includes a browser smoke test and service-worker contract checks. Those tests exercise caching and update behavior; they don't establish that every browser offers the same install experience.

PR #6022 restores the capability, and the JavaScript guide explains manifest customization. A web deployment can be a useful first distribution channel for your application, with native apps alongside it when their device integration matters.

Discussion

What should your app still let a user do after the connection drops?

title: Amazon RDS for Oracle now supports September 2026 Monthly Recommended Patch
description:
Amazon Relational Database Service (Amazon RDS) for Oracle now supports the September 2026 Monthly Recommended Patch (MRP) for Oracle Database version 19c and 26ai. An MRP is a minor engine version that builds on a quarterly Release Update (RU), bundling Oracle's Critical Security Patch Update (CSPU) with additional Oracle-recommended fixes. The September 2026 MRP is applied on top of the July 2026 RU and includes the Oracle September CSPU. We recommend upgrading to the September 2026 MRP as it includes the latest security updates for Oracle Database.

This release also includes the updated Oracle time zone file (DST version 46), which reflects the latest daylight saving time rule changes in several regions, including British Columbia and Alberta in Canada (effective November 1, 2026) and Morocco and Western Sahara (effective September 20, 2026), which are moving to permanent UTC offsets. If you store timestamps that include time zone information for these areas, the updated time zone file keeps that data aligned with the new rules.

You can apply the September 2026 MRP for new database instances, or upgrade existing instances to engine version 19.0.0.0.ru-2026-07.mrp-2026-09.r2 or 26.0.0.0.ru-2026-07.mrp-2026-09.r2 from the Amazon RDS Management Console, or by using the AWS SDK or CLI. To learn more about Oracle MRPs supported on Amazon RDS for each engine version, see the Amazon RDS for Oracle Release notes.

title: Two checks worth adding when you rewrite a checkout modal
description:
While rebuilding the free-preview and checkout flow in CrawlGraph, our review caught two details that are easy to miss: inherited disabled state and native email validation.

The browser APIs covered both cases. We added checks for the pending request state.

I build CrawlGraph, a backlink research and outreach tool. Here are the two checks from the interface work we just released.

1. A fieldset can disable an input without changing its attributes

Our checkout has a plan chooser. While its request is pending, the chooser's fieldset is disabled.

A focus-trap selector like this looks reasonable:

panel.querySelectorAll('button:not([disabled]), input:not([disabled])');

But an input inside a disabled fieldset can match that selector while still being disabled by the browser. It may have no disabled attribute of its own.

That matters when your trap treats the input as its last focusable element. Shift+Tab can try to focus a control that cannot receive focus. Forward Tab can leave the dialog because your calculated boundary is wrong.

Check effective state as well as visibility:

const controls = [...panel.querySelectorAll(focusableSelector)]
  .filter((element) => element.getClientRects().length > 0)
  .filter((element) => !element.matches(':disabled'));

Use a delayed checkout response, then press Tab and Shift+Tab from the close button while the request is pending.

MDN describes how disabled fieldsets affect their descendant controls.

2. Inline errors should keep the browser's email validity check

We wanted an inline error instead of the browser's validation bubble, so the rewritten form used noValidate.

That makes the submit handler responsible for validation. A check that only asks whether the string contains @ accepts user@@example.com far enough to start a request.

For an email input, the browser still exposes its validity state:

const invalid =
  !email.trim() ||
  input.validity.typeMismatch ||
  !input.validity.valid;

if (invalid) {
  showInlineError();
  input.focus();
  return;
}

// Track the valid action and start the request after this guard.

Keep the visible label, associate the error with the field, and preserve the typed address. Client validation improves the interaction; the server still validates the request independently.

The typeMismatch documentation explains the email and URL checks.

One more check for nested dialogs

Our free preview can open checkout. Escape should close the top dialog, preserve the preview beneath it, and return focus to the button that opened checkout. Background scrolling should remain locked until the final dialog closes.

We now render one responsive panel per modal instead of separate desktop and mobile copies. A shared stack owns focus and scroll behavior.

The WAI modal-dialog pattern is a useful baseline for Tab, Shift+Tab, initial focus and Escape behavior. We checked the Stripe backlink lookup against the live API and covered pending, error and already-paid checkout states with controlled responses.

The updated CrawlGraph preview lets you try up to five referring-domain rows without creating an account. Paid retrieval and CSV/JSON exports support up to 100,000 referring-domain rows per lookup. Paid users can also save outreach targets, find published contact emails and open a draft in their mail app.

The updated flow is live. Try a stripe.com lookup and follow the results into the outreach workflow.

title: Dockerfile multi-stage para Go: de 800 MB a menos de 20 MB
description:
Si tu Dockerfile de Go empieza con FROM golang y termina con CMD ["./app"], tu imagen probablemente pesa más de 800 MB: incluye el compilador, el código fuente y la caché de módulos. Nada de eso hace falta para ejecutar un binario. Con un build multi-stage compilamos en una imagen y copiamos solo el binario a otra mínima.

El Dockerfile 

# syntax=docker/dockerfile:1
ARG GO_VERSION=1.24

FROM --platform=$BUILDPLATFORM golang:${GO_VERSION}-alpine AS build
WORKDIR /src

COPY go.mod go.sum ./
RUN --mount=type=cache,target=/go/pkg/mod \
    go mod download

COPY . .

ARG TARGETOS
ARG TARGETARCH
RUN --mount=type=cache,target=/go/pkg/mod \
    --mount=type=cache,target=/root/.cache/go-build \
    CGO_ENABLED=0 GOOS=${TARGETOS} GOARCH=${TARGETARCH} \
    go build -trimpath -ldflags="-s -w" -o /out/app .

FROM gcr.io/distroless/static-debian12:nonroot
COPY --from=build /out/app /app
USER nonroot:nonroot
EXPOSE 8080
ENTRYPOINT ["/app"]

Qué hace cada parte

Dos FROM = dos etapas. La primera (build) tiene Go completo. La segunda parte de una imagen casi vacía y solo recibe /out/app con COPY --from=build. Todo lo demás se descarta.

go.mod y go.sum antes que el código. Docker cachea cada instrucción. Si copias todo de una vez, cualquier cambio en un .go invalida la descarga de módulos. Separándolos, go mod download solo se repite cuando cambian tus dependencias.

RUN --mount=type=cache. Es una función de BuildKit (activado por defecto desde Docker 23). Monta una caché persistente durante el build sin guardarla en la imagen. La caché de compilación de Go (/root/.cache/go-build) hace que recompilar tras un cambio pequeño tarde segundos.

CGO_ENABLED=0. Genera un binario estático que no depende de la libc del sistema. Es lo que permite usar una imagen final sin libc.

-trimpath -ldflags="-s -w". -trimpath quita las rutas de tu máquina del binario y -s -w elimina la tabla de símbolos y la información de depuración. El binario queda notablemente más chico.

--platform=$BUILDPLATFORM + TARGETOS/TARGETARCH. Go compila de forma cruzada sin esfuerzo. Con esto, el compilador corre nativo en tu máquina y genera el binario para la arquitectura que pidas, sin emular con QEMU:

docker buildx build --platform linux/amd64,linux/arm64 -t mi-servicio .

distroless/static-debian12:nonroot. Una imagen de unos 2 MB que contiene certificados CA (para llamar APIs HTTPS), datos de zona horaria y un usuario sin privilegios. No tiene shell ni gestor de paquetes: si alguien compromete tu app, no tiene herramientas para moverse.

Un detalle importante

Como distroless no tiene shell, no puedes usar HEALTHCHECK CMD curl .... Define el healthcheck en Kubernetes o compose apuntando a tu endpoint, o haz que tu binario acepte un flag como -healthcheck y usa HEALTHCHECK CMD ["/app", "-healthcheck"].

Compruébalo 

docker build -t mi-servicio .
docker images mi-servicio

Para un servicio HTTP típico verás una imagen de entre 10 y 25 MB. Menos tamaño significa despliegues más rápidos, menos costo de almacenamiento y menos superficie de ataque.

¿Te sirvió? Este ejemplo es parte del Pack Dockerfiles Optimizados: paga lo que quieras, desde 2 USD. Más recursos gratis en GitHub.

title: Dive into MobX with Flowik: how auto-tracking works
description:
In the first post I introduced Flowik, a MobX-style state library for Swing and Vaadin. Its pitch fits in one sentence: reading is subscribing. You read count.value inside an autoRun, and the autoRun re-runs when count changes. There is no subscribe() call anywhere.

The first time you see this it looks like magic. It isn't. The whole mechanism is a stack, a couple of sets and a counter, and it fits in about a hundred lines of Kotlin.

In this post we will build a toy version from scratch in three steps: observables with autoRun, then computed, then action. After that we will open Flowik's real Tracking.kt and see what changes when the toy has to survive a real UI. If you already use MobX in JavaScript, this is also a tour of what MobX does under the hood.

The picture in your head: a dependency graph

Every MobX-style app is a graph with three kinds of nodes:

  • Observables: the source state. They are mutable and know who reads them.
  • Computeds: values derived from other nodes. They are cached, and they are both readers and things being read.
  • Reactions (autoRun in Flowik): the leaves, where effects happen, such as updating a label. 
flowchart LR
    subgraph S["Observable state"]
        F(["firstName"])
        L(["lastName"])
        A(["age"])
    end
    subgraph D["Derivations"]
        N["fullName<br/><i>computed</i>"]
        R1{{"autoRun:<br/>update header label"}}
        R2{{"autoRun:<br/>update age field"}}
    end
    F --> N
    L --> N
    N --> R1
    A --> R2
    classDef obs fill:#e7f1fb,stroke:#3b78c4,color:#10243e
    classDef comp fill:#efedff,stroke:#6b5bd2,color:#1d1640
    classDef react fill:#e5f4e4,stroke:#3d8c40,color:#12300f
    class F,L,A obs
    class N comp
    class R1,R2 react

Arrows point the way changes flow. Change age and only the age field updates. Change firstName and the header updates, while the age field is left alone.

The interesting part is that you never draw this graph. Nobody writes "fullName depends on firstName". The library discovers each arrow at runtime, by watching what each derivation reads while it runs. Let's build the machinery that does that.

Step 1: who is reading right now?

The whole trick is one piece of global state: a stack of derivations that are currently running. When an observable is read, it looks at the top of that stack and adds whoever is there to its observers.

interface Derivation {
    fun onDependencyChanged()
}

object Tracking {
    private val stack = ArrayDeque<Derivation>()

    val current: Derivation? get() = stack.lastOrNull()

    fun <T> track(derivation: Derivation, block: () -> T): T {
        stack.addLast(derivation)
        try {
            return block()
        } finally {
            stack.removeLast()
        }
    }
}

It is a stack rather than a single variable because derivations nest: a reaction reads a computed, which runs its own function while the reaction is still running.

An observable is a value plus a set of observers. The getter records the current reader. The setter notifies everyone, but only if the value really changed:

class Observable<T>(initial: T) {
    private var _value = initial
    private val observers = mutableSetOf<Derivation>()

    var value: T
        get() {
            Tracking.current?.let { observers += it }   // reading is subscribing
            return _value
        }
        set(newValue) {
            if (newValue == _value) return
            _value = newValue
            observers.toList().forEach { it.onDependencyChanged() }
        }
}

And an autoRun simply runs its effect inside Tracking.track, and runs it again whenever told that something changed:

class AutoRun(private val effect: () -> Unit) : Derivation {
    fun run() = Tracking.track(this, effect)
    override fun onDependencyChanged() = run()
}

fun autoRun(effect: () -> Unit) = AutoRun(effect).also { it.run() }

That's it. Let's try it:

val count = Observable(0)
autoRun { println("count = ${count.value}") }   // count = 0
count.value = 1                                  // count = 1
count.value = 1                                  // nothing: the value did not change

Here is what happened during that first run:

sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant R as autoRun
    participant T as Tracking stack
    participant O as count (observable)
    R->>T: push(this)
    R->>O: read count.value
    O->>T: who is reading? current
    T-->>O: the autoRun
    Note over O: observers += autoRun
    O-->>R: 0
    R->>T: pop()
    Note over O: later: count.value = 1
    O->>R: notify, run() again

Notice that the subscription is a side effect of reading. That is why dependencies can be conditional. In autoRun { if (showDetails.value) println(details.value) }, the reaction only depends on details while showDetails is true. Our toy doesn't handle the other half of that yet, which is forgetting old dependencies. We'll come back to it.

Step 2: computed, the node with two faces

A computed sits in the middle of the graph, so it plays both roles. To its readers it looks like an observable: reading it records the current derivation. To its inputs it looks like a derivation: it evaluates its function inside Tracking.track(this, ...).

class Computed<T>(private val compute: () -> T) : Derivation {
    private var cached: T? = null
    private var dirty = true
    private val observers = mutableSetOf<Derivation>()

    val value: T
        get() {
            Tracking.current?.let { observers += it }   // observable to its readers
            if (dirty) {
                cached = Tracking.track(this, compute) // a derivation to its inputs
                dirty = false
            }
            return cached as T
        }

    override fun onDependencyChanged() {
        if (dirty) return             // already stale, downstream already told
        dirty = true                  // push: mark stale, compute nothing
        observers.toList().forEach { it.onDependencyChanged() }
    }
}

fun <T> computed(compute: () -> T) = Computed(compute)

The key design choice is push invalidation, pull evaluation. When an input changes, the computed does not recompute. It only marks itself dirty and passes the news downstream. The actual work happens later, when someone reads value. If nobody reads it, it never runs.

sequenceDiagram
    participant A as firstName
    participant C as fullName (computed)
    participant R as autoRun
    Note over A: firstName.value = "Bob"
    A->>C: invalidate()
    Note over C: isDirty = true<br/>(nothing recomputed yet)
    C->>R: schedule
    R->>C: read fullName.value
    C->>A: recompute: read firstName
    A-->>C: "Bob"
    C-->>R: "Bob Smith"
val firstName = Observable("Alice")
val lastName = Observable("Smith")
var evaluations = 0
val fullName = computed { evaluations++; "${firstName.value} ${lastName.value}" }

autoRun { println("Hello, ${fullName.value}") }   // Hello, Alice Smith
firstName.value = "Bob"                             // Hello, Bob Smith
println(evaluations)                                // 2

Two evaluations for two distinct states. Add ten more readers of fullName and it still evaluates once per change. That is the caching MobX is known for.

Step 3: action, or "not yet, please"

Our toy has a problem. A user renames a person, so we write two fields:

firstName.value = "Carol"   // Hello, Carol Smith   <- a name that never existed
lastName.value = "Jones"    // Hello, Carol Jones

The reaction ran twice, and the first run showed a half-updated state. In a UI that is wasted work and sometimes a visible flicker.

The fix is a batch: a depth counter and a set of pending reactions. While the depth is above zero, reactions are queued instead of run. When the outermost batch ends, each queued reaction runs once. A LinkedHashSet keeps the order and removes duplicates for free.

object Batch {
    private var depth = 0
    private val pending = linkedSetOf<AutoRun>()

    fun schedule(autoRun: AutoRun) {
        if (depth > 0) pending += autoRun else autoRun.run()
    }

    fun <T> action(block: () -> T): T {
        depth++
        try {
            return block()
        } finally {
            if (--depth == 0) {
                val toRun = pending.toList()
                pending.clear()
                toRun.forEach { it.run() }
            }
        }
    }
}

fun <T> action(block: () -> T): T = Batch.action(block)

The only change elsewhere is one line in AutoRun: instead of running directly, it asks to be scheduled.

override fun onDependencyChanged() = Batch.schedule(this)

Now:

action {
    firstName.value = "Carol"
    lastName.value = "Jones"
}                              // Hello, Carol Jones  (once)

sequenceDiagram
    participant U as action { }
    participant T as Tracking
    participant O as observables
    participant R as autoRun
    U->>T: beginBatch() depth = 1
    U->>O: firstName = "Carol"
    O->>T: schedule(autoRun)
    Note over T: batching: add to pending set
    U->>O: lastName = "Jones"
    O->>T: schedule(autoRun)
    Note over T: already pending, set dedupes
    U->>T: endBatch() depth = 0
    T->>R: flush: run() once

The counter, rather than a boolean, lets actions nest. A store method that is an action can call another action, and nothing flushes until the outermost one ends.

The diamond: why batching is about correctness, not only speed

Here is a shape that appears constantly in real screens: one input, two derived values, one view that shows both.

flowchart LR
    A(["price"]) --> B["net<br/><i>computed</i>"]
    A --> C["tax<br/><i>computed</i>"]
    B --> R{{"autoRun:<br/>show net + tax"}}
    C --> R
    classDef obs fill:#e7f1fb,stroke:#3b78c4,color:#10243e
    classDef comp fill:#efedff,stroke:#6b5bd2,color:#1d1640
    classDef react fill:#e5f4e4,stroke:#3d8c40,color:#12300f
    class A obs
    class B,C comp
    class R react
val price = Observable(100)
val net = computed { price.value }
val tax = computed { price.value / 5 }
autoRun { println("net=${net.value} tax=${tax.value}") }   // net=100 tax=20

price.value = 200
// net=200 tax=20   <- glitch: tax is stale
// net=200 tax=40

Without a batch, price notifies net first. net schedules the autoRun, which runs immediately and reads tax. But tax has not been told about the change yet, so it returns its old cached value. Then tax is notified and the autoRun runs a second time. For a moment the screen showed a net price and a tax that never belonged together. In reactive systems this is called a glitch.

Inside an action the problem disappears. Both computeds are marked dirty before any reaction runs, so the single run sees a consistent world:

action { price.value = 300 }   // net=300 tax=60  (once)

MobX handles this by treating every write as a tiny batch of its own, and by tracking stale and ready counts on each node so that a reaction waits until all its inputs are settled. The practical rule for our toy, and for Flowik today, is simple: change state inside actions. That is good style anyway, because an action names the intent ("rename", "delete") and gives you one place to put it.

From toy to Flowik

Our toy is about 90 lines and already has the right shape. Open Flowik's Tracking.kt and you will recognise it immediately: a stack of Trackers, a batch depth and pending sets. What the real version adds is mostly about surviving a long-lived UI.

Concern Toy Flowik
Tracking context One global stack A ThreadLocal stack, so each thread has its own context. State is meant to be used from the UI thread.
Stale dependencies Never forgotten Before each re-run, AutoRun and Computed unsubscribe from all old dependencies, then re-subscribe to what they actually read
Reaction kinds autoRun only autoRun, reaction(supply, effect) and whenThen, each with its own pending queue
Change detection == equals by default, plus observableRef (identity), observableStruct (deep) or a custom comparer
Derived values that notify only on real change Not possible computedStruct / computedRef, refreshed at the end of a batch before reactions run
Errors Exception escapes into the writer Caught per reaction, passed to onError or logged; the reaction stays alive
Lifetime Lives forever dispose() stops a reaction and releases its subscriptions

A few details are worth reading in the source.

Batches end even when things throw. endBatch() refreshes derived values inside a try/finally, so a failing derivation can't leave the thread stuck in batching mode, where it would silently swallow every later reaction.

Derived values settle before reactions run. Policy-based computeds such as computedStruct have to evaluate to know whether they changed, and one refresh can invalidate another downstream. So flushRefreshes() loops until nothing is left, with a guard of 100 rounds to report a cycle instead of hanging. Only then are reactions flushed.

untracked is a stack swap. Reading without subscribing needs no special flags on observables. Flowik just replaces the stack with an empty one for the duration of the block:

fun <R> untracked(block: () -> R): R {
    val saved = stack.get()
    stack.set(ArrayDeque())
    return try {
        block()
    } finally {
        stack.set(saved)
    }
}

Errors are reported outside tracking. AutoRun.run() pops itself off the stack before calling the error handler, so whatever the handler reads does not become a dependency of the failed reaction.

Two ways to listen. Observer.kt is just a fun interface with onChange(). It is the explicit subscribe() channel, which the UI bindings and collections use to forward changes, for example from a list element up to its list. Auto-tracking and explicit subscription live side by side, and you rarely need the second one in application code.

Wrapping up

The "magic" of MobX comes down to three ideas:

  1. A stack of who is running. Reading an observable subscribes whoever is on top.
  2. Push invalidation, pull evaluation. Changes only mark things dirty; work happens when someone reads.
  3. Batching. An action delays reactions until the state is consistent, then runs each one once.

Everything else (disposal, error handling, comparison policies, async loading) is engineering around those three. Once you have built the toy yourself, the real source stops being intimidating. Flowik's whole core is under 3,000 lines of Kotlin, and Tracking.kt is about 150 of them.

The complete toy from this post fits in a single file, so paste it into a scratch file and break it. Try making the observable setter wrap its notifications in action { } and watch the diamond glitch disappear.

  • Flowik on GitHub: jreznot/flowik
  • The gist of MobX
