title: Nobody saw the flying sword, so I redesigned the first sky crossing
description:
Development covered 19 Sep 2026 to 20 Sep 2026 (commit dates).

Myriad Immortal Sect is a shared world without being a live multiplayer game. You never fight someone in real time, but the people around you on the map are real players: cultivators from the rankings walking the land near you, and now and then someone crossing the sky on a flying sword. That layer exists for one reason. An idle game played alone in a tab can feel like a spreadsheet with a background, and seeing other people is the cheapest way to say "this place is lived in".

This week I found out that the most important instance of it, the first one, was not working. Not broken. Working exactly as written, and unseen.

On cue, on screen, unnoticed

Shortly after you first reach the map, a toast says "Look up, someone rides the wind", and a rider crosses the sky. I measured it in the 1280 by 720 frame of an itch.io embed. The crossing launched on time. It cut a 21 degree diagonal through the player's own head height at 250 pixels a second and was gone in 2.8 seconds. A blind five-minute first play never noticed it.

Three things worked against it. It was fast. It moved diagonally through the busiest part of the screen, the area around your own character, where the eye is already full. And when it passed over land you had not explored yet, it was drawn under the fog, a faint shape behind a grey tint.

Making a figure in the sky readable

The opening crossing now runs nearly horizontally through the upper band of the view, away from the clutter around the player. It is paced to cross the full width of the view in six seconds whatever the window size, which I checked at five different sizes, because a fixed speed in pixels means a phone sees a blur and a wide monitor sees a crawl.

It also had a staging problem. The rider started far enough outside the view that it spent 3.4 seconds flying towards the frame after the toast had already told you to look up, so the prompt arrived, you looked, and there was nothing yet. It now starts just outside the edge and is in frame within half a second of the toast. And riders, their vessels and their glow draw above the fog while their shadow stays on the ground, so a crossing over unexplored land is as visible as one over home.

None of this changed what a crossing is. It changed whether the player's attention and the event were in the same place at the same time.

A warm-up cadence for the first three minutes

Normally someone crosses the sky about once a minute. That rhythm is right for the long session and wrong for the first one. If the opening crossing is missed, the next chance is a minute away, and a new player decides how a world feels in much less time than that.

So the first three minutes on the map have their own cadence: a crossing every 22 to 35 seconds, then it settles to the normal rate. All three of those numbers are settings rather than constants, because I fully expect to move them after watching more first sessions. Riders travel on different vessels depending on their sect, and one you may see overhead is the Black Iron flying sword, which has its own codex entry.

The embed is part of the design surface

Most of the measuring this week happened inside the itch.io page rather than on my own site, and the frame around the game turned out to matter more than I expected.

Whenever the game scrolled something into view inside itself, the sect offers after the spirit test for instance, the browser also scrolled the itch page around it. On the draft page that dragged the whole host page 221 pixels and pushed the top of the game out of the window. The game now only ever scrolls its own content and never the page it lives in.

And the defaults a new player hears changed. Music and effects both started at 70. Music now starts at 20 and effects at 50, because the first thing many people do in a browser game is reach for the mute button, and I would rather they kept the sound of a tribulation than lost it to a loud menu theme.

What to take from this

If your design depends on a moment, measure the moment in the smallest, busiest frame a real player will use, and check three things: is it where the eye already is, does it last long enough to find, and does the prompt arrive with the event or before it. For a wider view of what the map holds, the overview of exploration in an idle cultivation game is the place to start.

Look up in your first three minutes: the world is free to walk in your browser.

title: umux v1.7.7 ships Core Session
description:
umux v1.7.7: Core Session, a sleep block with an end time

Quick context for anyone new here: umux is an open-source terminal workspace manager. One desktop app (Tauri v2) with its own embedded terminal. You group terminals into named workspaces, each workspace holds tabs, and every tab splits into as many resizable panels as you need. Linux, Windows, macOS.

v1.7.7 ships Core Session, and it fixes a human problem more than a technical one.

umux Core keeps the machine awake while agents run long jobs. It shipped as a toggle: ON until someone flips it OFF. That someone is you, hours later, and until then the hardware runs for nothing.

Core Session puts a clock on the hold:

umux core-session start 90m

The machine (not just the screen) stays awake for exactly that window, 24 hours max per session. umux core-session extend 30m adds time mid-flight. umux core-session stop ends it early. When the deadline passes, the daemon releases the hold on its own and posts one desktop notification. Settings shows the countdown and, after the fact, when the session ended and why.

The deadline is absolute. It is stored the moment the session starts, and a restart brings the session back with whatever window remained. A crash can never stretch the hold by accident. umux status --json carries the same truth for scripts: active, endsAt, remainingSecs.

Under the hood, nothing new holds the machine. The same three backends as before: an IOKit assertion on macOS, SetThreadExecutionState on Windows, a logind inhibitor on Linux. The new part is the deadline on top.

Platform details worth knowing. On macOS, the persistent Core switch retires. Settings now shows Core Session (BETA), and umux core on refuses with a pointer to the new command. On Windows and Linux, Core stays as shipped, and Core and a session never run at the same time.

Also in this release:

  • Clicking a notification on macOS navigates to the panel it came from.
  • Windows gets a umux-owned notification banner, because the old toasts ignored clicks.
  • Daemon replay no longer answers a fresh terminal's hardware probes, so a restored session starts clean instead of printing probe garbage.
  • A fix for the keyboard freeze some setups hit when the app resolved a working directory.

I'm running this build on my Mac as of today. Install and build steps live in the README, and the full notes are here: https://github.com/CrystalPlatforms/umux/releases/tag/v1.7.7

title: Resolving Go Application Performance Issues: CPU Usage and Memory Leaks with pprof and Flame Graphs
description:
Introduction to Golang Profiling with pprof

Profiling Go applications is not just a debugging exercise—it’s a survival skill in modern software development. As Go’s runtime schedules goroutines onto OS threads, the system’s efficiency hinges on how well these threads are utilized. pprof, Go’s built-in profiling tool, acts as a microscope, capturing runtime data via sampling to expose CPU, memory, block, and mutex behaviors. Without it, performance issues like high CPU usage or memory leaks remain invisible, silently degrading application reliability and scalability.

Consider CPU usage: inefficient algorithms or busy-waiting loops force the CPU to execute redundant instructions, consuming cycles that could be allocated to other tasks. pprof’s CPU profiles reveal this by sampling the call stack at regular intervals, showing exactly which functions are hogging the CPU. Flame graphs then visualize this data, mapping function execution time to a hierarchical structure. Hotspots in these graphs often point to unexpected culprits—functions inlined or deferred, masked by Go’s compiler optimizations.

Memory leaks, on the other hand, are a silent killer in Go’s garbage-collected environment. While the GC reclaims unused memory, leaks occur when objects are retained unnecessarily, often via global variables or unbounded buffers. pprof’s memory profiles track heap allocations, exposing objects that persist across GC cycles. However, detecting leaks requires long-running applications to observe gradual heap growth, a constraint in production environments where profiling overhead is a concern.

The interplay between CPU and memory is critical. Frequent GC pauses, for instance, are often triggered by excessive object allocation in specific code paths. By correlating CPU and memory profiles, you can pinpoint operations that allocate heavily while consuming CPU, a double hit on resources. External dependencies exacerbate this—unoptimized libraries or database queries without indexes introduce hidden performance costs, masked in application code but visible in pprof data.

To profile effectively, enable runtime profiling flags (-cpuprofile, -memprofile) in your Go application. This activates pprof’s sampling mechanism, but beware: in production, this overhead can distort results. Instead, profile under controlled load conditions to simulate real-world behavior. Tools like go tool pprof and perf then process the collected data, generating flame graphs or textual reports. However, external dependencies lacking profiling support may require dynamic tracing or vendor-specific tools to uncover their impact.

In summary, pprof is not just a tool—it’s a lens into Go’s runtime mechanics. By understanding its sampling methodology and interpreting its output in context, you can diagnose performance issues with surgical precision. Ignore it, and you’re flying blind, risking inefficient resource utilization, increased operational costs, and a degraded user experience. The choice is clear: if you’re serious about Go performance, pprof isn’t optional—it’s mandatory.

Analyzing CPU Usage with Flame Graphs

Flame graphs are a powerful visualization tool for understanding CPU usage in Go applications. By mapping the call stack hierarchy and function execution time, they reveal hotspots where CPU cycles are consumed excessively. This section guides you through generating and interpreting these graphs using pprof, enabling precise identification of performance bottlenecks.

Generating CPU Flame Graphs

To generate a CPU flame graph, follow these steps:

  • Enable CPU profiling: Start your Go application with the -cpuprofile flag to activate pprof’s sampling mechanism. This flag instructs the Go runtime to periodically capture the call stack, providing data for CPU usage analysis.
  • Simulate workload: Run your application under a controlled load to ensure the profiling data reflects typical usage patterns. Avoid profiling in idle states, as this can distort results.
  • Process profiling data: Use go tool pprof to convert the raw profiling data into a format suitable for flame graph generation. For example: 
  go tool pprof -svg cpuprofile.out > cpu.svg
  • Visualize with flame graph tools: Utilize external tools like FlameGraph (available in Perl or Python) to generate the final visualization. This step transforms the hierarchical call stack data into a layered, color-coded graph.

Interpreting Flame Graphs

Flame graphs provide a visual breakdown of CPU usage, with each layer representing a function in the call stack. The width of each block corresponds to the time spent executing that function. Key insights include:

  • Hotspots identification: Wide blocks indicate functions consuming significant CPU time. These are often caused by inefficient algorithms, busy-waiting loops, or unoptimized external library calls. For example, a function with a wide block may be performing redundant calculations or blocking on I/O operations.
  • Inlining and deferred execution: Flame graphs may show unexpected hotspots due to function inlining or deferred execution. In Go, the compiler may inline small functions, causing their execution time to appear under the caller’s block. Similarly, deferred functions execute as part of the caller’s stack unwinding, which can skew the graph.
  • Concurrency effects: Goroutine scheduling and mutex contention can manifest as CPU inefficiency in flame graphs. For instance, a mutex lock held for an extended period may appear as a wide block, indicating a concurrency bottleneck.

Optimizing CPU-Intensive Code

Once hotspots are identified, apply targeted optimizations:

  • Algorithmic improvements: Replace inefficient algorithms with more performant alternatives. For example, switching from a nested loop to a hash-based lookup can reduce CPU usage significantly.
  • Eliminate busy-waiting: Replace busy-waiting loops with asynchronous patterns or channel-based communication. This reduces redundant CPU cycles and improves overall efficiency.
  • Optimize external dependencies: Profile external libraries using dynamic tracing or vendor-specific tools. If a library is unoptimized, consider replacing it or contributing optimizations upstream.

Edge Cases and Limitations

While flame graphs are invaluable, they have limitations:

  • Profiling overhead: Enabling profiling flags introduces overhead, which can distort results in production. Always profile under controlled conditions and compare against baseline measurements.
  • External noise: External dependencies without profiling support may introduce noise. Use dynamic tracing or isolate their impact by profiling with and without them.
  • Concurrency masking: Concurrency issues like mutex contention may appear as CPU inefficiency. Correlate CPU profiles with block and mutex profiles to diagnose such cases.

Decision Dominance: When to Use Flame Graphs

Flame graphs are optimal for:

  • Identifying CPU-intensive functions in complex call stacks.
  • Diagnosing performance regressions after code changes.
  • Comparing CPU profiles before and after optimizations to quantify improvements.

Avoid using flame graphs for:

  • Memory leak detection (use memory profiles instead).
  • Profiling applications with minimal CPU usage, as hotspots may be insignificant.
  • Diagnosing issues in external dependencies without profiling support.

Rule of thumb: If CPU usage is high and the cause is unclear, generate a flame graph to pinpoint hotspots. If X (high CPU usage) -> use Y (flame graphs) to identify and resolve bottlenecks.

Detecting and Resolving Memory Leaks

Memory leaks in Go applications, despite the garbage collector (GC), occur when objects are unnecessarily retained, often via global variables or unbounded buffers. This retention forces the GC to skip these objects during cleanup, leading to gradual heap growth. The mechanism here is straightforward: the Go runtime’s memory allocation tracking identifies objects allocated but not garbage collected, which pprof captures in memory profiles. Over time, this unchecked growth deforms the application’s memory footprint, causing increased GC pauses as the collector struggles to reclaim memory from a shrinking free heap.

To detect leaks, enable memory profiling with the -memprofile flag, which activates pprof’s sampling of heap allocations. However, this approach has a critical edge case: profiling overhead in production. The act of profiling itself can distort memory behavior, making detection unreliable. Instead, profile under controlled, long-running conditions to observe trends. Use go tool pprof to process the profile data, generating reports that highlight objects persisting across GC cycles. For example, an unbounded channel buffer will show continuous growth in allocated memory, as objects are added but never removed, breaking the GC’s ability to reclaim them.

Practical Strategies for Mitigation

Once a leak is identified, the optimal solution depends on the root cause. If the leak stems from global variables, refactor to use local variables or explicitly nil references when objects are no longer needed. For unbounded buffers, introduce size limits or implement eviction policies. However, a common error is prematurely optimizing without understanding the leak’s mechanism. For instance, reducing buffer size without addressing the underlying retention logic merely delays the issue. The rule here is clear: if memory growth correlates with specific objects in profiles → inspect their lifecycle and retention paths.

External dependencies pose a unique challenge. Libraries without profiling support may introduce hidden leaks, as their memory behavior remains opaque to pprof. In such cases, dynamic tracing or vendor-specific tools become necessary. However, this approach has limitations: it requires deep familiarity with the dependency’s internals and may not integrate seamlessly with Go’s profiling ecosystem. The trade-off is between precision and practicality—if the dependency is critical and unoptimizable, consider replacing it with a profiled alternative.

Decision Dominance in Leak Resolution

  • If the leak is caused by global variables → refactor to use local scope or explicit nil references.
  • If unbounded buffers are the culprit → enforce size limits or implement eviction policies.
  • If external dependencies are leaking → profile with dynamic tracing or replace with profiled alternatives.

Avoid the common error of focusing solely on GC tuning (e.g., adjusting GC percentages) without addressing the root cause. While reducing GC pressure can alleviate symptoms, it does not fix the leak. The mechanism of risk here is clear: unchecked leaks will eventually exhaust memory, leading to application crashes or degraded performance. The optimal solution is always to eliminate the retention path, ensuring objects are reclaimed by the GC.

Finally, correlate memory profiles with CPU profiles to identify resource-intensive operations that trigger excessive allocations. For example, a function allocating large objects in a tight loop will show up in both CPU and memory hotspots. This interplay highlights the causal chain: high CPU usage → frequent allocations → increased GC pressure → memory leaks. By addressing both CPU and memory inefficiencies, you not only resolve leaks but also optimize overall application performance.

Practical Scenarios and Case Studies

1. High CPU Usage in a Web API: Uncovering Inefficient Algorithms

A Go-based web API experienced sustained CPU spikes under moderate load. Flame graph analysis revealed a hotspot in a JSON serialization function, consuming 40% of CPU time. The root cause was an inefficient recursive algorithm for encoding nested structures, generating redundant instructions. Replacing it with a hash-based lookup reduced CPU usage by 65%, as the new algorithm minimized stack operations and eliminated redundant memory accesses.

Mechanism: Recursive calls inflated the call stack, causing frequent context switches and cache misses. Hash-based lookup flattened the execution path, reducing stack depth and improving cache locality.

Rule of Thumb: If flame graphs show wide blocks in recursive functions → replace with iterative or hash-based alternatives.

2. Memory Leak in a Long-Running Service: Global Variable Retention

A long-running Go service exhibited gradual heap growth, leading to GC pauses every 5 minutes. Memory profiling identified a 200MB buffer retained in a global variable, never garbage collected. The buffer was initialized during startup but never cleared, accumulating data indefinitely. Refactoring to a local scope and adding explicit nil references resolved the leak, stabilizing heap usage.

Mechanism: Global variables bypass Go’s garbage collector, as they are always reachable. Explicit nil references break retention paths, allowing GC to reclaim memory.

Decision Dominance: For global variables causing leaks → refactor to local scope or nil references. Avoid GC tuning without addressing retention paths.

3. Unbounded Channel Buffer: Continuous Memory Growth

A messaging system used an unbounded channel to queue messages, leading to 1GB/hour memory growth. Memory profiling showed the channel buffer persisted across GC cycles, as messages were not consumed fast enough. Enforcing a size limit and implementing an eviction policy (e.g., dropping oldest messages) capped memory usage at 200MB.

Mechanism: Unbounded buffers accumulate objects indefinitely, as Go’s GC cannot reclaim them until explicitly removed. Size limits force eviction, breaking retention paths.

Rule of Thumb: If unbounded buffers cause leaks → enforce size limits or eviction policies. Avoid relying on GC alone.

4. External Library Bottleneck: Unoptimized Database Queries

A Go application using an external database library experienced 500ms latency spikes. CPU profiling showed 30% of CPU time spent in the library’s query execution function. Investigation revealed missing indexes on queried tables, forcing full table scans. Adding indexes reduced CPU usage by 70% and latency to 50ms.

Mechanism: Full table scans generate excessive I/O and CPU load, as the library processes all rows. Indexes reduce query scope, minimizing I/O and CPU overhead.

Decision Dominance: For external library bottlenecks → profile dependencies and optimize at the source. Avoid replacing libraries without root cause analysis.

5. Mutex Contention Masking CPU Inefficiency

A Go application showed high CPU usage in a critical section, but flame graphs pointed to a mutex lock function. Block profiling revealed 90% of goroutines were blocked on the mutex, causing 50% CPU underutilization. Replacing the mutex with a lock-free algorithm eliminated contention, increasing throughput by 200%.

Mechanism: Mutex contention serializes access, forcing goroutines to wait. Lock-free algorithms enable concurrent execution, maximizing CPU utilization.

Rule of Thumb: If CPU inefficiency coincides with mutex hotspots → use block profiles to diagnose contention. Replace locks with lock-free alternatives if feasible.

6. Frequent GC Pauses: Excessive Object Allocation

A Go application experienced 2-second GC pauses every minute, despite low memory usage. Correlating CPU and memory profiles identified a tight loop allocating 1MB objects every second. Optimizing the loop to reuse objects reduced allocations by 90%, eliminating pauses.

Mechanism: Frequent allocations shrink the free heap, triggering GC cycles. Reusing objects reduces allocation rate, preserving heap space and minimizing GC pressure.

Decision Dominance: For frequent GC pauses → correlate CPU and memory profiles to identify allocation hotspots. Optimize allocation paths before tuning GC settings.

title: What a from-scratch browser actually trusts: webpki-roots, exact pins, and the eMudhra week
description:
We're writing a browser from scratch in Rust. It's called Mars: own HTML parser and layout engine, own JS engine, own HTTP framing on top of rustls, native macOS shell. When you own the network stack you also own the question Apple is getting shouted at about this week: which certificate authorities does the thing trust, and who updates that list?

How Mars gets its roots

Our network crate, Relay, builds a rustls RootCertStore from webpki_roots::TLS_SERVER_ROOTS once at startup and keeps it in a OnceLock. That's it. No OS keychain, no /etc/ssl/cert.pem, no runtime download. The trust anchors are whatever the webpki-roots crate contained the day the lockfile was written. That's a normal choice for rustls users, and it has one property worth saying out loud: the trust store ships inside the binary, so it only changes when you rebuild.

What I found today

The eMudhra / emSign compromise is around ten days old. Mozilla, Google, Microsoft and most Linux distros dropped the roots within days. Apple blocked the certificates in Safari and Mail but left the macOS command line tools reading a cert.pem that still trusts them, which is why Hacker News is on fire.

In that thread someone asked whether there's a Rust crate that compiles root certs into binaries. There is, and we use it. So I checked. Both crates that do TLS in Mars pinned webpki-roots = "=1.0.9", released July 18. Grepping src/lib.rs in each release:

  • 1.0.9 (Jul 18): emSign Root CA - G1, emSign Root CA - C1, emSign ECC Root CA - G3, emSign ECC Root CA - C3
  • 1.0.10 (Oct 19): removed emSign ECC Root CA - G3
  • 1.0.11 (Oct 23): removed emSign Root CA - C1 and emSign ECC Root CA - C3, tracking the CCADB removals

So Mars, as of this morning, had the same hole as /usr/bin/curl on a Mac. Nothing at runtime would have told us. rustls does no revocation checking unless you hand it CRLs, and we don't. There is no blocklist. The bundle is the whole story.

The fix and the lesson

The fix took four minutes: bump both pins to =1.0.11, cargo update -p webpki-roots, cargo check. It compiles and it's in the tree.

The lesson is the uncomfortable one. Mars pins dependencies to exact versions, and an exact pin on a root bundle is a decision to stop receiving CA removals. It means someone has to watch that crate's releases the way an OS vendor watches the CCADB. For a browser that isn't optional, so it goes on the release checklist. I'd like to know how other rustls users handle it: Dependabot on that one crate, a CI job that diffs root names between versions, or just reading the release notes.

Repo: https://github.com/OyadotAI/oya-browser, folder mars/. Source-available under a Sustainable Use License, SDK and CLI MIT.

title: Object Storage for App Data Backups: A US/EU S3-Compatible Restore Test
description:
Short answer: object storage is a sensible low-cost home for app data backups when you keep buckets private, use signed download links for restores, and accept retention measured in whole days. It is the wrong tool when immutable recovery, public URLs, or a provider-managed compliance program is the actual requirement.

I make the decision with a restore-window SLO, not a storage-rate leaderboard. A nightly database dump or ZIP export is only useful if an operator can find it, download it from the right region, and restore it under pressure. Storage, egress, and request charges all belong in the estimate; the smallest monthly byte price alone tells me very little. I've watched estimates miss the transfer leg because someone counted stored gigabytes and ignored the restore path, so I write down the worker region, expected restore frequency, and the person who can authorize a download before I approve a bucket.

What should US/EU app backups require from private S3-compatible storage?

Start with a private bucket and a naming convention that carries the metadata your operator needs: prod/postgres/2026-07-31/tenant-42.sql.gz is easier to list by prefix than an opaque UUID. Scheduled dumps, archive exports, and restore downloads fit this pattern. A restore service authenticates the operator, then mints a short-lived signed URL; the bucket never needs a public-read policy.

US and EU placement still needs an explicit decision. Put each workload and its restore worker in the region you operate and document the residency assumption in the runbook. “US/EU” is a deployment constraint, not proof of compliance, and I'm not sure a vendor label can answer the legal question without your contracts.

Lifecycle rules can expire a prefix, but the smallest interval is one day. There is no hour-level expiry, automatic cleanup for multipart fragments, or server-side metadata search beyond prefix listing. If the application needs those controls, a catalog, queue, or cleanup worker has to own them.

That naming choice becomes a capacity signal as well as a lookup aid. I would separate prod/ from staging/, keep the database engine and date in the key, and record the compressed byte count in the backup manifest. During a restore drill, an operator can list one prefix, select a date, and compare the manifest before pulling a large archive across regions. The same convention makes a lifecycle rule narrow enough to review: expire prod/postgres/ after the agreed number of days while leaving a separate audit prefix alone. It also avoids pretending that object metadata is a query index. If the retention decision depends on a customer, legal hold, or checksum that is not in the key, keep that fact in a database and make the cleanup worker consult it before deletion. This is slower to design than “list everything and inspect names,” but it gives the on-call person a bounded operation and a measurable restore path.

Private means private.

The production-shaped restore path

The implementation should make retries boring and observable. The storage API uses a bearer key, an explicit HTTP method, and a client idempotency key for writes. A 429 is a scheduling signal: honor Retry-After when it is present, back off, and surface the error when attempts are exhausted. Don't turn a retry loop into an unbounded worker; a backup that cannot report failure is worse than a backup that fails loudly.

package main

import (
    "context"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "time"
)

func call(ctx context.Context, method, path string, body io.Reader, idem string) (*http.Response, error) {
    baseURL := os.Getenv("INFRAI_BASE_URL")
    if baseURL == "" { panic("INFRAI_BASE_URL is required") }
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 5; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequestWithContext(ctx, method, baseURL+path, body)
        if err != nil { return nil, err }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY"))
        req.Header.Set("Idempotency-Key", idem)
        resp, err := http.DefaultClient.Do(req)
        if err != nil { return nil, err }
        if resp.StatusCode != http.StatusTooManyRequests { return resp, nil }
        resp.Body.Close()
        delay := time.Duration(1<<attempt) * 200 * time.Millisecond
        if retry := resp.Header.Get("Retry-After"); retry != "" {
            if seconds, parseErr := strconv.Atoi(retry); parseErr == nil { delay = time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second }
        }
        select { case <-ctx.Done(): return nil, ctx.Err(); case <-time.After(delay): }
    }
    return nil, fmt.Errorf("storage request remained rate limited")
}

func main() {
    ctx := context.Background()
    resp, err := call(ctx, http.MethodPut, "/v1/storage/object/put/{bucket}/{key}", nil, "backup-prod-2026-07-31")
    if err != nil { panic(err) }
    defer resp.Body.Close()
    if resp.StatusCode < 200 || resp.StatusCode >= 300 { panic(fmt.Errorf("upload failed: %s", resp.Status)) }

    link, err := call(ctx, http.MethodPost, "/v1/storage/object/presign/{bucket}/{key}", nil, "presign-prod-2026-07-31")
    if err != nil { panic(err) }
    defer link.Body.Close()
    if link.StatusCode < 200 || link.StatusCode >= 300 { panic(fmt.Errorf("presign failed: %s", link.Status)) }
    // Read the returned URL and use it without the Infrai Authorization header.
}

The sample keeps the data plane narrow: upload the archive, then request a presigned response for the restore. In production, send the archive bytes as the PUT body and parse the response before issuing the download. Do not attach the API bearer token to that returned URL.

Which storage option fits the backup SLO?

I compare the real alternatives by operational promise. Amazon S3 has the broadest S3 tooling; Cloudflare R2 can be convenient when the application already depends on Cloudflare; Backblaze B2 is a straightforward archive target; Veeam and Rubrik are dedicated backup products with a different control plane.

Option Good fit Trade-off to price and test
Amazon S3 Mature S3 tooling and broad ecosystem Model requests, egress, region, and lifecycle together
Cloudflare R2 Workloads already centered on Cloudflare Validate residency, restore path, and migration needs
Backblaze B2 Simple object backup archives Test the chosen S3-compatible restore tooling
Infrai storage A platform team that wants one key and one bill across backend services It is not a public-link, version-recovery, or WORM system
Veeam or Rubrik Compliance-heavy recovery and ransomware-resilience programs Higher product and process overhead than dump-to-object storage

Infrai's relevant advantage is administrative: one REST API, one key, and one bill can cover storage alongside other backend capabilities. That can reduce credential and invoice sprawl for a small platform team. It does not change the durability or retention guarantees, so the acceptance test remains a real restore drill.

Where this design is not suitable

The catch is material. There is no object versioning or object lock (WORM), so an accidental overwrite is not recoverable as a prior object version; regulated retention should stick with a dedicated backup platform or an external immutable copy. Conditional If-Match writes are unavailable, which means strict concurrent exclusion belongs in a queue or database coordinator.

Public or public-read ACLs are unavailable, so static website hosting, permanent public links, and image-hosting are poor fits. Browser direct-upload workflows also need caution because there is no independently exposed CORS configuration route. There is no cross-region automatic replication or cross-cloud bulk migration tool, and the storage vendor coverage does not include GCS or B2. Finally, trial credit cannot pay for persistent writes; plan for a funded account before the first backup run.

My exit criterion is simple: upload a representative dump, list it by its prefix, mint a signed link, download it from the intended US or EU worker, and restore it into an isolated target. Record elapsed steps against the restore SLO. If the drill needs object lock, version recovery, or public delivery, choose a different option before production.

Test it before you trust it.

References

  • https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Guides/CORS
  • https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/mpuoverview.html
  • https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/object-lock.html
  • https://developers.cloudflare.com/r2/
  • https://www.backblaze.com/docs/cloud-storage

title: SaaS Application Logging via JSON API: Choosing a Simple Service for Import Freshness
description:
Short answer: Choose a simple JSON logging service only if it can preserve structured run events, support safe retries, and expose enough retention and queryability to detect missing import results; the alert rule still belongs to your application.

A scheduled import should page someone when it stops producing results, but a log line saying job finished is not enough. The least complex design is a structured event for each run, a durable count of accepted results, and an alert based on the absence of a successful result within the expected window. JSON over an HTTP API can carry the event; it cannot decide what success means.

The useful alert is the one that tells the on-call engineer which schedule went quiet, when it was expected, and what evidence is missing. That distinction matters in B2B SaaS, where a scheduler can keep firing while an upstream cursor, tenant filter, or validation step quietly yields zero records.

Can a simple logging service with a JSON API serve SaaS applications?

Imagine the page arrives at 09:20. It says: import produced no successful result for tenant acme-prod; expected every 15 minutes; last success 08:45; run 6f3b. That is enough to start an investigation. A page saying HTTP 200 from logging endpoint is not.

I keep these facts separate because they answer different questions:

  • Did the scheduler start a run?
  • Did the run reach the source and finish its protocol?
  • Did it accept at least one result, or was an empty result valid?
  • Can the run be joined to the tenant, schedule, and deployment?

The first three are domain events. The HTTP response from a log collector is transport evidence. Treating transport success as job success is how a healthy logging path hides a failed import.

A hosted endpoint is a poor fit when policy requires data to remain inside a private network, when retention must be customized beyond its contract, or when the import must continue during a prolonged telemetry outage without a local buffer. In those cases, a self-managed collector or queue can be the better boundary, even though it adds patching and capacity work.

A simple service is still useful for teams that value a small integration surface and can accept those limits. The limitation is operational ownership: a hosted boundary reduces collector maintenance, while a self-managed queue gives more control over residency, buffering, and retention.

Keep it boring.

A compact event can make that distinction explicit:

type ImportRun struct {
    RunID       string `json:"run_id"`
    Tenant      string `json:"tenant"`
    Schedule    string `json:"schedule"`
    StartedAt   string `json:"started_at"`
    FinishedAt  string `json:"finished_at"`
    Status      string `json:"status"`
    ResultCount int    `json:"result_count"`
    ErrorCode   string `json:"error_code,omitempty"`
}

Use a stable run ID. It gives retries and duplicate deliveries one identity, which is more useful than trying to infer a run from a timestamp and a message string. Keep tenant and schedule fields bounded and intentional; high-cardinality labels copied into every metric can create a second operational problem.

Where should the earlier signal come from?

The earlier signal is the completed-run event, not the page. Emit one event when the import reaches a terminal state, with status set to a value such as succeeded, empty, or failed. Then define the alert from the business rule: a schedule that normally produces data must have a recent successful result.

That rule needs an explicit exception for legitimate emptiness. A tenant with no new records can be healthy. If empty and failed are collapsed into one status, the alert will page on normal quiet periods and the team will eventually tune it out. Signal quality is a policy decision before it is a threshold decision.

A JSON API is a reasonable ingestion boundary when the client can set timeouts, retry safely, and preserve the event body for diagnosis. The event should be append-oriented. A retry may deliver it twice, so the consumer needs a uniqueness key such as (tenant, schedule, run_id) or an equivalent idempotency key. Do not use a random request ID as the only deduplication key; it changes on every retry.

For the log record, I would include the same correlation fields in every terminal event and keep the message for a human. The machine-readable fields carry the decision. This follows the broader observability model in which logs are a signal that can be correlated with traces and metrics, rather than a replacement for either one.

How do you instrument the path without creating noise?

Start at the scheduler boundary and trace the state transitions. A minimal sequence is scheduled, started, source_read, and one terminal event. Do not emit a full payload for every imported row. Log counts, bounded error categories, source offsets when safe, and a reference to the run. The raw records belong in the application data path, not in an alerting stream.

Here is a small Go helper that sends a terminal event. It leaves retries to the caller so the caller can apply the same run ID and idempotency key on every attempt.

func postRun(ctx context.Context, client *http.Client, endpoint string, run ImportRun) error {
    body, err := json.Marshal(run)
    if err != nil {
        return fmt.Errorf("marshal import run: %w", err)
    }

    req, err := http.NewRequestWithContext(ctx, http.MethodPost, endpoint, bytes.NewReader(body))
    if err != nil {
        return fmt.Errorf("create import event request: %w", err)
    }
    req.Header.Set("Content-Type", "application/json")
    req.Header.Set("Idempotency-Key", run.RunID)

    resp, err := client.Do(req)
    if err != nil {
        return fmt.Errorf("send import event: %w", err)
    }
    defer resp.Body.Close()

    if resp.StatusCode < 200 || resp.StatusCode >= 300 {
        return fmt.Errorf("import event endpoint returned %s", resp.Status)
    }
    return nil
}

The important details are boring: context cancellation, a bounded client timeout configured outside this function, and a response check. A successful network write does not prove that a downstream consumer has indexed the event. The service should expose a health and delivery signal that can be monitored separately from import success.

One trap is logging the retry itself as a new business run. That creates duplicate alerts and inflates counts. Keep transport attempts in a separate diagnostic field or metric, while the terminal business event retains the original run ID.

Which threshold separates a quiet tenant from a broken import?

Use the schedule contract, not a universal five-minute threshold. For a 15-minute schedule, the rule might allow one missed interval and page after the next expected completion plus a bounded grace period. For a daily schedule, the same fixed threshold is meaningless. Record the expected interval with the schedule configuration and evaluate the freshness of the last valid result per tenant and schedule.

The decision table should be explicit:

Observed state Operational meaning Page?
Recent succeeded result Import is producing data No
Recent empty result and emptiness is allowed Healthy quiet period No
Recent failed result Run completed with an error Usually, based on impact
No terminal result past the grace window Missing output or missing instrumentation Yes

The last row deserves special attention. No event can mean the scheduler did not run, the worker stalled, the source call hung, or the logging path failed. The alert should say “no terminal result,” then link the operator to scheduler and worker evidence. It should not pretend to know which failure occurred.

A short test matrix catches most alert mistakes: successful run, valid empty run, failed run, timeout before terminal emission, duplicate delivery, late delivery, and two tenants with different schedules. Run it in CI with fixed clocks. Then exercise one production-like canary schedule during deployment so a schema change cannot silently remove the fields the alert reads.

What does a practical selection checklist look like?

For a simple logging service with a JSON API, I would evaluate the boundary against the workflow rather than a feature count. Can it accept structured records without forcing message parsing? Can the client set a timeout and retry with a stable idempotency key? Can operators retain and query tenant, schedule, run ID, status, and timestamps? Can access controls separate tenants? Can the retention policy match the investigation window?

Also check the failure behavior. If the logging endpoint is unavailable, the import worker should not blindly block a business-critical run forever. Decide whether terminal events go to a local durable buffer, a queue, or a bounded retry loop. Make that choice visible in the runbook. Losing an observability event is bad; turning an observability outage into data loss is worse.

I initially treated the JSON endpoint as the main design decision. The harder part was defining a result that could be trusted by an alert. Once empty, failed, and “no terminal event” had separate meanings, the transport became replaceable and the false-positive discussion became concrete.

A good page is therefore a small contract between the scheduler, the importer, and the on-call engineer. It names the missing evidence, preserves a stable identity across retries, and respects each schedule’s expected cadence. That is enough to make a simple JSON logging boundary useful without asking it to become the source of truth for application state.

Further reading

  • OpenTelemetry, “Logs signal concepts”: https://opentelemetry.io/docs/concepts/signals/logs/
  • OpenTelemetry Specification, “Logs Data Model”: https://opentelemetry.io/docs/specs/otel/logs/data-model/
  • RFC 9110, “HTTP Semantics”: https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110
  • RFC 9457, “Problem Details for HTTP APIs”: https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9457

title: AWS Lambda supports Seekable OCI (SOCI) lazy loading for Lambda Managed Instances
description:
AWS Lambda now supports Seekable OCI (SOCI) for lazy loading Event Functions packaged as Open Container Initiative (OCI) images running on Lambda Managed Instances. With SOCI support, Lambda fetches only the files needed at each stage of the execution environment startup rather than downloading the entire image upfront, reducing container startup times by up to 70%.

Customers building compute-intensive applications such as data processing pipelines, high-throughput API backends, and batch computation workloads require substantial memory and CPU resources to process large datasets, serve low-latency responses at scale, and run complex computations efficiently. Container images for these workloads can reach several gigabytes, and downloading and preparing the full image can take several minutes when provisioning new execution environments. SOCI support on Lambda Managed Instances eliminates this bottleneck by streaming only the required files at each stage of the execution environment startup, so your functions start faster as you scale.

To get started, create a SOCI index (a table of contents for the files in your image layers) for your container image and push it to Amazon ECR. When creating or updating your function, set the image URI to the SOCI-indexed tag in Amazon ECR (for example, my-function:v1-soci) and publish a function version. Lambda automatically detects the SOCI index and enables lazy loading with no additional configuration. If you use a coding assistant such as Kiro, Claude Code, or Codex, install the Lambda Managed Instances skill from the Agent Toolkit for AWS to configure and deploy functions through your agent.

The feature is available in all AWS commercial Regions where Lambda Managed Instances is available. To learn more, visit the AWS Lambda Managed Instances developer guide.

title: Flowik: MobX-style reactive state for Swing and Vaadin
description:
Why I wrote this

I have spent most of my career writing UIs on the JVM. For nine years I built ERP and OLTP systems with Vaadin and Swing: order entry, warehouse screens, master/detail forms with dozens of fields that depend on each other. Today I work at JetBrains on the IntelliJ Platform team, and the IDE is still, to a large extent, a Swing application.

Along the way I also wrote frontends in GWT and React, and I fell in love with functional programming. That mix left me with an itch. On the web, state management is a solved and widely discussed problem. On the JVM desktop and in server-side UI frameworks, most of us still wire things together by hand.

This post introduces Flowik, a small Kotlin library that brings MobX-style reactive state to Swing, Vaadin and the IntelliJ Platform.

The problem: listeners all the way down

If you have built a non-trivial Swing or Vaadin form, you know this code:

quantityField.addChangeListener { recalcTotal(); updateSaveButton() }
priceField.addChangeListener { recalcTotal(); updateSaveButton() }
discountCheckBox.addActionListener { recalcTotal(); updateDiscountRow(); updateSaveButton() }

Every derived thing on the screen (a total, an enabled flag, a label) needs someone to remember every source it depends on. Add a field and you hunt down every listener that should now also call recalcTotal(). Forget one and the UI shows stale data. Remove a panel and forget to unregister, and you leak it.

The dependency graph is real, but it lives only in your head and is scattered across addXxxListener calls. In an ERP screen with 40 fields it is the main source of bugs. In an IDE with hundreds of settings panels and tool windows, the same pattern repeats at scale.

React taught a generation of developers a different model: describe the UI as a function of state and let the framework keep it in sync. MobX took that one step further for state itself.

MobX in one paragraph

MobX sums itself up in one line:

Anything that can be derived from the application state should be derived. Automatically.

You mark some values as observable. You write derivations, which are plain functions that read them. MobX records which observables each derivation actually read while it ran, and re-runs it when, and only when, one of those changes. There is no subscription code and no dependency list to maintain. Reading is subscribing.

What appeals to me as a fan of functional programming is that your UI becomes close to a pure function of state, while the state itself stays ordinary mutable objects. You get most of the benefit of the functional model without forcing immutable data structures onto a 15-year-old domain model.

The second thing I realised is that none of this is JavaScript-specific. The tracking mechanism needs only a place to record "who is reading right now" and a way to batch writes. The project that convinced me was RomanPozdeev/MobX, a compact Kotlin implementation of observables, computed, autorun and action with property delegates. Seeing the whole idea fit into a small, readable Kotlin library showed me that MobX is very portable, and that the JVM UI world could have it too. Flowik grew from that starting point, with a focus on the toolkits I work with every day.

Meet Flowik

A Flowik app has two parts. The store is a plain Kotlin class that holds observables and computed values. The view only reads from the store. It never registers a listener.

import flowik.core.*

class CounterStore {
    val count = observable(0)
    val doubled = computed { count.value * 2 }

    fun inc() = action { count.value += 1 }
}

The store knows nothing about Swing or Vaadin. The same class drives both UIs below.

Swing 

import flowik.core.*
import flowik.layout.uiFrame
import flowik.swing.*

fun main() {
    val store = CounterStore()
    val bindings = Bindings()

    uiFrame("Counter", width = 240, height = 120, bindings = bindings) {
        center {
            vbox(gap = 4) {
                Label { "Count: ${store.count.value} (×2 = ${store.doubled.value})" }
                Button("Increment") { store.inc() }
            }
        }
    }.disposeOnClose(bindings)
}

The Label lambda reads count and doubled, so it re-renders whenever either changes. That is the whole binding.

Vaadin Flow 

@Route("counter")
class CounterView : VerticalLayout(), Bindings by Bindings() {
    private val store = CounterStore()

    init {
        val label = Span()
        label.text { "Count: ${store.count.value} (×2 = ${store.doubled.value})" }
        add(label, Button("Increment") { store.inc() })
        disposeOnDetach()
    }
}

You will notice Bindings in every example. It is the owner of the subscriptions a window, view or panel creates, so they can be released together. Flowik makes that lifetime explicit instead of guessing from attach and detach events, which in Vaadin also fire when a component is merely moved.

Building blocks

The core module, flowik-core, has no UI dependency. Its vocabulary will be familiar to anyone who has used MobX:

Block Flowik API What it does
Observable state observable, observables, observableSet Mutable values that track who reads them
Cached derivation computed { } A value derived from others, recomputed only when an input changes
Side effect autoRun { }, reaction, whenThen Code that re-runs when what it read changes, usually a UI update
Batch action { } Groups writes so derivations fire once, at the end

A short tour:

val name     = observable("Alice")
val greeting = computed { "Hello, ${name.value}" }

autoRun { println(greeting.value) }      // prints "Hello, Alice"

action {
    name.value = "Bob"
    name.value = "Carol"
}                                        // prints "Hello, Carol" once

Two things are worth noticing. The autoRun never says which values it depends on. And the action produced one update, not two, which matters a lot when a single user gesture touches ten fields of an order.

Kotlin helps make this pleasant. Observables work as property delegates (var name by observable("")), bindings accept property references (TextField(store::name)), and observable(person) turns each property of a data class into its own reactive atom, so a label showing only the name does not re-render when the age changes.

Where it pays off: screens with many parts

A counter proves nothing. The real test is whether you can split a large screen into small parts that know nothing about each other, and still have them stay in sync. That is exactly where my ERP screens used to rot.

The Vaadin demo contains a port of the master/detail page from the Vaadin docs' "Compose with Components" example: an employee list on the left, the selected person on the right, plus editing, adding and deleting. Its shape is:

EmployeeStore            the only place state changes
└── EmployeesView        the one stateful component: wires store → children
    ├── EmployeeMaster   search + list, owns no state
    │   └── EmployeeRow × N
    └── EmployeeDetail   tabs, manager card, Edit / Delete, owns no state

One store, state down, events up

The store is plain Kotlin. Its setters are private, so nothing writes state past it. The filtered list is a derivation, not something anyone updates:

@SpringComponent
@UIScope
class EmployeeStore : Store {
    val employees = observables(*sampleEmployees().toTypedArray())

    var search by observable("")
    var selected by observableRef<ObservableEntity<Employee>?>(null)

    val visibleEmployees by employees.filter { employee ->
        val query = search.trim().lowercase()
        query.isEmpty() || employee.fullName.lowercase().contains(query)
    }

    fun select(employee: ObservableEntity<Employee>?) = action { selected = employee }
    fun updateSearch(query: String) = action { search = query }
}

The route view hands each child the slices it shows and a callback for each event it raises:

class EmployeesView(private val store: EmployeeStore) : Div(), Bindings by Bindings() {
    init {
        add(
            register(EmployeeMaster(
                employees = store::visibleEmployees,   // a computed slice
                query = store::search,
                onQueryChange = store::updateSearch,
                selected = store::selected,
                onSelect = store::select,
                onAddNew = ::addNew,
            )),
            Div().apply {
                childSwitch(store::selected) { employee ->
                    if (employee == null) NoSelection() else detail(employee)
                }
            },
        )
        disposeOnDetach()
    }
}

EmployeeMaster and EmployeeDetail never reference the store or each other. Both follow store.selected, so clicking a row, adding a person and deleting one all move the detail pane the same way. There is no code that keeps the two panes in sync, because there is nothing to sync.

Why the parts stay small

  • Inputs are Supplier<T>, not framework types. EmployeeMaster takes a Supplier<List<ObservableEntity<Employee>>>. Every observable and computed is a Supplier, and so is any lambda that reads them. A caller can pass a store property, derive a value inline (isSelected = { selected.get() === employee }) or pass a constant, and the child cannot tell the difference. Tracking flows straight through the lambda.
  • Entities are live, and fine-grained. A row, a person card and the detail tabs all receive the same ObservableEntity<Employee>. Each field reads only the property it shows, so changing someone's phone number re-renders only the places that show the phone number, on every page that shows it.
  • Editing is a transaction. The editor dialog gets a buffered createViewModel(employee). Nothing reaches the model until submit(), so Cancel needs no code, and the same dialog creates a new person from a draft that joins the list only on Save.
  • Lifetimes follow the composition tree. Every part is Bindings by Bindings(). register(child), items { } and childSwitch { } dispose what they drop. Whoever creates a component owns it.

Derived state is shared the same way. The Teams and Locations pages are one generic GroupsView fed with store.groupedBy { ... }. Change someone's title on the Employees page and the Teams page regroups, with no code connecting the two pages.

Testable without a browser

Because a part depends only on suppliers and callbacks, and bindings run without a Vaadin UI, it can be tested in plain JUnit, with no store and no browser harness:

val people = observables(*sampleEmployees().take(3).toTypedArray())
val selected = observableRef<ObservableEntity<Employee>?>(null)

val master = EmployeeMaster(
    employees = people::items,
    query = { "" },
    onQueryChange = {},
    selected = selected,
    onSelect = { println("select ${it.fullName}") },
    onAddNew = {},
)

master.rows()[1].click()                      // only reported: the master does not select by itself
action { selected.value = people.items[1] }   // its owner does, and the row follows
assertTrue(master.rows()[1].hasClass("selected"))

This is the part I missed most in nine years of enterprise UIs. Flowik lets you design the state (fine-grained entities, derived slices, edit buffers) and hand it to components that do not know where it comes from. The more parts a screen has, the more that matters. The whole demo is about 900 lines of Kotlin across ten files, and the source is on GitHub.

Status and how to try it

Flowik is experimental. The API is still moving between releases, and I would not put it under a production system yet. What it does have: bindings for Swing, Vaadin Flow and the IntelliJ Kotlin UI DSL, tests, and several demos. These include a Todo app, an Obsidian-like notes UI in Swing, and an employees master/detail screen in Vaadin.

Releases are published through JitPack:

repositories {
    mavenCentral()
    maven("https://jitpack.io")
}

dependencies {
    implementation("com.github.jreznot.flowik:flowik-swing:v0.5.0")
    // or flowik-vaadin, flowik-intellij
}

The bindings use Kotlin context parameters, so modules that depend on them compile with -XXLanguage:+ContextParameters.

If you build UIs on the JVM, I would love to hear how you manage state today. Try a demo, open an issue, or tell me in the comments what you would want covered next.

Source: github.com/jreznot/flowik
